Predicting Chemical Stressor Effects on Conjugative Plasmid Transfer Rates Using Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Chemical stressors in environmental and clinical settings can alter conjugative plasmid transfer, which is a key process driving antibiotic resistance dissemination. However, predicting these effects across chemically diverse compounds is challenging. Here, we compiled and curated data on the effect of chemical stressors on RP4 plasmid transfer, extracting compound identity, concentration, conjugation frequency, and experimental metadata from 73 in vitro studies. Chemicals were characterized by functional use categories and molecular descriptors, including physicochemical properties, MACCS keys, Morgan fingerprints, and extended descriptors from the OCHEM platform (AlvaDesc, Dragon 7, and 3D-shape descriptors). An exhaustive evaluation of 1022 feature set combinations across 3066 models showed that chemical concentration alone provides no meaningful predictive signal (Q2ext <0), whereas integrating Morgan fingerprints substantially improves predictive performance. The best-performing model combined concentration, Morgan fingerprints, and experimental conditions using extreme gradient boosting (XGB), achieving Q2ext = 0.373 on a held-out compound-aware test set and a median Q2ext of 0.319 within the defined applicability domain across 20 independent splits. SHAP analysis revealed that Morgan fingerprints account for 69% of total predictive weight, with quaternary ammonium compounds and long-chain alkyl structures associated with inhibition of conjugation and sulfonamide and amine-containing compounds associated with promotion. These results demonstrate that chemical structural features provide critical information for predicting the chemical modulation of conjugative plasmid transfer. This work highlights that combining chemically informed descriptors with machine learning (ML) anticipates chemical contributions to antibiotic resistance dissemination, providing a scalable framework for the prioritization and risk assessment of chemicals.

title: A Multi-Stage Deep Learning Framework for Daily PM2.5 Estimation at 100 m Resolution Across the Contiguous United States, 2000–2024 (A Quarter Century of Data)
abstract: Abstract Accurate high-resolution estimation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) remains challenging because of sparse monitoring networks and missing satellite observations. We developed a multistage deep learning framework to generate daily PM2.5 concentrations at 100 m resolution across the contiguous United States (CONUS) from 2000 to 2024. The framework first reconstructed missing satellite aerosol optical depth (AOD) using a U-Net-based encoder–decoder informed by reanalysis data, refined temporal dependencies using a bidirectional long short-term memory network, and downscaled reconstructed AOD to 100 m using terrain information. Daily PM2.5 was subsequently estimated using a multistream deep learning architecture integrating reconstructed AOD, meteorological, spatiotemporal, and geospatial predictors. Evaluation using strict site-level data partitioning yielded strong predictive performance (R2 = 0.82, RMSE = 2.85 μg/m3, MAE = 1.84 μg/m3), with high spatial (R2 = 0.94) and temporal (R2 = 0.78) performance. The framework generated spatially continuous daily PM2.5 surfaces across more than 766 million 100 m grid cells while capturing broad spatial gradients and fine-scale variability. These long-term, high-resolution estimates provide an exposure surface suitable for epidemiological, environmental justice, and air-pollution assessment applications.

title: Multidimensional Cardiac Phenotyping of Daphnia magna Enables One-Hour Effect-Based Screening of Aquatic Toxicity
abstract: Abstract Operational water quality management relies on physicochemical monitoring and targeted chemical analysis, but routine surveillance covers only a prioritized subset of high-risk contaminants and does not capture biological activity from unmonitored chemicals, transformation products, or complex mixtures. Whole-organism bioassays provide complementary effect information, yet the conventional Daphnia magna (D. magna) acute immobilization end point requires 48 h. Here, we introduce D-HEART (Daphnia-based Heartbeat Evaluation and Analysis for Rapid Toxicity Screening), a microfluidic imaging and analysis framework that converts high-speed cardiac recordings into 116 descriptors spanning morphology, pumping, wall motion kinematics, and synchrony. Within the tested response space, D-HEART assigns cardiac-response classes using a six-contaminant reference library, while its Heartbeat Toxicity Index (HTI) estimates 48 h immobilization from the predicted class and phenotype. Transcriptomic profiles provided molecular context for differentiated 1 h cardiac states. Post-training Cd(II) tests across environmental water matrices tracked immobilization with greater uncertainty than in laboratory water, and two untreated industrial wastewaters showed dose-responsive HTI estimates for mixed exposures from unseen contaminant classes. By linking early physiological states to transcriptional responses and later apical toxicity, D-HEART provides a rapid, cross-time scale effect-screening layer for operational water-quality evaluation, reducing the detection window by approximately 98% relative to the conventional 48 h immobilization end point.

title: Reactive Oxygen Species Trigger Rapid Natural Purification of Soils and Water in Wetlands
abstract: Abstract Wetlands, often referred to as the “Earth’s kidneys”, are essential ecosystems that filter pollutants and regulate biogeochemical processes. However, the mechanisms underlying their rapid self-purification are still in their infancy and lack deep understanding. Here, we propose that reactive oxygen species (ROS) constitute an intrinsic oxidative network that drives accelerated pollutant transformation in wetlands. We summarize that ROS are generated through coupled photochemical and redox-driven processes and are highly concentrated at environmental interfaces, including soil–water, fluctuating redox boundaries, and rhizosphere. These interfaces function as reactive hotspots where the colocalization of organic matter, minerals, oxygen, and microorganisms amplifies ROS production far beyond bulk water levels. Interfacial ROS enrichment can shorten pollutant half-lives and alter oxidative pathways, as illustrated by a representative pesticide. Advances in in situ and real-time ROS imaging have enabled direct observation of these microscale hotspots, providing new insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of ROS-driven processes. We further identify key challenges in resolving and monitoring fine-scale ROS dynamics, interfacial electron transfer, and scaling microscale processes to ecosystem-level functions. This perspective reframes wetlands as interface-driven oxidative systems, highlighting ROS-mediated processes as significant regulators of pollutant transformation and providing a conceptual basis for developing wetlands as controllable biogeochemical reactors.

title: Redox Properties of Structural Fe in Clay Minerals: 5. The Role of Fe in the Tetrahedral Sheets of Synthetic Smectites
abstract: Abstract Iron-bearing smectite clay minerals are important redox-active phases in soils and sediments. Yet, the influence of iron substitution in the tetrahedral sheets (TetFe) of smectites on their redox properties remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the repeated reduction and re-oxidation of synthetic Fe-rich smectites, known as synthetic nontronites (SyN), with constant content of Fe in the octahedral sheet (OctFe) but variable initial content of TetFe. The redox properties of redox-cycled smectites were characterized using mediated electrochemical analysis. The resulting Fe2+/FeTotal ratios determined over a wide range of reduction potentials were analyzed using a process-based model to extract thermodynamic and kinetic descriptors of the interfacial electron transfer and subsequent charge redistribution processes that occur during the redox reaction. The fitted standard reduction potentials and apparent diffusion coefficients for charge redistribution were insensitive to TetFe content, indicating that thermodynamics and bulk charge transport within the smectite crystal are predominantly governed by the Fe–O–Fe networks in the octahedral sheet. Conversely, samples containing TetFe exhibited fitted interfacial electron-transfer rate constants approximately an order of magnitude higher than the TetFe-free sample. Comparison of these thermodynamic and kinetic descriptors between synthetic nontronites and natural reference smectites showed that parameter values converge within a narrow range across iron-rich dioctahedral smectites. These model-based results highlight the distinct roles of OctFe and TetFe in controlling smectite redox reactivity in subsurface environments, with OctFe governing the thermodynamics and TetFe primarily influencing interfacial electron-transfer kinetics.

Application of machine learning algorithms for seasonal and annual perchlorate risks in groundwater of the Arjunanadi River Basin (India): drinking water quality assessment and human vulnerability
abstract: Machine learning algorithms were used to analyze and predict the seasonal perchlorate content in groundwater of the Arjunanadi River Basin (ARB) in South India and associated health risks. The CaMgCl type of majority samples reflected secondary salinity from prolonged rock-water interaction and prominent anthropogenic influence. Perchlorate concentrations ranged from 0.001 to 0.21 ppm. In post-monsoon season (POMS) 2023, 24.4% of the groundwater samples were classified as at risk and 8.5% as high risk, with corresponding area mapped to an extent of 280 and 80 km 2 , respectively. Similarly, in pre-monsoon season (PRMS) 2024, 22.5% and 1.0% of the samples were classified as at risk and high risk with corresponding area mapped to an extent of 244 and 2.5 km 2 . In POMS 2024, 29.8% and 8.5% of the samples were classified as at risk and high risk with corresponding area mapped to an extent of 274.5 and 46 km 2 . In PRMS 2025, 23.4% and 3.2% of the samples were classified as at risk and high risk with corresponding area mapped to an extent of 242 and 34 km 2 . Among all the machine learning algorithms, Random Forest (RF) showed the moderate performance with a mean accuracy of 71.5% compared to others. Health hazard assessment indicated that children are more vulnerable to perchlorate exposure, with 72% (POMS 2023), 67% (PRMS 2024), 87% (POMS 2024), and 80% (PRMS 2025) of samples showing a total hazard index (THI) >1. Additional managed aquifer recharge (MAR) structures in the higher concentration area away from the pre-existing check dams would be helpful to raise the static level and improve the water quality. This study provided valuable understanding on perchlorate levels among the seasons and a trend of health risk over a year with a view to implement effective and safe water management practices under the sustainable development goals (SDG) of 3 and 6.

title: Role of Neighborhood Vulnerability and Opportunity in the Association Between Prenatal Air Pollution and Autism-Related Traits in the ECHO Cohort
Meandering shorelines: The potential for multi-level habitat complexity to ecologically enhance artificial coastal defences
abstract: Artificial coastal defences simplify, linearize, and homogenize the coast, leading to reduced species diversity, ecological functioning, and ecosystem services. Previous active management research has shown that greater habitat complexity at millimeter to decimeter scales increases the diversity of fauna and flora living on constructed shores, however, little is known regarding the potential effects of increasing the scale of complexity on larger marine species. Testing this experimentally is challenging, hence, as a first step, we conducted a meta-analysis on movement patterns, home ranges, and body size for a wide range of coastal marine species. We found that as mean body length of species increases, so does the distance travelled, home range, and core activity areas. To widen the variety of niches created and reduce a key negative aspect of coastal engineering, we argue that the design and planning of future coastal defences should consider incorporating more complex structures across scales from millimetres to kilometres.

title: Current status and future perspectives on fungal solid-state fermentation scale-up
Meiyu intensity modulates cyanobacterial bloom dynamics in sub-deep reservoirs via synergistic hydrological and nutrient regulation
abstract: Meiyu is a persistent rainy weather phenomenon in East Asia caused by a subtropical monsoon front. Under global climate change, the intensity and extremity of Meiyu have increased markedly, posing severe challenges to the water safety and management of regional reservoirs. However, the impacts of Meiyu intensity on cyanobacterial blooms in regional sub-deep reservoirs remain poorly understood. Here, we used Qishu Reservoir, a typical sub-deep reservoir in Yi County, Huangshan City, Anhui Province, China, as the study area. Based on monitoring data from two contrasting Meiyu years (normal, 2023; wet, 2024) and using multivariate statistics and partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM), we revealed how Meiyu intensity regulates summer reservoir hydrodynamics, thermal stratification, nutrient dynamics, and phytoplankton communities. Results showed that frequent and intense rainfall during the wet Meiyu generated strong hydrological pulses and markedly shortened hydraulic retention time. TN was primarily driven by rainfall-induced non-point source inputs and increased with Meiyu intensity. In contrast, TP was markedly diluted during the wet Meiyu due to limited sources and strong hydrological pulses, making TP the key regulator of interannual differences in phytoplankton density. Thermal stratification stability was the core physical control of Microcystis -dominated cyanobacterial blooms. Hydrometeorological factors regulated phytoplankton dynamics mainly via indirect pathways. During the wet Meiyu year, these factors naturally suppressed cyanobacterial blooms via the synergistic effects of weakened thermal stratification and reduced TP. We propose a hierarchical bloom control strategy based on Meiyu intensity, providing a scientific basis for managing similar reservoirs in the East Asian subtropical monsoon region.

title: The effect of fire regimes on above-ground biomass change in Baikiaea-dominated woodlands of the Chobe region, northern Botswana, 1991 – 2023
Response of ecosystem service supply–demand dynamics to urban expansion patterns on the loess plateau, China
abstract: Urban expansion alters ecosystem service (ES) supply–demand relationships, yet pattern-specific responses remain unclear in ecologically fragile regions. Using land-use data for 2000, 2010, and 2020, we identified edge expansion (EE), leapfrog expansion (LE), and infill expansion (IE) on the Loess Plateau (LP), quantified supply and demand for four ES, and compared patch-level changes in the ES supply–demand ratio (ΔESDR) among patterns using nonparametric tests. From 2000 to 2020, construction land expanded substantially, with EE remaining the predominant expansion pattern (49.10%), followed by LE (42.33%) and IE (8.57%). After 2010, expansion accelerated and the share of LE increased markedly, becoming dominant in several ecological subregions. Food production (FP) showed negative median ΔESDR under all three patterns. Carbon sequestration (CS) showed a near-zero median ΔESDR under LE but negative median ΔESDR under EE and IE, whereas water yield (WY) and soil conservation (SC) showed positive median ΔESDR under all three patterns. For FP, CS, and WY, median ΔESDR followed LE > EE > IE, with all pairwise differences significant. For SC, median ΔESDR was significantly higher under LE than under EE and IE, whereas EE and IE did not differ significantly. Overall, LE was more often associated with weaker deterioration or more positive changes in ES supply–demand balance than IE, with EE mostly intermediate, although these relationships varied across services and subregions. These findings advance understanding of how ES supply–demand responses vary among urban expansion patterns and ecological subregions, and provide regional evidence for sustainable land-use planning in ecologically fragile regions.

Effect of Stand Density on Soil Microbial Carbon and Nitrogen Use Efficiency in Robinia pseudoacacia Plantations in the Loess Hilly‐Gully Region, China
abstract: ABSTRACT Soil microbial carbon (CUE) and nitrogen (NUE) use efficiency are critical for soil carbon (C) sequestration and nitrogen (N) availability. However, how microbial CUE and NUE respond to stand density is unclear. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether the response of microbial CUE and NUE to stand density could be mediated by soil depth. This study investigated the impact of stand density (low‐density, 625~1000; medium‐density, 1001~1625; high‐density, 1626~2100 trees ha −1 ) on microbial CUE and NUE in topsoil (0–10 cm) and subsoil (10–20 cm) of Robinia pseudoacacia plantations in the loess hilly‐gully region, China. In the 0–10 cm soil layer, microbial CUE decreased with increasing stand density. Specifically, microbial CUE under low‐density stands was significantly higher than that under medium‐ and high‐density stands, with increases of 4.9% and 7.1%, respectively. Microbial NUE in low‐density stands was significantly markedly lower than that in medium‐ and high‐density stands, with decreases of 19.9% and 27.8%, respectively. In the 10–20 cm layer, microbial CUE in medium‐density stands was 4.8% and 6.4% higher than that in low‐ and high‐density stands, respectively. In contrast, in the 10–20 cm layer, microbial NUE in medium‐density stands was 24.5% and 32.1% lower than that in low‐ and high‐density stands, respectively. Hierarchical partitioning analysis revealed that the relative importance of environmental factors on microbial CUE and NUE differed markedly across soil depths. Specifically, enzymatic C:N ratio and soil organic C:total N ratio explained the largest proportions of variation in microbial CUE and NUE at the 0–10 cm (19.2%) and 10–20 cm (19.5%), respectively. Results from multiple linear regression indicated that microbial metabolic limitation was the main driver of microbial CUE and NUE at the 0–10 cm layer; however, microbial biomass C:N ratio was the primary driver of microbial CUE and NUE at 10–20 cm soil layers. Overall, these results highlighted that stand density regulates microbial nutrient use efficiency by driving variations in nutrient limitation caused by the stoichiometric imbalances across soil depths.

The Value of an Attorney: Collateral Source Rule Changes as an Invalid Instrument
abstract: ABSTRACT The value of lawyers to their clients is notoriously difficult to estimate because of endogeneity. We utilize modifications to the collateral source (CS) rule that require reducing trial awards by the amount of payments from first‐party insurance as an instrument for hiring a lawyer. The problem with our instrument is that modifications to the CS rule have a direct effect on recovery and, hence, violate the exclusion restriction required for a valid instrument. We develop a new identification and estimation method that uses CS rule changes as an invalid instrument and bounds the impact of lawyers. We find that our estimated impact's upper and lower bounds are lower than estimates that do not correct for endogeneity. Our estimates of the impact of lawyers on total payment are consistently negative, although not precise enough to claim statistical significance. The upper bound of the effect of hiring a lawyer on total payment received is negative after fees in our preferred specification. This suggests that even in the most optimistic scenario, lawyers appear to reduce total recovery.

Income inequality as a barrier to the CO2-reducing potential of public investment: evidence from Latin America
abstract: This paper aims to empirically analyze the association between public investment and carbon emissions relative to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for a panel of Latin American countries from 1994 to 2019. Given that reduced income inequality can enhance the effectiveness of environmental policies, the estimations are carried out under two income inequality regimes: higher and lower. A nonlinear Local Projections model with a threshold is employed, dividing the sample into two groups based on the Gini index. The results show that, during periods of relatively low income inequality, the estimated response of carbon-intensity growth to changes in public investment is negative over time. In contrast, under conditions of relatively high income inequality, the estimated association is not statistically significant at the 10% level. Our estimates suggest that a 10% increase in public investments is associated with an approximately 4.40% reduction in the growth rate of carbon intensity in the low-inequality regime, as measured by the Gini index, until the fourth year following the increase in public investment. These empirical findings support existing literature highlighting the positive association between income inequality and carbon emissions.

title: The politics of environmental peacebuilding: global agendas, advocacy networks, and domestic policy arenas
abstract: This article examines how environmental conflict narratives emerge and are used in peacebuilding policies. It advocates for a multi-level perspective that systematically connects global intervention agendas to political struggles in domestic policy arenas. Through a comparative analysis of four case studies—Liberia, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Lebanon—it investigates how environmental considerations are framed as security issues and incorporated into peacebuilding agendas. It explores how actors construct causal stories linking environmental issues to conflict, and how these narratives shape policy design, implementation, and resistance to change. It highlights how environmental conflict narratives are shaped by security concerns and donor-recipient relationships. While such narratives can support policy change by providing advocacy coalitions with a platform, their effects vary significantly depending on the domestic political context. This article contributes to environmental peacebuilding research by highlighting the strategic and contested nature of how environmental concerns enter peacebuilding discourse and practice.

abstract: Abstract We address the interconnected issues of externalities in the use of a natural common‐pool resource system and adverse effects of environmental uncertainty on risk‐averse resource users. We set up a simple analytical model and derive conditions such that insurance by means of an income sharing mechanism mitigates externalities and hence achieves a socially optimal outcome. For this to materialize, we show that the sharing rule must be sufficiently sensitive to individual contributions and specifically show that a simple proportional sharing rule can provide incentives for both efficient contributions to the income pool and efficient use of the resource system.

Behavioral Financial Responses to War Threat and Geopolitical Uncertainty
abstract: While war and geopolitical instability reconfigure household economic behavior, the psychological mechanisms underlying conservative online spending and financial planning in conflict-affected economies remain insufficiently understood. Drawing mainly on Protection Motivation Theory (PMT), this study examines whether threat appraisal (perceived vulnerability and severity) of war and geopolitical uncertainty, accompanied by coping appraisal (financial self-efficacy and response efficacy), is associated with online conservative spending, and whether coping appraisal is related to financial planning in Lebanon. Based on survey data from 262 relatively active Lebanese online consumers, perceived war threat vulnerability, rather than its severity or broader geopolitical instability, is found to be significantly related to online conservative spending. Perceived war severity and both geopolitical threat dimensions show no significant association. Regarding coping appraisal, the findings indicate a positive association between financial self-efficacy and both conservative online spending and financial planning, while financial response efficacy is strongly associated with financial planning but not with conservative online spending. These findings indicate that perceived personal vulnerability to war, rather than perceived threat severity or broader geopolitical instability, is associated with online consumption restraint in the present sample. Moreover, spending restraint is positively associated with perceived financial capability, while structured financial planning is more strongly associated with beliefs in the effectiveness of financial strategies. The study provides context-specific empirical evidence on the differential relevance of PMT components in a prolonged instability context, with vulnerability and severity, as well as the two coping-appraisal components, exhibiting different associations across behavioral outcomes. From a supplementary prospect-theory perspective, the observed association may be consistent with heightened sensitivity to potential financial losses; however, loss aversion was not directly measured. Practically, the results underscore the importance of reducing actual household financial vulnerability through financial safety nets, access to reliable financial information, emergency liquidity mechanisms, and financial literacy initiatives, while strengthening both financial capability and confidence in financial strategies in fragile, low-trust economies.
journal_name: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance

title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: When money isn't everything: Identifying stage‐based patterns of entrepreneurial resource acquisition
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Scholars often examine how entrepreneurs' existing ties predict resource acquisition. We investigated the reverse: How does the act of pitching generate new ties with investors? Using the context of the Slow Money community, we analyzed social entrepreneurs' pitches to impact investors. Rather than identify a single strategy that benefited all firms, we found that “stage‐appropriate framing” facilitated resource acquisition by aligning with investors' expectations. Late‐stage entrepreneurs who emphasized financial process framing acquired more financial capital. Conversely, early‐stage entrepreneurs who emphasized social process framing developed more investor ties. By shifting attention from the importance of pre‐existing networks to the potential of entrepreneurial pitches, our research explains how pitch framing can facilitate the acquisition of both financial capital and investor ties, thereby mitigating liabilities for early‐stage firms. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs know that pitches help raise money, but we discovered that they also foster investor ties. In studying pitch competitions in the Slow Money community, we found that different messages resonated with investors depending on a firm's stage. Early‐stage entrepreneurs gained more investor ties when their pitches highlighted a willingness to collaborate and engage in true partnerships. Late‐stage entrepreneurs attracted more funds when they focused on their business track record. In both cases, matching the pitch framing to the firm stage—and using engaging behavioral cues—helped founders attract stage‐appropriate resources. Our research shows that entrepreneurs can raise not just financial capital but also build investor ties without relying on pre‐existing networks—when their pitch aligns with their stage.

title: From project value creation to firm-level appropriation: Who captures economic value, and under what conditions?
abstract: Projects create value for multiple stakeholders, yet project management research offers limited insight into how this value is converted into economic value appropriated by project-based firms and their stakeholders. Drawing on the Value Creation and Appropriation framework, we develop an accounting-based approach to measure stakeholder value appropriation over time and apply it longitudinally to project-based firms in Finland and Sweden. The findings show that economic value is neither automatically nor evenly appropriated by the focal firm but varies across stakeholder groups and institutional and procurement contexts. Customer appropriation can decline while firms protect appropriation by employees and strategic suppliers. The study links project-level value creation with firm-level economic value appropriation, showing that creation and appropriation can diverge across stakeholders and that stable appropriation by critical stakeholders during turbulent periods may indicate organizational resilience and stakeholder buffering. The study extends the Value Creation and Appro-priation framework to project-based firms and provides a replicable longitudinal approach to analyzing value appropriation.

title: Selecting the best, yet following the crowd: coevolution of project‑based collaborative networks and digitalization behavior
Benefit shortfalls in information technology projects: A configurational view of explicitness, organizational change, beneficiaries, and project size
Advertising with HAART: Introducing Human–AI Asymmetric Relationship Theory
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)is rapidly reconfiguring advertising from message delivery and optimization to relationship-like exchanges between consumers and brands. While existing work has explained these interactions through social response accounts and interpersonal relationship theories, this lens risks overlooking a defining structural mismatch: AI agents convincingly enact relational characteristics but cannot experience relational benefits, costs, or commitment. Perceived mutuality can be high even when the underlying relational capacity for reciprocity is absent. We introduce human–AI asymmetric relationship theory (HAART), which conceptualizes AI-mediated relationships as relationally expressive yet structurally one-sided. HAART advances three tenets: (1) inherent AI agent characteristics limit relational reciprocity; (2) AI agents mask these limits through performative relationship actions, defined as linguistic, paralinguistic, and interactional behaviors that simulate relational engagement; and (3) when this masking succeeds, an asymmetric relationship emerges, characterized by asymmetries in dependence, risk, and control. We develop six propositions that detail the positive (e.g., enhanced support) and negative (e.g., heightened vulnerability) consequences for consumers and brands, and provide implications for theory, practice, and policy.

title: A process theory of data-centric marketing innovation
Blockchain Technology Adoption and Audit Pricing: The Influence of External Regulatory Intensity
Balancing Stability and Transparency: Macroprudential Policies and Opacity Puzzle in Banking
abstract: This study examines the trade-off between financial stability and transparency by analysing the unintended effects of macroprudential policy adjustments on bank financial reporting behaviour. Using a global dataset of 1,179 listed banks across 84 countries over 1990-2023, we find that macroprudential tightening is associated with greater financial reporting opacity, reflected in increased discretionary use of loan loss provisions. This relationship is particularly evident for capital-based and asset-side instruments. We further explore two mechanisms that may help explain this pattern. First, the results are consistent with capital-management interpretation: income-decreasing discretionary provisioning associated with macroprudential tightening is particularly evident among better-capitalised banks, in line with incentives to build regulatory buffers and manage capital ratios. Second, during periods of macroprudential tightening, discretionary provisioning is more closely related to subsequent earnings. This pattern is consistent with a forward-looking signalling interpretation, although it may also capture changes in banks’ expectations of future risks and performance. Our findings reveal a potential opacity dimension of macroprudential policy adjustments. The results contribute to the literature by showing that changes in the macroprudential policy stance relate to banks’ reporting behaviour and by highlighting the challenges of pursuing financial stability objectives while maintaining transparent risk disclosure.

title: Assessing inter-rater agreement among large language model judges: Evidence from persona evaluation across varying educational risk contexts
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as automated judges for evaluation, yet their reliability remains unclear. This study examines the inter-rater agreement of three LLM judges (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro) when evaluating fairness, lack of stereotypicality, and diversity in user personas across varying educational risk contexts. We analyzed 60 individual personas and 12 persona sets to assess whether these judges demonstrate sufficient consistency to function as reliable evaluators. Although inter-rater agreement was moderate at the individual persona level, three critical limitations emerged. At the set level, agreement ranged from .39 to .63 across persona generators and therefore did not show a uniform decline relative to individual-level agreement. Mean dimension-support scores were 41% to 61% lower, although the individual- and set-level tasks are not directly comparable. Second, non-compliance rates, where judges could not provide textual justification for their ratings, ranged from 9.6 to 26.7% at the individual level and increased to 34% to 49% at the set level. Third, agreement differed across the three educational scenarios classified by risk: individual-level agreement declined from the lower- to higher-risk scenarios, while set-level agreement showed no monotonic pattern. We conclude that, under the tested protocol, current LLM judges demonstrate poor-to-moderate inter-rater agreement for persona evaluation. These findings contribute a descriptive characterization of LLM evaluation behavior across risk contexts and provide a foundation for future validation studies comparing LLM agreement against human judgment.

title: Corruption Distance and Chinese OFDI: Sanding or Greasing the Wheels?
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between corruption distance and the outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) decisions of Chinese firms. We develop a two-stage sequential game model predicting an inverted U-shaped relationship between corruption distance and Chinese OFDI, and test this prediction using OFDI data on firms listed on China’s A-share market from 2004 to 2021 to construct a country-year panel for OFDI frequency and a firm-country-year panel for OFDI volume. The empirical results show a robust inverted U-shaped association at both the country and firm levels. Chinese OFDI is highest at moderate corruption distance and lower at either extreme. Further analyses reveal that this nonlinear association is evident in both developed and developing host countries, is strongest in Asia, and is not significant among Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries following the Initiative’s launch. At the firm level, the association is more pronounced among state-owned enterprises (SOEs), resource-seeking and cost-seeking investors, and firms in industries with higher corruption-risk exposure, non-manufacturing sectors, and non-high-tech industries. These findings contribute to the literature on OFDI determinants by documenting a robust nonlinear effect of corruption distance that reconciles the competing “grease-the-wheel” and “sand-the-wheel” views.

title: ESG Performance and Continuous Green Innovation: A Perspective from Export-Oriented Enterprises
abstract: Against the backdrop of increasingly stringent green governance in global supply chains, this study examines whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance enhances continuous green innovation (CGI) among export-oriented firms. Using data on Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2024, we define export-oriented firms as those whose overseas business revenue accounts for at least 5% of total operating revenue and construct a CGI measure. The results show that ESG performance significantly improves CGI, and the conclusion survives endogeneity and robustness tests. Mechanism analyses indicate that ESG operates by increasing overseas business revenue, strengthening export stability, and promoting outward foreign direct investment (OFDI). The effect is stronger among state-owned and politically connected firms, whereas it does not strengthen with auditor size. This study extends research on the economic consequences of ESG from contemporaneous green innovation to intertemporal innovation persistence and clarifies the roles of export operations and international resource allocation.

title: Psychological Effects of Air Pollution: Evidence from House Viewings
abstract: We investigate the effect of air quality on the day of house viewing on final transaction prices. Using transaction-level data from Beijing that link individual house viewings to transaction outcomes and daily pollution levels, we find that higher pollution on the viewing day is associated with significantly higher final transaction prices, which does not appear to be driven by long-run local air quality. This price premium is especially pronounced for properties near amenities that can mitigate pollution exposure. We interpret these findings as evidence of projection bias, highlighting a novel behavioral channel through which transient environmental conditions may distort real estate valuation and decision-making.

title: Hindered From Making a Difference: How Increasing Organizational Constraints Undermine Public Servants' Perceptions of Prosocial Impact and Why It Matters
abstract: ABSTRACT Public servants often work under organizational constraints that hinder how they experience and carry out their work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, this research examines how changes in these constraints affect public servants' perceptions that their work benefits others and, in turn, their well‐being and withdrawal behavior. Using data from two longitudinal studies conducted in the United States and France, the findings show that increases in organizational constraints are associated with declines in perceived prosocial impact, which in turn predict lower well‐being and greater withdrawal over time. These results identify perceived prosocial impact as a key psychological resource that links changing work conditions to employee functioning. By emphasizing the dynamic nature of organizational constraints, this study advances the understanding of how evolving administrative conditions can weaken the psychological foundations that sustain meaningful and effective public service.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Punctuated Equilibrium: Shaping Government Attention in the Digital Age
abstract: ABSTRACT How do government attention and policy agendas shift when information constraints are relaxed through technological advancement? Punctuated equilibrium theory links agenda‐setting dynamics to governments' limited information‐processing capabilities, yet we know little about whether and how technology improvement such as artificial intelligence (AI) influences policy agendas. This article proposes a conditional digital punctuation framework to specify the conditions under which technological advancements drive agenda shifts. Using China's implementation of AI initiatives as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that government attention exhibits a punctuated pattern. AI increases technology‐focused attention, signaling incremental changes, while having minimal impact on general government attention. This selective impact stems from AI's asymmetric effects on information processing. Specifically, AI significantly increases the procurement‐based indicator of information quantity, which is associated with greater attention to technology sectors; however, no significant change is observed in the corresponding indicator of information quality, consistent with its limited impact on general government attention.

title: Interpretive leadership skill as the meaning-making leadership competency in public service organizations: content, construct, and criterion validity
abstract: This research examines the conceptualization and measurement of interpretive leadership skill (ILS) in public service organizations. ILS is conceptualized as an individual leadership competency for meaning-making whose function is interactive: the leader’s capacity to read the working context, build shared understandings that promote coherent action for the organization, and revise those understandings as conditions change. This research reports three studies using two large-scale samples to validate the psychometric and predictive properties of ILS in the public service logic. Study 1 develops and validates a multidimensional measure of ILS and demonstrates its content validity. Study 2 establishes construct validity by situating ILS within a three-level model of leader development. Study 3 demonstrates criterion validity by showing ILS’s predictive property on organizational public service performance. Together, these studies validate ILS as the meaning-making competency of public service leaders and provide implications for leadership theory and practice across public and non-profit organizations.

title: From reform to reality: governance mechanisms and social capital development in mandated healthcare networks
abstract: Mandated healthcare networks are introduced to achieve reform objectives through collaboration, yet imposed arrangements may not generate the social capital needed for collective action. We examine how governance mechanisms activate key sources of social capital (opportunity, ability, motivation) and shape its subsequent development. Using a longitudinal case study of a mandated hospital network governed by a Network Administrative Organization (NAO), we analyse 55 interviews along with documentary data. We find that while the NAO expanded opportunities for social capital development through network governance mechanisms, these were pseudo-opportunities that failed to enhance the ability and motivation of network members to collaborate. We contribute to theory by explaining how imposed governance can simultaneously appear to provide a key condition for social capital (interaction opportunities) and nevertheless inhibit successful collective action and generate disenchantment. The study highlights the need to distinguish between technical integration and meaningful collaboration in the implementation of governance mechanisms.

title: Two-dimensional dynamic analysis of vehicle sideway lane changing based on size-dependent driving risk potential field
“Nothing but a pair of shorts and a lifetime of trauma”: Trauma-related concerns of US foster caregivers
Generative artificial intelligence and commercial sexual exploitation of children: Implications for healthcare providers
How cultural world views moderate policy framing on Universal Basic Income
abstract: Universal Basic Income (UBI) has gained global attention as a potential policy response to the AI revolution, yet public support remains divided. While existing research highlights the role of political predisposition in shaping attitudes towards UBI, such explanations rely on the presence of partisan/ideological cues. In contexts where UBI is not yet politicized, ideological alignment may offer limited explanatory power. This article examines how individuals’ cultural predispositions, as conceptualized by Cultural Theory (CT), shape responses to different UBI framings in Taiwan, a non-Western democracy where partisan cues on UBI are less salient. Using an online survey experiment, the article tests how cultural world views interact with framing conditions to influence support for UBI. Findings demonstrate framing effects are conditioned by cultural orientations, supporting CT that individuals filter policy information through stable value lenses. This study advances a theoretical framework for understanding how public opinion forms in the absence of partisan cues.

title: Power, politics, and policy agency: towards a Functional Theory of Agency
abstract:
This article examines how political position shapes policy agency in local policy making. Specifically, it asks: what patterns of policy agency functions do municipal councillors (
 regidores
 ) exhibit in the local policy process? Drawing on the Functional Theory of Agency framework and a sequential mixed-methods design combining a national survey of Mexican municipal councillors with follow-up semi-structured interviews, we analyse how councillors exercise four modes of policy agency: steering, innovation, intermediation, and intelligence.
 
 Our findings reveal systematic differences between majoritarian and opposition councillors. Majoritarian councillors dominate commissions, align with mayoral priorities, and primarily act as steerers and brokers of executive policy. By contrast, opposition councillors, who are often excluded from formal decision-making arenas, engage in disruptive innovation, cultivate vertical alliances beyond the municipality, and invest more heavily in knowledge production as a counter-power strategy. These distinct patterns suggest that political position shapes the policy agency functions available to local legislators and influences how they seek to affect policy outcomes.
 The article contributes to the consolidation of a Functional Theory of Agency by demonstrating how unequal access to formal policy-making authority structures actors’ behavioural repertoires within policy-making processes. It also advances comparative research on legislative actors by showing how local representatives adapt their policy agency strategies under conditions of unequal access to formal policy-making authority.

title: Explaining the policy advisory success of non-governmental organisations in unlikely settings: a complexity-oriented approach
Extending the Advocacy Coalition Framework: measuring within-coalition belief variation in offshore wind policy conflicts
abstract: This study advances the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) literature by introducing new approaches to capture variation in actors’ belief expression and to analyse how such expressions are constrained by actors’ organisational affiliations. Moving beyond existing accounts of constrained belief expression, it reconceptualises constraint as measurable differences in the breadth and intensity of beliefs articulated by actors within a coalition. Drawing on debates over US offshore wind energy, the study examines how organisational affiliation shapes patterns of constrained belief expression in public discourse. To do this, the article develops two quantitative metrics – the Belief Variety Score and the Belief Extreme Score – which capture the range and intensity of belief expression within coalitions. These are complemented by network-based measures of cohesion across actor types. The findings show that purposive (value-oriented) groups are more cohesively connected in their belief-sharing, draw on a narrower range of concepts, and express more extreme beliefs than material (profit-oriented) groups. This suggests that actors in purposive groups may be more constrained in their belief expressions. These results provide empirical support for, and refinement of, ACF expectations regarding constrained belief expression, while demonstrating how within-coalition variation can be systematically measured. The study contributes a more precise conceptualisation and a novel measurement strategy for analysing belief expression in policy conflicts.

title: A systematic review of policy conflict and its (un)productive consequences
abstract: Like most collective decision-making processes, the formulation, adaptation, and implementation of public policies are not immune to conflict. Recently, various authors have lamented the lack of explicit attention to conflict in the policy process and called for more research into how policy conflicts unfold and what consequences they produce. This article contributes to that scholarship in two ways: first, through a systematic discussion of empirical studies on the consequences of policy conflict since 2000; and second, by bringing into conversation insights that are currently dispersed across fragmented research traditions. The systematic literature review focuses on three aspects: how and where policy conflicts have been studied; whether and how they have been conceptualised; and what their consequences are. In doing so, the article highlights the often overlooked productive potential of policy conflicts. Policy conflicts are studied primarily in relation to issues of the (built) environment, where contestation has been shown to produce detrimental effects such as trust erosion, frustration, and disengagement. Supporting an agonistic understanding of conflict, however, they have also been shown to drive productive outcomes such as policy change, stakeholder engagement, policy learning, and innovation. This study contributes to bridging policy conflict scholarship across theoretical perspectives, advancing empirical understanding of policy-conflict consequences, and raising awareness of their productive character in both theory and practice.

title: Not yet partisan: Cultural Theory explains attitudes about solar radiation management in the US
abstract: This article investigates the role of cultural theory (CT) in explaining attitudes towards solar radiation management (SRM) in the US. Partisanship traditionally provides a clear lens through which to view favourability to climate change policies; however, the lack of partisan attention to geoengineering policies, such as SRM, suggests other belief systems may be better explainers of attitudes. Previously, scholars have found climate attitudes to vary based upon cultural types, which are a function of how individuals see the role of authority in policy making and the extent to which individuals see themselves as part of a social unit. We find that partisanship is a weak predictor of SRM attitudes, while cultural affinities provide strong influences over SRM attitudes. Specifically, we find strong group affinities (particularly egalitarians) to lead to more favourable impressions of SRM research and deployment in the case of climate emergencies. Attitudes towards hierarchy, specifically cultural affinities that disfavour hierarchy, explain SRM scepticism. We contrast these results with a separate analysis of more widely known mitigation policies: carbon taxes, regulations on carbon emissions, taxes on higher income earners for green investment, and carbon cap and trade. For these better-known policy positions, partisanship is far more important. Our work contributes to the application of CT to policy attitudes as well as to explaining the shifting landscape of attitudes towards geoengineering and a variety of climate mitigation policies.

title: Repurposing gas power stations for modular nuclear and hydrogen systems: a techno-economic assessment
abstract: In the UK, many fossil-fuel power stations are approaching retirement, yet these sites retain valuable brownfield assets, notably developed industrial land and high-capacity grid connections, and can be repurposed for low-carbon generation. Repurposing such sites for low-carbon generation could therefore offer three linked advantages: lower upfront capital requirements through reuse of grid connections and developed industrial land; shorter project delivery times by reducing permitting needs and avoiding lengthy grid-connection queues; and higher system value through the provision of dispatchable flexibility and improved asset utilisation. This study examines repurposing end-of-life gas power stations into modular nuclear plants and further enabling hydrogen integration via high-temperature electrolysis, where the electricity-heat split is governed by endogenous reactor choice. A repurposing-oriented optimisation framework is proposed to embed inherited brownfield constraints, particularly land availability and grid-export limits, while co-optimising technology selection with hourly unit commitment and economic dispatch. Under the selected representative-week simulations, results show that the repurposed modular nuclear can deliver system-level flexibility comparable to that of gas turbines while meeting brownfield constraints. Nuclear‑hydrogen integration further increases reactor utilisation by using co-located electrolysis as a flexible local demand for nuclear-derived electricity and heat, eliminating renewable curtailment and substantially reducing plant-level levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) relative to power-only repurposing under these simulations. Among the electrolyser options, high-temperature electrolysis coupling gives the lowest plant-level levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH), while producing the largest hydrogen output with the lowest plant-level upfront investment. This advantage arises from the ability of high-temperature electrolysis to use both electricity and cost-effective nuclear heat, reducing reliance on electricity-priced input energy. Sensitivity analysis identifies nuclear and high-temperature electrolyser capital costs as the main upward cost drivers, while stack lifetime remains the key durability-related lever. Overall, the findings indicate that brownfield nuclear‑hydrogen integration can provide a valuable pathway for converting retiring thermal power station sites into flexible low-carbon power and hydrogen production assets.

title: Ownership structures shape climate-policy effectiveness in electricity generation
The impact of international clean energy finance and public policies on the low-carbon energy transition: Evidence from Egypt and Brazil
A coupled production-removal approach for Spirulina-derived biochar: Life cycle assessment and implications for carbon accounting
abstract: Value-chain emissions constitute the majority of environmental impacts across industrial systems, yet scalable, life-cycle-based strategies for reducing these impacts remain limited. Biochar has been widely studied as a functional material with climate benefits, but its contribution to supply-chain decarbonization is typically constrained by moderate inclusion rates and limited impact per unit mass. This study evaluates a coupled production-removal system in which Spirulina biomass is simultaneously valorized into biochar and a waste-derived biostimulant for soil organic carbon enhancement, thereby directly linking microalgal production with land-based carbon removal. A comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) with a focus on climate impact (GWP100) is conducted on a cradle-to-gate basis, with 1 kg of biochar at the factory gate as the functional unit, including Spirulina cultivation, downstream processing and drying, pyrolysis, and waste-stream valorization through field application as a biostimulant for soil carbon enhancement. Soil carbon removal is based on primary field measurements of soil organic carbon, assessed using a 100-year GWP horizon and incorporating a 20% non-permanence discount and ± 20% uncertainty for the sequestration estimate. The results show a strongly net-negative climate impact of −613,428.6 kg CO₂-eq per kg biochar (GWP100), driven primarily by biostimulant-induced soil carbon removal of −615,690.6 kg CO₂-eq per kg biochar, while the non-climate impacts are mainly linked to the upstream cultivation rather than to the biochar itself. These impacts should therefore be seen as a part of the overall system. At product level, the low inclusion rates required (<7 g·t −1 ) result in negligible contributions to other impact categories, suggesting limited risk of burden shifting under the conditions assessed. Application across four supply chains - cotton textiles, cement/construction, corrugated cardboard packaging, and virgin ABS plastics - illustrates how integrating functional ingredients into upstream materials could generate system-level mitigation potential relevant to value chain decarbonization, provided that emissions, removals, and carbon storage are transparently reported and not treated as interchangeable within corporate inventories. These findings highlight the potential of coupled production-removal systems to contribute to sustainable production, while emphasizing the importance of site-specific conditions and robust monitoring frameworks.

title: Life cycle greenhouse gas emissions of aluminium production in import-dependent countries: Supply chain effects and implications for vehicle lightweighting
Acid Leaching for Carbon Sequestration with Prospects for Critical Metal Recovery
abstract: Abstract Reducing carbon emissions and supplying critical metals for the green energy transition are essential to limiting global warming to below 1.5 °C. Here, we propose heap leaching ultramafic material with sulfuric acid followed by sequential precipitation for nickel recovery and carbon sequestration. Ultramafic materials were subjected to benchtop-scale acid leaches using 0.08–0.8 M H2SO4. The leachates were combined with NaOH to precipitate Ni (oxy)hydroxide minerals and then with NaOH + Na2CO3 to precipitate Mg carbonate minerals. The carbon sequestration potential of each sample and the efficiency of each experimental stage were calculated to estimate carbon sequestration using these techniques. The acid leaching released 2–57% of the Mg2+ along with 6–64% of the Ni2+ into the leachate, depending on acid strength and tailings mineralogy, while carbonation precipitated up to 95% of the dissolved Mg2+ and 90% of the CO32– + HCO3– in solution, depending on initial Mg2+ concentrations. Techno-economic analysis demonstrates that treatment cost and Ni production are the most important factors determining the profitability of the process, with CO2 removal being less important due to the relatively low value of carbon credits compared to Ni, but still contributing to the sustainability of this process.

title: Biochar–Straw Interaction Drives Soil Carbon Accrual by Modulating Microbial Metabolic Pathways
abstract: Abstract Straw and biochar additions can enhance long-term carbon storage, yet how their interactions regulate carbon mineralization and allocation remains unclear. We conducted a 360-day microcosm incubation employing a reciprocal 13C-labeling design that paired 13C-labeled straw with unlabeled biochar and unlabeled straw with 13C-labeled biochar and used single-cell Raman spectroscopy and 13C-labeled cell metagenomics. At day 360, biochar reduced cumulative straw-derived 13CO2 from 1391 to 1199 mg C kg–1 soil, while increasing straw-C allocation to fulvic acid (FA) and humic acid (HA) fractions. This shift was associated with enrichment of bacterial taxa such as Chitinophagales and increased abundance of genes involved in phospholipid metabolism, the phenylacetyl-CoA pathway, and potential polyphenol-related processing. Conversely, straw increased biochar-derived dissolved organic carbon from 1.5 to 5.5 mg C kg–1 soil and cumulative 13CO2 release from 17 to 23 mg C kg–1 soil, increasing FA and HA allocation. This shift was associated with the enrichment of genes involved in oxidative degradation, membrane transport (for substrate uptake), exopolysaccharide (EPS) formation, and quinone biosynthesis. Overall, the biochar–straw interaction redirected exogenous carbon from rapid mineralization toward humic substance associated soil organic matter fractions, thereby enhancing soil carbon accrual.

title: Haloacetic Acid Disinfection Byproducts in Follicular Fluid and In Vitro Fertilization Outcomes: A Prospective Cohort Study in China
abstract: Abstract Drinking water disinfection byproducts (DBPs), particularly haloacetic acids (HAAs), can exert adverse effects on oocyte quality and embryo development. However, there has been a paucity of human evidence. We included 1176 women who underwent 1306 in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles from the Tongji Reproductive and Environmental cohort (2018–2021). Dichloroacetic acid (DCAA) and trichloroacetic acid (TCAA) concentrations in follicular fluid were assessed. Elevated quartiles of DCAA and TCAA concentrations in follicular fluid had significant inverse exposure-response associations with all IVF outcomes (e.g., 16.67% and 10.14% reductions in proportion of clinical pregnancy for the highest vs lowest quartiles of DCAA and TCAA concentrations, respectively; both P for trend <0.01). The effects were more pronounced in women undergoing non-long GnRH agonist regimens and IVF insemination technology. The serial mediation analyses identified that a sequential pathway (oocyte → mature oocyte → zygotes with two pronuclei → good-quality embryos) mediated 21.1%–33.9% of HAA exposure-related inferior clinical pregnancy outcomes (implantation, clinical pregnancy, and live birth). Our findings suggest that elevated levels of HAAs in follicular fluid are associated with decreased oocyte quality and subsequent inferior IVF outcomes, strengthening human evidence that exposure to drinking water DBPs has detrimental effects on early reproductive outcomes.

title: Decentralized Solar-Driven Plant Factories Secure an Adequate Global Vegetable Supply beyond the Electricity Grid and Water Limitations
abstract: Abstract Conventional open-field vegetable production is increasingly constrained by climate volatility and natural resource endowments, creating supply instabilities and shortages that threaten global food resilience and human health. Here, we integrate solar photovoltaics and atmospheric water harvesting with plant factories, creating a technically mature off-grid agricultural system using plant factories (OASIS). By decoupling production from local water and grid infrastructure, OASIS significantly expands the area suitable for cultivation. Globally, OASIS can meet the recommended upper vegetable intake (600 g capita–1 day–1) for at least 98.3% of the population, leveraging mostly non-arable land. Cropland substitution could spare approximately 578,000 km2 for staple food production and, under the idealized zero-operational-loss case, reduce agricultural nitrogen and phosphorus losses by up to 9.90 and 0.95 Tg yr–1, respectively. Estimated global, production-weighted levelized costs were 3.8–4.0 USD kg–1 across six scenarios. Under the 600 g capita–1 day–1 scenario with cropland substitution, OASIS offered cost advantages over existing production benchmarks in 115 of 166 comparable countries, including all 26 low-income countries, which could meet modeled supply targets with a 32.2% average cost advantage. These results highlight OASIS’s potential to advance resilient, clean vegetable production and the Sustainable Development Goals across food security, health, and land conservation.

title: Integrating Supply Chain Life Cycle Decisions: Empirical model validation for a large-scale case
Valorization of spent coffee grounds into metal–phenolic coatings for producing spray-dried microbial biostimulants for sustainable agriculture
abstract: Dry microbial biostimulants offer a convenient and sustainable approach to enhancing crop health and yield. However, their efficacy is limited by the challenge of stabilizing microbes into dry products because scalable dehydration methods such as spray drying impose substantial thermal and osmotic stresses that often result in substantial viability losses. In this work, metal-phenolic network (MPN) coatings were applied to Klebsiella michiganensis M5al, a Gram-negative, plant-beneficial bacteria, prior to spray drying to enable their survival during the rapid thermal dehydration process. Uncoated cells lost 5.0 ± 0.21 log viability during spray drying, whereas tannic-acid-iron coatings reduced this loss to 3.2 ± 0.34 log with a streamlined, single-coat process, and 2.1 ± 0.47 log with a two-coat process. Furthermore, phenolics present in water extracts of spent coffee grounds (SCG) were shown to form MPNs with protective performance comparable to those formed from purified tannic acid, reducing viability loss during spray drying to 3.5 ± 0.19 log. Nano-scale infrared spectroscopy confirmed the presence of metal-phenolic coatings on cell surfaces, while atomic force microscopy indicated improved structural preservation during spray-drying. These findings show that SCG-derived phenolics can serve as sustainable feedstocks for protective MPN coatings and demonstrate the feasibility of using waste-derived phenolics as functional substitutes for purified reagents in MPN coatings. This approach simultaneously enables scalable production of dry microbial biostimulants and valorization of abundant, phenolic-rich agro-industrial residues.

title: Supply-side perceptions of demand for natural food products in regional sustainable food systems: evidence from Finland
abstract: Natural food products, items foraged from the wild that have been only minimally processed, are becoming more closely associated with sustainability transitions in food systems. However, their integration remains limited, and demand's influence on adopting such products is not well understood. We examine how supply-side actors in Finland understand and interpret demand for natural food products and how these interpretations shape sourcing and coordination within the regional food system. Based on 22 semi-structured interviews with nine restaurants, ten producers, processors, and wholesalers, and three sector experts, we show how supply-side stakeholders develop an understanding of demand through indirect signals amid uncertainty and low market transparency, and how these constructed perceptions, in turn, affect sustainability-related practices. The findings indicate that supply-side actors rely on indirect signals, such as perceived customer preferences, direct customer interactions, and product differentiation, to interpret demand, and that price sensitivity, seasonal availability, and infrastructure limitations further shape these interpretations. Price and infrastructure came out as the most mentioned barriers to sourcing, while collaboration and shared infrastructure were strongly identified as development opportunities.The way stakeholders interpret demand was found to affect their sourcing strategies, collaboration practices, and the degree to which natural food products are included in supply chains. This study contributes to the field of Sustainable Supply Chain Management by explaining how perception-based demand signals influence supply-side responses, and by stressing the importance of coordination, information flow, and the empirical verification of proposed development paths in sustainability-focused regional food systems.

title: Mitigating seed sedimentation for sustainable sulfur hexafluoride hydrate formation using cyclopentane hydrate seeds
abstract: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF 6 ) is a highly potent greenhouse gas with a long atmospheric lifetime, necessitating efficient and low-energy capture strategies. Hydrate-based SF 6 capture has emerged as a promising alternative due to its low operating cost and high uptake capacity compared with conventional technologies. This study investigates a static hydrate-based SF 6 capture process employing cyclopentane (CP) hydrate seeds and evaluates the synergistic effects of CP seeds and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) under varying driving force (DF) conditions. Visual observations revealed an unfavorable seed-drowning phenomenon under 5 K DF, where SF 6 hydrate accumulation on CP seeds induced early sedimentation. Increasing CP seed concentration suppressed sedimentation by reducing the overall density and increasing the seed stability. Higher DF promoted vertical growth and wall adhesion, mitigating sedimentation even at low seed loadings. The optimized condition (0.0556 mol% CP seed and 500 ppm SDS, 10 K DF) achieved high SF 6 uptake (51.009 mmol SF 6 /mol H 2 O) and rapid formation ( t 90 = 0.492 h) without retardation. Compared with agitated or porous media systems, the CP seed process achieved comparable uptake while exhibiting significantly lower energy demand and improved volumetric efficiency. These findings demonstrate the application of CP seeds to static SF 6 hydrate formation while providing mechanistic design criteria for clean and feasible SF 6 capture.

title: Experimental characterization of a scroll expander under two-phase conditions within a micro PE-ORC system

Pilot-scale investigation of a convective fixed-bed reactor for CaO/Ca(OH)2 thermochemical energy storage
abstract: The CaO/Ca(OH) 2 system is considered as one of the most promising thermochemical energy storage systems due to its high energy storage density and low material cost. However, existing studies are mainly limited to numerical simulations or laboratory-scale reactors, while pilot-scale investigations remain scarce. In addition, the high decomposition temperature of Ca(OH) 2 aggravates material sintering and limits the utilization of low- and medium-temperature heat sources. In this study, a pilot-scale convective fixed-bed reactor capable of loading 334.14 kg of CaO is proposed. During the heat storage stage, high-temperature N 2 directly transfers heat by convection while simultaneously removing reaction steam to reduce the decomposition temperature, whereas during the heat release stage, heat is indirectly extracted by heat transfer oil flowing inside finned tubes. Total 4 cyclic performance tests have been conducted with the max and final conversion ratio of 98.18% and 91.75%, respectively. For a typical heat release stage, it lasts for 105 min with maximum/average heat release powers of 75.03/52.89 kW and 318.17 MJ of energy is released. The overall/particle-side heat transfer coefficients are 97/107 W/(m 2 ·K). During the heat storage stage, it lasts for 1135 min with maximum/average reaction heat storage powers of 7.97/4.68 kW and 321.03 MJ of energy is stored. In addition, the decomposition temperature decreases to 420 °C. Based on energy balance analysis, the heat release, heat storage, and cycle efficiencies are 95.85%, 79.11% and 76.65%, respectively. This work demonstrates significant advantages in storage scale, conversion performance, and decomposition temperature, promoting practical applications of thermochemical energy storage technology.

title: Wake and power-performance responses of high-altitude wind farms to air-density variations
Investigation of complex hydraulic fracture behavior for natural gas hydrate using tri-axial fracturing experiments
An expert-informed framework for participatory soundscape design: From Interviews to co-design application
abstract: Participatory approaches are widely recognised in soundscape standards and policy, yet their application remains fragmented and underreported. This study developed an expert-informed conceptual framework for participatory soundscape design, with a co-design experiment demonstrating its application. Semi-structured interviews were analysed using a Straussian grounded theory analytical procedure, identifying six categories: Stakeholder roles, Soundscape design elements, Assessment and design brief, Design and demonstration, Discussion and optimisation, Documentation and validation. Stakeholder roles describe participatory soundscape design as a dynamic multi-actor process involving soundscape specialists, local experts, clients, and planning authorities. Soundscape design elements are described as multimodal, linking sound with visual-spatial context and supported by interactive audio-visual tools. The four process phases are Assessment and design brief, where stakeholders assess the soundscape and develop the design brief; Design and demonstration, where proposals are developed and compared; Discussion and optimisation, where stakeholders discuss and refine proposals; and Documentation and validation, where design process and outcomes are documented and evaluated. Overall, the framework provides insights for organising participatory soundscape design, and its applicability should be evaluated across project contexts in future studies.

title: Urban ethnopedology: Integrating community soil knowledge into environmental justice and urban greening policy
AN ALTERNATIVE CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK OF THE PROXIMATE SOURCES OF GROWTH ACCELERATIONS IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICAN COUNTRIES
Cross-national institutional divergence in ESG ratings and corporate green innovation
Supply chain digitalization and ESG greenwashing: A signal reliability perspective
Dance as destination infrastructure: Toward a progress agenda

Employee Activism, Then and Now
abstract: We review research on employee activism, with particular attention to developments over the past decade, and identify avenues for future research that reflect the evolving nature of the phenomenon. We first define employee activism and distinguish it from related forms of employee behavior. We then identify three themes in the evolution of research on employee activism: an expansion from organizational-change goals to also include society-oriented goals, from persuasive tactics to also include disruptive tactics, and from in-person mobilization to also include activism through online digital platforms. We next synthesize research on five central features of employee activism—participants, goals, contexts, behaviors, and outcomes—drawing on scholarship across social movement sociology, organizational theory, organizational behavior, and strategic management. We conclude by identifying opportunities for research that better captures contemporary forms of employee activism and advances understanding of its consequences for employees, organizations, and society.

title: A Response to Don Kettl's Debate Article on the Future of Public Administration and Democracy
abstract: ABSTRACT This commentary critically engages with Kettl's analysis of the crisis of public administration (PA) scholarship and its relationship with democratic decline. It argues that both phenomena should be understood within broader global developments rather than primarily as problems specific to the United States. While acknowledging the role of governance failures in facilitating autocratization, it questions the claim that autocratization results predominantly from the failures of PA scholarship and practice. Rather, it emphasizes that broader societal phenomena, such as the erosion of societal trust and the power‐consolidating objectives of authoritarian leaders play a key role. Drawing on Hungary's experience, the commentary illustrates how authoritarian governance may perpetuate administrative instability and institutional transformation long after the (perceived) failures of democratic governance have been addressed in the early phase of illiberal transformation. However, it also argues that poor governance and declining policy performance can eventually undermine authoritarian rule, as illustrated by Hungary's 2026 political transformation. The commentary thus highlights the complex and potentially self‐undermining relationship between authoritarianism and public governance.

Child neglect from a legal perspective: A quantitative analysis of Israeli court judgments over half a century

A Data-Driven Approach for the Development of a Time-Informed Adverse Outcome Pathway Network for the Cardiotoxicity of Environmental Chemicals
abstract: Abstract We developed a bottom-up, data-driven approach for constructing a time-informed adverse outcome pathway (AOP) network for environmental chemical-induced cardiotoxicity. Mechanistic end points were systematically extracted from 339 in vitro and in vivo studies, yielding 1759 Key Event (KE) entries and 4938 Key Event Relationship (KER) entries, together with study metadata and essentiality evidence from intervention experiments. After quality filtering and minimum support thresholding, 62 unique KEs and 256 unique KERs were retained for network construction. Network analysis highlighted oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction as prominent, highly connected KEs linking diverse upstream perturbations to downstream cardiomyocyte injury, inflammation, cardiac remodeling (fibrosis and hypertrophy), decreased myocardial contractility, and reduced left ventricular function. A central methodological finding was that temporal information was more informative at the level of KERs than at the level of KEs. The same KE could occur across multiple durations depending on the relationship in which it was embedded, whereas KER-level time-scale annotation resolved distinct acute, subacute, and chronic pathway patterns not apparent from KE timing alone. This framework provides an evidence-weighted synthesis of the most consistently supported cardiotoxicity mechanisms and introduces a temporal layer for the mechanistic interpretation of heterogeneous evidence.
