Meeting lifestyle recommendations among cancer survivors – a cross-sectional descriptive analysis from the Swedish CArdioPulmonary BioImage study (SCAPIS)
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study aimed to describe lifestyle patterns in relation to recommendations —including physical activity, diet, smoking, alcohol consumption, and sleep quality—among Swedish cancer survivors, stratified by sex and age. Method A descriptive cross-sectional study was performed using data from the Swedish CArdioPulmonary BioImage study (SCAPIS). Questionnaires and accelerometers were used to collect data. SCAPIS data were linked to the Swedish in- and out-patient registry. Descriptive statistics were used to describe proportion meeting lifestyle recommendations in different cancer diagnoses. Results In total, 2576 individuals were identified as cancer survivors in the SCAPIS-cohort. The median age was 59 years, 57% were females, the median time since diagnosis was 13 years, and malignant melanoma was the most common cancer type (50%). Most cancer survivors in the sample met at least one lifestyle recommendation. Meeting multiple recommendations were significantly ( p < 0.001) more common among breast cancer and malignant melanoma survivors than among other cancer types. Females were significantly ( p < 0.001) more likely to meet multiple recommendations and were twice as likely (53%) to meet the dietary recommendation compared to men (26%). Conclusions In this study of cancer survivors, differences across cancer types were observed in meeting multiple lifestyle recommendations. Most survivors met at least one recommendation, while the lowest proportion meeting the recommendations was observed for diet and alcohol consumption. Implications for Cancer Survivors These findings suggest that cancer survivors might benefit from secondary prevention strategies targeting lifestyle factors in general and diet and alcohol consumption in particular.

Lattice-Oxygen-Mediated Electronic Reconstruction of High-Entropy Oxides for Durable Fenton-like Water Treatment
abstract: Abstract High-entropy catalysts offer broad compositional tunability for peroxymonosulfate (PMS)-based water treatment, yet achieving rapid, selective, and durable oxidation remains challenging because metallic bonding in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) limits electronic communication among metal sites. Here, we construct a quinary high-entropy oxide (HEO, (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4) featuring an oxygen-bridged M-O-M framework that enables local electronic coupling among neighboring metal centers. X-ray absorption spectroscopy and theoretical calculations support oxygen-mediated charge redistribution, with Hirshfeld analysis indicating 0.46e of charge transfer toward adsorbed PMS. Temperature-dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy reveals a substantially lower apparent activation energy for interfacial charge transfer in the HEO (0.43 eV) than in the HEA (1.15 eV). Mechanistic experiments support a predominantly nonradical PMS activation pathway involving high-valent cobalt-oxo species and singlet oxygen. The HEO achieved near-complete phenol degradation and 87.9% total organic carbon removal within 10 min, with an apparent rate constant of 0.359 min–1 versus 0.113 min–1 for the HEA. The system maintained >90% phenol removal across pH 3–11, sustained activity over 30 reuse cycles, and retained effective contaminant removal during continuous-flow operation and 50 L bench-scale treatment. These results support lattice-oxygen-mediated electronic reconstruction as a strategy for coupling efficient PMS activation with structural durability in high-entropy oxide catalysts.

title: Combined Residues of Frequently Detected Herbicides are Stronger Predictors of Soil Resistome and Virulence Potential than Single Residues
abstract: Abstract Overuse of herbicides has resulted in a global epidemic of evolved resistance in soil ecosystems. While single herbicide risk has been documented, the impact of multiple herbicide residues on the soil resistomes remains poorly understood. Our study quantified the residues of 24 herbicides, profiled antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and virulence factor genes (VFGs), and reconstructed 1086 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from 93 agricultural soils across China. The analytical results demonstrate that the frequently detected herbicide residues (e.g., 60–90% detection frequency) are stronger predictors of soil antibiotic resistomes than total herbicide load, unsupervised mixture based on principal component analysis (PCA), or single-herbicide models. For VFG abundance, the same mixture outperformed the best single herbicide and total herbicide concentration, although PCA–PC1 showed a moderately stronger correlation. Specifically, these commonly detected herbicides showed positive associations with ARG abundance through both direct linkages and bacterial community-dependent indirect pathways. Similar patterns were observed for virulence potential, where frequently detected residues maintained strong predictive performance and were predominantly associated with indirect pathways. Functional annotation patterns further suggest a concurrent enrichment of traits related to antioxidant defense, mobility, adherence, and immune modulation under elevated herbicide exposure. Notably, multiple herbicide residues were linked to the abundance of a Trinickia taxon, which was identified as a candidate ARG-VFG co-occurrence MAG carrying a high ARG load. Our findings highlight the need to integrate compound exposure of frequently detected herbicides into future risk assessment methodology for preventing the dissemination of ARGs in agricultural soils.

title: Aging of Urban Traffic Fine Particles Modulates Toxicity Mechanisms and Oxidative Stress Responses
abstract: Abstract Vehicular emissions are an important source of urban air pollution that can age through atmospheric processes, but how their health effects change during atmospheric aging remains poorly understood. To simulate realistic urban emissions, we sampled air in a parking garage where cold-start and urban emissions coexist. Following aging in an oxidation flow reactor (OFR), we studied the cellular and acellular effects of the fresh and aged aerosols. Photochemical aging in the OFR increased secondary organic aerosol (SOA) mass by up to 6.9-fold, the oxygen-to-carbon (O:C) ratio from 0.26 to 0.79, and both the intrinsic oxidative potential (OPm) and the volume-normalized oxidative potential (OPv). In contrast, the peroxide-sensitive DCF activity decreased following aging. Cellular exposure to aged aerosol extracts increased cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation in lung (A549) and liver (HepG2) cells, whereas fresh extracts strongly reduced cellular respiration, particularly in HepG2 cells. Cell painting analysis showed distinct morphological profiles. Exposure to aged extracts showed greater oxidative stress and DNA damage responses than those of exposure to fresh extracts. These findings suggest that atmospheric aging shifts the toxicity of fresh emissions from suppression of mitochondrial respiration toward oxygenated organics that can drive intracellular oxidative stress and DNA damage phenotypes. In conclusion, atmospheric aging of cold-start and urban vehicular emissions contributes to enhanced SOA formation and leads to distinct biological outcomes that depend on the degree of oxidative aging.

Generative AI and Firm Values
abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.

title: Why do people migrate irregularly? Evidence from a lab-in-the-field experiment in West Africa
abstract: Irregular migration to Europe by sea, though risky, remains one of the most popular migration options for many Sub-Saharan Africans. This study examines the drivers of irregular migration decisions using an incentivized lab-in-the-field experiment in rural Gambia, the African country with the highest per-capita rate of irregular migration to Europe. Potential migrants substantially overestimate the probability of dying en route , reporting an average belief of 51 percent compared with a best available estimate of about 20 percent. In the experiment, reducing the probability of dying en route from 50 to 20 percent raises willingness to migrate irregularly by 3.0 percentage points, while reducing the probability of obtaining legal residence from 50 to 30 percent lowers it by 2.1 points. Our results highlight the importance of potential migrants’ prior beliefs in shaping responses to information and suggest that information policies that fail to account for these beliefs may backfire.

title: Morality and climate policy attitudes
abstract: This paper studies the moral roots of climate policy attitudes. We fielded a survey with a representative sample in the US to study the predictive power of moral universalism in explaining heterogeneity in specific climate policy attitudes. Our results reveal that universalism is significantly related to support for various policy measures that prevail in current policy debates in most countries, including domestic policies such as a carbon tax and a green infrastructure program, as well as international policies such as international burden-sharing. Supporting evidence comes from simple bystander allocation decisions in which respondents are asked to decide “who should pay” to fight climate change or to mitigate the adverse consequences of global warming. Open-text elicitations further corroborate these results and identify moral universalism as a key aspect of how people reason about climate policies.

When Trade Policy Shocks Hit the Pit: Pricing, Volatility and Speculation in the 2025 Soybean Futures Market
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper explores responses to major trade policy shocks in the soybean futures market in 2025. Using an event‐study framework, we analyse short‐run movements in soybean futures prices, historical volatility, implied volatility and speculative positioning around three major policy shocks: the U.S. tariff announcement targeting China on February 1, the reciprocal tariff announcement on April 2, and Argentina's temporary suspension of soybean export taxes on September 22. Broader in scope, the April reciprocal tariff package was associated with the clearest and strongest response. Futures prices fell by about 6% within two trading days, while implied volatility rose sharply. Following the February announcement, implied volatility increased immediately and then receded, while downward repricing became evident only after China's retaliatory tariffs took effect, suggesting that uncertainty rose before the implications for U.S. export demand became clearer. Argentina's export‐tax suspension, by contrast, was followed by limited repricing, a later decline in implied volatility, and greater speculative positioning relative to commercial hedging needs. The cross‐event comparison suggests that the timing and composition of market adjustment vary with the scope, directness and subsequent evolution of each policy episode.

title: Revealing tax evasion: Experimental evidence from a representative survey of Indonesian firms
abstract: Measuring tax evasion by firms is notoriously difficult: direct questions yield biased responses while administrative data captures only detected violations. This paper examines the prevalence of reported tax non-compliance in Indonesia through a randomized, double-list experiment embedded in a nationally representative survey of 2,955 registered firms that preserves anonymity. The results indicate that around one-quarter of firms indirectly report not paying all taxes they are required to pay. An indicative back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the associated revenue losses could be economically meaningful, in the order of two percent of GDP. Heterogeneity analyses suggest higher reported non-compliance among firms that do not export, face informal-sector competition, and view tax administration as a major obstacle. These findings help inform tax authorities, which face substantial challenges in estimating levels of tax evasion and identifying non-compliant taxpayers, by providing the first representative estimates of firm tax evasion in a major middle-income country.

title: Political elites and access to economic opportunities in China’s rural market transition
The Olympic effect revisited: 1950–2019
abstract: Rose and Spiegel (2011) identified a positive trade-promoting effect of hosting the Olympic Games, yet they did not account for multilateral resistance terms in their analysis, which are emphasized in the structural gravity model by Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). This paper revisits the trade effects of the Olympics using a nonparametric matching method developed by Chang and Lee (2011), analyzing a comprehensive gravity dataset encompassing 187 economies from 1950 to 2019. Our findings suggest that hosting the Olympics is positively associated with bilateral trade. For pairs in which both countries have hosted, the matching estimate corresponds to a long-run trade difference with an implied increase of approximately 15 times relative to matched nonhost pairs. Under an assumed trade elasticity of 4, this estimate corresponds to an illustrative trade-cost equivalent of approximately 50%.

title: Drought, women’s time poverty, and the development costs of water collection in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Drought can impose development costs that are not fully captured by income, production, or formal water access indicators. This paper examines one such hidden cost in Sub-Saharan Africa by focusing on women’s time poverty arising from household water collection. Combining harmonized Demographic and Health Surveys with geocoded drought exposure measured at the survey cluster level, we estimate how local drought conditions are associated with women’s annual water collection burden and broader household adjustments. We find that drought exposure is associated with higher water-collection time for women, with larger estimated increases among women living in poor households, women with no formal education, and women living in households without piped-water access. Intermediate-outcome evidence shows that drought is associated with lower local water availability and a higher likelihood of very long collection trips, particularly journeys exceeding 60 minutes. These water-time burdens are also associated with greater engagement in flexible, household-based, family-based, and self-employed forms of work among women rather than with a simple expansion of protected paid employment. In addition, higher community water burdens are associated with poorer schooling outcomes among girls, including a greater likelihood of being out of school and larger grade-for-age gaps. Household-linked evidence further shows that poorer girls’ schooling outcomes are associated with larger household shares of adult women in unpaid or in-kind work, self-employment, and family work. The findings suggest that drought-related water insecurity can redistribute adaptation costs within households, making women’s unpaid time a key margin through which climate stress produces hidden development costs.

The Depositary of Last Resort
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits. Deterrence or Self-protection: Effects of Anti-mafia Campaign on Corporate Fraud
abstract: This paper identifies a novel channel—corporate fraud—through which local firms protect themselves during anti-mafia periods. We initially explore the impact of the anti-mafia campaign on mafia-like forces captured by accepted mafia-like criminal cases. The results indicate that the average number of accepted mafia-like criminal cases increases by 10.03%. More importantly, the accepted mafia-like criminal cases committed by firms also exhibit a notable increase, mainly within the first 30 months of the anti-mafia campaign. We then theorize that the anti-mafia campaign may have two contradictory effects on corporate fraud: deterrence and self-protection. The main results show that the self-protection effect prevails over the deterrence effect and that firms are more likely to commit fraud to strategically protect themselves from potential losses. The baseline findings reveal that the fraud occurrence of an average firm increases by 44.07% during anti-mafia periods.

title: How Strategic Leaders Drive Firms in Ecosystems: Envisioning Value, Orchestrating Knowledge, and Shifting Roles
abstract: Abstract Research on business ecosystems has illuminated how ecosystems emerge, evolve, and transform, revealing ecosystem‐level dynamics and the central actors that orchestrate them. Yet, it is individual firms that continuously attempt to establish and shift the roles they play within ecosystems through the vision and choices of their strategic leaders. How do strategic leaders drive these shifts? Through a longitudinal case study of Dallara Automobili (1972–2025), we trace how the CEO's prior professional experience shaped an evolving theory of value – a set of conjectures about how value should be created that guided the development of organizational routines enabling progressively more expansive knowledge orchestration. This process shifted Dallara from a peripheral component supplier to a boundary‐spanning knowledge orchestrator. Our recursive process model theorizes how the leader's conjectures drive firm role shifts within an ecosystem: experience shapes the leader's theory of value, which drives organizational routines and knowledge orchestration; knowledge orchestration, in turn, redefines the firm's ecosystem role. Ecosystem responses then feed back, augmenting prior experience and, in turn, refining the theory of value so that each round operates at a broader scope. We contribute to ecosystem research by identifying knowledge orchestration as the mechanism through which a leader's theory of value translates into shifts in the firm's role and by showing how this process unfolds recursively as ecosystem responses reshape the leader's conjectures.

Collective Activism
abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation features multiple equilibria. Small changes in coordination costs significantly influence ICAO formation and activism. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. Yang thanks the support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grants 435-2021-0040, 435-2026-0060] and the Bank of Canada [Fellowship]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02975 .

title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

title: Worker Repositioning and Technological Change: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
abstract: Technological change reshapes labor markets not only by changing labor demand but also by altering labor supply, as workers reallocate effort across tasks and opportunities in response to technological advances. Yet research has focused more on demand-side effects than on how workers themselves adapt. In this research, we examine worker repositioning on a large online labor market following the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. We argue that the launch of ChatGPT reduced expected returns to labor in exposed skill domains and develop and test a series of hypotheses regarding how this shock is associated with participation, horizontal positioning, and vertical positioning among workers on the platform. Using proprietary data on incumbent freelancers and a difference-in-differences design that leverages cross-sectional variation in pre-period AI exposure and skill-level, we show that freelancers more exposed to AI shift away from prior domains and reorient bidding toward higher-value contracts. In contrast, high skill-level freelancers, who face greater adjustment costs, are less likely to reduce participation on the platform, reposition across domains, and move upmarket. These findings highlight how technological shocks reshape labor markets through supply-side adaptation and how domain-specific human capital constrains worker responses.

title: The Sustainability Claim Paradox: When Green Marketing Encourages Greater Consumption
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainability claims are assumed to promote responsible consumption, yet consumption itself drives environmental harm. Drawing on moral licensing theory, this study asks whether such claims instead licence greater consumption across the purchase, use/replacement and disposal stages of one cycle. A between‐subjects experiment ( N = 303) manipulated claim strength (control, light, strong) in a product advertisement, and the hypothesised effects were estimated jointly using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Stronger claims raised perceived environmental impact, which raised intended purchase quantity, and this belief carried the total purchase effect entirely, consistent with static moral licensing. The evidence is mixed thereafter: Claim strength had no net effect on intended use or replacement, and although it showed a small total effect on justifying earlier disposal, perceived impact did not carry that effect, and the direct path was inconclusive under the inferential rule adopted here. Environmental concern attenuated rather than amplified the effect.

title: When Premium Product Strategy Meets Sustainability: Environmental–Economic Trade‐Offs in Japanese Manufacturing
abstract: ABSTRACT Corporate sustainability has become a central concern for business stakeholders, yet little is known about how premium product strategies shape firms' sustainability orientations and performance. Drawing on stakeholder theory, this study examines whether pursuing premium products is associated with firms' adoption of environmental and economic sustainability orientations and how these orientations, in turn, relate to corporate performance. Using survey data from 128 directors and managers responsible for overseas operations in manufacturing firms listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, analyzed with structural equation modelling, we find that a premium product strategy is positively associated with both environmental and economic sustainability orientations. However, their performance implications differ: economic sustainability is positively related to firm performance, whereas environmental sustainability shows a significant negative association. These results suggest that, among Japanese manufacturing exporters, premium product strategies simultaneously foster sustainability ambitions and expose firms to short‐term trade‐offs between environmental and economic outcomes.

title: Digitalisation, Organisational Innovation and Firms' Environmental Protection Expenditures: Evidence From Spanish Manufacturing
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how digitalisation and organisational innovation shape firms' routine environmental protection efforts in Spanish manufacturing. Using an unbalanced panel of 2348 firms and 7603 firm‐year observations from 2009–2023 drawn from the Survey on Business Strategies (ESEE), the study examines the determinants of current environmental protection expenditures as a recurrent form of operational green capability rather than radical eco‐innovation. The empirical analysis relies on panel‐data logit models that relate firm characteristics at time (2009–2022) to current environmental protection expenditures at time (2010–2023), with firm‐level controls and sector and period effects, and reports average marginal effects. The results show that digitalisation is strongly and consistently associated with routine environmental protection efforts. Firms that use robotics in production, invest in external ICT training and implement software‐based process innovations exhibit around 8–11 percentage points higher predicted probabilities of undertaking current environmental protection expenditures than otherwise similar firms. Organisational innovation, measured through the introduction of new work‐organisation practices, also displays a positive and significant association, with an average marginal effect of about 8–9 percentage points. Participation in EU research programmes is likewise positively associated with environmental protection expenditures, although this result applies to a relatively small share of firms and should be interpreted with caution, as it likely reflects the behaviour of a self‐selected subset of highly capable, outward‐oriented firms. The findings indicate that digital and organisational capabilities, together with cooperative engagements, act as key enablers of operational green practices, even though interaction terms provide only weak evidence of strong complementarities in this specific outcome. The paper contributes novel firm‐level evidence on how the twin green–digital transition materialises in ongoing environmental management within a manufacturing sector dominated by SMEs in Spain, shifting attention from one‐off eco‐innovations towards the stabilisation of everyday environmental routines and highlighting the role of capability bundles in supporting sustained environmental protection efforts.

title: Contracting as Sensemaking Infrastructure: Enacting Sustainability Strategy in Business‐to‐Business Relationships
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms articulate sustainability objectives but depend on suppliers and business partners to enact them. As commitments cross organizational and professional boundaries, their meaning may fragment even when parties agree in principle. This theory‐synthesis article examines B2B contracting as sensemaking infrastructure for enacting sustainability strategy across interorganizational relationships. Integrating sensemaking, proactive contracting, and contract design, it develops the sensemaking‐based contracting framework. The framework identifies four interdependent functions: framing clarifies what the relationship seeks to govern; translation connects that understanding to responsibilities, data, and routines; adaptation organizes legitimate revision; and signaling connects relationship‐level performance to external credibility. The article repositions contracting from downstream compliance to strategy enactment. It shows that preserving contractual wording is insufficient when purpose becomes disconnected from performance and directs managerial attention to connections among purpose, responsibility, capability, review, and evidence. Whether this infrastructure supports shared meaning depends on power, network position, and actors' ability to question established interpretations.

title: Warehouse logistics and task switching theory revisited: asymmetric height switching costs in order picking systems
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the impact of pick location height switching on task performance time in manual order picking systems. Drawing on task switching theory, we examine whether switching between ground- and chest-level pick locations increases task performance time, whether switching costs are asymmetric, and whether item weight strengthens possible differences between ground-to-chest and chest-to-ground switches. Design/methodology/approach We adopt a two-stage approach that combines internal validity and operational generalizability. First, a controlled eye-tracking experiment simulates a simplified order picking scenario to explore the cognitive mechanisms underlying visual search when repeating versus switching pick location heights. Second, we analyze 3,537,973 pick location visits from a German grocery retail warehouse to test the effects of pick location height switching in a real-world operational environment with professional order pickers. Findings The eye-tracking experiment provides mechanism-oriented evidence that switching between pick location heights increases visual search time and reorientation demands under controlled conditions. The archival field study complements these behavioral insights by showing that height switching is associated with longer task performance time. It further shows that switching costs depend on direction, with ground-to-chest switches being more time-consuming than chest-to ground switches. This directional difference becomes more pronounced as item weight increases. Practical implications The findings suggest that warehouse managers should consider not only the frequency but also the direction of height switches when designing picking sequences. Batching and routing algorithms could incorporate switching costs as a weighted parameter, with particular attention to ground-to-chest switches involving heavier items. However, reducing height switches should be balanced against ergonomic risks, as long sequences of ground-level picks may increase repetitive bending and musculoskeletal strain. Originality/value This study provides the first empirical evidence on pick location height switching in warehouse operations and extends task switching theory to a new operational context. By combining mechanism-oriented eye-tracking evidence with large-scale field data, we show that height switching is associated with asymmetric switching costs and provide insights into the cognitive and motor reorientation processes that may underlie these effects.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: Understanding the mixed consequences of diversity practices: A typology of migrant employees
Understanding and Confronting Organizational Corruption and Wrongdoing in the Era of Grand Societal Challenges: Past, Present, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Organizational corruption and wrongdoing remain persistent problems in contemporary life and are closely linked to the grand societal challenges humanity faces. This Special Issue, therefore, asks: How are organizational corruption and wrongdoing linked to grand societal challenges? We posit that corruption and wrongdoing are dynamic forces that interact reciprocally with grand societal challenges. In an inside-out dynamic, organizational corruption and wrongdoing hinder, distort, or reverse progress on grand societal challenges. In an outside-in dynamic, grand societal challenges and broader societal transformations reconfigure the incentives, opportunities, pressures, justifications, and visibility conditions through which corruption and wrongdoing emerge. This editorial traces the evolution of corruption research from classic economic and public-sector accounts toward a business-and-society perspective and develops a dynamic framework of the corruption–grand societal challenges nexus. We analyze how the Special Issue articles advance this conversation and conclude with a research and practice agenda for scholars and practitioners.

title: Corporate strategic distinctiveness in the aftermath of natural disasters
abstract: Purpose This study examines how natural disasters affect corporate strategic distinctiveness and investigates the moderating roles of CEO early-life disaster experience and CEO tenure. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on organisational adaptation theory, we construct a multidimensional measure of strategic distinctiveness using quarterly data on Chinese listed firms from 2009 to 2019. We estimate difference-in-differences models, with disaster data web-scraped from the National Disaster Reduction Centre of China. To address endogeneity and robustness concerns, we conduct placebo tests, propensity-score matching, subsample analyses and textual analysis of earnings conference call transcripts. Findings We find that natural disasters reduce corporate strategic distinctiveness, indicating that firms adopt more conforming strategies to secure legitimacy and resources. This effect is stronger for climate-related disasters and is amplified when CEOs have early-life disaster experience or longer tenure. Further analysis shows firms conform more strongly when disasters recur. Originality/value This study highlights how firms adapt to risks posed by natural disasters. By showing the tendency of firms to converge towards industry norms and the role of CEO characteristics in shaping this response, this study enriches the broader discourse on management accounting and corporate governance in the context of major external shocks.

title: State ownership, media sentiment, and the completion of cross-border acquisitions
The AI CEO: A conceptualisation and outline for future research

Interdisciplinary modelling in support of people-centred transitions: Forecasting citizen adoption of rooftop PV systems under alternative sociopolitical future-world evolutions
abstract: Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems are central to decentralised solar transitions in Europe, yet their diffusion depends on more than technical potential, technology costs, or the formal design of support schemes. As Member States move from guaranteed remuneration mechanisms towards more market-reflective compensation, rooftop PV adoption increasingly depends on how citizens perceive policy credibility, profitability, social influence, and uncertainty. This article investigates citizen adoption of rooftop PV systems in the Greek residential sector by 2030 under three alternative sociopolitical storylines representing citizen-driven, government-directed, and market-driven future-world evolutions. We operationalise an interdisciplinary modelling framework that sequentially couples sociopolitical storyline development with agent-based technology adoption modelling. The framework is applied to assess the recently introduced net billing scheme, both as a standalone policy and in combination with battery energy storage system subsidisation, and to benchmark its performance against former feed-in tariff and net metering designs. Results show that the former net metering scheme remains the most effective design by 2030, while net billing ranks second and remains comparatively robust when combined with storage. However, none of the analysed schemes is sufficient, on its own, to achieve the national target of 1 GW of residential rooftop PV capacity by 2030. Adoption outcomes vary across storylines and behavioural profiles, indicating that policy effectiveness is shaped by perceived profitability, policy maturity, social learning, investment resistance, and trust in the stability of the support framework. The study shows how compensation mechanisms translate into adoption trajectories under behavioural and sociopolitical uncertainty, supporting more adaptive and citizen-centred policy designs.

title: How the social capital of influencers drives social media engagement?
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of the influencer-follower relationship on engagement, integrating social capital theory and consistency theories to assess how social capital affects user engagement. Design/methodology/approach This study collected publicly available data on the TikTok platform, including 278 target posts and 5,722 past posts. Based on these data, the authors measured bonding, bridging, contributing, creating and post frequency and examined the relationships among them. Findings Bonding social capital is positively related to contributing and creating engagement, whereas bridging social capital is negatively related to both. Post frequency mitigates the positive effects of bonding and the negative effects of bridging. Research limitations/implications This study discussed the relationship between social capital and user engagement from the influencer’s perspective and revealed the double-edged effect of post frequency, providing valuable insights for influencer marketing strategies. Future research could further consider psychological factors to complement the role of social capital in the context of influencer marketing. Practical implications Influencers can strategically control their posting frequency based on their social network relationships to boost user engagement. Originality/value By measuring social capital using online metrics, this study examines the relationship between social capital and user engagement from an influencer’s perspective. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of social capital in influencer marketing.

title: When Co-Branding breaks down: strategic misalignment, symbolic rupture, and consumer resistance
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how and under what conditions co-branding in collaboration-saturated markets is associated with negative consumer responses. Moving beyond fit- and synergy-based explanations, it theorizes consumer negative agency (CNA) as agentic, tactic-focused resistance toward co-branding episodes. Design/methodology/approach A sequential, multi-method design is used. Study 1 applies grounded, Gioia-based analysis to walking interviews (n = 55), in-depth interviews (n = 12) and netnographic materials (n = 186) from young Chinese consumers in a high-frequency co-branding environment. Study 2 constructs 29 co-branding episode cases and applies fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and necessary condition analysis to identify degree-based bottlenecks and sufficient configurations associated with high CNA. Findings Study 1 reveals four dimensions underpinning resistance: strategic misalignment, identity and cultural disconnect, emotional and cognitive strain and CNA. Study 2 identifies equifinal, largely conjunctural configurations associated with high CNA: resistance is organized around distinct configurations labeled practical value distortion, conflict of meaning interpretation and emotional experience split, with image erosion also exhibiting a standalone sufficient set relationship with high CNA in one pathway. Research limitations/implications The study reconceptualizes co-branding breakdown as a consumer-interpreted collaboration stream in which governance, pacing, symbolic legitimacy and experiential costs shape resistance. It introduces CNA and provides a configurational framework explaining when co-branding shifts from engagement to backlash, offering actionable guidance for collaboration governance, symbolic coherence and experience design. Practical implications Three operational priorities follow from the configuration logic: brand managers could strengthen collaboration governance with explicit partner screening, reputational due diligence and a documented rationale; implement symbolic legitimacy checks by auditing meaning coherence and image erosion risk before launch; and reduce experiential strain by controlling release density, simplifying menu/interface presentation and aligning promotional claims with product experience. Originality/value The study reframes co-branding breakdown as a consumer-interpreted collaboration stream in which governance, pacing, symbolic legitimacy and experiential costs shape resistance. It conceptualizes CNA as a context-specific form of tactic-focused resistance and provides a configurational framework explaining when co-branding shifts from engagement to backlash, offering evidence-informed guidance for collaboration governance, symbolic coherence and experience design.

title: Coordinating the Frontlines: An Interdisciplinary Agenda for Extending Organizational Frontlines Research
abstract: Organizational frontlines research (OFR) has generated significant insights into the interactions between organizations and customers, the service interfaces through which these interactions occur, and how they unfold over time. However, less attention has been directed toward the mechanisms through which organizations coordinate these frontline dimensions. Building on Schneider and Bowen’s three-tier view of service organizations, we extend the OFR literature with a specific focus on the coordination tier, which consists of mechanisms responsible for integrating the boundary tier with the customer tier. Drawing on industry benchmarking survey data from senior service leaders and mapping these findings to established and emerging service research priorities, we identify six coordination-tier domains. These domains relate to the management of customer experience, service innovation, new technology exploration, service operations, culture and climate, and talent. By delineating key coordination challenges and a set of future research directions for each domain, we offer an integrated research agenda to advance interdisciplinary OFR scholarship. Additionally, we highlight the role of managers in coordinating resources and processes to deliver value across multiple touchpoints.

title: Tourist Safety Intelligence: Scale Development, Validation, and Prediction
abstract: Safety intelligence is critical for navigating security challenges but remains unexplored in tourism. This study conceptualizes the structure of tourist safety intelligence, develops a measurement scale, and investigates its behavioral influence mechanisms. Study 1 confirmed a triarchic structure of analytical, practical, and creative intelligence based on Sternberg’s Successful Intelligence Theory and validated a scale with adequate fit for both first-order and second-order models. Study 2 revealed that analytical intelligence positively predicts safety compliance but negatively predicts safety participation, while practical and creative intelligence both positively predict safety participation. Analytical and practical intelligence also indirectly influence both behaviors through sequential mediation of social and personal norms. Practically, these findings enable tourism authorities to design targeted training programs enhancing specific intelligence dimensions, develop tailored safety communication strategies based on tourists’ cognitive profiles, and implement differentiated interventions to promote both safety compliance and participation.

title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
abstract: ABSTRACT The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

title: Independent Agencies, Regulation‐Compliant Citizens? Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Vaccine Authorization in the EU
abstract: ABSTRACT The effectiveness of regulatory policy in many areas is contingent on citizens adhering to the scientific advice of regulatory bodies. This in turn depends on whether they perceive this advice as credible . One of the biggest threats to regulatory credibility is the concern that regulatory policy can be tainted by short‐term political interests. Consequently, regulation literature points to agency independence as a crucial resource to securing regulatory credibility, which in turn fosters citizen compliance. We test this assumption both observationally and experimentally in the case of the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) risk assessment for the first COVID‐19 vaccine—a prime example of reliance on credibility in regulation under conditions of controversy and concerns over political interference. We conducted a pre‐registered survey experiment with 4000 EU citizens from four countries timed shortly after the vaccine's approval and before its mass distribution. The results provide partial support that independence is beneficial to regulatory credibility and by extension, to regulatory compliance. Citizens who perceive the EMA as more independent found its risk assessment to be more credible and were more willing to take the vaccine. However, our experimental evidence is less conclusive. Thus, while independence might not in and of itself be a “silver bullet” to ensure regulatory credibility and compliance, it does play an important role, and its real‐life substantive significance would scale up considerably at population levels.

title: Executive Aggrandizement: Understanding the Silent Erosion of Democratic Constraints
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies of executive aggrandizement face a double measurement problem. Measures of aggrandizement may include institutions that constitute liberal democracy, while broad composites may treat substantively different executive practices as interchangeable. This article develops a measurement‐oriented classification that reduces direct overlap with the V‐Dem Liberal Democracy Index and compares distinct practices under common analytical rules. Using V‐Dem v15 data and a common sample of 17,404 country‐years across 179 countries from 1901 to 2024, country‐ and year‐fixed‐effects models estimate conditional within‐country associations for five lagged practices. Patronal‐distributive allocation, judicial purges, and personalist/mobilizational legitimation are negatively associated with liberal democracy. Executive corruption is consistently imprecise, whereas politicized administrative appointments are negative only in some specifications. Item‐level, restricted‐period, timing, and first‐difference analyses document practice heterogeneity but also show exceptional persistence; negative future‐lead estimates prevent a causal or sequential reading. The primary contribution is a bounded measurement and modeling strategy that preserves comparability while reducing, rather than claiming to eliminate, outcome overlap. Its linked theoretical contribution is a practice‐family account of executive aggrandizement: politically coordinated practices may coexist and remain interdependent without becoming interchangeable indicators or stages in a common causal sequence.

title: Regulatory Learning or Regulatory Privilege? How Sandbox Design Shapes the Governance Value of Experimental Regulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory sandboxes are controlled, time‐limited environments in which selected innovations are tested under regulatory supervision. This article asks how sandbox design can make selective experimentation capable of generating public regulatory value rather than regulatory privilege. It develops regulatory learning asymmetry to distinguish private, supervisory, and public regulatory learning and unequal distributions of access, information, learning, and benefits. A structured reading of public documents from five deliberately diverse FinTech and artificial intelligence cases illustrates a six‐element operational framework. The case material is not used to infer private or supervisory learning; it records only publication, generalization mechanisms, and documented uptake. The framework identifies a public‐learning configuration, a supervisory‐learning configuration that public documents cannot verify, and a regulatory‐privilege risk configuration. Market signaling is treated as a cross‐cutting dynamic. The article offers a bounded diagnostic for assessing whether case‐specific experience becomes contestable and institutionally usable knowledge.

title: Achievements amidst asymmetries: power dynamics in Swedish civil-military collaboration - an exploratory conceptualization
abstract: This article examines how power dynamics are shaped and managed in day-to-day civil-military collaboration in Swedish total defence. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with key civilian and military actors involved in total defence planning, the article investigates the interplay of power asymmetries, the collaboration’s institutional and relational conditions and how collaborating actors perceive and manage asymmetries in practice. Using thematic analysis, we demonstrate that civil-military collaboration is characterized by imbalances in authority, resources and discursive legitimacy. The paper further sheds light on micro-level practices of power enactment and details how collaborating actors negotiate and manage power asymmetries. The main finding suggests that when the relatively more powerful actors engage in power moderating practices, which we conceptualize as Strategic Power Moderation (SPM), collaborations can perform productively despite asymmetrical relations. The results offer a nuanced understanding of how collaborations fare under conditions of power asymmetry and have implications for both research and practice.

title: A Practical Guide to Conditional Mediation Analysis with GSCA: Method, Simulation, and Software
abstract: Conditional mediation (CoMe) analysis integrates mediation and moderation to examine how an indirect effect transmitted through a mediator varies across levels of a moderator. In this tutorial, we show how to conduct CoMe analysis in generalized structured component analysis (GSCA), a component-based structural equation modeling approach. We first outline the technical foundations of GSCA-based CoMe analysis and then report a simulation study evaluating its performance relative to partial least squares path modeling, another component-based approach. We also present an empirical illustration that provides step-by-step guidance for implementing GSCA-based CoMe analysis using GSCA Pro, a free, user-friendly software package.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: From mobilization to diversion: a comparative study of wartime communication tactics of Ukrainian and Russian political elites on Telegram
abstract: This study examines how Ukrainian and Russian political elites communicate on Telegram during the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. Using a dataset of Telegram public posts from 2019 to 2024, we analyze changes in communication volume, thematic content, and actor engagement before and after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. While the invasion triggered a massive spike in elites’ activity on Telegram in both countries—most notably among actors associated with Russia’s ruling pro-regime party—the focus of this communication diverged sharply. While Ukrainian elites initially prioritized war-related mobilization, this emphasis has declined over time. By contrast, Russian elites from the start adopted a tactic of strategic diversion, avoiding discussion of the war and shifting public attention to unrelated issues, such as crises in the West. Finally, we show that communication patterns are stratified by party size, with smaller parties specializing in narrow policy niches. These findings shed light on how political elites adapt their communication strategies in online environments during wartime.

title: Data benefits? Attitudes and aspirations of recipients towards social security administrative data sharing
abstract: This paper outlines benefit recipients’ views towards the sharing of data that is collected about them when they routinely interact with social security services. Sharing this administrative data between public bodies promises to transform the delivery and evaluation of social security. However, there remains a lack of research into public attitudes, understandings, and aspirations for the sharing of this data, particularly from those whose data would be shared. Drawing on discussions from deliberative focus groups with 41 individuals, we reflect on the scope for increased data sharing to deliver improvements for recipients.While participants were aware of how their data is currently shared and how increased data sharing might have advantages, they expressed strong distrust in government agencies to manage their data and concerns about being placed in a position of increased vulnerability. We argue individuals’ views towards data sharing cannot be separated from their lived experiences of data systems – their data realities – which are often markedly different from system designers. We conclude by offering considerations against data systems re-introducing paternalistic policy, unintentionally, via automation – which we term ‘automated paternalism’.

title: Framework for integration of regional transportation model (RTM) with collision prediction model (CPM)
abstract: Traditional road safety planning is largely reactive, while existing Collision Prediction Models (CPMs) often function as disconnected post-processing tools. However, a growing body of research has highlighted the need for proactive safety assessment at the transportation planning stage. Building on this research, the present study demonstrates a large-scale, automated framework that integrates CPMs with a calibrated, tour-based Regional Transportation Model (RTM), enabling travel demand and network-wide collision outcomes to be evaluated within a unified modelling workflow. Using the Calgary metropolitan region as a case study, Negative Binomial models were developed to estimate Fatal/Injury (FI) and Property-Damage-Only (PDO) collisions at mid-block segments and intersections. To ensure seamless operational integration, all explanatory variables used by the CPMs were derived exclusively from the RTM’s multimodal outputs, thereby eliminating the need for additional external data collection . Validation against independent historical data from 2017 to 2019 demonstrated robust predictive accuracy at both the aggregate network level and the individual facility level. The framework was then applied to a 2028 planning horizon to evaluate twelve demand-side policy scenarios involving changes in fuel prices, parking costs, and transit fares. The results revealed a consistent, monotonic dose–response relationship across all interventions. Increases in fuel prices produced the largest network-wide reductions in collision, while lower transit fare and higher parking costs generated more targeted safety benefits. Intersections were particularly sensitive, especially with respect to FI collisions under the transit fare scenarios. By generating severity-stratified safety estimates alongside conventional demand outputs, without requiring additional data inputs or manual post-processing, the framework enables planners to evaluate mobility and safety trade-offs for proactive, data-informed long-range transportation planning.

title: Why does the medical staff remain silent? Preventing child abuse begins with reporting: A cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Despite mandatory reporting laws, discrepancies between the estimated prevalence of child maltreatment and official reports may reflect both under-identification and failure to report recognized concerns. Healthcare professionals face emotional, cognitive, and institutional barriers that may influence reporting willingness. Methods This cross-sectional study examined sociodemographic, professional, cognitive, emotional, perceptual, and institutional factors associated with healthcare professionals' self-reported willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. The sample included 272 healthcare professionals caring for children (44% physicians, 43% nurses). Data were collected using a validated anonymous questionnaire. Results Years of experience were positively associated with identification ability ( r = 0.24, p < .001). Women reported higher willingness to report than men (M = 20.97 vs. 18.77, p < .001). Hospital-based staff demonstrated higher self-reported willingness to report than community-based staff (M = 20.74 vs. 18.95, p < .001), and managerial staff demonstrated higher self-reported willingness to report than non-managerial staff (M = 20.96 vs. 20.18, p = .03). Anger toward the child's family was the most common emotional response (44%). More positive perceptions and attitudes, together with greater emotional readiness, were associated with greater self-reported willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. Conclusions Female healthcare professionals, professionals with greater clinical experience, hospital-based healthcare professionals, and those in managerial roles reported greater willingness to report suspected child maltreatment. Targeted training incorporating clinical exposure, emotional processing, and ethical decision-making is recommended, particularly for community-based and male professionals. Stronger leadership and organizational support may enhance reporting willingness.

title: From silence to sharing: A six-month prospective study on adult disclosure of childhood sexual abuse
abstract: Background Disclosure of childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is often assumed to be beneficial. However, prospective research examining outcomes associated with disclosure remains scarce, limiting evidence-based guidance for adults considering disclosure. Objective The primary aim was to examine changes in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms following first-time disclosure of CSA to personal contacts and to test whether perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses moderated these changes. The secondary aim was to explore characteristics of CSA disclosure. Methods Forty adults with a history of CSA who had not previously disclosed the abuse to personal contacts completed two assessments, at baseline and at follow-up six months later. Participants who disclosed their CSA to a personal contact during the follow-up period were classified as disclosers, whereas those who did not were classified as non-disclosers. Results During the follow-up period, 60% ( n = 24) disclosed for the first time to personal contacts, after on average 31.5 years ( SD = 16.2), most often to friends (47%). Disclosers showed a clinically relevant, greater reduction in PTSD symptoms than non-disclosers. Perceived supportiveness of confidants' responses was moderate to high but did not significantly moderate changes in PTSD symptoms. Conclusions First-time disclosure of CSA in adulthood to personal contacts was associated with a clinically relevant reduction in PTSD symptoms. Nevertheless, individual differences in symptom change indicate that outcomes following disclosure vary. Guidance should therefore move beyond the question of whether to disclose and consider when, under what circumstances, and for whom disclosure may be beneficial.

title: Screening for suspected child physical abuse in a Colombian pediatric emergency department: Clinical characteristics and performance of SPUTOVAMO-R
abstract: Background Physical abuse causes morbidity and mortality in young children, yet Latin American emergency data are scarce. Objective To describe characteristics associated with a multidisciplinary child-protection panel's classification and estimate SPUTOVAMO-R sensitivity relative to ICD-10 coding and panel classification. Participants and Setting Children aged 1 month–18 years with emergency department records at a pediatric referral hospital in Bogotá, Colombia (2015–2017), coded with physical-abuse ICD-10 diagnoses. Methods Retrospective cross-sectional study. High- and low-probability classifications were compared using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 coded children, 59 (18.3%) were classified as high probability. An internally inconsistent account (OR 34.7, 95% CI 12.0–124.0), history inconsistent with injury (OR 18.0, 8.3–40.7), and disclosure by the child (OR 56.1, 12.7–516.7) were strongly associated with high-probability classification. Absence of an adult witness was not associated among children aged 0–4 years and was associated with low-probability classification in older children (OR 0.08, 0.00–0.58). All four high-probability children with high-specificity fractures, and none of three low-probability children, had a history inconsistent with injury. SPUTOVAMO-R sensitivity was 34.2% (110/322; 95% CI 29.0–39.6) relative to ICD-10 coding and 91.5% (54/59; 81.3–97.2) relative to the panel. Conclusions ICD-10 abuse coding corresponded poorly with panel classification. Panel classification was most strongly associated with history coherence. SPUTOVAMO-R was negative in two-thirds of coded children and should be evaluated in unselected populations.
authors: Diana Carolina De la Hoz-Díaz Granados

title: Towards a nutrition-enhancing and water-conserving diet: insights from China
Evidence and knowledge gaps on pumpkin in sub-Saharan African food systems: a scoping review
abstract: Abstract Pumpkin holds significant potential to improve food security, nutrition, and economic development in sub-Saharan Africa, yet is one of many neglected and underutilized crop species which has received limited attention from researchers and policymakers. This scoping review synthesizes findings from 44 peer-reviewed and grey literature sources across multiple disciplines to appraise the state of research on pumpkin within sub-Saharan African food systems. It explores value chain dynamics, dimensions of the food environment, consumer behaviour, and policy factors, alongside outcomes for nutrition, health, economic development, environmental sustainability, and social equity. The evidence base is geographically concentrated – with 41 studies (93%) having a single-country focus and the majority conducted in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa—and shows limited methodological diversity, with 33 (75%) employing cross-sectional observational designs. Fifteen documents examined value chain activities, 18 focused on consumer behaviour, and 37 provided insights into external and personal dimensions of the food environment – although none explicitly applied a food environment framework. Most studies centred on consumers and the use of pumpkin leaves and fruit. Production was the most frequently analysed value chain component, with other areas significantly underexplored. Insights on vendors, processors, and policymakers were largely absent, as were urban and peri-urban contexts. Of food environment dimensions, findings on availability, product properties, and desirability were most common. Evidence on outcomes of pumpkin production, value chain participation, and consumption remains limited: with a primary focus on social equity and food and nutrition security. Our review identifies the need for an interdisciplinary, systems-oriented approach in future research, covering the entire value chain and incorporating gender, market, and policy dimensions. Collated evidence supports the need for targeted interventions to improve processing, enhance food safety, shift cultural perceptions, and strengthen governance mechanisms, for pumpkin to contribute more substantially to resilient, equitable African food systems.

title: Who Is Afraid of ChatGPT? A Natural Experiment on the Effect of ChatGPT Release on Labour-Market Concerns
abstract: The public release of ChatGPT on November 30th, 2022 revived the public debate on technological change and, particularly, on its impact on the labour market. Despite the sudden growth in AI salience after the launch of the new chatbot, to our knowledge, no empirical investigation has assessed the impact of this technological breakthrough on citizens’ first concerns. By means of a unique survey fielded between November and December 2022 in five European countries, we use an Unexpected Event During Survey (UEDS) design to causally test the effect of ChatGPT’s launch on individual perception of unemployment risk. We rely on statistical matching techniques, combined with regression analyses to explore heterogeneity in responses between socioeconomic groups. We show that the release of the new chatbot mildly but significantly increased unemployment concerns in advanced industrial democracies, particularly among individuals with low and middling levels of income and education, as well as poorly exposed to AI. By capturing reactions before informational framings consolidate and widespread adoption occurs, this study provides a rare window into citizens’ genuine response to technological change, indicating that its socioeconomic consequences are perceived as immediately salient.

title: Managed Multiplicity: The Political Versatility of Assisted Reproductive Technologies in Singapore’s National Imaginary
abstract: This article presents a discourse analysis of reproductive policy in Singapore, a small Southeast Asian country with ultra-low fertility rates. Focusing on assisted reproduction between the 1980s and 2024, it shows how egg freezing and in vitro fertilization emerged as “politically versatile technologies” that are simultaneously associated with women’s reproductive choice and patriarchal pronatalism. It theorizes that such versatility arises through shifting and stratified policy provisions, the interplay of different policy domains, and discursive processes conditioned by the political regime. Enmeshed with foreign policy goals, social policies and regulatory approaches to assisted reproduction are justified via an increasingly global interpretation of competing gender ideologies. Furthermore, media policy supports the naturalization of heteronormative and patriarchal “family values,” as state-regulated media deploy emotional frames while spotlighting the connections between assisted reproductive technologies, egalitarianism, and pronatalist social policies that selectively benefit heterosexual or married women. By demonstrating how the ideological versatility of assisted reproductive technologies is discursively maintained by state-regulated media and government actors amid policy change, this article advances the concept of “managed multiplicity” to characterize the patriarchal state’s organization of gendered meanings across policy tools, domains, actors, and broader projects concerning national and international legitimacy.

title: Who speaks up? Voice and community belonging in Australian local government
abstract: Much has been written about the value of responding to community voice, yet we know far less about who expresses that voice. Using a nationally representative dataset of 65,336 observations, we analyse the association between direct local political voice and individual characteristics, distinguishing occasional from frequent engagement. Occasional voice is relatively common, but sustained participation is rare. Consistent with theory, educational attainment and community belonging are positively associated with speaking up. Unemployment is also positively associated with voice, while gender differences emerge across the models. We further observe a marked reduction in voice in 2022, a period marked by COVID-19. Overall, around one-third of citizens voice opinions, but participation is concentrated among specific groups. These patterns matter because many promised benefits of participation depend not merely on whether citizens speak, but on who speaks. We conclude by outlining implications for practitioners seeking broader and more equitable engagement.

title: Screening-based siting and metocean-aware O&M routing for floating offshore wind farms
Unlocking the green power of the North Sea: Identifying key energy infrastructure synergies for 2030 and 2040
abstract: The North Sea will play a key role in providing clean and secure energy for Europe. This not only requires the development of new offshore wind farms, but also their successful integration into the onshore system. In this work we analyze and compare three key integration options and their preferred siting (onshore vs. offshore): grid expansions, electricity storage, and the production, storage and transport of low-carbon hydrogen. We focus on their potential to reduce emissions and energy system costs – individually and in combination with each other. Additionally, we study the consequences of constraints on their implementation. We analyze the years 2030 and 2040, starting from the projections of installed energy infrastructure and demand from the Ten Year Network Development Plan (TYNDP) 2022 of the European Network of Transmission System Operators (ENTSO-E). Results show that cross-border electricity grid expansions across the North Sea are a no-regret measure, resulting in significant reductions in system costs and emissions compared to national grid expansions. By comparison, the production, storage and transport of hydrogen have a lower cost and emission reduction potential. In both the short and long term (2030 and 2040), electricity storage can help to reduce emissions, but it is not cost competitive unless emission reduction targets are enforced. Combining the three integration measures at optimal capacities provides additional benefits. Overall, the highest emission reductions can be achieved by combining electricity storage with an expansion of the grid, while the highest economic benefits can be achieved with a combination of grid expansions and hydrogen production for direct use in industry.

Institutional risk, finance, and the limits of techno-economic optimality in green hydrogen deployment
abstract: Green hydrogen is widely positioned as a key option for deep decarbonization, yet large-scale deployment remains limited despite growing techno-economic potential. This review examines how non-technical conditions influence the feasibility of green hydrogen business models, using the Netherlands as an illustrative case. A review-driven mixed-methods framework integrates evidence from a systematic literature review, semi-structured expert interviews, and an established hourly-resolved techno-economic optimization model to examine how policy design, investment risk, infrastructure constraints, and demand formation influence both the levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) and deployment feasibility. A multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is employed to synthesize qualitative and quantitative evidence and prioritize the principal drivers and barriers identified across the different sources. The synthesized evidence, supported by the illustrative techno-economic analysis, indicates that LCOH values below €6 kg −1 are attainable under favorable assumptions, including low renewable electricity prices, reduced weighted average cost of capital (WACC), and access to underground hydrogen storage. However, regulatory fragmentation, grid congestion, weak demand coordination, and limited institutional legitimacy substantially constrain the realization of such conditions in practice. The findings demonstrate that techno-economic assessments alone may overestimate the deployability of green hydrogen when institutional risk and market coordination challenges are not explicitly considered. The proposed integrative framework provides a structured approach for assessing hydrogen market readiness in early-stage European contexts and supports the alignment of techno-economic competitiveness with governance capacity, investment conditions, and social acceptance.

title: Pathways for fulfilling global extended producer responsibility: a data-driven optimization for sustainable and circular electric vehicle battery supply chains
abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates, managing end-of-life (EOL) batteries is critical for EPR implementation. This study optimizes recovery networks for China's exported EV batteries across 172 destinations. We develop a bi-objective MILP framework with Weibull-based forecasting, processing capacities from 156 Chinese recyclers and CAPEX of 24 automakers (2025–2060). Evaluating Ship Back, Local Plant, and Formal Outsource, results show cumulative EOL demand of 57.96 Mt over 2025–2060 and demand of 4.78 Mt in 2060. Domestic capacity constraints force profit-driven systems toward localized overseas recycling. Relative to PROFIT_MAX, CARBON_MIN advances local investment by ten years, raises local processing by 11.2 percentage points, and improves net GHG mitigation by 16.3%, but reduces NPV by 54.4%. PARETO_KNEE captures 66.7% of additional mitigation with a 13.2% NPV loss. CARBON_MIN yields the highest Li, Co, and Ni recovery, revealing synergy between environmental optimisation and resource circularity.
