Soil Protists Consume Viruses to Drive Microbial Nutrient Cycling: Overlooked Trophic Pathways in Soil Food Web
abstract: Abstract Soil viruses are traditional top-down regulators that redistribute organic matter through host lysis and the viral shunt, implicitly positioning them as terminal sinks rather than active trophic components. Here, we show, for the first time, that soil viruses can also be direct prey for protists, establishing an overlooked pathway for the transfer of viral-derived nutrients and energy within soil food webs. In controlled cocultures, the ciliate Tetrahymena pyriformis actively ingested the soil bacteriophage HRZ04p, with viral abundance declining by 0.66-log within 24 h at a virus-to-protist ratio of 5:1. Under high viral availability (104:1), viral consumption enhanced protist population growth by 2.24-fold relative to virus-free controls. Viral grazing altered nutrient dynamics, characterized by ammonium peaking at 1,206 μg L–1 (a 92% increase compared with protists alone) and coordinated shifts in nitrogen-metabolizing enzymes. Untargeted metabolomics revealed extensive metabolic reprogramming, with amino acid catabolic pathways upregulated. In contrast, amino acid biosynthesis and aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis were simultaneously activated, reflecting recycling of viral-derived substrates into new protein synthesis. These findings confirm the existence of a soil “viral consumption” pathway, reposition viruses as active nodes within microbial food webs, and provide a mechanistic and conceptual foundation for incorporating virus-mediated nutrient fluxes into soil biogeochemical models.

Public stockpiling, offtake, and the value of domestic rare earth midstream capacity: A calibrated policy valuation for South Korea
abstract: For import-dependent manufacturing economies, the policy value of domestic rare earth midstream readiness depends on whether it can provide useable supply that reduces shortages remaining after external supply and public stockpiles have been used. This study evaluates that condition for South Korea by comparing a BASELINE of external supply and a common public stockpile with an ENHANCED state that adds a pre-established joint neodymium–praseodymium (NdPr)–Dy 2 O 3 separation/refining pathway, domestic operating inventory, and public offtake. A 20-year monthly material-flow and inventory model is evaluated under a deterministic disruption and 10,000 stress-test paths, using 0.5 t/year of joint oxide output as a functional scale anchor. Under the deterministic full-usability benchmark, ENHANCED reduces the 2466.18 t BASELINE residual priority-demand shortage by 1.375 t (0.056%), with USD 9.584 million in incremental real-resource cost and a required USD 8974.7/kg break-even value, not an estimated economic benefit. Public offtake improves facility finance, but facility net present value remains negative under all three contracts, including OT-3 at −USD 1.478 million, while government fiscal burden reaches USD 8.913 million. At the same break-even unit value, economic net value is non-negative in 81.58% of full-usability paths, 59.27% of partial-usability paths, and 0% under pathway failure. These are conditional stress-test outcomes, not probabilities of policy success. Taken together, these diagnostics identify a bounded role for public offtake in improving the financial conditions for maintaining readiness, while downstream usability remains necessary for shortage reduction; they do not establish facility viability or economic justification.

Spatial trajectories and land-use potential of China's utility-scale photovoltaic expansion toward 2035
abstract: China aims to reach 3600 GW of combined wind and solar capacity by 2035, requiring substantial expansion of utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) deployment. Quantifying the geospatial footprint of this expansion is essential for sustainable land-use planning and ecological protection. This study develops a nationwide assessment framework that integrates multi-source remote sensing observations, Random Forest (RF) suitability modeling, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for model interpretation, and scenario-based spatial allocation. Historical PV data from 2000 to 2025 show that China's utility-scale PV farms expanded to 13,800 km 2 , with growth concentrated in northwestern mega-bases and emerging decentralized installations in central-eastern regions, indicating a dual-track spatial trajectory. Scenario projections suggest that Scenario B (NDC Update-Aligned Pathway) requires an additional 21,420 km 2 , whereas Scenario C (Wind-Slowdown Compensation) increases land demand moderately to 24,405 km 2 . Scenario A (Business as Usual) could require up to 63,990 km 2 and would disproportionately affect croplands and forests. However, China retains more than 206,000 km 2 of high-potential land, indicating that ecological conflicts are driven mainly by spatial mismatch rather than absolute land scarcity. These findings underscore the need for integrated spatial governance, optimized ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission, and distributed PV deployment. By linking observed spatial trajectories, interpretable suitability modeling, and capacity-to-land translation, this study provides a transferable framework for assessing the land-use potential of utility-scale PV expansion toward 2035.

Mechanisms of circularity: How epistemic, financial and material flows construct new waste geographies
abstract: Circular Economy (CE) initiatives originate predominantly in the Global North, yet their material, epistemic, and financial effects increasingly manifest in Global South contexts. Using Dutch–Kenya waste relations as a critical case study, this article examines how CE interventions transform waste materials into a marketized commodity through three interconnected variables: an epistemic variable, reframing waste and circularity through market-oriented knowledge systems; a financial, channelling investment towards formalized circular infrastructure that excludes informal and community-based actors; and a material variable, establishing new waste geographies that concentrate processing activity in the Global South. Kenya's dual position as a destination for Dutch waste exports and a recipient of Dutch CE development funding, makes it a relevant site for observing how these variables operate and interact. Drawing on interviews with Dutch and Kenyan government, donor, and civil society actors, the article argues that CE interventions restructure the governance of existing waste markets not through Dutch influence alone, but through negotiated convergence between Dutch donor priorities and the Kenyan state's own regulatory capacity constraints and economic interests. This restructuring concentrates control over the terms of participation among formal, internationally connected, and resourced actors, while progressively marginalizing informal workers who have long managed waste through community-based practices. Through an environmental justice lens drawing on Schlosberg's (2007) tripartite framework of distribution, recognition, and participation, the article demonstrates that the critical question is not only who governs the new waste geographies and on whose terms material recovery proceeds, but how donor and recipient-state interests jointly produce the exclusion of informal actors from that governance. The article contributes an integrated analytical framework for studying the shift from conventional waste trade to circular trade in North–South relations, and positions this contribution within political ecology and critical CE scholarship.

title: Selective nostalgia: development through ‘shared heritage’ diplomacy in post-colonial Sri Lanka
abstract: Developing nations are increasingly inscribing urban heritage sites to UNESCO’s World Heritage List for global recognition, political legitimization, and economic development. Sri Lanka’s ‘Old Town of Galle’ is a colonial-era site inscribed to the List as an outstanding example of a fortified city built by Europeans in Asia. Although Galle Fort’s colonial-era heritage is attributed to three European traditions – Portuguese, Dutch, and British – its Dutch ancestry is prioritized by experts, the State and its residents. This “selective nostalgia” in the parsing of layered colonial pasts through heritage conservation reveals how heritage operates as a medium for pursuing diplomatic relations and developmental agendas. Using evidence from interviews, observational data, and documents, I show that through its production as World Heritage, colonial-era heritage is reinterpreted as a shared heritage to serve diverging diplomatic and developmental agendas. For the Dutch, the construction of a shared heritage narrative neutralizes this past by boosting colonial accomplishments while underemphasizing colonial exploitations. For Sri Lanka, Dutch-aided conservation of Galle Fort provides a marketable commodity that is a magnet for global tourism. However, the cultivation of ‘shared heritage’ is also restructuring the Fort’s socio-spatial fabric with rampant gentrification and touristification marginalizing the local community of this living heritage site.

title: An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
From Green Culture to Sustainability Performance: Unpacking a Sequential Capability Pathway Through Environmental Leadership and Circular Economy Practices
abstract: ABSTRACT Although green organizational culture has been associated with sustainability outcomes, less is understood about the mechanisms through which sustainability‐oriented cultural values are translated into organizational action and performance. Drawing on the Natural Resource–Based View (NRBV) theory, this study examines how environmental leadership and circular economy practices independently and sequentially transmit the effects of green organizational culture to sustainability performance. Using a quantitative explanatory design, survey data were collected from 1209 employees across Ghana's oil and gas, power generation, transmission and distribution, and regulatory segments and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM), supplemented by cluster‐robust sensitivity analyses. The findings show that green organizational culture positively influences sustainability performance and environmental leadership. Environmental leadership, in turn, enhances circular economy practices and sustainability performance, while circular economy practices positively influence sustainability performance. However, circular economy practices do not independently mediate the green organizational culture–sustainability performance nexus. Instead, significant indirect effects operate through environmental leadership and sequentially through environmental leadership and circular economy practices, while the direct effect remains significant. These findings extend the NRBV by revealing how sustainability‐oriented culture translates into performance through interconnected leadership and operational capabilities rather than through cultural orientation alone. The study provides large‐sample evidence from an under‐researched emerging‐economy energy context and demonstrates the practical importance of aligning green organizational culture, environmental leadership, and circular economy implementation to enhance sustainability performance.

title: Sustainable Building Operation and Maintenance as a Strategic Environmental Capability in Net‐Zero Office‐Type Buildings: A Web of Science–Based Bibliometric–Systematic Review (2009–2025)
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable building operation and maintenance (O&M) is increasingly supported by digital technologies; however, research remains fragmented across technical, organisational and behavioural domains, limiting understanding of how performance gains are sustained in net zero energy (NZE) office‐type buildings. This study maps, critically synthesises and theorises this interdisciplinary evidence base. An integrated bibliometric–systematic literature review combined descriptive bibliometric analysis and science mapping of 137 Web of Science records with a systematic qualitative synthesis of 30 purposively selected studies, supported by search‐sensitivity and cross‐database robustness checks. The analysis identified 17 bibliographic clusters that were consolidated into eight research streams and four higher‐order socio‐technical themes. The findings indicate that sustained performance depends on the recursive integration of technological sensing, organisational interpretation and governance, behavioural–operational enactment, verification and learning. Building on these insights, the study develops the dynamic socio‐technical capability (DSTC) framework, offering an integrative and empirically testable explanation of sustainable building O&M as a strategic environmental capability, defined here at the building operational level.

title: Trust in algorithms biased appraisal and boosted affect in online dating

How experiential knowledge becomes evidence in lawmaking through consultations with incarcerated people
abstract: Experiential knowledge, grounded in lived experience, is increasingly recognized as an important source of evidence in policy making and legislative drafting. Yet questions remain about how knowledge derived from consultations with affected individuals can legitimately inform broader lawmaking. This article examines how experiential knowledge from targeted consultations with incarcerated individuals is transformed into context-specific legislative knowledge through the interplay of propositional system knowledge, procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system, and implicit analogical reasoning. Drawing on consultation memoranda and a draft Bill produced during the reform of the Finnish Imprisonment Act, we analyse consultations concerning incarcerated individuals’ use of communication technologies to manage essential practical matters beyond prison under conditions of administrative burden. We first construct a narrative from the consultees’ propositional and procedural experiential knowledge and then examine how this knowledge was incorporated into legislative arguments alongside official expert knowledge. Our analysis shows that the draft Bill employed implicit analogical reasoning to transform procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system into propositional claims applicable to broader prison populations sharing similar contexts, institutional routines, and practical needs. By demonstrating how analogical reasoning links propositional and procedural knowledge to generate context-specific generalizations, the article offers a novel conceptual framework for understanding how experiential knowledge can become legitimate evidence in lawmaking. We suggest that this approach is applicable to other institutional settings characterized by standardized living conditions, shared procedures, and common systems of navigation.

Desert dust storm, ambient temperature, and pulmonary function among children with asthma in the Eastern Mediterranean
abstract: Background Climate change has contributed to increased dust events and rising ambient temperature, posing potential health risk for susceptible populations including children with asthma. The study aims to examine associations between exposure to desert dust storm (DDS) and higher ambient temperature with pulmonary function indicators, including forced expiratory volume in 1s (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC) and FEV 1 /FVC% among asthmatic children during the dust season in the Eastern Mediterranean. Methods We conducted exploratory secondary analyses of repeated pulmonary function measurements from schoolchildren with asthma in Cyprus and Crete, Greece during spring of 2019 and 2021. Dust exposure was defined using short-term (at least one DDS day on the assessment day or during the preceding 7 days) and cumulative days (over the spring season) metrics based on site-specific DDS classifications as well as ambient temperature assessed from the nearest meteorological station. Associations were examined using linear mixed-effect models. Results Among the 135 children included, short-term DDS exposure was associated with a non-significant decrement in FEV 1 (-20.46 mL, 95% CI: -50.38, 9.46) and FVC (-27.21 mL, 95% CI: -59.45, 5.02). Cumulative dust exposure was associated with -3.52 mL (95% CI: -5.90, -1.14) difference in FEV 1 per DDS day. Ambient temperature averaged over 0-7 days before assessment was inversely associated with FEV 1 (-19.77 mL; 95% CI: -37.91, -1.63 per 5°C increase) and FEV 1 /FVC% (-0.81; 95% CI: -1.36, -0.25 per 5 °C increase), with no statistical evidence of effect modification by short-term DDS exposure. Conclusions This exploratory secondary analysis demonstrated inverse associations of cumulative DDS exposure and ambient temperature with pulmonary function among children with asthma, while short-term DDS associations were not statistically significant. These findings may inform the management of children with asthma during desert dust seasons, but confirmation in larger studies is required.

title: Hydroxyapatite mineralization-driven granulation enables rapid start-up and stable operation of the one-stage partial nitritation/anammox process
abstract: Severe biomass washout remains a major bottleneck limiting the rapid startup and long-term stability of one-stage partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) processes. In this study, a novel hydroxyapatite-based partial nitritation/anammox (HAP-PN/A) strategy was developed to enhance biomass retention and improve operational stability through HAP mineralization-driven granulation. An HAP-PN/A reactor was established using anammox sludge and partial nitrification sludge as inocula, and the effects of different Ca/P ratios on reactor startup, nitrogen removal performance, sludge characteristics, and microbial community succession were systematically investigated. The results demonstrated that Ca/P regulation promoted HAP precipitation and facilitated granular sludge reconstruction, enabling successful startup within 40 days at a Ca/P ratio of 3. The HAP-PN/A system achieved a maximum nitrogen removal efficiency of 85.24% at a nitrogen loading rate of 1.25 g N/(L·d), while simultaneously achieving an average phosphorus removal efficiency of 59.52%. The developed HAP-based granules exhibited excellent settleability, with an average particle size of 346 μm and a sludge volume index of 15.11 mL/g. Microbial analysis revealed that Ca. Brocadia became the dominant anammox genus after reactor acclimation, accounting for 9.6-13.9% of the microbial community, indicating successful enrichment of functional AnAOB within the HAP matrix. Overall, this study demonstrates that HAP mineralization-driven granulation provides an effective approach for accelerating PN/A startup, enhancing microbial retention, and achieving simultaneous nitrogen removal and phosphorus recovery from ammonia-rich wastewater.

title: Sustainable upcycling of ferrous sulfate waste into functional Fe7S8 via COS-mediated controlled sulfidation
Differences between PM2.5 chemical sources at semi-closed transport environments: comparing bus depots and metro platforms
abstract: Chemical composition and source contributions of PM 2.5 were investigated at a public-restricted bus depot in Valladolid (Spain) and two metro stations (Alto dos Moinhos and Quinta das Conchas) in Lisbon (Portugal) using positive matrix factorization (PMF). Locally derived sources dominated PM 2.5 in both environments, with OC-rich combustion emissions prevailing at the bus depot and Fe-rich wear processes at the metro stations as major components. Trace element signatures (ng m -3 ) differed accordingly, with Zn dominating at the bus depot, reflecting tire wear and maintenance, and Mn prevailing at the metro stations, indicative of metro wear (e.g. rail–wheel–brake wear). Seven sources were resolved at the bus depot, led by mineral/construction (27.6%), followed by secondary sulfate (15.8%), tire wear (14.8%), exhaust (11.5%), washing/resuspension (11.4%), maintenance (9.9%), and brake wear (8.9%). However, both metro stations were dominated by metro wear emissions (∼45–46%), with additional contributions from sea spray (∼16–17.5%), secondary sulfate (8.4–16.5%), and mineral/construction (11.5–20.6%). Traffic-related infiltration was identified only at Alto dos Moinhos (8.1%), whereas biomass burning was resolved at Quinta das Conchas (9.7%). The different source profiles indicate the need for specific exposure-control strategies targeting indoor emissions, particularly combustion- and activity-related sources at the bus depot and mechanically generated metal-rich wear particles at the metro stations. Source-specific responses to air purifier operation suggest that filtration can complement source-control measures, although its effectiveness may depend on particle characteristics, spatiotemporal distribution, and continuous source generation. These findings support targeted air quality management in semi-closed transport environments.

Intensifying compound drought–heatwave events weaken ecosystem water-use efficiency in the Nile River Basin
abstract: Climate warming has intensified compound drought–heatwave (CDHW) events worldwide, posing growing threats to ecosystem carbon–water dynamics. However, the impacts of CDHWs on ecosystem water-use efficiency (WUE), particularly event sequencing, drought memory, and climatic heterogeneity, remain poorly understood at large river-basin scales. This study investigated the spatiotemporal evolution of CDHW events and their impacts on ecosystem functioning across the Nile River Basin (NRB) during 2000–2025 using SPEI, heatwave detection, harmonized MODIS-derived GPP and ET, phase-space trajectory analysis, and machine-learning approaches. CDHW frequency, duration, severity, and spatial extent generally increased across the basin, with heatwave-leading events showing a 29.5% increase in spatial extent compared with 12.9% for drought-leading events. A chronological Pettitt test identified 2014 as a significant change point in CDHW frequency. Although basin-wide GPP and ET increased, WUE declined across 58.6% of valid WUE grid cells, indicating substantial spatial heterogeneity in ecosystem carbon–water coupling. CDHWs were generally associated with stronger reductions in GPP and ET than individual drought or heatwave conditions, while WUE commonly increased at the event scale because ET declined proportionally more than GPP. WUE responses varied across SPEI accumulation timescales, with longer antecedent timescales prevalent across much of the basin. Precipitation contributed most in arid and semi-arid regions, whereas temperature, radiation, and VPD contributed relatively more in wetter environments. These findings provide a comprehensive basin-scale assessment of ecosystem WUE responses to CDHWs in the NRB, highlighting spatial heterogeneity, event-scale impacts, and antecedent hydroclimatic associations, and inform ecosystem management under a changing climate.

abstract: Synthetic phenolic antioxidants (SPAs) are emerging contaminants of concern in coastal environments, yet their multimedia distribution and integrated risks remain insufficiently characterized. We investigated 10 SPAs in seawater, suspended particulate matter (SPM), sediment, and Ruditapes philippinarum at 10 sites in three bays during May and August 2025. Total operationally dissolved concentrations ranged from 948 to 9851 ng/L in May to 19,585-42311 ng/L in August, and the across-site arithmetic mean was 6.35-fold higher in August. Sediment and clam concentrations across both campaigns ranged from 26,190 to 126425 and 28,666-117083 ng/g dry weight, respectively. Structural equation modeling indicated season-dependent associations between SPA concentrations and hydrochemical and nutrient variables. Positive matrix factorization resolved four factors tentatively associated with plastics, rubber, personal care products, and petroleum/lubricants. Biomarker associations in field-collected clams indicated co-occurring physiological stress but did not establish SPA-specific causation. In the provisional weight-of-evidence screen, BHT was classified as major in both campaigns, whereas AO1010 was classified as major in May and severe in August based on the sediment partitioning parameters, dietary exposure assumptions, and toxicological screening benchmarks. The integrated assessment supports targeted monitoring of BHT and AO1010 and investigation of their probable product-related inputs, with quantitative risk prioritization conditional on these methodological uncertainties.

Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

title: Too little too late? Nationwide carbon trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021. Covering the world’s top CO₂ emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap. We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter. Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO₂ emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants. Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise). Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China’s high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant. This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of high-efficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants. Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of high efficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China. To curb the level of China’s carbon emissions and thereby slow climate change, benchmarks need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system adopted that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production.

The unseen pain of the Vietnam War: long-term effects of Agent Orange on labor market outcomes
abstract: Abstract We examine the long-term labor market consequences of exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War, focusing on cohorts whose childhoods overlapped the spraying period. Exploiting district-level variation in herbicide exposure intensity, we find exposed individuals attain lower levels of schooling and reduce their labor supply by 7% relative to the mean. Among individuals who remain in their birth provinces, labor income is reduced by 26.7%. We show that cognitive and physical health impairments do not fully explain the effects. Exposure also reduced household income and pushed individuals toward primary industries, away from wage employment. We further document intergenerational effects, as children of exposed parents exhibit lower educational attainment and reduced labor supply. These findings highlight the lasting and multigenerational economic costs of wartime chemical exposure.

title: A Century and a Quarter of Stock Market Liquidity and Trading Costs
abstract: ABSTRACT A widely cited working paper from the 2000s, now published (Jones, 2026), documents a substantial decline in trading costs and a positive relation between bid–ask spreads and excess returns from 1900 to 2000. We update the analysis and find that over the next quarter century, turnover surges, spreads decline sharply and subsequently cluster near zero, and excess returns become negatively related to spreads. Additional analysis attributes the reversal of the excess returns relation to distortions in the time‐series analysis created by the sudden reduction and clustering of spreads. We find similar distortions using the Amihud illiquidity measure and in simple cross‐sectional analyses, which suggest the effects we highlight might be pervasive.

Biodiversity risk premium
abstract: We identify a biodiversity risk premium (BRP) in investment strategies designed to mitigate biodiversity risks. To capture this premium, we construct optimised portfolios by reweighting approximately 3,000 constituents of the MSCI All Country World Index, using their MSCI biodiversity risk scores as a key screening criterion. Analysing data from 2013 to 2023, we find that biodiversity-screened portfolios exhibit lower risk-adjusted returns compared to randomly selected portfolios. This suggests the presence of a biodiversity risk premium: screening at three different intensities reduces the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio by 1.19 % to 4.14 %, a return loss of 16 to 60 basis points per year, of which 1, 5, and 11 basis points per year are attributable to the biodiversity criterion itself rather than to the reduced universe size. Our findings provide valuable insights into the pricing dynamics of biodiversity risk, enhancing the understanding of how natural capital considerations impact financial markets and investment strategies.

title: To Acquire or to Ally? Foreign Competition and Firm Boundary
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how foreign competition influences firms’ external growth strategies. Exploiting staggered US import tariff reductions as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that heightened competition leads firms to expand their use of strategic alliances. This pattern is more pronounced for firms with limited financial or operational flexibility, weaker competitive positions, and firms operating in low‐entry‐barrier industries. Under competitive pressure, firms predominantly form alliances with partners in the same industry, as well as with firms in high‐tech, business‐to‐consumer (B2C), and product‐differentiated sectors. In the long term, alliance‐active firms exhibit higher R&D intensity and patent outputs. Overall, the study highlights how domestic firms reshape their external growth choices, partner selection, and long‐term innovation outcomes in response to global competition shocks.

title: Rhetorical Contests Over Environmental and Social Proposals in Proxy Statements
abstract: ABSTRACT Activists push firms to improve their environmental and social (ES) performance using shareholder proposals. These ES proposals threaten managerial legitimacy and control, so management argues against activists to deflect their threat. We quantitatively examine how activists and management use rhetorical strategies in proxy statements to persuade shareholders to vote for or against ES proposals. Drawing on Aristotle's On Rhetoric , we study how appeals to ethos , logos , and pathos persuade proxy advisors and shareholders. We utilize natural language processing to develop replicable measures for each type of appeal, which we use to examine 1708 ES shareholder proposals in 1055 proxy statements from 2007 to 2021. Management at firms with higher levels of insider control and block ownership uses less persuasive rhetoric. Rhetorical strategies by activists and management are associated with proxy advisor recommendations and shareholder votes that support their respective sides. Activist and management rhetoric affect votes incrementally to proxy advisors’ recommendations, suggesting that the contesting parties are able to influence individual investors through their rhetoric.

title: Random Disclosure Costs: A Unified Theory of Disclosure
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a unified framework for a class of evidence games in which a sender, seeking to increase posterior expectations (e.g., a market price), chooses whether to reveal or withhold her information. Our model nests several classic models, including type‐dependent disclosure costs or benefits, uncertain information endowment, and the market for lemons. Frictions are captured as random disclosure costs that are privately known to the sender and noisily inferred by the receiver. We derive a simple characterization of the equilibrium and show that it features increasing disclosure for lower frictions or greater fundamental uncertainty. Further, with high uncertainty or low frictions, greater uncertainty about disclosure costs decreases the likelihood of disclosure. Positive costs do not necessarily rule out unraveling to full disclosure, especially when outcomes have heavy tails or when disclosure costs are not constant. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be estimated with a simple probit, suggesting that cost uncertainty is descriptive of real‐world behavior.

title: The Bank for International Settlements innovation hub: infrastructural power or innovation theatre?
abstract: Financial technology (FinTech) is disruptive not only for banks and payment providers, but also for public authorities. Although the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has produced extensive research on FinTech since 2000, it took on an experimental new role in 2019 with the launch of the BIS Innovation Hub. This hub brings together multidisciplinary teams of economists, computer scientists and design thinkers in seven centres across the world to develop FinTech prototypes, products and public goods. This article contributes to debates about the legitimacy of international financial institutions and the global governance of FinTech by asking why the BIS has reimagined itself as an innovator despite its limited experience of innovation. Through a mixed methods study, which includes a thematic analysis of 50 hub projects and case studies of Projects Nexus, mBridge and Genesis 1.0, it finds that the BIS has become an innovator to bolster its legitimacy and reassert greater public control over money and payments systems in the era of FinTech disruption. Even though its projects have struggled to achieve scale, the BIS has avoided the risk of innovation theatre and put itself at the centre of debates about infrastructural power in an era of rapid technological change.

title: Shareholder empowerment and ownership structure in a free-contracting environment
Competing Digital Money
abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system (FPS) or a central bank digital currency (CBDC), may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits. This contrasts with entry of PSPs on the merchant side, which disciplines incumbent fees instead.

title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.

EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
abstract: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

title: Digital Inclusion in Corporate ESG Communication: A Text‐Mining Analysis of Global AI Companies
abstract: ABSTRACT As digital platforms increasingly mediate nearly all human activities, artificial intelligence (AI) exhibits dual potential: It can enhance digital inclusion or intensify the exclusion and inequality faced by digitally vulnerable populations. This study examines digital inclusion and accessibility in the ESG reports of eight AI technology companies representing diverse business models. By applying a text‐mining method to analyze reports from these eight companies covering 2019–2024, we found that ESG disclosures are dominated by environmental topics. The coverage of digital inclusion and accessibility increased alongside major regulatory developments, suggesting a temporal alignment between disclosure practices and the evolving regulatory environment. Moreover, a comparative analysis with the WBA Digital Inclusion Score revealed selective disclosure and divergences between disclosure emphasis and external benchmark assessments across business models. This study recommends institutionalizing digital inclusion and accessibility as measurable ESG metrics to support practical assessment and industry‐level governance.

title: Water as a Strategic Design Variable for Climate‐Resilient Urban Farming: Reconfiguring Sustainable Business Models Through the Water‐Enabled Resource Architecture Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how water sourcing and management can be embedded within urban farming business models to enhance environmental sustainability, climate resilience, and economic viability. It introduces the water‐enabled resource architecture (WERA) framework, which conceptualizes water as a strategic design variable capable of reshaping value proposition, governance arrangements, value capture logic, feasibility conditions, and performance indicators. The framework is illustrated through a comparative case study of an urban aquaponics installation in which two structurally equivalent systems operate under closely aligned conditions and different water sourcing strategies: centralized potable water supply and rainwater harvesting. Within the analyzed case, the decentralized configuration is associated with greater water autonomy and estimated operating‐cost reductions, while also redistributing organizational responsibilities and requiring additional infrastructure, treatment, and monitoring routines. WERA therefore provides an analytical lens for examining how water choices reshape governance, stakeholder value, cost‐risk mechanisms, and resource resilience within urban farming business models. It also clarifies how water choices reshape governance, stakeholder value, and cost‐risk mechanisms in urban systems.

title: Sustainable Corporate Loans: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper presents a systematic literature review of sustainable corporate loans (SCLs), including green loans and sustainability‐linked loans, to synthesise current academic knowledge and outline future research directions. Using a PRISMA protocol and a bibliometric analysis of 102 peer‐reviewed articles published in AJG‐ranked journals (3 and above) between January 2009 and May 2025, the review examines publication trends, theoretical perspectives, methodological approaches, thematic patterns and research gaps. The literature shows rapid growth after 2020, with substantial regional concentration in China, the United States and Europe. Stakeholder theory is the most frequently invoked explicit theoretical lens, although many studies do not anchor their analysis in a clearly stated theory. Quantitative designs prevail, but longitudinal, mixed‐method and experimental approaches remain scarce. Four main themes emerge: borrower ESG and financial outcomes, lender incentives and risk management, loan contract features, and macroeconomic implications. Key gaps relate to causal identification, ESG metric standardisation and borrower–lender dynamics in emerging markets.

How Complementarities Affect Technological Innovation Within Platform‐Based Innovation Ecosystems: The Role of Orchestrators' Platform Capability and Interorganizational Trust
abstract: ABSTRACT Complementarities in Platform‐based Innovation Ecosystems (PIEs) are crucial for collaborative technological innovation (TECI), yet how they influence TECI remains underexplored. Therefore, by integrating Resource Dependence Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study empirically examined the relationships between two key complementarities (supermodular and unique) and TECI. With a sample of 203 technology firms, this study demonstrates that: (a) supermodular complementarities are more strongly positively associated with TECI than unique ones; (b) orchestrators' platform capabilities and interorganizational trust significantly moderate these complementarities–TECI links, with moderating effects varying by complementarity type. Theoretically, this study advances literature on complementarities–TECI relationships in PIEs. Managerially, it provides practical insights into effectively managing complementarities for TECI performance.

title: Promotion and prevention regulatory focus in equity crowdfunding reinvestment decisions
An integrative theoretical framework of strategic marketing solutions for resolving social dilemmas
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how marketing can help resolve firm-level social dilemmas. The authors synthesize insights from sociology, psychology, economics, political science, management and marketing to conceptualize firm-level marketing social dilemmas, organize marketing solution levers into an integrative taxonomy and develop a testable framework with antecedents, marketing solutions, boundary conditions, consequences and propositions. Design/methodology/approach The authors conduct a systematic review to identify core social-dilemma constructs and diagnostic attributes (e.g. observability, externality dispersion/reversibility, coordination/free-rider risk, short–long payoff gap). Building on this base, the authors propose an integrative taxonomy of marketing solutions − communication and norm activation, regulation, group-structure and governance and strategic marketing − and illustrate generalizability with four cases: climate change, pandemic, data privacy and DEI. The authors then develop an integrative framework and associated propositions. Findings The authors offer a firm-level conceptualization of social dilemmas that links diagnostic dilemma attributes to matched marketing solution bundles and specifies boundary conditions that shape effectiveness. The framework explains how marketing efforts translate antecedents into firm-level outcomes, while positioning employee-, consumer- and society-level consequences as broader downstream implications of firms’ efforts to resolve social dilemmas, yielding clear, mechanism-based propositions for explanation and prediction. Research limitations/implications Future research could expand on this research by empirically testing the proposed framework and exploring marketing solutions for resolving different social dilemmas. Practical implications This study offers actionable strategies for marketers and marketing to address social dilemmas, foster stakeholder relationships, enhance organizational outcomes and benefit society. Social implications Addressing firm-level social dilemmas through marketing activities fosters long-term societal benefits while enhancing firm performance. Originality/value This research advances the understanding of social dilemmas within the marketing domain through a novel framework and a taxonomy of marketing solutions that address firm-specific challenges. By bridging gaps across disciplines, it contributes foundations for innovative marketing strategies that can resolve complex social dilemmas.

title: Public Interest Capacity: The Case of Direct File
abstract: ABSTRACT This article describes the conditions for creating and undermining public interest capacity, that is, the ability of the state to generate public goods with widely distributed benefits. The creation and elimination of Direct File, a free, online public tax reporting system in the United States, offers an instrumental case. The creation of Direct File depended upon political commitment sufficient to overcome private interests: both the traditional dependence on private contractors to produce digital products, and the opposition of the private tax preparation industry which saw Direct File as a competitor. Political will was not enough: creating internal capacity in the form of skilled government tech teams who could build a quality digital product was also necessary. But without this political commitment in the Trump administration, which instead pursued downsizing and was receptive to the tax preparation industry arguments, both Direct File and the team that built it were eliminated.

title: Partisan composition and public spending on adult education: An event study analysis using German county-level data (2008–2022)
abstract: Political parties vary in their education policy preferences, with public spending on education serving as one indicator of these policy priorities. We hypothesise that centre-left parties in local government increase public spending on adult education. To test this, we analyse public data on expenditures for adult education at the local level and data on party participation in county and city councils in Germany (n = 390; N = 5534). Using the seat share and party affiliation of the head of the administration as measures of partisan influence, we employ two-way fixed-effects models and heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimators to account for variation in treatment timing and duration of parties’ local government participation. The investigation covers the period from 2008 to 2022. For counties where centre-left parties hold a majority of seats, we observe a statistically significant positive effect, whereas where they have the head of administration the effect is not significant.

Unlocking the potential of nanocellulose: Promising substrate materials for electrocatalysts
abstract: Nanocellulose as substrate materials have garnered considerable interest for developing high-performance carbon-based electrocatalysts toward hydrogen evolution and oxygen evolution/reduction reactions, due to their many advantages including unique fibrous nanoarchitecture, mass production capacity, environmental benignity, cost effectiveness and sustainability. However, the intricate relationships between structure, design and catalytic activity in nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts have yet to be comprehensively discussed and deciphered, which hinders their practical application and further development of nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts. Therefore, this review summarizes and analyzes the latest development for electrocatalysts integrated on nanocellulose substrate. Herein, the design and application of nanocellulose as substrate materials for electrocatalysts closely related to its structure characteristics and chemical properties are fully discussed, highlighting the unique merits of nanocellulose substrate in the field of electrocatalysis. Simultaneously, the commonality and individuality of nanocellulose categorized into three types with diverse structure properties are analyzed. Moreover, the viable optimization strategies for enhancing catalytic activity have been systematically explored based on the coupling of nanocellulose substrate and active sites, focusing on the core structure-performance relationship. Centering on these topics, the future research challenges and prospects for designing high-performance nanocellulose-based electrocatalysts is presented, aiming to pave the way for new research directions of this attractive field.

When heat hits: Short-run saving and withdrawal behavior among microfinance clients in Benin
abstract: Increased access to finance is widely viewed as a key driver to increase adaptive capacity in response to climate change. However, apart from limited studies on borrowing behavior, little is known about how exposure to extreme heat impacts microfinance clients’ financial behavior. This study addresses this gap by investigating the short-run effects of unusual heat on microfinance clients’ saving and withdrawal behavior. In a case study, it combines geo-located temperature data with a unique dataset of around 50,000 clients of a leading Microfinance Institution (MFI) in Benin. Applying two-way fixed effects, seemingly unrelated regression, and ordinary least square models, the study finds that exposure to extreme heat is heterogeneously associated with microfinance clients’ financial behavior. Specifically, non-agricultural clients show suggestive evidence for the accumulation of precautionary savings after extreme heat days in the precedent quarter, while agricultural clients statistically significantly reduce their savings following exposure to extreme heat in the precedent quarter. Microfinance clients increase their withdrawals when exposed to extreme heat within the precedent quarter, but the association is not robust to agricultural clients’ withdrawals in response to an increase in annual extreme heat days. Addressing the heterogeneous financial responses across different clients to extreme heat consequently requires explicit policy attention. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the impact of extreme weather events on individual economic outcomes, how financial behavior relates to weather risk, and how microfinance clients respond to shocks.

abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.

Limits to LTD, loan supply, and real effects: Banks vs. nonbanks
abstract: We study the transmission of macroprudential policy to loan issuance by banks and nonbank financial intermediaries, and the associated real effects on firm-level outcomes including mergers and acquisitions. We use loan-level data from the global syndicated credit market, information on the type of participating lenders between banks and nonbanks, and shocks to regulatory limits to the banks’ ratio on loans-to-deposits (LTD) to document that a LTD policy tightening reduces credit supply by banks and simultaneously shifts financial intermediation to nonbanks. We show that this credit migration is driven by banks facing high pre-regulation LTD ratios and by nonbanks that are less regulated and free from leading the loan arrangements when issuing term loans. We also find evidence that in response to tighter LTD, borrowing firms with stronger nonbank relationships are shielded more by the decline in bank credit with ensuing relative increases in corporate debt, assets, and capital investment. Finally, firms in countries with better access to nonbank credit differentially increase the number of acquisitions they undertake when LTD policy intensifies.

abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) safety is becoming increasingly critical as UAV operations are integrated into urban service and transportation systems, creating an urgent need for risk representations that can support refined low-altitude airspace management. Existing urban safety maps are still mainly expressed as two-dimensional or height stratified representations, which cannot capture the continuous variation of risk with altitude and therefore remain inadequate for continuous low-altitude flight scenarios. This paper develops a continuous three-dimensional spatiotemporal safety mapping framework for urban low-altitude environments. The framework integrates semantic information, digital surface model (DSM) and digital terrain model (DTM) derived morphology, pedestrian related exposure, and meteorological conditions within a unified geo-referenced support. A vertical continuous interpolation function is introduced to transform discrete risk representations into a continuous three-dimensional spatiotemporal risk field, thereby enabling continuous risk analysis across space, altitude, and time. Experiments in a real urban scene show that risk values vary significantly across different regions, time periods, and scene conditions, and that the resulting field reveals clear vertical differentiation and temporal redistribution patterns that conventional planar safety maps cannot represent consistently. These findings show that the proposed reusable continuous three-dimensional and time varying risk model offers a practical basis for refined low-altitude airspace management and has the potential to support future high density UAV operations.

title: Balancing adversariality and naturalness in autonomous vehicle testing scenario generation via multi-objective reinforcement learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL)-based adversarial scenario generation through dynamic agent–environment interactions has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. However, existing RL approaches struggle to balance adversariality and naturalness because naturalistic driving behaviors avoid risk whereas adversarial behaviors intentionally induce it. The reward-driven nature of RL can further lead to objective polarization under linearly weighted rewards, resulting in scenarios biased toward a limited range of adversariality–naturalness trade-offs. This study proposes a preference-conditioned safety–critical scenario generation framework based on multi-policy multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL), which models adversariality and naturalness as separate components of a vectorized reward and jointly optimizes them across the preference space. The adversariality reward incorporates risk–liability screening to filter two predefined invalid-risk patterns, while the naturalness penalty leverages a computationally efficient shadow-mode evaluation to provide real-time behavioral-deviation feedback relative to a reference driving policy. Envelope Q-learning is adopted to learn multiple preference-conditioned policies and is enhanced by a Kullback–Leibler divergence–based policy differentiation mechanism that mitigates policy mode collapse and encourages diverse behavioral evolution. Experiments in highway car-following and lane-changing environments show improvements in the evaluated scenario-quality and diversity metrics over the RL baselines. Compared with multi-round linearly weighted RL, the proposed method achieves 2.70 times the Pareto-front hypervolume, increases the valid safety–critical scenario success rate from 4.4% to 14.6%, and achieves 2.83 times the feature-space coverage volume. The results support the framework’s ability to generate diverse safety–critical scenarios across testing preferences within the studied highway operational design domain.

title: Role-Playing as Immigrants for Learning to Trust: Constructing a Theory of Experiential Contact
abstract: This research examined whether a computer-based role-playing game in which participants created immigrant characters from Mexico and took them through the process of naturalizing to the United States could be used to promote trust. A posttest-only experiment with a control group was conducted in Fall 2024 ( N = 98). Results indicate that participants who played the game had significantly higher levels of trust in immigrants in general, as well as those from Mexico, Central/South America, India, China, and the Middle East specifically, compared to the control condition. Parasocial connections to characters in game-based settings strengthened the effect of role-playing on trusting immigrants from Mexico. Half of the role-playing participants also saw a thank-you video from an outgroup representative, as a form of mediated indirect contact. The video condition appeared to drive the interaction between role-playing and sensing parasocial connections to characters in predicting Mexican immigrant trust. Results demonstrate the potential for role-playing games to foster trust between groups who may struggle to interact in person, along with the additive effect of mediated indirect contact at high levels of parasocial connection.

A broad review of metal/metal oxide based integrated thermal, biochemical and electrochemical systems for waste into hydrogen conversion
abstract: Global efforts to turn waste into useful fuels have accelerated due to the growing demand for clean and sustainable energy, with hydrogen emerging as a vital energy carrier. Metals and metal oxides have shown remarkable promise as catalysts and functional elements in a variety of Waste-to-Hydrogen (WtH) pathways among the materials studied. The functions and mechanisms of metals and metal oxides in the three main processes of hydrogen generation via thermal, biochemical, and electrochemical conversion are critically examined in this review. Metal oxides aid in cracking, reforming, and tar reduction in thermal pathways like pyrolysis and gasification, increasing hydrogen yields and lowering carbon emissions. Metal oxide additives enhance microbial activity and electron transfer efficiency, which promotes the production of biohydrogen in biochemical processes, especially anaerobic digestion and dark fermentation. Metal and metal oxide-based catalysts are essential for enhancing electrocatalytic activity, stability, and overall system efficiency in electrochemical systems, such as water electrolysis and microbial electrolysis cells. Recent developments in hybrid catalyst systems, process integration techniques, and nanostructured and doped metal oxides are also covered in this review. The three WtH approaches are compared, with important considerations like economic viability, scalability, environmental impact, and energy efficiency assessed. Additionally, the incorporation of WtH technologies with carbon capture and circular economy principles is explored. By addressing current challenges and identifying future research directions, this review underscores the transformative potential of metal/metal oxides in advancing sustainable hydrogen production from waste resources.
authors: P. Sri Bala Jeya Krishna Sri

title: Comparative review of multi-energy systems modeling tools for scenario analysis toward climate neutrality: Case studies, achievements, and challenges
abstract: Climate-neutrality planning requires modeling tools that connect long-term investment, multi-sector demand and emissions, power-system operation, and grid-security assessment. This structured review examines six widely used platforms such as PyPSA, Julia/JuMP, GAMS, TIMES, DIgSILENT PowerFactory, and LEAP for large-scale multi-energy-system analysis. Based on 100 cited sources, the platforms are qualitatively compared in terms of temporal and geographical resolution, optimization structure, data requirements, sector coverage, solver flexibility, and application domains. Kazakhstan's coal phase-down and renewable-energy expansion toward 2060 provide the practical context for discussing their suitability and complementarity. The review demonstrates that no single platform can fully represent all planning, operational, environmental, and engineering aspects of a climate-neutral energy system. TIMES and LEAP are particularly suitable for long-term demand, policy, and emissions scenarios; PyPSA, Julia/JuMP, and GAMS support investment and dispatch optimization with different levels of flexibility and transparency; and DIgSILENT PowerFactory provides detailed power-flow, contingency, protection, and dynamic-security analysis. The findings support a staged modeling workflow in which long-term transition pathways are linked to network-constrained optimization and subsequent engineering validation. This application-oriented comparison clarifies the respective strengths and limitations of the reviewed tools and provides guidance for selecting complementary platforms for large-scale energy-transition studies.
