Performance improvement and operating mechanism analysis of a vertical axis wind turbine with adaptive blades
abstract: Wind energy has been recognized as a promising energy source for broadly distributed electronics, due to its widespread availability and sustainability. Vertical axis wind turbines (VAWTs) are more suitable for harvesting wind energy in urban environments compared to horizontal axis wind turbines (HAWTs), owing to their omni-directional, low noise emission and lightweight characteristics. In our previous study, a novel VAWT with adaptive blades (consisting of flaps that open and close in response to the flow conditions) has been designed and constructed. The current study extends our previous study by further improving the rotor performance and by investigating the operating mechanism of the adaptive rotor. Wind tunnel experiments were conducted to compare the conventional rotor and the adaptive rotor under different wind speeds. The effects of inclination and pitch angle on the aerodynamic performance were investigated, and a favourable pitch angle of −8° was identified under the adjustable-beam configuration at 6 m/s. Based on this selected angle configuration, the improved rotor increased the maximum power coefficient from below 5% in the previous prototype to approximately 11% at 6 m/s, and reduced the self-starting wind speed from 8 m/s to 4 m/s. With this configuration, the adaptive blades further improved the low-speed torque performance compared with the conventional blades, increasing the minimum torque coefficient by 23% at 6 m/s, and thereby accelerating the self-starting process, while maintaining a comparable maximum power coefficient at high rotation speeds. However, the adaptive blades did not further reduce the self-starting wind speed. The analysis indicates that the transition rotation speed (representing the transition from drag-based to lift-based operation) of the adaptive blade is a key factor for further improvement.

Does artificial intelligence improve social stability risk performance in China?
abstract: This paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to improving the social stability risk level in China. Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation and increasingly complex governance challenges, AI has been widely adopted in areas such as public security, social management, and risk monitoring. However, its actual effectiveness in mitigating social stability risks remains underexplored. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions in China, this study constructs an empirical framework to evaluate the impact of AI policy on social stability risk levels. The analysis integrates indicators of technological capacity, governance performance, and socio-economic conditions, and applies quantitative methods to identify both direct and indirect effects. The findings suggest that AI policy significantly reduces social stability risks by promoting digital economy development, increasing wage levels and investment in education. At the same time, the results reveal notable regional heterogeneity. The AI policy significantly reduces social stability risk in the central and western regions, and areas with moderate digital economy development, but has no statistically significant effect in economically developed and digitally advanced areas. The study also highlights potential challenges, including data governance concerns and uneven technological access, which may offset some of AI's benefits. This research contributes to the literature by linking technological innovation with social governance outcomes and provides policy implications for leveraging AI to promote social stability. It suggests that policymakers should not only invest in AI infrastructure but also address institutional and regional disparities to ensure inclusive and effective risk management.

title: Steel plant-level technology innovations could diffuse cascading carbon emission reduction: Taking an iron and steel enterprise in Northwest China as a case study
abstract: Deep decarbonization of the iron and steel sector is essential to achieving national net-zero targets. However, national and sectoral roadmaps provide limited guidance for individual plants with diverse operating conditions and technical configurations. This study develops a plant-level model for a representative Chinese steelmaking process. The model combines a multi-technology spectrum with a two-way cascading transmission model to quantify the diffusion of technological impacts and identify priority pathways towards carbon neutrality. The 76 low-carbon innovation technologies provide an indirect carbon reduction potential of 15,208 t/d, 2.1 times their direct potential. Technologies for energy-mix adjustment, intelligent control, and energy recovery and utilisation technologies account for 75% of thecomprehensive reduction potential. Blast furnace (BF)-related technologies account for 83% of this amount, and 76% is transmitted through one-step and two-step pathways involving the BF, coking, and basic oxygen furnace (BOF). The BF, BOF, and coking nodes together account for 80% of the comprehensive potential and diffuse 9133 t/d (60%) indirectly. This plant-level evaluation provides a scientific basis for the targeted decarbonization of comparable integrated steel plant and offers transferable evidence for regional and national low-carbon transitions.

title: Evaluating clean energy strategies for national carbon neutrality: An interdisciplinary policy-focused decision framework
abstract: This study aims to evaluate and prioritize clean energy strategies to support Türkiye's national carbon neutrality goals. Achieving carbon neutrality requires adopting clean technologies and effective environmental policy tools. This study presents a novel multi-criteria decision-making context that combines the Picture Fuzzy Best-Worst Method (PiF-BWM) and Picture Fuzzy Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (PiF-TOPSIS) to evaluate and prioritize renewable energy strategies under uncertainty systematically. The empirical application focuses on Türkiye and is based on the evaluations of nine experts. Using Türkiye as the test bed, we assess alternatives such as climate-resilient low-carbon development plans, policy frameworks for low-carbon fuels, large-scale and distributed renewables, green jobs programs, and building electrification via heat pumps. Criteria span environmental impact, cost and financial viability, technological feasibility, socioeconomic effects, resilience, energy efficiency, energy security, and policy alignment. The methodology first applies PiF-BWM to determine the criteria weights, and then uses PiF-TOPSIS to rank the alternative strategies. Results show that environmentally effective and policy-enabled strategies deliver the highest urban decarbonization benefits, while building-focused electrification provides targeted gains when integrated with local grid constraints and building codes. The findings further indicate that climate-resilient low-carbon development plans and policy frameworks for low-carbon fuels are the most suitable strategic options, whereas heat pump-based building electrification receives the lowest score among the evaluated alternatives. This study positions energy as an instrument for sustainable development by foregrounding affordability, access, equity, and institutional capacity in strategy selection. From a policy perspective, the results suggest that governments should prioritize policy-supported and resilience-oriented clean energy pathways while aligning investment decisions with affordability, implementation capacity, and long-term sustainability goals. The policy-oriented framework supports sustainable development goal (SDG) 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and is tailored to the realities of developing-country contexts.

title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI ?
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

title: Decarbonizing the Food Supply Chain in Emerging Market Economies: A Transition Management Framework for Carbon Neutrality
abstract: ABSTRACT Decarbonizing the food supply chain in emerging market economies is vital for meeting national and global carbon neutrality commitments. This study identifies 15 key challenges hindering this transition and examines their structural interrelationships using interpretive structural modeling. The results identify lack of robust government policies and regulations, lack of low‐carbon facilities, and lack of R&D capabilities as the most influential challenges hindering the decarbonization transition. Grounded in transition management theory, these challenges are hierarchically organized into three interconnected transition levels: formulating carbon neutrality programs, deploying carbon neutrality measures, and implementing carbon neutrality practices. Further, based on the best‐worst method and VIKOR analyses, strategies including policy and regulatory framework, supply chain optimization and digitalization, and research and innovation ecosystem emerge as the highest‐priority strategic interventions. Thus, this study provides a theoretically grounded and practically actionable roadmap for businesses, policymakers, and other stakeholders seeking to accelerate the transition toward a carbon‐neutral food supply chain.

title: Green absorptive capacity and environmental sustainability: unveiling the interplay and moderating roles of blockchain and supply chain finance
abstract: Purpose Drawing on dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view, this study aims to examine how green absorptive capacity (GAC) enhances environmental sustainability performance (ESP) through financial performance (FP) and operational performance (OP) and how blockchain technology (BCT) and supply chain finance (SCF) strengthen these indirect relationships. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 522 organisations in Egypt and 508 in Jordan. Covariance-based structural equation modelling was used to test the moderated mediation model. Findings The results show that in both Egypt and Jordan, GAC improves ESP indirectly through FP and OP. In Jordan, blockchain technology strengthens the indirect relationship through both financial and operational performance, whereas in Egypt these blockchain effects are not supported. Supply chain finance strengthens the indirect relationship through operational performance in both countries, but not through financial performance. The nested model comparison indicates that whilst the overall model applies to both contexts, BCT and SCF exert varying degrees of influence in Egypt and Jordan. Research limitations/implications The results can support policymakers and organisational stakeholders by showing how digital technologies and green financing mechanisms can be used to strengthen the impact of green knowledge on performance and accelerate progress towards environmental sustainability. Originality/value This study develops and tests an integrated moderated mediation framework explaining how green absorptive capacity enhances environmental sustainability performance through financial and operational performance and how blockchain technology and supply chain finance strengthen these indirect relationships. By comparing Egypt and Jordan, the study extends dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view through context-specific evidence from two Arab emerging economies and reveals country-specific differences in the effectiveness of digital and financial enablers.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management An International Journal

title: The evolution of CFO role-identities under financialisation
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how chief financial officer (CFO) role-identities evolve in contexts of increasing financialisation, how they are sequentially reconfigured over time, and how prior identities continue to shape the way new role-identities are enacted. The article thus develops a dynamic perspective on how CFOs experience and navigate role-identity transitions throughout their careers. Design/methodology/approach The study is based on 50 career narrative interviews with CFOs, respondents' résumés, observations and documents from the French national professional association of CFOs. The analysis combined constant comparison and narrative reconstruction to identify recurring role-identities and trace their evolution across career trajectories. Findings The analysis identifies six CFO role-identities and shows how they developed successively during the rise and intensification of financialisation. Prior identities often persist, shaping how subsequent roles are experienced. As a result, financialisation appears as an ambiguity-generating process whose effects may shift over time for the same individual and be experienced as opportunity or threat at different moments. Originality/value The paper offers a processual account of how CFO role-identities have evolved during financialisation. The study makes three main contributions: it advances CFO research by developing a trajectory-based understanding of role-identity evolution; it shows how financialisation generates differentiated identity outcomes across CFO careers, depending on the lingering influence of prior identities; and it enriches financialisation research by illuminating its micro-foundations through the lived experience of professionals and their career trajectories.

title: Socio-spatial inequality: the case of Indonesian railway's reform
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how accounting practices as tools of governance reproduce inequality by reshaping relational spaces which intersect with colonial legacies, local contexts and neoliberal logics. Design/methodology/approach This study investigates organisational reforms of PT Kereta Api Indonesia (Persero) (KAI) during 2009–2014. It focuses on the transformation of station areas where neoliberal imperatives of efficiency and customer orientation reshaped socially vibrant, informally sustained spaces into purified, commercially driven zones, displacing long-standing occupants and disrupting local economies. Employing 28 semi-structured interviews with employees, passengers, consultants and experts, complemented by annual reports and public documents, the study validates methodological triangulation. By situating stations as socially and historically constructed spaces, the analysis demonstrates how accounting and governance practices intersected with spatial restructuring to produce and legitimise socio-spatial inequalities. Findings The findings reveal that neoliberal reforms generate structural inequalities by redefining who and what is recognised within organisational spaces. Accounting functions as a powerful instrument in this process, shaping the criteria through which actors are rendered visible, accountable and authorised to occupy the contested spaces. In doing so, previously established actors along with their culturally, historically and socially constructed livelihood were marginalised and rendered invisible and became vulnerably underrepresented upon their occupational rights as spatial value was recalibrated according to neoliberal logics. Accounting thus actively legitimises spatial reconfiguration and purification by embedding exclusionary logics. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by attributing neoliberal reform's structural consequences as inequality particularly pertaining to socio-spatial accounting. It empirically extends our understanding on accounting's centrality as a socio-spatial power as it actively constructs organisational realities, defining what is legible, permissible and valuable in both spatial and social life.

title: Energy management strategies for fuel cell vehicles: Advances, challenges, and future directions for the prediction-control hierarchical architecture
Integrated hydrogen production and liquefaction via alkaline electrolysis: Conceptual design and life cycle assessment under geothermal and hybrid renewable energy scenarios
The divergent roles of humic- and fulvic-acid DOM in regulating Hg methylation/demethylation in paddy soils
An analytical framework for assessing wind farm siting suitability in China under future climate scenarios
The hologenomic stress legacy: A framework for soil as a transgenerational memory bank of plant immunity
Flyway-scale migration phenology identifies mismatches between migration timing and European hunting regulations
abstract: The study of bird migration timing is pivotal for the identification of the onset of pre-breeding migration, when, according to the European regulatory framework, the hunting seasons should end following Article 7.4 of the EU Birds Directive. Member States may use different data sources, including citizen science platforms, to determine this onset. Here, we used data from eBird, a citizen science platform, to describe the timing of pre- and post-breeding migration of the Song Thrush ( Turdus philomelos ) across the Western Palearctic. For EU Member States, we compared the onset dates of pre-breeding migration we derived from eBird with those obtained from ringing data published in the Eurasian-African Bird Migration Atlas and with those reported in the EU Key Concepts Documents (KCD). We found high agreement between eBird and Atlas estimates, but substantial differences between KCD-defined onset dates and those identified in the Atlas and this study. This suggests that, in many EU Member States, hunting remains open after the onset of pre-breeding migration, with potential negative effects on breeding populations. This mismatch highlights the limitations of current country-specific definitions and the need for harmonized flyway-scale assessments of migration timing. As required by current EU legislation, hunting closure periods should rely on up-to-date scientific evidence and transparent national data-collection mechanisms. The systematic application of the method presented here to citizen science or ringing data provides a reproducible and standardized approach that can be adopted at the EU level, easily upgradeable as new data become available.

title: Biogeochemical and seasonal nutrient dynamics of restored estuarine oyster reefs in Mobile Bay, Alabama
abstract: Nutrient overloading in aquatic environments can degrade water quality and cause eutrophication, disrupting ecosystem function and local economies, including Mobile Bay, Alabama. Oyster reef restoration is a promising strategy for nutrient sequestration and estuarine recovery. Yet, few studies have examined how oysters affect the biogeochemical dynamics of nutrients such as nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and carbon (C), limiting our ability to develop restoration best management practices (BMPs). This study investigated the effects of eastern oyster ( Crassostrea virginica ) size class (juvenile and adult) and set style (single and floret) on nutrient removal through a one-year field experiment across 32 experimental plots in Mobile Bay, Alabama. Seasonal water, sediment, and oyster tissue samples were collected quarterly, which were analyzed for total N, P, and C to assess nutrient dynamics, biogeochemical processes, and oyster bioassimilation. Sediment nutrient concentrations showed strong seasonal variability for P and C, which peaked in April (0.019 ± 0.001% and 1.66 ± 0.18% respectively), whereas sediment N varied less markedly and reached its highest concentration in July (0.09 ± 0.011%). Oyster tissue nutrient content followed similar patterns, with the highest total P and C (0.82 ± 0.04% and 49.15 ± 0.39%, respectively) occurring in April, while the highest total N (7.95 ± 0.23%) in July, indicating coupling between oyster bioassimilation and sediment processes. Furthermore, nutrient removal varied among oyster treatments, with adult single oysters showing the lowest nutrient uptake, whereas floret configurations, particularly those incorporating juvenile oysters, supported greater nutrient retention. These findings demonstrate that nutrient removal benefits of oyster restoration depend not only on oyster presence, but also on life stage, reef configuration, and seasonal biogeochemical conditions. For restoration BMPs, deploying juvenile oysters in clustered floret configurations and accounting for seasonal nutrient dynamics may enhance nutrient capture and retention compared with restoration strategies dominated by individually set adult oysters.

title: Attributing the changes in evapotranspiration and its components to climatic factors and vegetation dynamics in the Three-River Headwaters Region
Establishing in-situ water quality criteria for assessing ecological risk of labile As in the Three Gorges Reservoir during low-water level period
Compound fire–meteorology extremes drove megacity air pollution during the 2024 South American fire season
abstract: Extreme air pollution increasingly threatens major cities, yet the relative roles of urban emissions and biomass-burning smoke transported across multiple spatial scales remain difficult to quantify. Here, we investigate three multi-day pollution extremes that affected São Paulo State during the 2024 South American fire season, when daily fine particulate matter (PM 2 . 5 ) reached 80–100 μg m −3 in the Metropolitan Area of São Paulo. We combined surface observations, aerosol optical thickness measurements, backward trajectories, and controlled global atmospheric simulations differing only in fire-emission representation to quantify the biomass-burning contribution. Simulations without fire emissions failed to reproduce the observed PM 2 . 5 and carbon monoxide (CO) peaks, whereas fire-attributable PM 2 . 5 increments reached 17–21 μg m −3 at the state scale and the ensemble-mean cumulative metropolitan fire-attributable burden reached ∼547 μg m −3 day across E1–E3 combined. The three events revealed contrasting source–receptor configurations: regional and longer-range transport combined with weak receptor ventilation during E1 (15–24 August), greater fire activity during E2 (29 August–5 September) produced a comparatively weaker receptor response under less persistent transport pathways, and E3 (7–15 September) occurred when intense fire activity across multiple spatial scales coincided with favourable transport configurations, anomalous heat and dryness, and weak ventilation. Fire-emission configurations producing larger aerosol enhancements generally showed better agreement with observations, although all inventories underestimated the most extreme episode. These results show that megacity pollution can arise from the combined effects of biomass-burning emissions, atmospheric transport, and adverse meteorological conditions, while highlighting substantial sensitivity to fire-emission representation in operational atmospheric-composition systems.

title: Relational values across land–sea interactions: Insights from a forest–river–ocean nexus watershed in northeastern Japan
Asymmetric Response of Soil Heterotrophic Respiration and Its Temperature Sensitivity in a Desert Steppe Under Climate Change
abstract: ABSTRACT Soil heterotrophic respiration ( R h ) and its temperature sensitivity ( Q 10 ) are important variables reflecting the intensity of feedback between the grassland carbon cycle and climate change. However, the factors regulating R h and Q 10 in desert grasslands under climate change remain unclear, and the asymmetric response of R h during warming and cooling remains unquantified. We collected and measured the physicochemical properties of soils after 8 years of elevated temperature and precipitation (ambient temperature, T0, +2°C, T1, +4°C, T2, ambient precipitation, P0, +25%, P1, and +50%, P2). To quantify the asymmetric response of R h , we continuously monitored R h during warming and cooling at six incubation temperature levels in the laboratory (5°C, 10°C, 15°C, 20°C, 25°C, and 30°C). Results indicated that elevated temperature and precipitation significantly affected soil moisture, soil organic carbon, R h , and Q 10 . Compared with the T0P0 treatment, the T2P2 treatment enhanced R h and Q 10 by 11.72% and 1.56%, respectively. In addition, R h was significantly affected by periodic changes in incubation temperature during both warming (5°C–30°C) and cooling (30°C–5°C), and R h was 15.05% higher under warming than cooling. Variation partitioning analysis showed that R h was primarily governed by soil carbon content, whereas Q 10 was largely driven by soil water content. In summary, soil carbon and water content are limiting factors for R h and Q 10 in the desert steppe, and periodic temperature changes should be taken into account when quantifying R h and Q 10 .

Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations
Investment-goods market power and capital accumulation
Capturing international influences in U.S. monetary policy through a Natural Language Processing approach
TESTING FOR ENDOGENEITY: A MOMENT-BASED BAYESIAN APPROACH
abstract: A standard assumption in the Bayesian estimation of linear regression models is that the regressors are exogenous in the sense that they are uncorrelated with the model error term. In practice, however, this assumption can be invalid. In this article, using the exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) framework, we develop a Bayes factor test for endogeneity that compares a base model that is correctly specified under exogeneity but misspecified under endogeneity against an extended model that is correctly specified in either case. We provide a comprehensive study of the log-marginal ETEL. We demonstrate that our testing procedure is consistent from a frequentist point of view: as the sample grows, it almost surely selects the base model if and only if the regressors are exogenous, and the extended model if and only if the regressors are endogenous. The methods are illustrated with simulated data and problems concerning the causal effect of automobile prices on automobile demand and the causal effect of potentially endogenous airplane ticket prices on passenger volume.

title: Patent agglomeration and environmental efficiency: effects and mechanisms in Africa
Optimizing environmental taxes for synergistic governance: From tax-rate to tax-system optimization
Predicting individual stock crashes via extreme return probabilities: Machine learning with Bayesian optimization
Identifying heterogeneous decision rules from choices when menus are unobserved
abstract: Consider aggregate choice data from a population with heterogeneity in both preferences (or more general decision rules) and in menus, and where the analyst has limited information about how menus are distributed across the population. We determine what can be inferred from aggregate data about the distribution of preferences by identifying the set of all distributions that are consistent with the preceding. Our main theorem strengthens and generalizes existing results on such identification and provides an alternative analytical approach (using convex capacities) to study the problem.

title: Extreme weather and human capital formation: evidence from Qing China
abstract: Weather shocks can constrain educational investment and human capital formation. In Qing China, education spending rose and fell with weather-sensitive farm income. Using a two-century panel (1646–1904) covering 234 prefectures, we find that a drought occurring one year before the examinations and additional droughts within the past five years reduce jinshi (the highest degree in the imperial examination system) density by approximately 6 % and 2.6 % per period, respectively. Adaptive measures such as the introduction of sweet potatoes, savings from surplus years, and flexible pricing mechanisms prove effective in mitigating drought effects. For robustness, we proxy regional recording capacity with the word count of meteorological entries and augment the baseline with controls for social unrest and epidemic shocks, with results remaining stable. By bringing long-run historical evidence to bear, this study enriches the literature on how extreme weather affects human capital formation.

title: Shared value vs plural values. Contesting renewable energy projects of the Enel Group
abstract: The energy transition triggers urgent questions about what values are important, who controls transitional processes, and who has the power to define the answers to the climate crisis. Energy companies claim their central role in the development of renewable energy as the ultimate solution. However, communities affected by large-scale renewable energy projects have extensively raised environmental and social justice concerns and denounced the industry's poor practices and abuses. In this article, we analyse 15 socio-environmental conflicts around renewable energy projects owned by the Enel Group, one of the world's largest energy utilities, through the values and valuation languages of the affected communities. We map them onto five dimensions: environmental, health-related, socio-economic, ontological, and political. We build on environmental justice and ecological economics literature on valuation languages and employ counter-accounting to gather bottom-up evidence of grievances. We argue that, while the company claims that RE is the ultimate solution and the ‘Creating Shared Value’ approach is beneficial to all parties, those impacted by Enel's projects question the corporate model of energy transition and defend a plurality of values embedded in relational worldviews that are systematically misrecognised. We eventually criticise the corporate self-attributed moral and value-centred mandate in the energy transition and call for inclusive research about desirable energy futures rooted in plural and relational value systems.

title: Evaluating the influence of climate finance on reducing water, energy, and food vulnerabilities driven by climate change in African countries
abstract: Climate finance flows disproportionately toward Africa's most climate-exposed economies, yet this targeting rarely yields commensurate reductions in vulnerability, a “targeting-impact paradox” that raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of global adaptation and mitigation funding. Using an original panel dataset covering 23 African countries from 2000 to 2019, this paper models the joint determination of water, energy, and food (WEF) vulnerabilities and climate finance through a simultaneous-equations framework, estimated via three-stage least squares and two-step efficient IV-GMM. The results show that both global and mitigation-specific climate finance significantly reduce vulnerability, with the strongest effects in food and water systems, yet these gains are neither uniform nor unconditional: they are powerfully mediated by income level, institutional quality, and the tight interdependencies binding the WEF nexus together. Food vulnerability emerges as a critical amplifier of energy and water risk, while energy vulnerability feeds back through food and water systems, revealing a self-reinforcing architecture of risk that undermines siloed policy responses. For African economies confronting escalating climate stress, these findings carry a clear imperative: climate finance can fulfil its transformative promise only where it is deployed through integrated, cross-sectoral strategies explicitly aligned with national development plans and international finance flows, making the coherence of its design as decisive as its volume for building lasting, systemic resilience.

title: Digital Innovation and NextGenerationEU: Spatial Patterns in Italian Local Government Performance
Does Environmental Accountability Policy Enhance Urban Ecological Resilience? From the Perspectives of Industrial Structure and Environmental Regulation
The Unexpected Consequences of Clean Heating Policy in Northern China: A Study from the Perspective of Household Energy Poverty
From Stimulus to Strain: Provincial Fiscal Spending and TFP Growth in China, 2001–2018
Science-Finance Integration and the Formation of Patient Capital: Evidence from China's Sci-Tech Finance Pilot
The fragmented green state: state capacity, green macrofinancial regimes, and political contestation in Thailand’s energy transition
abstract: This paper contributes to debates on green states and green macrofinancial regimes in the Global South. It analyses Thailand, an upper-middle-income country that, although subject to international financial subordination, has sufficient domestic finance to support renewable energy rollout. However, despite consensus on the need for green transition, renewable energy remains low in Thailand’s energy mix. We explain this using the concept of the fragmented green state. State managers in macroeconomic and energy planning express support for green policies, but the fragmented state bureaucracy and contestation between competing coalitions lead to competing green macrofinancial regimes emerging. Fiscal hawks and green planners, linked to a reformist coalition, support weak derisking, including structural market-based reforms to the electricity sector. Geopolitical hawks, in alliance with state and large private energy firms, support limited robust derisking or Big Green State policies to maintain control over the power sector and advance renewables as supplementary to the core business of natural gas. This contestation prevents a green macrofinancial bargain that could support decarbonization. The fragmented green state could be relevant in understanding barriers to decarbonization in other Global South contexts.

title: Have billionaires become more tax-friendly since the financial crisis?
abstract: This article introduces the billionaire tax speech dataset, which provides comprehensive data on the tax speech acts of the hundred richest billionaires living in democracies over the past three decades. It has four major findings. First, the majority of these billionaires did speak publicly about wealth-based taxation, and the extent to which they did so rose explosively after the 2008 financial crisis. Second, while the billionaires became much more likely to weigh in, they have not become more tax-friendly in their public statements. In the first years after the financial crisis pro-tax speech outweighed anti-tax speech, but the trend has since been in the opposite direction. Third, there has, however, been a continuous rise in self-justifying speech: statements that sought to justify a billionaire's own tax record against concrete or diffuse allegations, since the publication of the Panama Papers in 2016. Finally, the terms of debate have shifted. Before the crisis, anti-tax billionaires were still seeking to slash wealth-based taxes further, while pro-tax billionaires sought to retain them. Afterwards, pro-tax billionaires pushed for new or higher wealth-based taxes, and anti-tax billionaires were more often on the defensive, opposing new or more taxation.

title: Stack disruption: Worldcoin’s standards for the world
abstract: Converging digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain, are challenging seemingly settled standards of trust, privacy, and identity within global finance. This article examines how financial technology (fintech) firms are disrupting established norms of financial governance by circumventing traditional actors, especially banks, through the case of World, an OpenAI-affiliated ‘proof of personhood’ initiative co-founded by Sam Altman. Headquartered in San Francisco, World provides digital passports and cryptocurrency (Worldcoin) in exchange for biometric data. Built to address challenges of human identification in the era of AI, World reconfigures informational governance and marginalises conventional authorities. We argue that World contributes to wider, ongoing disruption of longstanding conventions of trust and privacy in financial governance. World separates users from the fiduciary roles traditionally held by banks and governments, mediating value and identity with minimal oversight and increased risks for individuals. Rather than representing a peripheral experiment, World demonstrates how AI and blockchain technologies are contributing to attempts at redefining the boundaries between finance, data, and identity. This case highlights how fintech disruption not only challenges regulatory frameworks but also redefines the standards of trust and privacy that structure the contemporary political economy.

title: When Do Narratives Move Prices? Portfolio Allocation and Narrative Diffusion in Financial Markets
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do widely discussed market narratives sometimes trigger large asset‐price movements while at other times have little effect? We develop a dynamic equilibrium model in which narratives diffuse through investor communication networks and affect prices through portfolio reallocation. Narratives influence equilibrium prices only when adoption changes perceived asset values sufficiently to alter portfolio demand. The magnitude of their price effects depends on who adopts, is larger when existing narrative valuation is low, and remains bounded by aggregate wealth. Communication networks therefore shape prices indirectly by influencing the distribution of narrative views and investors' adoption decisions. An empirical application to four U.S.‐listed firms associated with the quantum‐computing investment narrative provides complementary reduced‐form evidence. More favorable narrative coverage is associated with higher contemporaneous abnormal returns, while greater narrative intensity is associated with excess volatility and a higher probability of extreme abnormal returns.

title: Investigating the Dependence Structure of Dirty and Clean Cryptocurrencies with Energy and Green Assets: Evidence from Markov-Switching Models
