title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: R. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant 31-R833984]. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07607 .

title: The Paradox of Inventors’ Job Security
Would a Balanced PCAOB Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.

title: How do audit committee members' and audit partners' communication styles jointly influence client managers’ negotiation behavior?
Service Recovery in Chatbot‐mediated Environments: Trust Dynamics and Customer Loyalty Intentions
abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

title: The Nexus of Green Behavior, Corporate Green Innovation Performance, and Industrial Green Value Co‐Creation: Insights for Green Business Strategies
abstract: ABSTRACT Drawing on the lens of green value co‐creation, this study investigates how such co‐creation mediates the relationship between employees' green behavioral intentions and corporate green innovation performance. By integrating internal and external moderating factors, the study constructs a comprehensive model of the green innovation process. Data from 448 survey responses were analyzed using covariance‐based structural equation modeling (CB‐SEM). The results demonstrate that green value co‐creation partially mediates the link between employee intentions and innovation outcomes. Furthermore, the study finds that market and policy orientations positively moderate the impact of employee intentions on value co‐creation. At the organizational level, leadership collaboration awareness and a corporate green innovation culture strengthen the transition from value co‐creation to innovation performance. These findings offer critical theoretical insights and practical pathways for firms seeking to alleviate environmental pressure and achieve sustainable development.

title: Mobilising AI Capability for Sustainable Supply‐Chain Transformation: The Mediating Role of Green Lean Six Sigma
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) capability can be mobilised as a strategic organisational capability for sustainable supply‐chain transformation. Integrating the Natural Resource‐Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study argues that AI‐enabled sensing and decision support do not automatically translate into sustainability outcomes; strategic value emerges when technological resources, managerial competencies, human expertise and process routines are aligned. Green Lean Six Sigma (GLSS) is therefore conceptualised as an organisational architecture that converts AI‐generated insight into disciplined problem definition, waste and variation reduction, process redesign, standardisation and continuous improvement. Survey data from 361 managers and executives in supply‐chain‐intensive organisations across multiple Southeast Asian countries and sectors were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. AI capability is positively associated with GLSS implementation, whereas GLSS is positively associated with environmental, economic and social supply‐chain performance. Significant indirect effects further show that GLSS acts as the transmission mechanism linking AI capability to all three triple‐bottom‐line outcomes. Because the estimated structural model did not include direct AI capability‐to‐performance paths, the evidence is interpreted as support for indirect effects rather than as proof of partial mediation. The study contributes to business strategy and sustainability research by explaining how an AI capability becomes strategically valuable when embedded in a sociotechnical improvement architecture. It also offers a staged managerial road map for harmonising AI investment, GLSS techniques and sustainable business transformation.

title: Environmental Sustainability–Oriented Employer Branding and Employer Attractiveness: The Role of Moral Meaningfulness Across Career Stages
abstract: ABSTRACT As organisations increasingly integrate environmental sustainability into strategic human capital management, understanding how environmentally oriented value commitments shape talent attraction remains important. Drawing on stakeholder theory, signalling theory and social identity theory, this study examines whether environmental sustainability–related employee value proposition attributes influence talent attraction through the moral meaningfulness of work and whether career stage conditions the relationship between moral meaningfulness and attraction. A three‐wave, time‐lagged survey of 242 part‐time higher education students with prior professional experience in the UAE shows that environmental sustainability–related employee value proposition attributes positively predict moral meaningfulness, which in turn predicts talent attraction. Moral meaningfulness significantly mediates the relationship between environmental sustainability–related employee value proposition attributes and talent attraction. Career stage significantly moderates the relationship between moral meaningfulness and talent attraction, with a stronger association among early‐career participants. However, the index of moderated mediation is not significant, indicating that the indirect effect through moral meaningfulness does not statistically differ across career stages. The findings clarify moral meaningfulness as a psychological mechanism linking environmental sustainability–oriented employer branding to talent attraction while identifying career stage as a boundary condition specifically for the moral meaningfulness–attraction relationship.

title: Time Management in Circular Construction: A Systematic Review of Secondary Materials Integration
abstract: ABSTRACT The transition of the building and construction industry towards a circular economy (CE) increasingly relies on the integration of secondary materials. This integration can disrupt the traditional cost, time and quality metrics of project success. While research has extensively examined the technical feasibility (quality) and economic viability (cost) of secondary materials, time implications remain underexplored. This study employs a systematic literature review approach to identify key time‐intensive activities associated with the use of secondary materials in construction, their underlying causes and potential mitigation strategies. Through a review of 41 relevant publications, the study found that time‐intensive activities occur across the project life cycle, including planning, design, predemolition, demolition, waste collection and processing, procurement and construction. These time demands largely arise from misalignments between conventional construction workflows and the requirements of circular practices, coupled with a lack of enabling digital, regulatory, logistical and contractual infrastructures, which increase uncertainty. Accordingly, this study provides recommendations for seven key stakeholder groups, namely, clients, architects and design consultants, builders, demolishers, project managers, procurement managers and policymakers, to help reduce or strategically invest time in ways that better support the integration of secondary materials in construction.

title: Advancing Industrial Symbiosis: The Dynamic Role of Public Organisations
abstract: ABSTRACT Industrial symbiosis is a key circular economy strategy that relies on collaboration among diverse actors to turn residual streams into new value. Although prior research acknowledges supportive public‐sector involvement, there is a lack of understanding of how public organisations' roles evolve over time as industrial symbiosis initiatives develop. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative case study of a regional industrial ecosystem in northern Sweden. Drawing on 25 interviews with public organisations, support actors and producers, five distinct public‐sector roles are identified (policymaker, facilitator, knowledge broker/data provider, participant and financier). The study shows that roles shift across industrial symbiosis development phases, and a framework is developed that links role configurations to phase‐specific barriers. The study contributes by conceptualising public organisations as dynamic ecosystem actors and by offering a practical framework that helps public organisations to align roles with evolving ecosystem needs to support long‐term circular economy transformation.

title: Repair in the Circular Economy: From Fragmented Practices to Strategic Repair Capability
abstract: ABSTRACT Repair is central to the circular economy, yet research remains fragmented across product design, consumer behaviour, business models, community initiatives and policy, limiting understanding of how these dimensions interact to enable repair at scale. This study systematically reviews 79 peer‐reviewed articles using bibliometric mapping, qualitative content analysis and actor‐network analysis. Three interconnected knowledge domains emerge: user and community practices; product design, manufacturing and business models; and policy and governance. Findings show that repair outcomes depend on the alignment of organisational capabilities, ecosystem actors, infrastructure and institutional conditions, while several potentially important actors remain underexplored. Integrating these findings, we conceptualise repair as an ecosystem‐dependent strategic capability for value retention and develop a framework explaining its enabling conditions and interdependencies. The study highlights implications for firms seeking to integrate repair into circular strategies and for policymakers designing supportive repair systems, while identifying research priorities on capability development, ecosystem governance, policy effectiveness and inclusive repair systems.

title: How Circular Economy Practices Drive Sustainable Performance: A Dual‐Moderator Model of Green Culture and Environmental Dynamism in the Hotel Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how circular economy practices (CEP) influence sustainable performance (SP) in the hospitality industry. It explores the mediating role of green supply chain management (GSCM) and investigates how green organizational culture (GOC) and environmental dynamism (ED) moderate the CEP–SP relationship. Data were collected from 425 employees of four‐ and five‐star eco‐friendly hotels in Türkiye using judgmental sampling. Data were analyzed using PLS‐SEM to test the measurement and structural models, including mediation and moderation. CEP did not directly improve sustainable performance. However, GSCM fully mediated the CEP–SP relationship, indicating that circular practices must be operationalized through supply chain processes to create sustainability outcomes. Furthermore, GOC strengthened the positive effect of CEP on SP, highlighting the importance of supportive internal culture. ED also amplified the CEP–SP link, suggesting that dynamic external conditions enhance the effectiveness of circular initiatives.

title: Peer Pressure in Green Innovation: Green Innovation or Greenwashing?
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether a firm engages in green innovation or greenwashing in response to pressure from its business rivals' engagement in green innovation. Using a sample of 2958 firm‐year observations from 720 US publicly listed firms from 2010 to 2023, we find that a gap in green innovation between a focal firm and its top business rivals is significantly and positively associated with the focal firm's greater greenwashing but not green innovation. This effect is more pronounced when the firm is financially constrained, operates in a non‐carbon‐intensive industry, or faces stronger product market competition. These findings provide new insights for investors, policymakers, and scholars into the externalities, showing that rival firms' positive environmental initiatives may generate negative spillovers when focal firms respond opportunistically.

title: Modeling Dynamic Capabilities and Firm Performance: The Moderating Role of Organizational Flexibility and Entrepreneurial Orientation
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates how multiple dynamic capabilities contribute to competitive advantage and firm performance among manufacturing firms in Malaysia. Drawing upon the dynamic capability view, the study examines the effects of research and development capability, big data analytics capability, information technology capability, innovation capability, and marketing capability on competitive advantage, alongside the moderating roles of organizational flexibility and entrepreneurial orientation. Data were collected through an online questionnaire survey involving 226 managers from medium and large manufacturing firms in Malaysia and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. An importance‐performance map analysis was additionally conducted as a complementary analysis to identify which capabilities constitute managerial priorities for strengthening competitive advantage. The findings reveal that all rigorously tested constructs, except marketing capability, positively influence competitive advantage. Entrepreneurial orientation positively moderates the relationship between innovation capability and competitive advantage, whereas organizational flexibility does not significantly moderate the relationship between big data analytics capability and competitive advantage. In addition, competitive advantage significantly improves both market performance and financial performance. This study contributes to the dynamic capability view literature by providing a broader understanding of how multiple complementary organizational capabilities support competitive advantage formation through the processes of sensing opportunities and market changes, seizing strategic opportunities through resource mobilization, and transforming organizational resources and routines under dynamic business environments. The study further extends contemporary strategy literature by highlighting the contextual roles of entrepreneurial orientation and organizational flexibility in influencing the effectiveness of dynamic capabilities within an emerging economy manufacturing context. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that manufacturing firms should prioritize capability alignment, innovation orientation, and digital capability development to sustain competitiveness and improve organizational performance under technological and market turbulence.

title: The paradox of withdrawal: How managerial turnover intention and attitudes shape performance appraisal quality in high-contact service
Too much of a good thing? The curvilinear effects of job clarity on career satisfaction and creativity among hospitality employees
The right endorser for the right stay: How human and AI endorsers shape accommodation booking
abstract: This research examines how endorser presence and endorser type influence consumers’ accommodation booking intention. Drawing on Embodied Cognition Theory, it shows that endorsers shape booking intention by activating embodied mental simulation. It further examines two hospitality-specific factors, booking purpose and service mode, that influence when human and AI-generated endorsers are more effective. Across five experimental studies, we demonstrate that endorser presence increases booking intention via embodied mental simulation. Human endorsers generally produce stronger embodied mental simulation and booking intention than AI-generated endorsers. However, this pattern reverses in high-privacy booking and self-service environments, where AI-generated endorsers are better aligned with the accommodation experiences consumers are imagining. This research extends Embodied Cognition Theory by showing that the effectiveness of embodied cues depends on the match between endorser type and the accommodation experience consumers mentally construct. It also offer practical guidance for hospitality marketers seeking to align endorser strategies with different booking contexts.

title: Bridging R&D project management and tax incentive assessment through a Frascati-based scoring model
Steady at the helm: how CEO early-life disaster experience shapes CEO resilience
abstract: CEOs’ central role in navigating crises makes their resilience—the capacity to withstand and positively adapt to adversity—highly consequential. Drawing on imprinting theory, we propose that CEOs’ early-life disaster experience can foster such resilience. Consistent with the ‘broaden-and-build’ logic, we expect this capacity is reflected in a CEO’s ability to sustain a optimistic orientation in times of crisis. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock, we perform a difference-in-differences analysis on S&P 500 CEOs over 2017–2022. We capture CEO optimism through the positive versus negative tone in CEOs’ emotional displays in earnings-call Q&A responses. We find that CEOs who experienced a disaster between ages 5 and 15 maintain a more optimistic orientation in crisis, and their firms exhibit stronger post-COVID performance recovery. By identifying early-life disaster experience as a foundation for CEO resilience, our findings advance research on the relationship between CEO private life experiences and firm outcomes.

title: From digital skilling to sustainable performance: How climate entrepreneurship and attitudes toward artificial intelligence shape the future of SME technological transitions
abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies respond to environmental pressure, yet two questions remain open. Research linking digital skilling to sustainability has largely tested direct effects without tracing the behavioral pathway such an effect would have to travel, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence have rarely been examined as a condition governing whether green entrepreneurial activity converts into performance. This study addresses both. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, and Contingency Theory into a single explanatory sequence, it models climate entrepreneurship (CE), green entrepreneurial behavior (GEB), and green entrepreneurial intention (GEI) as the mechanisms linking digital entrepreneurial education and training (DEET) to sustainable environmental performance (SEP) and sustainable organizational performance (SOP), with commitment to the environment (CTE) and attitude toward artificial intelligence (ATAI) as boundary conditions. Survey data from 648 Pakistani SMEs are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with a random forest robustness check confirming that the modelled relationships are linear and compensatory. DEET directly predicts organizational performance but has no significant direct effect on environmental performance; its environmental influence is transmitted entirely through the three behavioral mechanisms. Environmental commitment and favorable attitudes toward artificial intelligence each strengthen the conversion of green entrepreneurship into sustainability outcomes, though the interaction effects are modest in magnitude. The findings suggest that digital skilling initiatives are unlikely to yield environmental returns unless paired with entrepreneurial agency and technological openness, with implications for the sequencing of digital and AI-readiness policy in resource-constrained economies.

title: When Apologies Sound Closer: The Role of Brand Nicknames in Apologies Following Service Failure
abstract: ABSTRACT How do subtle self‐referential linguistic choices shape consumers’ responses to service recovery? When apologizing for service failures, firms may refer to themselves using either their formal brand names or brand nicknames. This research examines whether such self‐labeling influences recovery satisfaction. We propose a relational pathway through which firm‐initiated brand nickname usage increases consumers’ psychological closeness to the brand, enhances perceived brand sincerity, and ultimately improves recovery satisfaction. Across seven experiments involving real and fictitious brands and multiple service‐failure contexts, apologies using brand nicknames generally elicited greater recovery satisfaction than those using formal brand names. The indirect‐effect pattern was consistent with a sequential pathway through psychological closeness and perceived brand sincerity. The findings further identify theoretically meaningful boundary conditions: the nickname advantage was attenuated when sincerity was already salient through brand positioning, when apologies were delayed rather than timely, and among consumers with higher power distance beliefs. This research advances understanding of how firm‐initiated brand nickname usage interacts with characteristics of the message source, recipient, and communication context to shape consumer–brand interactions and service‐recovery effectiveness. The findings also offer practical guidance for the strategic design of apology communications.

title: Liquid Death, Moral Debt: Ironic Naming and the Effect on Healthiness Perception
abstract: ABSTRACT Ironic brand names such as “Liquid Death” and “Surreal Cereal” are increasingly common in the marketplace to compete for consumers’ limited attention. Yet, we know little about their downstream consequences for product inferences. Across experiments, we show that ironic names diminish perceptions of product morality, which in turn lowers perceived health. Importantly, we show that this “irony penalty” holds for virtue products (e.g., smoothies) but is attenuated for vice products (e.g., milkshakes), where moral judgment is less salient and expected. Further, we find that providing diagnostic attribute information on packaging reduces reliance on the name's negative semantics and attenuates the irony penalty. We find that although ironic names seem attention‐grabbing, they do not necessarily translate into purchase intention. Our findings contribute to research on brand naming and health inference by identifying when ironic naming backfires and how firms can mitigate this for products where healthfulness is most salient.

title: Scenic spot crowd flow prediction: Combining large language model semantic understanding and spatio-temporal network
Service–Sales Ambidexterity as a Double-Edged Sword: Dual-Path Effects of Frontline Employee Appraisals on Performance
abstract: While prior research suggests that service–sales ambidexterity (SSA) can produce both beneficial and harmful consequences, why it results in positive or negative outcomes is less well understood. Drawing on the transactional theory of stress and job demands–resources theory, we propose and empirically validate a novel conceptual framework of frontline employee (FLE) SSA appraisal. Specifically, we explain how FLEs appraise SSA as a challenge and/or hindrance, and how these appraisals, in turn, influence their performance. A field study reveals that psychological climate shapes FLEs’ SSA appraisals: a promotion climate fosters challenge appraisals, boosting performance via work engagement, while a prevention climate drives hindrance appraisals, reducing performance via burnout. Furthermore, work meaningfulness of serving customers acts as a psychological resource that strengthens the positive effect of SSA challenge appraisal on work engagement and mitigates the detrimental impact of SSA hindrance appraisal on burnout. An experimental study complements the field study by demonstrating the causal effects of psychological climate on SSA appraisal tendencies. The findings contribute novel insights into the dual processes underlying SSA appraisal tendencies and provide actionable guidance for managers seeking to optimize FLE performance.

title: Triangulation as Methodology and Mindset: Developing Practice-Based Guidance for Organizational Research
abstract: Aiming to inform organizational research practice, we scrutinize how scholars in management and business studies report triangulation: the systematic integration of multiple data sources, methodologies, measures, investigators, and/or theories, usually with the objective of enhancing the robustness, validity, richness, and/or complexity of research findings. We analyze 1,209 articles from the UTD24 journal list, using thematic analysis to assess scholars’ use and justification of triangulation as a term of art that spans disciplinary boundaries and qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, and nonempirical methodological approaches. Our findings elucidate triangulation types (method, data, investigator, theory, and measures triangulation); convergence (validity and corroboration) and divergence (richness and complexity) perspectives; and reporting practices at the manuscript level. From this analysis and our examination of exemplars, we abstract triangulation's dual nature: as a root methodology—a foundational tool that transcends methodological boundaries and is deployable across the research process—and a research mindset—an epistemological orientation that engages reflexivity and multiplicity to achieve rigor. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for how to plan for, conduct, report, and evaluate triangulation and discuss our contributions to organizational research methods.

title: The Two Faces of Janus: Dual-Path Moderated Mediation of Observer Responses to Abusive Supervision
The impact of pilot inland free trade zones on household income: Evidence from China
Training and productivity in micro-firms
abstract: This paper examines the effect of training on productivity of micro-firms, defined in official statistics as firms with less than 10 employees. While training may represent a crucial mode of knowledge accumulation in micro-firms, which usually lack resources or structure to devote to formal innovation activities, the specificities of micro-businesses suggest that training may even be detrimental to productivity of this category of firms. Yet, the received wisdom that training should foster their productivity, as it does in larger firms, remains un-tested, mainly due to difficulties in previous literature to analyze micro-firms separately from the wider groups of small or small-medium enterprises. Exploiting a unique administrative panel dataset that records training expenses of a large sample of micro-firms located in three Italian regions, we address whether micro-firms which train enjoy a productivity premium vis-a-vis micro-firms that do not. Our main finding, controlling for endogeneity of training via Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment methods, combined with firm fixed-effects, is a positive and sizable average treatment effect of training, stable across a series of robustness checks and heterogeneity analysis.

title: Promises, Threats, and Norms: A Mixed Methods Study on Bureaucratic Support for Public Participation
abstract: ABSTRACT Public participation can enhance policy quality and democratic legitimacy but may threaten bureaucratic control. We hypothesize that bureaucratic support for participation is higher when policies are less complex and participants are broadly representative. Using a mixed‐methods design involving Indonesian local public servants, we pursue complementarity by combining a 2 × 2 vignette‐based survey experiment with a Gioia analysis of qualitative reflections to explain the experimental results and further illuminate how bureaucrats evaluate participation. The experiment shows that participant representativeness significantly increases support, whereas policy complexity has no statistically significant effect. Integrating the experimental and qualitative data through joint displays reveals that bureaucrats rejecting participation frequently cite participant‐related risks, whereas supporters emphasize instrumental, procedural, and implementation benefits. Normative values, such as citizens' rights and democratic principles, are acknowledged regardless of bureaucrats' overall support. We conclude that bureaucratic support for public participation reflects how officials balance its promises, threats, and normative foundations.

title: Governing Reserves: Managerial Discretion and Government Creditworthiness
abstract: ABSTRACT A government's ability to generate surpluses and build reserves reflects prudent financial management, with the accumulation of reserves signaling sound budgeting practices. Reserves are essential for sound fiscal governance during economic downturns, and managerial discretion over these resources is crucial to minimizing disruptions in service delivery. While the counter‐cyclical benefits of formal reserves are well documented, less attention has been paid to the discretion managers retain over reserves. Using credit ratings as a proxy for creditworthiness, we find that managerial discretion over accumulated resources enhances fiscal flexibility and strengthens creditworthiness; however, the presence of formal reserves alone does not improve credit ratings. Our study contributes to an emerging literature exploring whether better financial reporting can help us understand the critical balance between management flexibility and accountability mechanisms in public‐sector organizations.

title: Economic Governance and Institutional Design
abstract: ABSTRACT How should institutions be designed to achieve compliance with behavioral rules, including laws, social norms, religious rules, or cultural traditions? This conceptual paper introduces a typology of economic governance institutions and explains how it can be used both by policy makers, administrators, and researchers in all social sciences to improve rule compliance. It explains how effective and efficient institutions can be identified for a given economic governance problem. The framework is built on the microeconomic foundations of economic governance theory, and its applicability extends to any compliance problem that can be formalized as a social dilemma or coordination game. The concepts are applied to two cases: how to create trust in cloud computing technologies, and how to implement data sharing of user‐generated information on data‐driven markets.

title: Ownership and Confusion in Employee‐Owned Firms: An Exploration of the EOT Model
abstract: ABSTRACT Based on interviews with employees in UK employee ownership trusts (EOTs), this article interrogates understandings of ‘ownership’ and explores confusion, tensions and frustrations in the lived experience of ownership stemming from employees' dual status as employees and owners. Employees assume that ownership brings various rights, but these often conflict with management understandings, the perspectives of other employees and the limited rights legally embedded in the EOT model. This emphasises the tensions between employee‐owners' legal status as beneficiaries and aspects of their ownership status that are dependent on norms and discourse. Relationships are crucial in developing shared understandings of ownership within the internal ‘community’ of employee‐owners. By showing how relationships shape such understandings and how ownership ‘works’ in practice, the study illuminates how conceptualisations of ownership impact the functioning of EOT firms.

title: Evaluating the validity of performance measurement systems in law enforcement: a pragmatic constructivism approach
abstract: This paper assesses the practical validity of a balanced scorecard-based performance measurement system in a UAE law enforcement agency by examining how well strategic priorities translate into departmental and individual measures. Drawing on pragmatic constructivism, we conduct a single-case qualitative study using manager interviews and archival documents. We find weak translation of strategy into operational indicators and appraisal criteria, uneven awareness of performance indicators, and limited integration of facts, logic, values, and communication, which undermines system validity and strategic alignment. Effective alignment requires clearer cascades from strategy maps to operational indicators and appraisal criteria, role-appropriate access to KPIs, and cross-unit forums connecting planning and appraisal owners. The study’s primary contribution is empirical: it provides evidence of how misalignment emerges between strategy, measures, rewards, and appraisal in a public law enforcement organization. It also elaborates ‘practical validity’ as a criterion for examining how performance measurement systems function in practice.

title: When women lead: women mayors and municipal police effectiveness in reducing homicide in Brazil
abstract: While research highlights women leaders’ influence in traditionally feminine domains such as health, education, and welfare, less is known about their impact in traditionally masculine fields such as policing and crime reduction. Using a Regression Discontinuity design and data from Brazilian municipalities, this study shows that, compared with male mayors, women mayors are more likely to adopt municipal police forces. Municipal policing, in turn, reduces youth homicide rates under women leadership, with this effect amplified by investments in socially oriented infrastructure. These findings demonstrate that women leaders can generate broader community-wide benefits beyond direct representation of women’s interests. The study extends scholarship on gender-responsive governance and women leadership by showing how elected women can shape policy choices and their effectiveness in traditionally male-dominated domains such as policing.

title: A Law of Iterated Expectation Primer for Causal Inference
abstract: The g-formula is a foundational tool for identifying causal effects in observational data. This tool is based on the law of iterated expectation, a key mathematical identity in statistics. However, the notation with which the law of iterated expectation and the g-formula is expressed can be opaque to those with little background in statistics. We provide a primer introducing the law of iterated expectation, the integration notation used to express it, and its role for causal effect identification via the g-formula. Combined with the assumptions of causal consistency, positivity, and conditional exchangeability, the law of iterated expectation yields a causal standardization formula (the g-formula) in two nonparametrically equivalent forms: a non-iterative conditional expectation (NICE) form involving a single weighted average of conditional outcome means, and an iterative conditional expectation (ICE) form involving nested expectations. We illustrate both forms using three progressively complex numerical examples: a time-fixed example with a single binary confounder, a time-fixed example with discrete and continuous confounders, and a time-varying example with two timepoints. We provide clarity on what the law of iterated expectation is, how it is related to the g-formula, and how to gain intuition of its mathematical formulations in actual data examples that can be generalized to a range of settings.

title: Estimate Optimal Dynamic Treatment Regimes with Partial Compatibility: An Application to data from a TREAT Asia HIV Observational Database (TAHOD) site in Pune, India
abstract: Dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) formalize sequences of treatment decision rules that adapt to a patient's evolving clinical status. In observational studies, estimation of the value of a DTR (i.e., the expected population-outcome of a treatment strategy) using inverse probability weighting (IPW) and augmented IPW can be unstable when strict regime compatibility yields few valid participant trajectories, leading to highly variable weights and noisy estimates. In this paper, we introduce two adaptive weighting frameworks: generalized compatibility weighting (GCW) and bootstrap compatibility windowing (BCW), that allow near-compatible trajectories to contribute information in limited samples, with diminishing information-borrowing in larger samples. We illustrate how these estimators reduce noise in estimation and stabilize empirical optimal treatment threshold identification. Using data from adults living with HIV in one site of the TREAT Asia HIV Observational Database in India observed from 2013-2024, we evaluate clinically interpretable threshold-based decision rules based on baseline CD4 count and weight. In this application, GCW and BCW produced more stable estimated regime values than standard IPW-based approaches, with reduced variability across candidate thresholds and more reliable identification of empirically optimal treatment rules. These methods provide practical tools for improving treatment rule evaluation in observational studies.

title: Racial discrimination and preterm birth subtype among a prospective cohort of nulliparous Black women in the United States, 2010-2013
abstract: Racial discrimination has been associated with an increased risk of preterm birth (PTB) among Black women. Few studies have examined whether this association differs by clinical presentation of PTB. We examined the association between racial discrimination and PTB subtype using data from a 2010-2013 clinic-based prospective cohort study of nulliparous women among women who self-reported Black race. Lifetime racial discrimination was measured with the revised Experiences of Discrimination scale. We used inverse probability of exposure and post-stratification weights with the cumulative incidence function to estimate associations between racial discrimination and spontaneous PTB and indicated PTB within a competing risk framework. We estimated standard errors via bootstrapping. We stratified by education and age group to examine effect modification. Compared to none, racial discrimination in ≥3 situations was associated with 1.66 (95% CI, 0.72, 3.82) times the risk of spontaneous PTB and 0.37 (95% CI, 0.15, 0.93) times the risk of indicated PTB. Point estimates between racial discrimination and spontaneous PTB were strongest among women with some college education and ≥20 year-olds. Future studies should consider clinical subtype in assessments of the association between racism and preterm birth and include in the study design late prenatal care initiators.

title: Child maltreatment and reentry of adolescents following reunification in the USA
abstract: Background Adolescents return to foster care for reasons that differ from younger children, yet little research has examined whether these reentries reflect newly reported maltreatment or ongoing behavioral health and family functioning challenges. Understanding these patterns is essential for designing age-appropriate reunification and post-reunification supports. Methods We used linked administrative data from the National Child Abuse and Neglect Data System (NCANDS) with the Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System (AFCARS). Together, these data identify all child maltreatment reports and foster care episodes nationwide. Using a sample of 16,261 adolescents who reunified between the ages of 13–17, we explore the patterns and predictors of rereport and reentry, with an emphasis on understanding variation in repeated system involvement. Among adolescents who reenter, we additionally examine the longitudinal patterns of removal reasons. Results 87% of the adolescent did not reenter foster care after their first foster care episode. Among those who did not reenter, 44% did have a new maltreatment report. Among those who reentered foster care, 36% did not have a new maltreatment report, indicating that maltreatment reports and reentry are only loosely coupled for this age group. Adolescents with more placement instability and shorter stays prior to reunification had higher reentry rates. Implications Adolescent reentry appears driven primarily by unmet behavioral health and family functioning needs, underscoring the importance of stability-focused interventions, behavioral health supports, and post-reunification monitoring tailored to adolescent risk profiles.

title: Understanding Changes in Child Welfare Service Needs in the United States: A Quarter-Century Perspective
abstract: This study examined how caregivers and child welfare professionals reported service needs over 25 years, focusing on housing, legal, mental health, and substance use supports. Using three cohorts of the National Survey of Child and Adolescent Well-Being (1999–2024; N = 6,102), we estimated longitudinal multilevel logistic regression models to assess trends in reported service needs and associations with child, caregiver, and child welfare professional characteristics. Reported housing and legal needs declined modestly, while reported mental health and substance use needs increased. Caregivers consistently reported fewer needs than professionals, and service need trajectories differed between caregivers and child welfare professionals. Racial/ethnic differences persisted, with Black and Hispanic caregivers more likely to report housing needs and less likely to report behavioral health needs relative to White caregivers. Findings highlight evolving perceptions of caregiver service needs and underscore the importance of multi-informant, equity-focused assessment practices within child welfare systems.

title: Fragile ties or sustainable partnerships? Linking social capital between community-based social enterprises and local governments
abstract: Community-based social enterprises (CBSEs) are increasingly recognised as important actors in addressing service gaps in deprived and rural areas. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on their relationships with local governments, particularly through linking social capital. This study examines conditions that shape the quality of linking social capital in CBSE–municipality relationships, adopting a public service ecosystem perspective. The multiple case study of three CBSE ecosystems identifies six interrelated conditions: accountability, recognition, fragmentation, conflicting logics, trust, and expectations, which shows that linking social capital is not a fixed resource but a dynamic and negotiated relational achievement. The study highlights that collaboration outcomes range from enabling to exploitative forms, depending on how these conditions are managed in practice. We contribute to the literature by showing how linking social capital manifests in CBSE–government relationships and provide practical insights for fostering more sustainable and reciprocal forms of collaboration in hybrid local governance contexts.

title: One Big Beautiful Bill? A Preliminary Assessment
abstract: The “One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025” (OBBBA) is a sweeping tax-and-spending package that could reshape federal fiscal policy for decades to come. This paper summarizes the act’s major provisions and provides preliminary analysis. Independent estimates find that the act is expensive, regressive, and unlikely to boost Americans’ income much over the long term. It uses up resources that would otherwise have been sufficient to resolve Social Security’s long-term shortfall. It raises the number of people without health insurance by 10 million. It is broadly unpopular. And it was enacted through a budget procedure that invites future budget abuses.

title: Accurately modeling long-term storage with minimum representative hours in large-scale renewable energy systems
abstract: Energy system optimization often relies on time series aggregation to ensure computational tractability. Aggregation generally loses the chronology of time steps, which renders the storage level representation challenging. Typically, this challenge is addressed by using representative days (RD) to utilize intra-day chronology, even though representative hours (RH) can describe the input time series more accurately at fewer representative time steps than RD. However, until now, the use of RH storage representation methods has been limited by either high computational complexity, poor accuracy in clustering and storage representation, or restricted applicability. Here, we present a novel storage representation method based on RH that combines the high accuracy of RH time series aggregation with the high computational efficiency of methods based on RD. Through benchmarking the four most established storage representation methods on a model of a net-zero European energy system, we find that the proposed method can reduce the solving time by over 95% for the same objective value compared to the most established RD and RH methods. The proposed method exhibits particular strengths at strong aggregations of around 100 to 500 representative hours per year, making the method especially applicable to large-scale and sector-coupled transition pathway models. The developed method for accurately modeling both short-term and long-term storage, along with the presented findings, is of practical relevance to energy system modelers who seek computational tractability in large-scale applications while avoiding the misallocation of storage and conversion capacities.

title: Transferable state-of-charge prediction across temperature domains for lithium-ion and semi-solid batteries
Causality-constrained hierarchical LLM agents for online rule adaptation in building HVAC control
Risk-aware cooperative planning of energy storage in multi-regional power systems under extreme weather: CVaR-based transfer pricing and contribution-based Nash bargaining
abstract: The increasing integration of renewable generation highlights the need for cross-regional resource sharing, especially during extreme-weather events that cause renewable droughts and supply shortages. However, regional differences in renewable profiles, load characteristics, flexibility resources, storage investment potential, and risk exposure make sustained cooperation difficult. System-level cost minimization can lead to uneven support obligations, risk burdens, and benefits among autonomous regions. This paper proposes a risk-aware cooperative energy storage planning framework for multi-regional power systems. The framework first introduces a physical planning model that jointly optimizes the siting and sizing of short- and long-duration energy storage, as well as cross-regional operations under both normal and extreme-weather scenarios. A risk-adjusted transfer-pricing rule combines a load-weighted conditional shadow-price signal with an average conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) allocation charge. The resulting recipient-side prices are used to value outward emergency support and determine contribution-based weights for asymmetric Nash bargaining, which allocates the cooperative surplus under individual-rationality and internal budget-balance constraints. A three-level C&CG–AOP–ADMM procedure is developed for distributed planning and exchange coordination, with exchange valuation and surplus allocation based on regional optimization outputs. Numerical studies on a four-region IEEE RTS-24 system show that cooperation reduces system physical cost by 29.14% and expected load shedding by 48.64% relative to independent regional planning, while the proposed allocation links regional surplus shares to recipient-valued support contributions and satisfies individual rationality and internal budget balance.

title: Learning scheduling-relevant joint uncertainty: Decision-aware compound-risk forecasting for microgrid dispatch
abstract: This paper studies joint probabilistic forecasting for renewable-rich microgrid scheduling, where costly operating outcomes are often caused by simultaneous high load and low renewable generation rather than by a large error in any single variable. The main challenge is to preserve calibrated load, wind, and PV marginals while assigning appropriate probability mass to the joint tail states that matter for dispatch. We propose a Compound-Risk End-to-End (CoRisk-E2E) framework that combines physically feasible marginal forecasting, conditional rank-diffusion scenario generation, compound-stress supervision, and decision-aware training. It preserves non-crossing marginals, captures temporal and cross-variable dependence, and emphasizes high-load and low-renewable conditions through progressive training with a continuous scheduling surrogate. The differentiable scheduling surrogate is used only for training, while all reported operating results are evaluated with the original exact two-stage CVaR MILP. The framework is evaluated in three data settings: the complete Rye load–wind–PV microgrid benchmark, a reduced IEEE load–PV case, and a public load–wind–solar transfer case. The results show that CoRisk-E2E improves joint-tail representation and exact-MILP operating performance, although NoDecision remains competitive on marginal and global scenario metrics. The operational benefit persists in the reduced-source case and the mapped transfer setting under the fixed Rye scheduler, but decreases with stronger domain shift. These findings indicate that explicitly learning scheduling-critical joint tails can improve microgrid decisions, while broader validation on additional complete microgrid systems remains necessary.

title: Environmental synergies and trade-offs in the rapid transition of China's electricity system
abstract: China's power sector is undergoing rapid decarbonisation while simultaneously expanding generation. Although the power sector's greenhouse gas (GHG) emission trajectories under various decarbonisation pathways have been extensively researched, other non-GHG environmental implications remain poorly investigated, particularly due to limited spatially resolved data to trace where the actual impact occurs globally. Therefore, this study employs a spatially explicit life cycle assessment method to evaluate the environmental synergies and trade-offs of China's power sector under two future scenarios in 2050. A comprehensive portfolio of provincial-level, technology-specific life cycle inventories for China's current and future power systems are compiled, incorporating country-specific supply chain processes for key materials. The results show substantial decreases in GHG Emissions, from 5.5 Gt CO 2 eq in 2020 to 3.2 and − 1.02 Gt CO 2 eq by 2050 under the two scenarios. Synergies are observed between GHG Emissions and Particulate Matter Formation, with the latter declining by 31–70% compared to 2020. However, these synergies are accompanied by significant environmental trade-offs, as Land Transformation, Freshwater Eutrophication and Mineral Resource Use increase significantly. Spatially, land and water related impacts are gradually concentrating in China, while mineral related impacts are increasingly spreading to other countries and regions. Provincial contributions to national total impacts are also significantly reshaped under future scenarios because different power system configurations redistribute the ultimate cause of environmental impacts. This study highlights the need for climate policies to balance climate targets with broader environmental considerations for sustainable decarbonisation and to coordinate tailored mitigation across technologies, provinces, and global supply chains to support a more equitable and just transition.

title: China’s dynamic layouts of carbon capture utilization and storage
abstract: Carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) is pivotal to China's carbon neutrality goal by 2060. A national-scale dynamic source-sink matching optimization model is developed to explore CCUS deployment across 31 provinces and 16 sedimentary basins under eight integrated scenarios, which combine two emission pathways (Announced Pledges Scenario, APS; Stated Policies Scenario, STEPS) with four storage growth pathways (CS1–CS4). The model quantifies CO₂ capture from coal-fired power, gas-fired power, steel, cement, and chemical plants, and evaluates storage via enhanced oil recovery (EOR), enhanced gas recovery (EGR), enhanced water recovery (EWR), and enhanced coal bed methane (ECBM). Under the CE1-CS1 pathway cumulative CO₂ capture and storage reaches 11.1 billion tons by 2060 with the Ordos Basin storing 4.24 billion tons. Coal-fired power plants dominate capture contributions, while EWR and EGR emerge as predominant utilization modes. In STEPS, the CE2-CS1 pathway featuring slower emission decline but sustained storage growth yields a cumulative capture of 32.59 billion tons. Hebei, Shanxi, and Shandong collectively account for 26.5% of national capture, with the Ordos Basin storing 8.29 billion tons. Here, EGR and ECBM become the dominant storage strategies, reflecting higher residual emission and extended capture timelines. Economic analysis shows that the CE1-CS1 pathway generates benefits totaling 4849.5 billion yuan. Proximity between major emitters (e.g., Shanxi) and large storage basins (e.g., Ordos) is critical for cost-effective transport. The study highlights that coal-fired power remains the primary CCUS target, while EOR/EGR offer high-value utilization opportunities. These findings provide a data-driven framework for scaling CCUS in China and insights for global carbon management.

title: Reviewing the implementation design of energy subsidy reforms: insights from novel cross-country data
abstract: Over the past two decades, energy subsidy reforms have increasingly gained importance as mitigation measures to fight climate change. Still, many countries subsidize fossil energy consumption, and reforms are often short-lived. This paper presents harmonized cross-country data on the design of energy subsidy reforms, obtained from a structured literature review of both implemented and failed consumption subsidy reforms between 1978 and 2021. This standardized data enables the identification and validation of key design characteristics, including the motivation for reform, the use of gradual approaches, communication strategies, pricing mechanisms, and social protection measures, as well as their use in implementing reforms. The data highlight significant regional heterogeneity and emphasize the importance of context-specificity in shaping reform designs. The study also demonstrates the connection between key aspects of reform design and reform implementation, as well as associations with subsidy levels. It offers lessons for middle-income countries, especially those planning to implement carbon pricing policies. Lastly, this paper lays the groundwork for future research to explore these factors in greater detail; one avenue is to link design characteristics and political economy factors.KEY POLICY INSIGHTS Many reforms fail to reduce subsidies sustainably, a pattern strongly linked to the pricing mechanisms that countries use. Automatic pricing systems and even liberalised prices can still generate subsidies, as the data on subsidy levels suggests, while government-controlled prices often lead to repeated reforms.Gradual subsidy removal improves implementation success compared to one-off approaches, especially in regions with fragile fiscal structures.Government-controlled pricing mechanisms are more often represented in successful implementations. Higher-income countries are better able to manage more complex reforms, such as automatic or liberalized pricing systems.Other insights from energy subsidy reforms are also relevant for countries – especially low- and middle-income nations – considering carbon pricing.

title: Optimizing grassland biodiversity and carbon co-benefits under climate change: An integrated climate-ecological-economic modelling framework
abstract: Managing grasslands for both carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation is increasingly challenging under climate change. We develop an integrated climate–ecological–economic modelling framework to evaluate biodiversity–carbon trade-offs in the Inner Mongolian typical steppe, where mowing and grazing are dominant management practices. Using butterflies as biodiversity indicators, carbon-sequestration estimates, regional opportunity-cost parameters, and downscaled climate projections under SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.5, we applied the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to identify Pareto-optimal mowing–grazing configurations from 2025 to 2050. The simulations indicated that, within the parameterized water-limited response functions, projected precipitation differences were associated with larger shifts in biodiversity–carbon co-management potential than temperature differences. Under the assumptions of our modelling framework, optimized configurations were generally mowing-dominated, with mowing accounting for 77%–94% of the management-allocation matrix in representative 2030 solutions, although grazing-oriented patches remained important in biodiversity-priority outcomes by maintaining habitat heterogeneity. Opportunity-cost accounting provided a regional economic comparison layer for Pareto-optimal configurations, with temporal cost increases mainly reflecting the assumed annual escalation and cross-scenario differences reflecting the cost ranges of feasible Pareto-optimal solutions. Overall, the framework provides a transferable approach for linking climate scenarios, land-use allocation, ecological outcomes, and economic constraints in grassland biodiversity–carbon co-management, subject to recalibration with local ecological, management, and economic parameters.

title: Accommodating electric vehicle charging and water heating within distribution networks: a case study of the Australian Capital Territory
abstract: Electrification and population growth are increasing electricity demand globally. While this makes some infrastructure expansion inevitable, the extent - and cost - of this expansion, is far from inevitable. Existing infrastructure utilization is highly irregular, creating periods of significant spare capacity. If electrified appliances can concentrate their demand within these times, infrastructure expansion can be minimized. This paper presents a reference point for the scale of this opportunity with a case study of the Australian Capital Territory. It uses granular, real-world data and a simple, intuitive approach to scheduling electric vehicle charging and residential water heating. The approach builds policy-maker intuition and parallels Australian government policy that incentivizes daytime demand with three hours of free power. The results indicate that this basic approach, in principle, enables the electrification of 100% of private vehicles and water heating without exacerbating demand beyond the peak demand due to other loads, particularly space heating and cooling. Noting that practical realization of such a result is dependent on specific local context and implementation pathways, two policy implications stand out. Firstly, simple approaches for incentivizing the flexibility of electrified appliances should be acted upon immediately, as a priority; there is no need to wait for more sophisticated solutions. Examples include electricity pricing and setting appliance defaults. Secondly, concerted investment in building thermal performance is required to reduce heating and cooling demand; otherwise heating and cooling demand will drive major network upgrades, even if other electrified appliances operate flexibly.

title: How justice-framed policy narratives shape citizen engagement: Evidence from a survey experiment on time and capital contributions
abstract: Under the dual challenges of global climate change and energy crises, the success of energy transition critically depends on substantive citizen engagement to secure social legitimacy and mobilize distributed resources. However, encouraging such engagement requires moving beyond mere material incentives to resonate with citizens' normative values. This study investigates how energy justice framed policy narratives serve as a key communicative mechanism to foster citizens' willingness to contribute time and capital. Based on a survey experiment with 927 participants, the study designed three narratives reflecting distributional, procedural, and recognition justice compared against a control group. The experimental results indicate that justice-framed narratives can significantly enhance citizens’ policy support, thereby promoting willingness to contribute time and capital, with the rights protection narrative representing procedural justice being the most prominent. Moreover, the effects of different justice-framed policy narratives also vary among citizens with different levels of trust in the government. This study advances the theoretical discourse on just energy transition by elucidating the roles of policy narratives, while offering practical insights to guide governmental communication strategies that foster citizen engagement and promote a just and sustainable energy transition.

title: Firms’ renewable energy adoption and energy taxes: How institutional quality matters
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between environmental energy taxes and firm-level renewable energy adoption, addressing existing literature gaps by providing microeconomic evidence and analyzing the moderating role of institutional quality, the effectiveness of formal and informal institutions in shaping incentives and reducing uncertainty in economic interactions. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data (2018–2020) across a large cross-country sample of firms, the empirical analysis finds that energy taxes are, on average, positively associated with firms’ renewable energy adoption, supporting the Porter Hypothesis. However, the extent of this impact depends on specific firm and country characteristics: it is significantly stronger for large corporations, as well as for firms in higher-income countries and those in environments with superior environmental performance, respectively, while remaining uniform across both manufacturing and service sectors. Additionally, energy taxation upgrades internal capabilities by stimulating R&D and strategic climate planning. Crucially, institutional quality operates through a dual pathway: it exerts a standalone direct influence that encourages firms' renewable adoption, while simultaneously acting as an indirect moderator that makes fiscal policy signals credible. The incentive effect of energy taxes is strictly contingent upon governance, becoming pronounced under higher levels of voice and accountability, control of corruption, and the rule of law. These findings carry clear policy implications, indicating that fiscal instruments and institutional reforms may need to proceed jointly, as energy taxation alone may fail to stimulate green adoption without robust institutional structures.

title: Residential electrification load modeling: A critical review of electric vehicle, heat pump, and integrated modeling frameworks
Deploying low-GWP refrigerants in vapor compression refrigeration systems: performance trade-offs, adoption barriers, and socio-technical pathways
abstract: The global phase-down of high-global-warming-potential (GWP) hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) is accelerating the transition toward low-GWP refrigerants. However, the deployment of low-GWP refrigerants remains constrained by trade-offs among energy efficiency, volumetric cooling capacity (VCC), flammability, cost, and serviceability. A comprehensive evaluation of these interrelated factors is therefore necessary to ensure that refrigerant selection considers not only GWP and thermodynamic performance but also broader practical and environmental considerations. The objective of this review is to provide a unified socio-technical approach to vapor-compression refrigeration cycles (VCRCs) that connects the intrinsic limitations of R744, hydrocarbons (HCs), hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), and refrigerant mixtures with suitable performance enhancement strategies and deployment requirements. The published experimental, numerical, thermodynamic, environmental, economic, and deployment studies are comparatively synthesized based on coefficient of performance (COP), VCC, compressor power, exergy efficiency, safety, cost, regulation, component availability, supply-chain readiness, and workforce capability. Enhancement techniques, such as subcooling, internal heat exchangers (IHXs), ejectors, vortex tubes, nano-lubricants, and multistage compression, are evaluated based on the refrigerant-specific limitations addressed. The representative results show that increasing the ambient temperature from 25 to 35 °C reduced the COP of the transcritical R744 system by 34.8 %, whereas the optimized vortex tube improved the COP by 20.3–21.1 %, cooling capacity by 7.8–11.3 %, and exergy efficiency by 7.9–11.3 %. Life-cycle assessment results also indicated that R744 reduced total emissions by 31.9 % compared with R134a. Overall, the review highlights that no low-GWP refrigerant is universally optimal; rather, refrigerant selection and deployment should be tailored to the refrigerant properties, enhancement technologies, application requirements, climatic conditions, and available infrastructure. The framework provides guidance on refrigerant selection and system design for domestic, supermarket, transport, and industrial refrigeration applications.

title: Overlooked methane in high-density cities: from detection to verifiable mitigation
Volatile and Semi-volatile Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS): Air–Water Partitioning, Atmospheric Emissions, and Environmental Fate and Transport
abstract: Abstract Volatile and semi-volatile per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (V/SV-PFAS) represent a class of PFAS that can partition into the gas phase, enabling atmospheric transport and inhalation exposure pathways that remain poorly understood. Recognizing that air–water partitioning is a fundamental determinant of environmental volatility, this review critically evaluates the current understanding of air–water partitioning coefficients (Kaw), atmospheric emissions, and subsurface occurrence and associated vapor intrusion (VI) risks of V/SV-PFAS. Experimentally determined Kaw values are compiled, highlighting variability spanning multiple orders of magnitude and uncertainties that may arise from limitations of conventional measurement techniques or differences in experimental methodologies. Recent advances, such as thermodynamic cycle methods, are assessed for their potential to expand the range of measurable V/SV-PFAS. Field observations from major atmospheric emission sources, including landfills, wastewater treatment plants, PFAS manufacturing facilities, vadose-zone soil gas at contaminated sites, and indoor environments, are evaluated. Fluorotelomer alcohols dominate V/SV-PFAS profiles, with concentrations of up to 105–106 ng/m3 in landfill and soil gas, 103–104 ng/m3 in industrial indoor air, 103–104 pg/m3 in ambient air near source regions, and 103 to 106 pg/m3 in indoor environments. Addressing critical knowledge gaps in air–water partitioning, source characterization, and subsurface fate and transport is essential for improving V/SV-PFAS exposure assessment and developing effective management strategies.

title: Issue Editorial Masthead
