Inland Migration Space Requirements for Maintaining Blue Carbon Stocks after Spartina Eradication under Accelerating Sea Level Rise
abstract: Abstract China’s nationwide Spartina alterniflora eradication program across 18,000 km of coastline aims to restore native biodiversity, but removing these carbon-rich invasive stands is estimated to release 21.4 Mt CO2. This challenge is compounded by accelerating sea level rise, which threatens the native replacements meant to restore blue carbon functions, and current restoration approaches lack systematic strategies to address both pressures. We coupled species distribution modeling with the Sea Level Affecting Marshes Model (SLAMM) to project the performance of two posteradication restoration strategies─Environmental Suitability (ES, prioritizing habitat preferences) and Optimized Carbon Stock (CS, prioritizing high-carbon species)─under SSP1–2.6 and SSP5–8.5 through 2100, and quantified the minimum inland migration area required to sustain a target carbon stock (2.16 Tg C). Across projections for 2060 and 2100, tidal marshes outside seawalls are projected to lose 23–50% of their area, with carbon stocks declining 12–51% relative to 2021 levels. The CS strategy maintained 6–16% higher carbon stocks than ES. Mainting the target carbon stock required 31–157 km2 of inland migration space, with CS’s advantage over ES in reducing migration requirements narrowing from 37% under SSP1-2.6 (2060) to 4% under SSP5-8.5 (2100). These results show that management strategies lose effectiveness under extreme climate conditions, underscoring the value of early intervention under low-emission scenarios, and offer practical migration-space targets for coastal planning wherever invasive species control intersects with accelerating environmental change.

title: Selective Destabilization of Mineral-Protected Organic Carbon Accompanies Iron Reduction across a Coastal Wetland Salinity Gradient
abstract: Abstract Climate-driven seawater intrusion is intensifying salinization in coastal wetlands, but its consequences for the stability of sediment organic carbon (OC) remain poorly constrained. Here, we combined field observations along a natural salinity gradient with spectroscopic and mineralogical analyses, mineral sorption–desorption experiments, and manipulative incubations to examine the stability of mineral-protected OC. Salt-marsh sediments contained 9.23% less OC than freshwater sediments, with a disproportionate difference in reactive iron-bound OC (FeR-OC). Across the 36 independent field plots, FeR-OC represented 9.80–22.95% of total OC, while the FW–SM FeR-OC difference was numerically equivalent to 64.28% of the corresponding bulk-OC difference. This disproportionate response was associated with a shift from reactive Fe(III)-bearing phases toward Fe(II)-rich products, as well as a weakening of mineral protection, supported by spectroscopic, mineralogical, and geochemical evidence. In salt-marsh incubations, molybdate addition decreased FeR-OC mobilization by 39.51%, identifying a molybdate-sensitive contribution consistent with the sulfate-reduction branch. Together, these results support an iron-unlocking pathway in sulfate-rich coastal wetlands, in which Fe reduction weakens mineral protection and mobilizes previously stabilized OC. This mechanism identifies iron-mediated mineral protection as an important geochemical vulnerability of blue carbon under increasing seawater influence, while the subsequent mineralization, export, or recapture of mobilized OC remains unresolved.

title: Putting Large Language Models into Environmental Context
abstract: Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.

title: A Call to Future-Proof Environmental Science and Engineering

title: Catalyst or Bystander? Disentangling True Catalytic Effects from Confounding Phenomena in Ozone-Based Wastewater Treatment
abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous catalytic ozonation has generated thousands of publications over two decades, with these publications articulating a consistent narrative: catalysts enhance ozone decomposition, generate hydroxyl radicals (or other reactive species), and improve contaminant removal beyond that achievable by use of ozone alone. Despite this narrative, performance gains demonstrated at laboratory scale are routinely inconsistent and poorly reproduced at pilot and industrial scale. This perspective argues that the field suffers from a systematic attribution problem with observed enhancements frequently misattributed to catalytic activity when, instead, they arise from gas–liquid mass transfer modification, pH effects, and/or metal leaching driving homogeneous reactions. Using quantitative modeling, we further demonstrate that faster catalyst-mediated reaction kinetics alone may not translate into meaningful process-level benefits, particularly in full-scale reactors where relatively long hydraulic retention times and constraints on O3 gas–liquid mass transfer can diminish the advantage of kinetic acceleration. A sustained catalytic advantage at scale, therefore, requires not only kinetic acceleration but also more efficient utilization of ozone, an important distinction that has received limited attention in the HCO literature. Based on these findings, we propose a framework that will assist in distinguishing true catalytic pathways from various confounders and will help establish process-relevant benefit of HCO at scale. Overall, this perspective establishes a more rigorous evidentiary basis for translating catalytic activity into reliable wastewater treatment performance.

title: Fate of Perfluoroalkyl Acids during Thermal Regeneration of Hydrotalcite
abstract: Abstract Calcined hydrotalcite (cgHT) is a promising PFAS adsorbent because it may enable PFAS destruction and sorbent regeneration at reduced temperatures. This study evaluated the thermal behavior of PFOS and PFOA adsorbed on cgHT at temperatures ranging from 125 to 550 °C and compared it with their behavior on sand (a reference carrier). Targeted PFAS, total fluorine, and fluoride analyses were used to quantify fluorine-containing products and establish fluorine mass balances across the solid, liquid, and gas phases. For both PFOS and PFOA, more than 75% of the initial fluorine remained associated with cgHT in an unextractable, likely inorganic form. In contrast, less than 40% of the initial fluorine was recovered as fluoride overall from the sand experiments, with less than 6% retained as solid-phase fluoride. Fewer types of volatile organic fluorine byproducts were detected in the cgHT experiments than in the sand experiments. Enhanced PFOS and PFOA degradation on cgHT may involve reactions with the bentonite binder, or the magnesium oxide and water generated from cgHT at elevated temperature. Adsorption and thermal regeneration performance did not change significantly over three adsorption–regeneration cycles. The results support further evaluation of cgHT as a thermally regenerable PFAS sorbent.

A comprehensive validation of an electrical–thermal model for bifacial photovoltaic modules
abstract: This study focuses on the representation of bifacial photovoltaic modules using electrical and thermal models. Various approaches in the literature propose modifications, such as incorporating rear-side irradiance, adjusting resistive parameters and diode currents, and adding series resistances. However, experimental evidence for evaluating these approaches under different operating conditions remains limited. Moreover, most studies concentrate on the maximum power point without analyzing the full IV curve, which can reveal shading-induced steps associated with rear-side frame shading in commercial photovoltaic modules. An integrated electrical and thermal model for bifacial modules is proposed, employing a single-diode model for the electrical component. To represent bifacial behavior, parameters for both front and rear sides are integrated using irradiance-based rescaling, including temperature corrections to derive IV curves and estimate power output. For the thermal component, two approaches are employed, culminating in a hybrid model that selects between the Gu and Faiman formulations according to irradiance conditions. Irradiance estimation is performed using Bifacial Radiance software. Validation of the proposed model involves two tests. The first employs laboratory measurements using an A+A+A+ solar simulator to generate IV curves under controlled conditions. The second uses an outdoor setup with a vertically oriented, east–west bifacial module that continuously monitors irradiance, temperature, voltage, and current. The proposed electrical model reproduced the indoor IV curves with deviations of approximately 3% at the maximum power point. Under outdoor conditions, additional discrepancies were observed and were associated with irradiance variability, temporal resolution, and shading from the module frame and surrounding structure.

title: A thermal battery assisted by proton exchange membrane fuel cell waste heat for coordinated heat and power supply in green industrial parks
abstract: Low-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cell waste-heat recovery is generally investigated through separate heat-supply, heat-pump, storage, or power-recovery routes, leaving the potential of a shared thermal inventory for time-shifted heat–power coordination insufficiently addressed. This study proposes a waste-heat-assisted, multi-output thermal battery for green industrial parks. Under baseline conditions, a 1 MW proton exchange membrane fuel cell with an electrical efficiency of 0.50 yields 850 kW of recoverable liquid-cooling waste heat at 60–65 °C while continuously supplying electricity. The system couples a heat-pump charging cycle with two-tank thermal-oil storage and parallel organic Rankine cycle and direct-steam discharge branches, enabling stored heat to be allocated between additional electricity and saturated process steam. Working-fluid screening combines thermodynamic performance with operating pressure, toxicity, flammability, and regulatory constraints. Although toluene and benzene maximize heat-pump coefficient of performance and organic Rankine cycle efficiency, respectively, cyclopentane provides a balanced engineering compromise and is adopted for the integrated analysis. As the hot-tank temperature increases from 160 to 200 °C, the heat-pump coefficient of performance decreases from 2.730 to 2.114, whereas the energy stored during two hours of charging increases from 2.575 to 3.097 MWh th ; the electricity generated by the organic Rankine cycle during a full-tank discharge simultaneously increases from 247.5 to 370.0 kWh. For the representative 180 °C design supplying 135 °C saturated steam with an organic Rankine cycle oil-flow fraction of 0.5, the thermal-battery-pathway exergy efficiency is 21.325 %; park-level net electricity supply is 0.384 MW during charging and 1.075 MW during discharging, accompanied by 0.294 MW th of steam heat. Over the rated four-hour cycle, net electricity and steam-heat supplies are 2.919 MWh e and 0.588 MWh th , respectively. The thermal battery therefore does not primarily deliver a net increase in cycle electricity; its central value is upgrading low-grade proton exchange membrane fuel cell waste heat and enabling time-decoupled, flexible allocation of heat and electricity through a shared thermal inventory.

title: Optimal design of a solar-driven multistage direct contact membrane distillation system under series and parallel arrangements
abstract: Solar-driven direct contact membrane distillation is promising for decentralized desalination, but limited attention has been given to the techno-economic comparison of series and parallel multistage arrangements within the same solar system. This study develops an hourly time-dependent model of a standalone system integrating photovoltaic/thermal and flat-plate collectors, thermal storage, an auxiliary heater, and multistage membrane distillation under NEOM climatic conditions. The novelty lies in the direct optimization and comparison of both arrangements under identical membrane capacity and common energy constraints. Following a parametric analysis, a single-objective optimization is performed to minimize the levelized cost of water for a fixed capacity of 10 membrane modules by optimizing the collector areas and feed flow rate. The optimized series arrangement achieves a water cost of 1.16 $/m 3 and annual production of 1484 m 3 /yr, compared with 1.61 $/m 3 and 625 m 3 /yr for the parallel arrangement, representing approximately 28% lower cost and 137% higher production. Solar radiation is identified as the most influential parameter, while membrane distillation and flat-plate collectors dominate the total cost. Overall, the series arrangement provides superior techno-economic performance under the investigated capacity and climatic conditions.

DARK FERMENTATION OF CHICKEN MANURE AND CITRUS WASTEWATER FOR RENEWABLE BIOHYDROGEN PRODUCTION: THE ROLE OF MICROBIAL FUNCTIONAL BALANCE
abstract: ABSTRACT Dark fermentation of chicken manure waste and citrus wastewater was evaluated as a strategy to enhance biohydrogen production from agro-industrial residues. Eight batch assays using autochthonous and allochthonous inocula were conducted to assess hydrogen production, metabolite profiles, and microbial community dynamics under different substrate and inoculum configurations. The highest cumulative H 2 production reached 2774 mL H 2 L -1 , corresponding to 0.186 L H 2 g -1 VS added, with faster kinetics and reduced lag phases in the best-performing assays. The observed hydrogen performance was consistent with the established importance of metabolic pathway selection and electron partitioning in mixed culture dark fermentation. High performing systems were characterized by acetate–butyrate fermentation, whereas propionate and C1-related pathways were associated with reduced or delayed hydrogen production. Metagenomic analysis revealed enrichment of hydrogenogenic KEGG Orthologs associated with pyruvate oxidation and [FeFe]-hydrogenases in high-performing reactors. Enhanced hydrogen production was linked to functionally complementary microbial consortia involving hydrolytic and fermentative genera, particularly Bacteroides, Clostridium , and Caldicoprobacter . Overall, the results are consistent with previous evidence highlighting the importance of microbial functional organization and metabolic pathway distribution in determining hydrogen production from mixed agro-industrial substrates, providing mechanistic insights for the optimization of dark fermentation systems.

Energy Crisis and the Renewable-to-Fossil Energy Balance in the European Union: Linear and Nonlinear Evidence, 2009–2024
abstract: Energy crises may either delay or accelerate the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, but the direction of the relationship remains unsettled. This study examines the association between energy-crisis intensity and the renewable-to-fossil energy ratio in 21 European Union countries during 2009–2024. A composite crisis index combines fossil-fuel consumption growth, electricity-price growth, fossil-fuel import dependence, realized declines in physical fossil-fuel imports, and energy inflation. Panel ARDL estimators, common correlated effects mean group (CCEMG), DOLS, FMOLS, a fixed-effects threshold model, and the Juodis–Karavias–Sarafidis predictive test are used. The preferred PMG estimate is negative, and DFE, CCEMG, DOLS, and FMOLS have the same direction; however, the MG estimate is statistically insignificant, and the CCEMG coefficient becomes insignificant when 2021–2022 are excluded. The linear result is therefore neither estimator- nor episode-invariant. The threshold model identifies a tentative, sample-specific regime boundary: the association is negative below it and positive above it. Because the dependent variable is a ratio, a higher value may reflect renewable expansion, fossil-fuel contraction, or both. The one-lag predictive test indicates feedback in both directions, whereas at two lags only crisis-to-ratio predictability remains; neither result establishes structural causality. The results reconcile the barrier and catalyst interpretations of energy crises while showing that policy recommendations concerning grids, storage, and permitting are interpretive implications rather than directly estimated infrastructure effects.

Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk,
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study the causal relationship between trade exposure and individual income risk, with emphasis on the role of human capital. We use a rich worker-level longitudinal dataset from Germany spanning the period 1976-2012, and find industry trade exposure to be causally related to income risk: Imports increase risk and exports decrease risk in an economically significant manner. Importantly, there is a complex interplay between human capital and the linkage between trade and risk: On average, individuals with higher levels of industry- or occupation-specific human capital experience lower risk. However, an increase in industry net imports increases risk more for workers with higher levels of industry tenure. Although net imports are also associated with declines in the mean income of these workers, the estimated effect on income levels is economically small. Our welfare framework, which jointly considers both mean income and income risk, shows that the welfare consequences of trade exposure are quantitatively dominated by the risk channel.

The Largesse design problem
abstract: Abstract Largesse design is a positive theory of what happens when players in a game, who have a limited willingness to sacrifice for the common good, can coordinate on a welfare-optimal solution. This theory provides an alternative to psychological theories in explaining why players engage in costly punishments and rewards. It also says that players will engage in other low-cost methods of encouraging pro-social behavior, for example, through reputation effects. In this paper, I study the properties and comparative statics of the largesse design problem. Despite a lack of concavity in the maximization problem, solutions are unique and continuous except on a lower-dimensional bifurcation set. In examples, I study these bifurcations, in which a small change in the parameters can lead to a large change in behavior or welfare.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: The New Rules of Brand Visibility in AI Search
abstract: As LLM-driven search grows, brands are facing two distinct challenges: visibility and accuracy. For AI search, SEO is now entwined with GEO, generative engine optimization. As zero-click LLM responses replace direct links on search result pages, new metrics are replacing traditional traffic analytics. New research suggests ways leaders can ensure that their brands become more visible, more accurately represented, and more competitively positioned over time.

title: Dual‐Audit Governance and Sustainability Reporting for Environmental Innovation: International Evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how external sustainability assurance (EA) and internal audit reporting (IA) relate to sustainability reporting (SR) and environmental innovation (GI). Using 10,092 firm‐year observations from 1937 firms across 18 countries over 2010–2024, we employ LASSO‐guided two‐way fixed‐effects models supplemented by fixed‐effects instrumental‐variable estimation, clustered bootstrap path analysis, interaction tests, multiway clustering, and propensity‐score methods. Results show that EA and IA are positively associated with SR, while SR is positively associated with GI. Both contemporaneous indirect associations are also positive and remain stable across alternative control sets and richer fixed‐effects structures. However, the preferred within‐firm interaction is insignificant, instrumental‐variable estimates do not support causal interpretation, and entry into a positive external assurance score predicts stronger reporting but not subsequent innovation. The findings position external assurance and internal audit as additive governance mechanisms linked to reporting within observed firms, rather than evidence of causal mediation, substitution, complementarity, or hierarchical dominance.

title: Navigating Carbon Accounting in Manufacturing From Compliance to Decarbonisation
abstract: ABSTRACT Carbon accounting is increasingly mandated in manufacturing; however, its implementation remains fragmented between corporate reporting and product‐level assessments, limiting its effectiveness for decarbonisation. This study analyses the regulatory landscape in the United Kingdom and the European Union, identifying a structural misalignment among reporting requirements, methodological choices and operational decision‐making. To address this issue, a decision‐oriented carbon accounting framework is proposed to enable consistent, decision‐relevant application across manufacturing systems. The framework connects reporting drivers, system boundaries and data availability to methodological selection through a structured decision architecture. It introduces data specificity as a guiding principle to facilitate the progression from spend‐based screening to hybrid and activity‐based life‐cycle approaches across Scopes 1, 2 and 3. Through a unified structure, the framework integrates corporate‐ and product‐level accounting, coherent under overlapping regulatory regimes. Scenario‐based applications illustrate that aligning methodological complexity with data availability enhances comparability, hotspot identification and supply chain engagement. These improvements support targeted interventions in production systems and the development of credible carbon reduction strategies. The framework repositions carbon accounting from a compliance‐driven activity to a core capability for cleaner production, enabling actionable emissions reduction measures and supporting industrial decarbonisation pathways.

Neighborhood walkability, green space, and incident hip fracture among older U.S. adults: The cardiovascular health study
abstract: PURPOSE: Neighborhood walkability and green space are associated with walking behavior and physical activity, but evidence linking them to fracture is limited and inconsistent, and potential sex differences remain understudied. We evaluated associations of neighborhood walkability and green space with incident hip fracture in older, community-dwelling U.S. adults. METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults aged ≥65 years from the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS). Neighborhood exposures were defined using 1-km radial buffers around geocoded residential addresses from 1992-1993 (baseline). Walkability was the sum of standardized population and walkable destination densities. Green space was the proportion of satellite-derived green land cover. Hip fractures were prospectively ascertained over 12 years using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9) codes from hospital discharge abstracts. Cox hazard models adjusted for individual-level (age, sex, race, weight, height, smoking status, current heavy alcohol use, medication use, diabetes, renal function, marital status, education level, annual household income) and neighborhood-level (median household income, median value of owner-occupied housing, proportion of persons in managerial/professional occupations) covariates evaluated associations, overall and by sex. RESULTS: Among 3,676 participants (58% women), 359 experienced hip fracture over a median 10-years observation. Greater neighborhood walkability was significantly associated with lower hip fracture incidence among women (hazard ratio per 1 standard deviation increase of 0.72 [95% confidence interval, 0.53-0.98]), but not overall or among men. Neighborhood green space was not significantly associated with hip fracture. CONCLUSION: Greater neighborhood walkability, but not green space, was associated with lower hip fracture risk among older women.

title: Hydrogen-rich syngas production via biomass pyrolysis catalyzed by iron co-loaded with biochar and aluminum smelting fly ash: Tar formation and component characteristics
abstract: Biomass pyrolysis for hydrogen production is generally regarded as a crucial technological pathway to achieve the carbon neutrality goals, whereas the corresponding system efficiency and environmental friendliness are significantly constrained by the generation of tar byproducts. In this study, the iron-based carbon-aluminum (Fe/Carbon-AWA) composite catalyst was prepared via the hydrothermal carbonization method using corn straw (CS) as the carbon-based precursor, and activated aluminum smelting ash (AWA) as the support. Besides. its catalytic effect on hydrogen production performance was systematically investigated, and the intrinsic relationship between tar conversion and hydrogen yield was further elaborated. The results demonstrate that when the Fe loading reaches 10%, the catalyst exhibits optimal catalytic activity with a hydrogen yield of 64.36 mL/g -biomass , a hydrogen selectivity of 39.96%. Meanwhile, the total gas yield of 161.06 mL/g -biomass can be achieved, accounting for 43.77% of the total product yield, whereas the liquid yield decreases to 36.44%. The full-component analysis of tar indicates that the light tar fractions are primarily composed of oxygenated compounds. In contrast, the heavy tar fractions are dominated by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with a pyrolysis weight loss rate of only 54.24%. This limited pyrolytic reactivity represents the critical bottleneck in the tar conversion. It reveals that the Fe/Carbon-AWA catalyst can remarkably promote the cracking and conversion of refractory heavy tar components, and thereby the chemical energy stored in tar is partially converted into the hydrogen-rich syngas, resulting in an energy recovery efficiency of 17.72% and a carbon efficiency of 8.02%. Accordingly, this comprehensive strategy with the combination of waste-to-waste catalyst design and full-component analysis of tar was established. This work provides a feasible pathway for the synergistic development of biomass-based hydrogen production and waste valorization, which contributes to the efficient process integration and systematic optimization of biomass energy systems.

title: Spatio-temporal characteristics of microplastics in river surface water: insights from multi-year field monitoring
abstract: Despite the well-established role of rivers as the primary pathway for microplastics from land to sea, the effect of seasonal hydrological signals on riverine microplastic loads is still a matter of considerable controversy. This study conducted four seasonal sampling campaigns (rainy and dry seasons) over two consecutive hydrological years to clarify the spatiotemporal patterns and key drivers of microplastic occurrence in rivers from an interannual perspective. Across both hydrological years, microplastic abundance was consistently higher during the dry season (49.13 and 51.45 n/m 3 ) than during the rainy season (36.38 and 29.70 n/m 3 ), a pattern primarily driven by the dilution effect of elevated river discharge. Urban point sources were identified as the dominant contributors to microplastic pollution, generating persistent contamination hotspots. Interestingly, we observed a pronounced spatial decoupling between abundance hotspots (W9 and W15) and flux hotspots (W11 and W15). Since microplastic flux is less sensitive to dilution, flux-based assessments more accurately reflect the in-situ pollutant loads and ecological risks than abundance-based ones. Additionally, we have established a linear relationship between microplastic flux and river discharge, offering a valuable tool for extrapolating results from short-term baseline studies to long-term flux dynamics. Collectively, these findings provide a scientific basis for developing long-term monitoring and mitigation strategies for microplastics at the catchment scale.

title: How ESG dimensions shape corporate green innovation: Necessary-condition thresholds, causal asymmetry, and the resource curse
abstract: Whether ESG dimensions shape green innovation through consistent mechanisms remains contested, in part because ESG rating divergence can alter empirical conclusions. Using three independent ESG data sources (Huazheng, CNRDS, Runling Global) and a multi-method design (fixed effects, NCA, fsQCA) covering Chinese listed firms (2015–2023), we document a construct-asymmetry thesis : ESG dimensions do not have uniform roles across rating sources. In the Huazheng sample, Governance (G) and Environmental (E) dimensions are necessary conditions for substantive green innovation (d > 0.28); in two independent ratings, the necessity pattern shifts toward the Social (S) dimension, while G necessity disappears. This divergence is not an artifact of sample composition — it persists in a matched same-firm sample — but reflects systematic differences in how rating agencies operationalize governance and social responsibility. Despite this measurement sensitivity, failure configurations are more identifiable than success recipes — a pattern consistent with the panel and NCA evidence across sources — and the average facilitative effect of G on strategic innovation is directionally consistent. Our findings suggest that the ESG–green innovation relationship is more method- and construct-dependent than previously assumed, and that multi-source validation is indispensable for credible ESG–innovation research.

Oxygen vacancy regulation and morphological engineering: Study on the construction and synergistic mechanism of Fe-doped BiOBr/activated carbon composite photocatalysts
abstract: A bulk photocatalyst (Fe-BiOBr/AC) was constructed by loading Fe-doped BiOBr onto activated carbon (AC). The synergistic enhancement mechanism of the material structure, photoelectrical properties, and catalytic performance induced by AC introduction was systematically investigated. Characterization results revealed that AC not only served as a high-surface-area support providing nucleation sites for in situ growth of Fe-BiOBr, but also promoted the formation of defect-related sites, including oxygen vacancies, on the composite surface through structural regulation. Meanwhile, Fe doping further modulated the local chemical environment of Fe-free counterpart and contributed to improved charge-transfer behavior. The optimal sample Fe-BiOBr/AC8 demonstrated significantly superior degradation efficiency to that of Fe-BiOBr for both the typical organic dye Crystal Violet (CV) and practical wastewater. This superior performance mainly originated from the enhanced adsorption capacity and defect-related active sites provided by AC loading, while Fe doping further promoted favorable charge-transfer characteristics. Moreover, AC loading facilitated the transformation of the catalyst from a powder state to a macroscopic bulk structure, successfully overcoming the technical challenge of nanocatalysts separation and recycling within suspension systems.

title: The conservation benefits of fallows for farmland birds depend on local farmland structure in Central Europe
abstract: Fallows are a cornerstone of farmland biodiversity conservation in Europe, yet their effectiveness varies regionally. In this study, we examined how local structural features of farmland, specifically field size and land-use heterogeneity, influence bird responses to fallows in Central Europe. We surveyed 408 study sites in agricultural landscapes of Slovakia and Austria, recording 2947 individuals of 51 bird species. We then quantified overall bird abundance, species richness, and the abundances of functional guilds defined by nesting strategy, trophic level, and habitat preference. Both bird abundance and diversity increased with increasing fallow area and land-use heterogeneity and decreased with increasing mean field size. However, the benefits of fallows were context dependent: the positive interaction between fallow area and mean field size indicated that the negative effect of large fields weakened as fallow area increased. Among bird guilds, ground-nesting species, open-habitat birds, and insectivores showed the same pattern, with fallows partly offsetting the negative effects of large fields. Fallows also had positive effects on the abundance of arboreal and hole-nesting birds, granivores, and insectivores, while land-use heterogeneity positively affected several guilds, including open-habitat species and granivores. These findings highlight the importance of tailoring fallow-based conservation to the local farmland context. In post-socialist regions dominated by large fields, fallows can partly compensate for the negative effects of field consolidation on bird communities and thus provide a pragmatic pathway for biodiversity recovery without requiring fundamental changes to land ownership or parcel structure. At the same time, land-use heterogeneity remained beneficial, supporting higher bird abundance and diversity in farmland.

title: Submarine groundwater discharge: An overlooked but quantifiable pathway for microplastics inputs to the coastal ocean
A Carbon–Water nexus framework for agricultural systems: Insights from Turkish agriculture
abstract: Agricultural sustainability is constrained by water scarcity and climate change, necessitating integrated approaches that move beyond single-indicator assessments. This review synthesizes carbon footprint (CF) and water footprint (WF) evidence within a carbon–water nexus perspective using Turkish agricultural as a case study. A literature-based dataset was constructed by combining reported CF values with observed and benchmark WF data from national and global sources. Three complementary approaches were applied: (i) carbon–water efficiency frontier analysis based on a Pareto framework, (ii) irrigation carbon penalty assessment using blue water use–emission relationships, and (iii) variability analysis of CF consistency across studies. The integrated comparison reveals a non-linear pattern between CF and WF, with agricultural systems clustering into distinct environmental regimes. Efficiency frontier analysis identifies non-dominated systems characterized by relatively balanced resource use, while irrigation-intensive systems consistently emerge as environmental hotspots. The irrigation carbon penalty perspective indicates that increasing blue water use is generally associated with higher carbon emissions due to energy requirements; however, the magnitude of this effect varies across crops, indicating strong system dependency. In addition, substantial variability in reported CF values highlights the influence of methodological choices and system boundaries on footprint estimates. These findings demonstrate that sustainability in agricultural systems cannot be adequately assessed through isolated metrics and require integrated, nexus-based approaches. The synthesis framework provides a basis for identifying priority mitigation areas and supports crop-specific and context-sensitive management strategies. While developed for Türkiye, the proposed approach is transferable to other regions facing similar challenges related to water scarcity, agricultural intensification, and decarbonization.

title: Incorporation of granulated organic materials boosts soil quality and multifunctionality in infertile croplands
Effects and driving mechanisms of short-term fertilization on the carbon pool management index in lightly degraded alpine marsh wetlands
abstract: The carbon pool management index (CPMI) is a sensitive indicator for assessing degraded ecosystem restoration, but how fertilization affects CPMI in alpine marsh wetlands remains unclear. We conducted a two-factor, three-level field experiment in a lightly degraded alpine marsh wetland using organic fertilizer (O0, O1800, and O2700, i.e., 0, 1800, and 2700 g m −2 ) and Bacillus subtilis (J0, J5, and J10, i.e., 0, 5, and 10 g m −2 ). Two-way ANOVA, correlation analysis, random forest, and structural equation modeling were used to investigate the effects and driving mechanisms of short-term fertilization on CPMI. The results showed that organic fertilizer and its interaction with bacterial fertilizer significantly affected CPMI, indicating that the effect of bacterial fertilizer depended on the organic fertilizer background. Under O0, J5 and J10 increased CPMI by 64.80% and 42.12%, respectively. In contrast, under O1800 and O2700, the addition of bacterial fertilizer showed a decreasing trend in CPMI. Correlation analysis indicated that easily oxidizable organic carbon, soil organic carbon, alkaline hydrolyzable nitrogen and pH were significantly correlated with CPMI. Random forest analysis showed that fungal Shannon diversity and available phosphorus were the most important predictors of CPMI, highlighting the roles of fungal communities and phosphorus availability. Partial least squares structural equation modeling indicated that fertilization indirectly influenced CPMI mainly through soil properties and labile carbon pools (GOF = 0.42). This study reveals how short-term fertilization regulates carbon pool management in lightly degraded alpine marsh wetlands. It also shows that bacterial fertilizer effects depend strongly on the organic fertilizer background.

title: How storage type and weather govern rainwater quality?
Scale dependent coupling and transfer limits of ecosystem carbon and water use efficiency across an inland river basin
abstract: Sustainable management of inland river basins requires joint assessment of carbon retention and water loss, yet the relation between these efficiencies across sites and within sites remains unclear. The study utilized data from 17 eddy covariance observation sites in the Heihe River Basin from 2008 to 2024 to reconstruct the carbon and water records. The study employed two indicators of ecosystem carbon use efficiency (CUE) and water use efficiency (WUE), and conducted a comprehensive analysis through gradient analysis, mixed models, specific scale coupling, XGBoost-SHAP, and year-site validation methods. The results showed that first environmental component explained 63.0% of the variance among site environments. Mean CUE was 0.578, 0.589, and 0.413 upstream, midstream, and downstream, respectively. The corresponding WUE means were 1.51, 2.26, and 1.22 g C/kg H 2 O respectively. Water supply and atmospheric demand accounted for 57 to 66% of absolute CUE model attribution across reaches, while energy variables accounted for 53 to 61% of absolute WUE attribution. When complete years were excluded, basin prediction R 2 was 0.377 for CUE and 0.689 for WUE. When complete sites were excluded, R 2 was −0.158 and 0.459, respectively. Annual CUE and WUE deviations were positively associated downstream, but spatial transfer of downstream WUE was poor. Joint assessment of both efficiencies therefore informs monitoring, while predictions at unmonitored sites require local validation.

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Disagreement of disagreement
abstract: We show that leading investor disagreement proxies have near-zero cross-correlation – making disagreement pricing inferences challenging. We develop a frictionless model that generates overpricing from latent disagreement, jointly rationalizes major proxies, and generates new testable predictions. Equilibrium interrelationships motivate a new disagreement measure, DIS, which is more predictive of returns cross-sectionally than major proxies and more consistently predictive across macroeconomic regimes. We provide evidence that the friction-based channel of Miller (1977) and a frictionless mechanism coexist and are empirically separable. DIS also provides a micro-founded, disagreement-based account of the IVOL puzzle, absorbing IVOL’s predictability while revealing its regime and friction dependence.

title: PROXIMAL ESTIMATION AND INFERENCE
abstract: Abstract We develop a convex-analytic framework for constructing and analyzing a broad class of penalized estimators. Our method defines penalized estimators by applying proximal operators to benchmark estimators, rather than by penalizing the benchmark criterion itself. We establish general finite-sample properties, derive unified asymptotic distribution results, and provide tractable conditions for oracle selection and oracle asymptotic efficiency. We then apply the framework to linear regression with irregular designs, including singular and nearly-singular cases. In this setting, where the coefficient vector need not be point identified, we motivate the Ridgeless estimand as the inferential target, construct a n $\sqrt {n}$ StartRoot n EndRoot -consistent modified Ridgeless benchmark estimator, and combine it with adaptive proximal penalization to obtain, to the best of our knowledge, the first penalized estimator achieving the oracle property under both regular and irregular designs.

title: The Dynamics of the Racial Wealth Gap
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race. We find that equalizing earnings is critical for permanent reductions in racial wealth inequality, and that one‐time transfers will have only transitory effects unless earnings are also equalized. Our results are robust to the introduction of racial differences in returns to saving, which only matter after earnings inequality is reduced.

title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life.

title: Violence and capital accumulation in Colombia: the dominant social bloc of the 2000s
abstract: This article addresses a puzzle in analysing Colombia’s political economy: the coexistence of macroeconomic stability with persistent armed conflict, illicit economies and high levels of inequality. Drawing on the concept of the Dominant Social Bloc (DSB) developed by Bruno Amable and Stefano Palombarini, it argues that violence and illicit economies were not external to Colombia’s accumulation regime during the 2000s but were incorporated into the coalition that sustained it. By adapting the DSB framework to Colombia, the article incorporates economic dependency, armed conflict, and drug trafficking into the analysis. Based on qualitative evidence from public discourse and political positioning, the article identifies a DSB comprising domestic and foreign capital, landowners, narco-paramilitary actors, and segments of subaltern groups. It shows how a political strategy centred on security and foreign investment aligned the expectations of these actors and secured their political support, articulating economic, coercive, territorial, and symbolic power into a relatively stable coalition. More broadly, the article contributes to political economy debates by showing how violence and crime can become embedded within the coalitions that sustain accumulation regimes.

title: The economic costs of green state derisking: evidence from Germany’s energy transition
