AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .

title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Financial support from the Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe Experiment Center Frankfurt [Grant 232406], the Interdisciplinary Public Policy Mainz [Grant A2021011], and the Mainzer Wissenschaftsstiftung is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01818 .

title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

title: When format boundaries collapse: Price reactions of conventional retailers to national-brand listings at hard discounters
Judge financial holdings and case outcomes: Evidence from judge financial disclosures
Video-Based Deception Detection and Financial Fraud
An Application of Machine Learning and Textual Analytics for Visualisation and Enhanced Interpretation of Sustainability Disclosure
abstract: ABSTRACT Social and environmental accounting provides accountability mechanisms through which organisations communicate their sustainability practices to stakeholders. However, the increasing volume, complexity and diversity of sustainability disclosures make manual content analysis both labour‐intensive and susceptible to subjectivity. Machine learning and textual analytics offer promising approaches for systematically processing and visualising large qualitative datasets with greater consistency and transparency. This study explores how machine learning‐based textual analytics can be used to collect, analyse and visualise sustainability disclosure data in ways that enhance public accountability. More specifically, it focuses on how local governments use language to construct and communicate their sustainability commitments and performance. The empirical material consists of 237 annual reports from 79 local government areas in Victoria, Australia, covering the period 2015–2017. Drawing on a realist constructionist ontology, machine learning theory and stakeholder theory, the authors develop a machine learning‐based approach that transforms unstructured qualitative data into measurable insights. The methodology integrates VADER sentiment analysis, Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modelling and Doc2Vec embeddings with cosine similarity to assess the comprehensiveness of sustainability disclosures. The analysis reveals that sustainability disclosures exhibit predominantly positive to neutral sentiment, with the dominant themes relating to financial and environmental challenges. The reports were categorised into three comprehensiveness levels, with the majority demonstrating a medium level of sustainability disclosure. Temporal analysis further suggests distinct patterns in how local governments frame sustainability initiatives and indicates that sustainability is conceptualised as a multidimensional construct. The study makes a methodological contribution by demonstrating how machine learning can enhance the rigour, scalability and transparency of sustainability accounting research. It also extends realist constructionist ontology into the domain of computational analysis and provides practical benchmarking tools for local governments. For stakeholders, the proposed visualisation techniques offer methods for assessing public sector sustainability accountability.

title: Competencies for Sustainable Development in Entrepreneurship: A Bibliometric Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainability has become one of society's main concerns and, with it, the development of the competencies necessary to achieve and contribute to sustainable development. In this sense, the entrepreneur as an agent of change toward a sustainable world is fundamental. This paper contributes to the knowledge on competencies for sustainable development in entrepreneurship by conducting a bibliometric analysis. The results show significant growth in the literature, especially since 2017, and reveal five thematic clusters linked to individual and strategic capabilities for sustainable performance, sustainable entrepreneurship ecosystems, education for sustainable entrepreneurship, social entrepreneurship and digital transformation in emerging economies, and women's empowerment and well‐being. This study demonstrates that competencies for sustainable development are a key element enabling entrepreneurs to transform social and environmental challenges into opportunities for innovation, value creation, and transition toward more sustainable business models. Furthermore, future research lines are suggested to further explore entrepreneurship based on sustainable competencies.

title: Barriers to Engagement in Circular Business Models Among Small and Medium‐Sized Enterprises: Evidence From the Irish Construction, Manufacturing and Retail/Wholesale Sectors
abstract: ABSTRACT Although circular business models (CBMs) are central to the circular economy (CE) transition, their adoption among small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) remains limited, and evidence on barrier variation across CBMs and sectors is scarce. This study examines barriers to engagement in five CBM activities, spanning secondary raw material use, takeback, repair/maintenance, remanufacturing/refurbishment and leasing/rental, using a survey of 452 Irish SMEs in construction, manufacturing and retail/wholesale, in which respondents rated barriers for each activity. Barrier importance proves strongly contingent on CBM activity and sector, with variation also evident across firm characteristics. Only two barriers, secondary raw material costs and upfront costs of leasing/rental, are high‐priority in all sectors; several recur across sector pairs, while most bind in single activity–sector combinations. Resource‐based, institutional and contingency perspectives help explain this patterning. The findings move CBM barrier research beyond descriptive classification, provide systematic evidence on SMEs and inform more effective CE policymaking.

title: When and How Do Women Directors Matter for Corporate Sustainability? The French Case
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines when and how board gender diversity matters for corporate sustainability. Using a sample of French listed firms over 2006–2024, we combine dynamic system GMM estimations with difference‐in‐differences tests around France's phased board gender quotas. The results show that greater female board representation is associated with stronger ESG performance, but that this relationship is highly contingent. It becomes substantially stronger once women attain meaningful representation, with the clearest evidence emerging around 30% of board seats and approximately four women directors. Consistently, the 20% regulatory threshold produces no significant ESG effect, whereas the 40% requirement is followed by significant improvements among initially non‐compliant firms. Decomposing ESG performance reveals particularly strong associations with social performance, stakeholder engagement, and product responsibility, but a negative association with environmental innovation. Finally, the relationship is concentrated among financially stronger firms and firms with powerful CEOs. Overall, the findings show that the sustainability consequences of board gender diversity depend on representation, the ESG dimension considered, and organizational context.

title: Circular Economy Disclosure in Europe's Automotive Sector: An Analysis of Reporting Patterns
abstract: ABSTRACT According to the European Circular Economy Action Plan, the automotive industry plays a key role in Europe's transition to a circular economy (CE). Industry‐specific legislation and upcoming reporting guidelines raise the question of the current CE implementation level, which is still an underexplored research field. Based on 77 corporate reports from European automotive companies, a content analysis is conducted using a mix of a deductive and inductive code system to examine CE disclosure in terms of its reporting patterns. Overall, a wide range of CE practices are already being pursued. However, the automotive industry focuses on more easily implementable practices such as reduce and recycle activities. Frequently disclosed CE practices are generally described in more detail than those reported less often. Furthermore, the reports lack specific targets and quantitative statements. Lastly, supply chain position, compliance with voluntary reporting guidelines, and external assurance are associated with CE disclosure.

title: Cultural value configurations and guests’ evaluations of AI-enabled service technologies
abstract: As Artificial Intelligence reshapes hospitality service delivery, understanding how culturally diverse guests evaluate AI-enabled encounters is critical. This study examines how cultural value configurations shape evaluations of service robots in hotels. Cultural value configurations are coherent combinations of orientations that jointly influence how individuals interpret and assess service encounters. Using more than 3000 robot-related hotel reviews from guests across 77 countries, we integrate Hofstede’s dimensions with Schwartz’s value theory to explain cross-cultural differences in sentiment. Masculinity and uncertainty avoidance predict more negative sentiment, individualism shows a positive association that is sensitive to model specification, and power distance shows no direct effect. One configuration is robust: masculinity combined with uncertainty avoidance amplifies dissatisfaction, and this interaction holds under multilevel and combined estimation and survives correction for multiple testing. Two further configurations remain suggestive: power distance combined with uncertainty avoidance attenuates risk aversion, and individualism combined with masculinity increases tolerance for imperfection. Both are marginal and do not persist under multilevel or joint estimation, so we report them as patterns for replication rather than as established effects. Hofstede’s indices provide the measurement, while Schwartz’s value theory serves as an interpretive lens rather than as a measured individual-level construct. Findings position culture as a configurational system and provide guidance for AI service design and communication.

title: When politics matter as a contingency factor: Comparing hotel customer satisfaction in Cuba and Western nations
abstract: This study explores differences in service delivery in hotels in Cuba, a collectivist economy, and in comparable hotels in Western countries, including Mexico, the Dominican Republic, and Spain. This research extends contingency theory in tourism by incorporating governance quality as a moderating contextual factor and introducing cultural decoupling as a mechanism explaining how governance contexts shape service outcomes across contexts. Customer satisfaction research in collectivist economies examines governance influences. Data was collected through web scraping of customer reviews from major hotel chains on TripAdvisor. robust regressions, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), multivariate analysis. Contextual differences and governance quality indicators were estimated using variance (MANOVA), and matching procedures with Mahalanobis distance. The study identifies contextual differences in customer satisfaction and service quality evaluations between Cuba and Western countries. The contingency factor of governance quality and its dimensions, regulatory quality and voice plus accountability, show negative and significant effects.

title: Pet-friendliness in hospitality and tourism: Definition, scope, and governance
abstract: Pet-friendliness is a widely used hospitality label, yet it remains poorly defined and inconsistently specified. This paper clarifies what pet-friendly tourism means and how its scope is delimited within hospitality and tourism. Drawing on a systematic literature review and evidence from a global mixed-method survey, it shows that pet-friendliness extends beyond unrestricted pet access or isolated amenities and operates as a governance-mediated form of conditional inclusion supported by clear rules, appropriate infrastructure, staff practices, welfare, hygiene, safety, and coexistence management. Respondents converge on a stable core meaning, with variation arising primarily around tolerance for partial or restrictive arrangements. The findings provide an operational definition that can guide more comparable hospitality research, policy development, and managerial decision-making.

title: A structured framework for improving digital transformation maturity in food supply chains
abstract: Purpose Digital transformation is the transition from traditional to digital supply chains, enabled by emerging technologies. A digital transformation maturity assessment is necessary to manage this transition effectively. However, existing maturity frameworks for digital transformation in supply chains lack a structured process with detailed actions guiding maturity improvement. This research, therefore, aims to develop a digital transformation maturity improvement framework with evidence from food supply chains (FSCs). Design/methodology/approach In-depth case studies conducted in two food companies were used to gain insights into the digital transformation journey. Adopting diffusion of innovation (DOI) theory, a seven-step maturity improvement process was established, taking into account context-specific influences. Insights obtained from 32 FSC practitioners through a workshop were used to confirm the framework and identify additional improvement actions. Findings The developed prescriptive digital transformation maturity improvement framework presents a circular improvement process, beginning with an evaluation of the current digital transformation status and progressing through the seven steps (initiation planning, alignment, preparation, configuration, pilot testing, scaling and sustaining), followed by re-evaluation to support continuous improvement. The identified internal and external contextual influences highlight their relevance to FSCs. Step-specific actions are provided for advancing digital transformation maturity. Originality/value This study extends the application of DOI theory to develop a maturity improvement process for digital transformation in FSCs. It enriches the understanding of DOI by emphasising the “sustaining” step, which aims to maintain achieved maturity levels and accommodate the evolving nature of digital supply chains.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: AI dependency and employee burnout: a nonlinear self-determination perspective
abstract: Purpose Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study aims to examine how employees’ artificial intelligence (AI) dependency is associated with burnout in hospitality. It tests the curvilinear nature of this association, the roles of competence and autonomy as need-related pathways and the moderating role of perceived organizational support (POS). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 375 AI-using hospitality employees in China through a three-wave time-lagged survey. The measurement model was validated using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypotheses were tested using hierarchical regression with quadratic and interaction terms, and conditional indirect effects were examined using a derivative-based approach with delta-method confidence intervals. Findings AI dependency was associated with burnout in a U-shaped pattern with burnout decreasing from low to moderate dependency and increasing at higher dependency. Consistent with SDT AI dependency was associated with competence and autonomy in inverted U-shaped patterns. Competence and autonomy helped account for this curvilinear association with moderate dependency linked to higher competence and autonomy and lower burnout and high dependency linked to the opposite pattern. POS attenuated the negative curvature in these relationships fundamentally altering how AI dependency relates to employees psychological needs at higher AI dependency levels. Research limitations/implications This study extends hospitality technology and employee well-being research by conceptualizing AI dependency as a nonlinear antecedent of burnout and by integrating SDT with POS as a boundary condition. It clarifies when AI-enabled work shifts from supporting psychological needs to undermining them, and offers a mechanism-based explanation of how organizations can preserve employee well-being as AI becomes embedded in hospitality workflows. Originality/value This study advances hospitality AI and employee well-being research by shifting attention from AI use and adoption to employees’ perceived AI dependency. It develops a nonlinear SDT-based framework that explains how AI dependency is linked to burnout through competence and autonomy and identifies POS as a contextual boundary condition in AI-enabled hospitality work.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Decoupling and recoupling through stakeholder actions: ESG washing in B2B contexts
Greening in weak contexts: How institutional voids, green strategic orientations and internationalisation drive eco-innovation
abstract: The role of macro-institutional factors in shaping entrepreneurial outcomes is increasingly receiving scholarly attention. Yet, most existing studies often adopt a restricted approach that overwhelmingly treats institutional voids as constraints. This study fills this gap by analysing the mechanism through which institutional voids influence eco-innovation, as well as the conditions under which this mechanism is more effective. Using a sample of 9867 small and medium-sized enterprises from 13 emerging economies, we find support for the dual role of institutional voids. Specifically, institutional voids are not just constraining factors; they also stimulate green strategic orientations (GSO), which in turn promote eco-innovation efforts. Furthermore, we find that international exposure enhances this mechanism, as export firms have higher levels of GSO and eco-innovation outcomes. Our findings contribute to entrepreneurship literature by revealing that GSOs are not mere background conditions, but essential organisational levers that allow eco-innovating firms to succeed in weak institutional settings. These findings are crucial for managers and policymakers seeking to improve the productivity and sustainability efforts of emerging economy firms.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: Choosing to stay small: Growth boundaries in lifestyle entrepreneurship
abstract: Venture growth is widely regarded as the defining outcome of entrepreneurship, yet many lifestyle entrepreneurs intentionally remain small despite viable opportunities to expand. While studies explain the motivations of entrepreneurs behind their preference for lifestyle over high-growth ventures, little insight is given to how founders utilize their values and beliefs to set venture growth boundaries and make sense for readjustments thereof. Using sensemaking theory and employing an abductive, multiple-case-study design of eight Vietnamese lifestyle ventures, this study draws on 36 in-depth interviews, eight focus groups, and a variety of other documentary evidence. Herein, entrepreneurs’ evaluations of potential expansion employ a number of value-based filters that, in turn, generate market, legitimacy, financial, and identity-related tensions and that, consequently, trigger value-driven sensemaking. These processes end up in strategic containment, an organizing logic for growth that tries to keep value while containing it. By repeatedly checking and adapting growth limits, the founders of these companies maintained and fine-tuned their growth boundaries. The study develops a process model, based on empirical research, of how lifestyle entrepreneurs come up with growth opportunities, limit their growth, and readjust these limits again when necessary. The model offers a process-based account of strategic smallness and connects value-based interpretation with the regulation of venture growth.

title: The relationship between technology transfer office role emphasis and outcomes across the technology transfer process
abstract: Technology transfer offices (TTOs) perform multiple roles within a shared personnel portfolio, yet little is known about how relative role emphasis relates to outcomes across the technology transfer (TT) process. This study examines the associations of internal and external interface emphasis with invention disclosures and licensing agreements. Using data from Brazilian TTOs, we measured internal interface emphasis as the share of personnel devoted to intellectual property prospecting and protection, while external interface emphasis captures the share devoted to technology transfer and facilitating collaborative projects with firms and other external actors. The results show that internal interface emphasis is positively associated with invention disclosures, while external interface emphasis is positively associated with licensing agreements. Because these measures are shares within a broader portfolio, greater emphasis on either focal cluster corresponds to a smaller share devoted to other TTO responsibilities, although not a direct substitution between internal and external interface work. By incorporating this allocation trade-off into a process-oriented analysis, the study contributes a portfolio-based understanding of TTO work. It identifies distinct associations between inward and outward facing role emphasis and upstream and downstream outcomes, highlighting the value of examining personnel attention across connected responsibilities rather than treating expansion of the TTO role repertoire as sufficient.

title: Reshaping global value chains in the digital era: a systematic review from a firm-based perspective
abstract: Purpose This study aims to systematically examine how digitalization reshapes global value chains (GVCs) from a firm-centric perspective. It seeks to integrate theoretical insights and identify the antecedents, transformation processes, outcomes and moderating factors of digital GVC restructuring. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 39 empirical articles (2014–2024) integrates the ownership–location–internalization (OLI) paradigm and stakeholder theory to construct a multidimensional framework that captures firms’ strategic responses to digital transformation. Findings The review reveals that digitalization reshapes GVCs through reconfiguration of ownership advantages (e.g. digital capabilities), location strategies (e.g. digital infrastructure and regulatory environments) and internalization mechanisms (e.g. platform integration and blockchain). Outcomes include enhanced firm performance and governance innovation, as well as social and environmental challenges. These effects are moderated by national institutions, industry characteristics and firm-specific capabilities, resulting in uneven digital dividends and risks. Originality/value This study contributes to international business research by (1) linking micro-level firm strategies with macro-level GVC changes, (2) offering an integrated theoretical lens combining OLI and stakeholder perspectives and (3) highlighting underexplored issues such as power asymmetries and ecological trade-offs in digitalized GVCs. It provides a clear agenda for future research and practical recommendations for firms navigating digital transformation in global contexts.

title: A Decision‐Support System for Prioritizing the Transformational Dynamics of Autonomous Trucks Deployment
Crafting and recrafting the self: Cycles of identity struggle in job crafting
abstract: Abstract Job crafting is widely regarded as a proactive approach for enhancing meaning and well‐being at work. This study challenges this view by examining the experiences of 24 change managers across six public‐sector organizations. Conceptualizing job crafting as identity work, we show that it unfolds as a cyclical process of identity management, through which individuals repeatedly respond to identity ambiguity, conflict and unvalidated self‐worth as roles evolve under conditions of change. We identify three recurring identity tensions and three corresponding cycles of identity‐driven job crafting that reflect an emotionally charged process of self‐preservation in response to misalignment and shifting expectations. Across cycles, both approach‐ and avoidance‐oriented crafting strategies generate unintended identity consequences that shape subsequent responses and redirect crafting over time. We further identify alternative value definitions as a novel, symbolic form of job crafting through which individuals sustain authenticity when behavioural adjustment proves insufficient. By reconceptualizing aspects of job crafting as a cyclical identity process marked by emotional strain, this study advances understanding of the darker side of job crafting beyond behaviour‐centred accounts that portray it as uniformly empowering.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: Audit Oversight under One Roof: The Impact of Engagement Quality Reviewer Proximity
journal_name: Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory

title: Do investors equally value women directors? Evidence from financial expertise
abstract: Evidence on whether women directors contribute to shareholder value is mixed. We contribute to this debate by examining the market reaction to the appointment of women directors with financial expertise. Using a sample of 5,018 new board appointment announcements by US public companies from 2002 to 2018, we find that investors react more favourably to the appointment of women directors with financial expertise than to those without such expertise. We also show that investors reward the appointment of women directors with accounting financial expertise (e.g. CFOs, auditors), whereas appointments of women directors with non-accounting financial expertise (e.g. CEOs, presidents) receive an insignificant market response. Our cross-sectional analyses further reveal that market appreciation of the benefits brought by appointing women experts is influenced by their independence, leadership role, type of financial expertise, the firm’s corporate governance environment, and managerial ability. Overall, we advance the literature by showing that it is not the mere presence of women directors in the boardroom that matters, but rather the expertise they bring. Accordingly, our results provide evidence-based insights with policy relevance for enhancing the value contribution of women directors in corporate governance.

title: Momentum in the Cryptocurrency Market: A Comprehensive Analysis under Realistic Assumptions
Exploring the platformization dilemma: How manufacturers leverage digital platforms for service business model innovation
abstract: Recent research has highlighted the growing significance of digital platforms in manufacturing, particularly in driving service business model innovation (BMI). However, research gaps persist in understanding how a manufacturer's platform business configuration as well as its platform experience influence its service BMI capability. This paper addresses these gaps by using the digital platform capability approach as a theoretical framework and introducing the concept of digital platform experience. To conduct our study, we first derive hypotheses from literature and test them in a cross-sectional, three-stage empirical analysis using descriptive, bivariate and multivariate regression analysis. For this purpose, we use the German Manufacturing Survey , a representative, large-scale firm-level database, which encompasses 1334 firms from the German manufacturing sector. Our findings reveal that digital platforms play a central yet ambivalent role – depending on experience and configuration – in manufacturers' service BMI. Overall, moving into the platform business generally triggers service BMI. However, these effects are mostly confined to product-related BMI, while customer-oriented models are only enabled through more complex platform configurations. Notably, these positive innovation effects tend to be short-lived: in the long run, innovation dynamics slow down considerably, and manufacturers may face what we refer to as the “platformization dilemma.”

title: The Effect of Beauty Work on Healthy Product Preferences: The Mediating Role of Fresh Start Mindset
abstract: ABSTRACT Consumers often enhance their appearance through beauty work. While prior research has primarily examined the effects of others' beauty work from an observer's perspective, less is known about how beauty work influences consumers themselves. Drawing on self‐perception theory, the current research demonstrates how engaging in beauty work shapes consumers' subsequent choices. Across five studies (total N = 1448), including one field experiment, we show that engaging in beauty work activates a fresh start mindset, which in turn increases consumers' preferences for healthy products. Study 1 provides field evidence for the main effect and demonstrates the mediating role of a fresh start mindset. Study 2 replicates this effect and shows that a general self‐improvement activity (e.g., reading a self‐improvement book) does not elicit the same effect. Study 3 shows that different forms of beauty work (e.g., make‐up and hair‐styling) generate similar effects, whereas no‐visibility personal care that does not involve visible appearance enhancement does not produce the same effect. Study 4 further shows that the effect is stronger when beauty work produces a salient perceived change relative to one's usual appearance. Finally, Study 5 shows that the effect emerges primarily among consumers with low self‐concept clarity. These findings suggest that healthy product marketers can strategically promote healthy options when consumers are engaged in beauty‐related consumption.

title: Crowded Decisions: How Environmental Density Shapes Mobile Investment Behavior
abstract: ABSTRACT Neo‐brokers have democratized access to the stock market, primarily through mobile platforms, attracting novice retail investors. However, research on the influence of environmental factors on mobile investment behavior is scarce. In this paper, we investigate how the immediate environment of potential investors influences their decisions and examine how the level of crowdedness influences the likelihood and amount of investment. Across three studies, crowdedness is associated with lower investment likelihood and lower investment amounts. This effect is mediated by investors’ feelings of pleasure, with dominance additionally influencing investment amount. Our findings suggest that mobile brokerage platforms may seek to mitigate the effects of environmental factors through privacy‐conscious, context‐aware design.

title: Mixed emotions enhance consumer acceptance of distant brand extensions: the role of dialectical thinking as a mediator
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how mixed emotions (simultaneous happiness and sadness) influence consumer evaluations of distant brand extensions, addressing a critical gap in low-fit extension strategies. Design/methodology/approach Four experimental studies were conducted employing diverse stimuli (e.g. advertisement materials and music clips) to manipulate mixed emotions, with their impact on extension evaluations and underlying mechanisms tested through measurement and manipulation. Findings The study found that consumers experiencing mixed emotions (simultaneously experiencing happiness and sadness) exhibit more favorable attitudes toward distant brand extensions than those experiencing happiness. This effect is mediated by dialectical thinking, which reconciles emotional conflicts and broadens cognitive processing to increase extension acceptance. Research limitations/implications The findings advance brand extension theory by revealing how internal emotional conflict systematically resolves extreme product incongruity through the specific cognitive pathway of dialectical thinking. Practical implications The study provides brand managers with an agile, highly actionable communication toolkit. Rather than relying on pure cognitive strategies or complex macro-segmentation, practitioners can leverage mixed emotions framing and contextual segmentation to proactively foster consumer acceptance of extreme product incongruity at the point of communication. Originality/value This research advances understanding of the cognitive consequences of mixed emotions by showing how affective conflict can translate into dialectical thinking in the context of distant brand extensions. It also offers practical guidance for firms and other market actors on using mixed-emotion communications to facilitate consumer acceptance of such extensions.

title: When emotions matter: the contextual effectiveness of emotional expressions in AI agents
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) agents’ emotional expressions (positive or neutral) interact with service task types (subjective or objective) to shape consumer service satisfaction, and explore the mediating roles of mind perception, including perceived agency and perceived experience, in this process. Design/methodology/approach This work uses four studies, including a secondary data analysis of relevant Weibo posts and three scenario experiments involving a total of 587 participants, to underline the interaction effect between AI agents’ emotional expressions and service tasks on service satisfaction, and demonstrate the dual-path mediating effect of mind perception. Findings Across four studies, the authors find that the effectiveness of AI agents’ emotional expressions depends on service task characteristics. The secondary data analysis of Weibo posts first documents consumers’ differential responses to AI emotional expressions across subjective and objective service contexts. Three scenario experiments then establish that positive emotional expressions are more effective for subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotional expressions are more effective for objective tasks. Further analyses show that these effects operate through distinct psychological pathways: positive emotions enhance perceived experience in subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotions strengthen perceived agency in objective tasks, ultimately increasing consumer satisfaction. Research limitations/implications This study, while strong in internal validity, faces external validity limitations. It focuses on AI communication in commercial service texts, neglecting other domains like education and health care, and overlooking the nonverbal emotional expressions of embodied AI. In addition, the research primarily uses service satisfaction as the sole dependent variable, thus missing a broader spectrum of consumer responses such as repurchase intentions and word-of-mouth. Practical implications This research informs managers that AI service agents should be designed as social actors with mind perception rather than as purely functional tools. Firms can leverage emotional expressions to shape consumers’ social evaluations of AI. But emotional design should align with service task types: positive emotional cues are more effective for subjective, experiential tasks, whereas neutral styles better support objective, data-driven tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the emotional AI literature by uncovering critical situational factors that shape the effectiveness of AI emotional expressions and advances the authors’ understanding of the underlying mechanisms through a dual-path mediation framework of mind perception. The findings also provide practical implications for the strategic deployment of emotional AI in service design.

title: The Emergence of the Service Techonomy: POPP at the Frontlines and the Rise of AI-Mediated Service Influence
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), data infrastructures, and platform technologies are reshaping services and organizational frontlines. We conceptualize this shift as the emergence of the “service techonomy,” in which omni-personalization manifests via Prescribed, Omnipresent, and Personalized Persuasion (POPP; e.g., such that AI-driven agents guide frontline service interactions, determine service access and offers for consumers, and monitor and steer frontline employees). We derive four functional forms of POPP—interactive, pre-emptive, allocative, and governing—and organize them in a 2 × 2 matrix based on the timing of influence (reactive vs. proactive) and mode of influence (constraining vs. supportive). Anchored in evolutionary economics and the multi-level perspective on socio-technical transitions, our framework shifts attention from isolated technology and personalization features toward broader configurations of AI-mediated influence that shape service value creation, extraction, governance, and potentially inequality across customers, employees, and collectives in service ecosystems. This perspective provides a foundation for future theory building, measurement, and responsible design of AI-mediated services and organizational frontline research.

title: Explaining Value Creation in Mental Health IT Configurations: An Integrated Framework
Between the Lines: Decoding Signaling Differences in Public and Private Sector Job Advertisements
abstract: ABSTRACT To compete in the “war for talent,” public sector employers must demonstrate advantages over private employers. While public service motivation (PSM) predicts sector preference, scholars disagree on whether public employers (can) effectively signal PSM in job advertisements. Consequently, this article examines how public and private job advertisements differ in language. We collected 5000 advertisements from both sectors and performed natural language processing (NLP) and qualitative content analysis. Both sectors use specialized language that can narrow the applicant pool. PSM signals appear more often in the public sector, but affective motives are rarely communicated; instead, self‐sacrifice is framed as a legal obligation. Public sector advertisements adopt a rational tone instead of explaining purpose and societal value. Legally mandated, saturated signals may be perceived as low‐cost and ineffective. The findings explain the mixed results concerning PSM signaling and underscore the gap between theory and practice in PSM‐related recruitment efforts.

title: How collaborative platforms shape power dynamics and outcomes in local collaboration: evidence from disaster mitigation planning
Means‐Tested Public Transportation Subsidies: Causal Evidence and Implications
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper evaluates the effects of a novel and large‐scale program in King County, Washington, that provides fare‐free public transportation to individuals with low incomes. Using both experimental and quasi‐experimental methods together with rich administrative and survey data, we find that providing free transit has very limited effects on mobility or downstream outcomes related to health and well‐being. We examine possible explanations for the modest effects, which contrast with findings from prior research. Our results suggest that changes in the external environment post‐COVID‐19 pandemic, including changes in norms around fare evasion, reduced the price elasticity of demand for travel by transit among individuals with low incomes.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Returns to Caring? Health and Well‐Being Effects of Subsidized Long‐Term Care
abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the health and well‐being effects of subsidized access to long‐term care (LTC). Our analysis exploits the staggered implementation of Spain's 2007 System of Autonomy and Care for Dependent People (SAAD), which expanded publicly funded and universal LTC subsidies and supports, as well as its subsequent reform. Using two decades of administrative and survey data and leveraging exogenous regional and individual‐level variation in program exposure, we find that access to SAAD benefits reduces the care receiver's depressive symptoms by approximately 10 percentage points, increases its survival probability by 2.6–3 percentage points, and raises its life satisfaction by 0.24–0.50 scale points. Cost‐effectiveness estimates indicate that the implied cost per quality‐adjusted life year (QALY) gained lies below commonly accepted efficiency thresholds for public health spending in Europe. These findings document sizeable health returns and efficiency gains from publicly subsidized LTC provision.
