title: Those Confounded Examples
The effect of hypothetical interventions to limit weight gain on incident type 2 diabetes mellitus among people with HIV initiating antiretroviral therapy in the United States, 2012-2021
abstract: Among people with HIV (PWH), initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) is associated with weight gain that might increase the risk of cardiometabolic outcomes. We estimated the effect of hypothetical interventions to restrict increases in body mass index (BMI) in the two years after ART initiation on the 7-year risk of incident type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) among PWH in the North American AIDS Cohort Collaboration on Research and Design (NA-ACCORD) clinical cohorts using the parametric extended g-formula. Among 13,822 normal weight or overweight PWH (BMI ≥18.5 and ≤29.9 kg/m2) who initiated ART between 2012-2021, the 7-year risk of T2DM was 5.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 4.8%, 6.3%). Compared to no intervention on BMI, if BMI increase during the first 2 years was capped at 5% of baseline BMI, the risk ratio (RR) for T2DM risk was 0.94 (95% CI, 0.86, 1.03); if BMI was capped at 29.9 kg/m2, RR=0.88 (95% CI, 0.80, 0.97); and if PWH were prevented from gaining any weight over the first 2 years, RR=0.81 (95% CI, 0.72, 0.92). These results provide preliminary evidence to promote studies of real weight maintenance interventions among PWH initiating ART.

title: Practical validation of synthetic pre-crash scenarios
abstract: The representativeness of synthetic pre-crash scenarios is crucial for assessing the safety impact of Driving Automation Systems through virtual simulations. However, a gap remains in the robust evaluation of synthetic pre-crash scenarios' practical equivalence to their real-world counterparts; that is, whether they are similar enough for the intended assessment purpose. Conventional significance testing is inadequate, as it focuses on detecting differences rather than establishing practical equivalence. This study addresses the research gap by extending our previous work on a Bayesian Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE)-based equivalence testing framework by introducing a binning-based approach to define appropriate statistics and equivalence criteria. Two binning-based statistics are proposed to measure practically meaningful distributional differences between datasets in the context of safety impact assessment. The framework's applicability is demonstrated through a case study, which tests the practical equivalence of two synthetic rear-end pre-crash datasets with a previously developed reference dataset in the context of the safety impact assessment of an Automatic Emergency Braking system. The results show that the framework provides informative quantitative assessments of practical equivalence as well as diagnostic insights into the divergence of datasets. Although the demonstration focuses on rear-end pre-crash scenarios, the framework is generic and extensible to broader validation contexts, providing an interpretable and principled basis for practical equivalence assessment across diverse synthetic data applications.

title: Safety risks in Advanced driver Assistance Systems (ADAS): A systematic review of causation and analysis methodologies
abstract: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) have achieved rapid technological advancement, yet their widespread adoption has introduced new and multifaceted safety challenges. This review provides a systematic synthesis of ADAS-related accident scenarios and risk factors. Based on multinational accident databases and detailed crash reports, collision types are classified into three major categories: vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-pedestrian, and vehicle-to-non-motorized interactions. The underlying causes of these accidents are traced to sensor performance degradation under adverse weather, algorithmic limitations in dynamic traffic environments, and excessive driver dependence on automated functions. Furthermore, this review examines mainstream analytical approaches, including statistical modeling, system-theoretic frameworks, and AI-driven techniques, and evaluates their applicability in risk identification and mitigation. Finally, a forward-looking framework is proposed to advance multi-sensor data fusion and privacy-preserving governance, strengthen dynamic scene modeling and open scenario databases, and incorporate human factors into causal inference for proactive risk management. The findings are expected to enrich the methodological foundation of ADAS accident analysis and support future improvements in intelligent vehicle safety.

title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs
abstract: Determining traffic crash liability relies on rigorous on-site evidence and legal provisions and involves substantial manual intervention and potential human error. However, intelligent traffic monitoring systems focus on detection and tracking and cannot provide structured, rule-grounded decision support for formal crash-liability analysis. Moreover, emerging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from object hallucination that distorts or omits physical evidence, and their opaque reasoning cannot produce explicit evidence-to-rule chains required for traceable and reviewable liability analysis. This paper proposes CrashLex, an explainable neural-symbolic decision-support framework that integrates visual perception with legal knowledge graph reasoning to align multimodal inference with predefined statutory rules and traceability requirements. Within CrashLex, a dual-query vision-language architecture employs parallel semantic and symbolic streams to mitigate object hallucination, utilizing Scene Queries for global context modeling and Perception Queries for fine-grained atomic feature extraction, respectively. The domain-specific legal knowledge graph maps these atomic facts from observable physical conditions to corresponding statutory elements, providing a structured basis for rule-grounded assessment. A logic-driven aggregation protocol then imposes explicit constraints derived from extracted facts and statutory provisions onto the inference process, thereby enabling traceable and interpretable preliminary liability assessment. On the held-out DeepAccident benchmark, CrashLex achieves a Legal Accuracy of 94.0% under the fixed legal-output evaluation protocol and an Object Hallucination Rate of 2.8%, corresponding to an 82.1% relative reduction from the 15.6% rate of the best-performing MLLM baseline on this metric. CrashLex grounds its assessment results in the deterministic execution of predefined legal rules rather than relying solely on unconstrained probabilistic generation, providing verifiable reasoning chains for rule-grounded human review.

title: What creates safe and efficient pedestrian–vehicle interactions? a naturalistic study to design human-like behaviour for automated vehicles
abstract: Safe and efficient interaction with pedestrians is critical for the successful deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs). While vehicle speed and acceleration are vital communication signals for this interaction, the ways in which human drivers use these kinematic communication signals remain under-explored. To design motion-based communication for AVs, this study aims to explore how drivers control their speed as a function of initial interaction conditions, and how this translates into more or less successful interaction outcomes. We analysed naturalistic trajectory data of vehicles and pedestrians from two zebra crossings in Leeds, UK, comprising 981 interactions. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to quantify the mediating effect of vehicle kinematics on the relationship between initial time gap and interaction outcomes (crossing order, efficiency, and safety). Based on these models, vehicle speed profiles associated with optimal and worst outcomes were identified and compared using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). PLS-SEM results confirmed that vehicle kinematics significantly mediate interaction outcomes, exerting a strong influence on efficiency and safety, and a weaker influence on crossing order. Minimum vehicle speed in particular exerted a strong influence on crossing order and safety, suggesting that the speed to which the driver drops is a key communication signal to pedestrians. The mediation results and trajectory analysis revealed that drivers used different strategies to achieve balance between their efficiency and interaction safety: in yielding scenarios (time gap > 3 s), they decelerated early and softly to maintain a low non-zero speed (∼1 m/s) at a far distance (>10 m) to ensure safety while conserving momentum to ensure efficiency; in ambiguous non-yielding scenarios (time gaps ∼ 1 – 3 s), they employed a two-stage strategy: a proactive initial deceleration to prepare for potential danger and reduce uncertainty, followed by an assertive acceleration for efficiency; in unambiguous non-yielding scenarios with a narrow time gap (< 1 s), they sacrificed a small amount of efficiency and adopted proactive deceleration before pedestrians displayed a clear crossing intention to ensure safety. This study expands the understanding of interaction beyond binary yielding choices, offering new insights into the proactive strategies human drivers use to negotiate right-of-way safely and efficiently. Emulating these kinematic strategies can support better integration of AVs into human traffic.

title: When Heritage Goes Playable: Digital Spectacle and Cultural Attention Externalities in Platform Markets
abstract: Digital platforms reallocate scarce consumer attention, yet the externalities generated within these ecosystems and their heterogeneous reception across culturally distinct audiences remain poorly understood. Against this backdrop, this study investigates whether major digital spectacles can trigger cultural attention spillovers, exploiting the release of Black Myth : Wukong as a quasi-natural experiment. Utilizing rich bilingual user reviews from the Steam platform, we deploy a supervised machine learning pipeline to construct a quantifiable metric of cultural utility attribution. Employing a difference-in-differences (DD) design coupled with coarsened exact matching (CEM) to address selection bias, we find that this profound cultural shock structurally recalibrates consumer attention. Robust to pre-trend validations and traffic controls, the incidence rate of culturally oriented reviews for incumbent games sharing Chinese cultural elements increased by approximately 11.9%. Crucially, these spillovers are highly directional and bounded. Pre-existing associative memory acts as a binding constraint for translating the technological shock into sustained cultural attention. Transforming heritage into interactive digital experiences offers an effective approach to activate dormant cultural assets. From a practical perspective, flagship digital spectacles can generate positive attention externalities that systematically reduce attention frictions for related digital goods.

title: Academic Passporting in Western Versus Non-Western Feminist Scholarship (1936–2024): Bibliometric and Thematic Landscapes
abstract: This study examines structural inequalities in feminist knowledge production by analyzing 11,060 Scopus indexed articles published between 1936 and 2024. Using bibliometric indicators, statistical citation analysis, and topic modeling, the study found that Western affiliated scholars dominate both output and recognition, whereas non-Western voices remain numerically and symbolically marginalized. The findings highlight how “Westernization” operates not only through citation advantage but also through thematic centrality: scholarship from Western institutions often sets the agenda in areas such as digital activism and intersectionality, while non-Western contributions, often centered on decolonial critique, grassroots mobilization, and local contexts, receive less global visibility. Mixed teams improve recognition among non-Western scholars but do not close the structural gap, suggesting that collaboration narrows inequalities without redistributing epistemic authority. To explain these dynamics, this study introduces the concept of academic passporting , whereby Western institutional affiliations function as strong passports that confer recognition and visibility, whereas non-Western affiliations operate as weak passports, unless stamped through Western collaboration. These findings have implications for diversifying scholarly practices, rethinking theoretical frameworks, and shaping equitable research policies.

title: The female choice fertility paradox: a mating equilibrium shift in contracepted high-choice environments
On the complexities of kissing
Vertical, horizontal, and discursive channels of subnational diffusion: institutional isomorphism and local ordinances supporting borderline intellectual functioning in Korea
abstract: How do newly visible vulnerable groups enter subnational legislative agendas in centralised unitary states, and why does recognition spread quickly without advocacy infrastructure, professional consensus, or a central mandate? This study examines the early diffusion of local ordinances supporting persons with borderline intellectual functioning (BIF) across 243 Korean general-purpose local governments in 2016–2023, a window covering the innovator and early-adopter stages of an ongoing process. Drawing on institutional isomorphism, we estimate panel logit and event history models of coercive (upper-tier adoption), mimetic (peer adoption share), and normative pressure, measured through national media coverage and local non-profit density. Upper-tier adoption, peer imitation, and media salience accelerated adoption, whereas non-profit density and partisan variables had no effect. The results identify a boundary condition of the normative channel: where professional communities have not yet organised, media discourse carries normative pressure. In unitary systems, vertical cues dominate even when horizontal imitation should be strongest.

title: An Analysis of Higher Education Budget Allocation and Student Success
abstract: Abstract The US higher education system comprises diverse institutions, making peer benchmarking essential for accountability and resource allocation. This study examines the budget structure of Purdue University Northwest relative to IPEDS peer institutions from 2017–2022, focusing on instructional and non‐instructional expenditures, staffing, and faculty composition. Using pooled panel regression models, we analyze associations between budgetary inputs and student outcomes, including retention and graduation rates. Results indicate that instructional expenditures, student–faculty ratios, and faculty composition are significantly associated with student success. The findings offer policy‐relevant insights for budgeting design, strategic planning, and resource allocation to improve institutional effectiveness and equity.

title: Effects of the Expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit for Childless Young Adults on Material Well-Being
abstract: In 2021, the US Congress temporarily expanded the earned income tax credit (EITC) for workers without qualifying children (the childless EITC) to mitigate the COVID-19 pandemic’s economic effects. The reform tripled the maximum benefit and, for the first time, lowered the minimum age of eligibility from 25 to 19. Using data from the Household Pulse Survey and a difference-in-differences design, this study examines the effects of the reform on material hardship among low-income young adults ages 19–24. We find that the expanded childless EITC primarily reduced housing hardship, with less robust evidence of reductions in food and expense hardship.

title: Node-aware spatiotemporal carbon tracing and carbon-responsive control of electrified railways for emission reduction and tertiary reserves
abstract: The decarbonization of electrified transportation reshapes the interaction between power systems and mobile energy loads. As a key component of this sector, electrified railways draw large, geographically distributed traction loads whose emissions are governed by the power system’s spatiotemporally varying carbon intensity (CI). However, existing carbon tracing methods typically use spatially uniform emission factors, obscuring nodal carbon intensity (CI) differences. Consequently, long-distance trains cannot perceive or exploit spatial carbon heterogeneity when allocating traction power along their routes. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a unified framework that transforms heterogeneous railway fleets into active, carbon-responsive resources within the power system. First, a node-aware spatiotemporal carbon tracing method integrates Power Transfer Distribution Factors (PTDF) with dynamic train-node mapping, enabling real-time quantification of the nodal carbon intensity (NCI) experienced by mobile loads. Building upon this, a two-stage hierarchical coordinated control strategy is formulated, embedding dynamic NCI signals into an online receding-horizon predictive controller to achieve joint carbon minimization and tertiary reserve. The controller autonomously executes spatiotemporal load shifting by dynamically regulating traction and braking power to avoid high-carbon zones while maintaining schedule adherence. Case studies on high-speed and freight railways demonstrate that traditional system-average carbon accounting systematically obscures local low-carbon zones, overestimating the fleet’s true carbon footprint by more than four times under severe spatiotemporal mismatch. By actively exploiting these spatial zero-carbon opportunities, the proposed NCI-aware control achieves substantial carbon reductions, of 37.14% for high-speed trains and 34.74% for freight trains, while maintaining schedule adherence. Crucially, the Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition reveals that these emission mitigations originate predominantly from the strategic utilization of low-carbon nodes, rather than mere energy conservation. These results demonstrate a promising framework for integrated power–transport system decarbonization, transforming electrified railways from passive loads into active carbon-aware grid participants.

title: A stochastic techno-economic framework for hydrogen-based maritime decarbonisation under market and policy uncertainty
Strategic scenario planning for hydrogen supply chains via graph convolutional networks: overcoming mid-stream infrastructure bottlenecks in energy transitions
abstract: : Hydrogen transitions require a combination of change in policy, production, distribution, and adoption, but current scenario consistency assessment only checks for trend coherence without incorporating the role of the relationships among the stakeholders in shaping those emerging pathways. This study introduces a Graph Convolutional Network-based Scenario Planning (GCN-SP) framework that extends scenario-consistency assessment by linking actor-node engagement with emerging trends to graph-based representations of representative hydrogen scenarios. Multi-driver interaction effects are transformed into strategic scenario graphs, clustered using k-means to derive representative configurations from cluster centroids, and classified using a graph convolutional network. The optimal model achieves weighted precision and recall exceeding 0.78 under both cross-validation and hold-out validation and outperforms two multilayer perceptron baselines. Three distinct structural configurations emerge. Coordinated: aligned actors across government, production, distribution, and adoption form a mutually reinforcing structure supporting system integration. Divergent: production and international connectivity advance while the producer becomes disconnected from the domestic network, creating an export-oriented pathway. Constrained: supply-side ambition and transport expansion outpace downstream adoption, leaving the value chain incomplete. Across scenarios, distribution emerges as a structurally important link whose connectivity determines whether production translates into integration. These results show that similar stakeholder activity can generate fundamentally different outcomes depending on interaction configuration. GCN-SP therefore enables structural distinction between coordinated integration, export-oriented divergence, and supply-led constraint.

title: Behavioural limits of market-led flood-risk allocation: Loss normalisation, investment discounting and planning-led land-use governance in urban China
abstract: Whether recurrent flood exposure deters demand for flood-exposed urban land, a deterrence logic well established in mature Anglo-American property markets, is a growing consideration for land-use planning under climate change. This question travels poorly to dense, platform-mediated Chinese urban housing markets, where households face repeated flooding at first hand while statutory hazard disclosure remains comparatively thin. Drawing on a pan-Chinese survey of 505 urban residents across 29 provinces, with 52 % in the coastal high-flood-risk belt, this paper develops and tests a structural model of housing purchase intention under urban flood risk. The model integrates a loss-normalisation block (perceived loss tolerability, investment discounting), a risk-cognition block (perceived flood risk, flood-information salience) and the proximal theory of planned behaviour. Covariance-based structural equation modelling yields three findings consequential for land-use planning. First, perceived loss tolerability raises purchase intention directly, while investment discounting raises it through attitude, so that both absorb the flood-risk signal rather than transmitting deterrence. Second, recurrent-event habituation and optimism bias depress perceived risk and feed both mechanisms, giving the levee effect a micro-level foundation. Third, the attitude-to-intention path is not significant, with subjective norm dominating intention, and objective flood knowledge does not moderate these effects. Taken together, the results suggest that demand-side responses alone are unlikely to steer development away from flood-exposed urban land, which points to a larger role for planning in risk-sensitive land allocation.

title: From rules to learning: A GIS-integrated agent-based reinforcement learning framework for simulating farmers’ land-use decisions and sustainable policy design
abstract: Developing countries face critical tensions between farmland-use policies prioritizing food security and environmental sustainability, and farmers’ livelihood-centered land-use strategies. To address these challenges, this study develops a human-centered agent-based model that integrates dual-layer Q-learning with GIS-based spatial representation. This framework simulates farmers’ adaptive decision-making under dynamic policy and environmental conditions while formalizing behavioral heterogeneity through Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)-informed typologies. Agents dynamically evolve land-transfer and cropping strategies via perception–action–feedback learning cycles. Applied to and validated against empirical observations from a representative Chinese case, the model reveals non-linear scale–efficiency relationships, with medium-scale farms exhibiting the comparatively balanced performance across yield and multiple resource-use efficiency dimensions. The analysis further identifies evolutionary pathways of adaptive behavior under policy incentives and quantifies trade-offs among area-weighted crop output, resource-use efficiency, and regional gross income. Scenario simulations show that rice-oriented subsidies increase rice output but reduce resource-use efficiency, rapeseed output, and gross income, whereas rotation-oriented incentives increase gross income while maintaining rice output near the baseline level. These findings support performance-linked subsidies based on multidimensional outcomes, tiered land-transfer regulation, and diversified cropping incentives. By linking adaptive behavioral dynamics with spatial and institutional constraints, this study provides a robust analytical framework for evaluating land-use policies and supports more effective governance strategies for balancing food security, environmental sustainability, and rural livelihoods.

title: Redistribution effects of Norwegian hydropower and Norway-Europe transmission upgrades
Transnational municipal network design and urban climate governance: Comparative evidence from 1019 CDP-reporting cities
Fluoropolymers across Their Life Cycle: Why “Emissions Reduction” Is Not “Safe”
Identification of Novel PFAS Transformation Products in AFFF-Impacted Surface and Groundwater
abstract: Abstract The widespread use of Aqueous Film-Forming Foams (AFFF) has left thousands of contaminated “hotspots” across North America. In Canada, only 25 per-/polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are regulated in drinking water at 30 ng/L. In the present study, cyclic ion mobility–tandem mass spectrometry (cIMS-MS2) was used to identify 17 regulated and 52 unregulated PFAS in surface waters near a former firefighting training facility in Atlantic Canada, including 6 new PFAS that have not been previously reported in environmental waters: hydrido-ketone-5:2-fluorotelomer sulfonate (FTS), ketone-8:2-FTS, unsaturated 8:2-FTS, N-methyl-perfluorohexane sulfonamido sulfinate, N-methyl-perfluorooctane sulfonamido sulfinate, and perfluorohexane sulfonamido propionate. Semi-quantitation of unregulated PFAS was enabled by a machine-learning model validated using a set of 21 targeted PFAS (R2 > 0.95). The total concentration of PFAS declined from 2500 ng/L to 364 ng/L as the surface water entered the North Atlantic approximately 5 km away from the hotspot. Seven of forty-two drinking water wells located along a 5 km transect from the source were characterized by exceedances between 30 and 191 ng/L. Twenty-seven PFAS were identified in the wells, including 13 that are unregulated and 5 that result from (bio)transformation of AFFF. While the fraction of unregulated PFAS was low (<18%), these transformation products may inform forensic studies aimed at establishing links between the source of pollution and its receptors.

title: Elevated Outdoor O3 Can Sustain New Particle Formation and Growth Indoors
abstract: Abstract Ultrafine particles and submicron aerosol mass negatively impact human health; while indoor primary sources are known, secondary aerosol formation from oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) is an important, but less understood, exposure source. Previous studies have suggested that indoor new particle formation (NPF) and growth are ozone-limited. However, we find that in an authentic aged unoccupied office in a region with high outdoor O3 concentrations, sufficient O3 is transported indoors that NPF and growth are instead limited by the availability of VOCs. Mechanical ventilation continuously supplies O3 in the summertime and sustains the subsequent growth so that particle growth rates upon the addition of limonene range from 20 to 100 nm h–1─rates 1–2 orders of magnitude greater than those observed outdoors. Additionally, we observe meaningful mass contributions from the growth of newly formed particles. Household use of limonene-containing products in rooms with elevated ozone─either from ozone-producing remediation and germicidal UV technologies, or during outdoor ozone exceedance events─will produce ultrafine particles and increase particle mass. The effect of ventilated O3 from outdoors on particle formation and growth highlights the value of continued efforts to reduce outdoor O3 pollution for moderating both indoor and outdoor sources of secondary pollutants.

title: Toward Recreating the Breath of Cities in the Atmospheric Simulation Chamber SAPHIR
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric simulation chambers are essential for studying oxidation processes, yet many experiments rely on single-precursor systems at concentrations that limit their representativeness for the chemical complexity of urban air. Here, we present a framework linking emission inventories, chamber experiments, and field observations by constructing emission fingerprints of major urban sources, including vegetation, volatile chemical products, cooking emissions, and gasoline and diesel exhaust. Applied during the CHANEL campaign in the SAPHIR outdoor chamber, these fingerprints advanced toward reproducing gas-phase mixtures representative of Los Angeles (gasoline-dominated traffic), a diesel-dominated city, and a future low-vehicle-emission scenario. The resulting mixtures generated peroxy-to-hydroperoxy radical ratios (RO2/HO2) close to unity, bimolecular RO2 lifetimes comparable with urban atmospheric observations, although lower NO levels favored RO2 + HO2 over RO2 + NO reactions. Comparison with aircraft measurements over Los Angeles using ammonium (NH4+) chemical ionization mass spectrometry showed reasonable agreement, with 465 organic product ions detected in both data sets, representing 78% of the product ions observed in the ambient air. Furthermore, 87% of common product ions agreed within a factor of 3 of the linear correlation, demonstrating that chamber experiments can capture key aspects of both atmospherically relevant radical chemistry and the oxidation product diversity of urban air.

title: Novel Insight into Organoarsenic Degradation and Inorganic Arsenic Sequestration in Ferrate Treatment: Unraveling the Role of Active Fe–As Complexes at the Molecular Level
abstract: Abstract Efficiently removing organoarsenic contaminants like p-Aminophenylarsonic acid (pASA) with their toxic inorganic byproducts remains a major challenge. Ferrate [Fe(VI)] can oxidize organoarsenic and immobilize inorganic arsenic, but the molecular mechanisms linking these functions are unclear. Here, using theoretical computational spectroscopy and stopped-flow analysis, we identified a critical pathway mediated by Fe(V/IV)–O-As(III) intermediates (INTs) that bridges oxidative degradation and heterogeneous sequestration. X-band EPR further confirmed the INTs (g-factors = 2.006, 1.928, 1.712), with rhombic peaks and quadruple hyperfine splitting. These INTs form barrierlessly between Fe(VI/V) and ·As(III)O(OH)2 released upon C–As bond cleavage in pASA. The thus-formed INTs exhibit superior reactivity to Fe(VI/V/IV), enabling more effective organoarsenic degradation and As(III) oxidation via outer-sphere electron transfer. Additionally, these INTs facilitate highly efficient inner-sphere electron transfer, forming Fe(III/II)–O-As(V) complexes that directly evolve into As-bearing Fe nanoparticles via Fe–O–As bond formation, a process with a lower energy barrier. The abundance of INTs during pASA degradation can be regulated by modulating Fe(VI) decomposition kinetics using common reagents: H2O2 accelerates and NaClO delays Fe(VI) decomposition. The Fe(VI)/NaClO system achieved 88% total As removal, higher than the 72% for Fe(VI)/H2O2 and 78% for Fe(VI) alone, and exhibited enhanced As–Fe coordination, indicating improved sequestration. Overall, this work reveals a pivotal mechanistic bridge in metalloid contaminant removal, offering new insights for designing oxidation-sequestration synergy in environmental remediation.

title: Establishment of a Novel Alternative Method Using the Gobiocypris rarus AhR for Toxicity Testing of the Dioxin-like Potency of Halogenated Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
abstract: Abstract Halogenated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (HPAHs) often exhibit distinct toxicity and mechanisms relative to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), yet most remain unassessed, particularly for dioxin-like effects mediated by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). This study characterized three rare minnow AhRs and established an efficient AhR-activation screening assay (using graAhR2, EC50 = 2.53 nM and Z′ factor = 0.58), and evaluated 40 HPAHs/PAHs with preliminary activity screening and ecotoxicity considered. HPAHs showed a median IC50 of 1.15 × 10–4 M for cellular viability (parent PAHs: 4.29 × 10–4 M), indicating greater cellular toxicity. Nine compounds were AhR-active. Notably, halogenated fluorene and pyrene exhibited AhR activation, whereas the parent did not. 4-bromobenz[a]anthracene exhibited 2028-fold higher activation potency than the parent. Acute toxicity (cell viability IC50) and AhR activation potency (EC50) exhibited a weak correlation, R2 = 0.21 and P = 0.22 in COS-7 cells, implying little AhR contribution to acute toxicity. All HPAHs/PAHs shared a similar binding direction within the AhR. AhR-active compounds possessed greater affinity than inactive ones (P = 0.0032). For instance, in fluorene-based HPAHs, a binding pose more similar to 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) may confer stronger activation potency. The results support the need for a tiered risk evaluation of HPAHs, e.g., considering acute and long-term aspects, and integrating dioxin-like potency into relevant regulatory frameworks, e.g., the toxic equivalency factor (TEF) or similar ones.

title: Anticipating the Environmental Impact of AI-Enhanced Robotics and Automation

title: Ice Converts Phenols into Persistent Mineral-Bound Polymers
abstract: Abstract Freezing fundamentally alters how minerals transform dissolved phenols in cold environments. As water freezes, solutes are excluded from the crystal lattice and concentrated into microscopic pockets of unfrozen liquid, creating reaction conditions far more extreme than those of bulk solution. Here, we compare catechol oxidation on a key soil manganese oxide under freeze–thaw versus room-temperature conditions. Freezing redirects products from soluble humic-like substances to thermally stable, mineral-bound polymers. Freeze–thaw conditions removed over 50% of dissolved organic carbon within 24 h compared to less than 10% at room temperature, with solid-phase carbon increasing over 50-fold. The attenuation of the effect with increasing salinity is consistent with freeze-concentration as a key driver and indicates that the pathway should be strongest in freshwater and low-salinity frozen environments. Freeze–thaw conditions also converted preformed soluble products into mineral-bound forms, demonstrating that the process operates on a range of substrates. These findings reveal an unrecognized abiotic carbon stabilization pathway that could operate when microbial decomposition is suppressed by freezing with direct implications for carbon dynamics in permafrost and seasonally frozen environments.

title: Decadal Biochar Legacy Stabilizes Paddy Soil Carbon by Reshaping Redox-Driven Reactive Oxygen Species Dynamics
abstract: Abstract Biochar (BC) displays great potential in stabilizing soil organic carbon, yet its decadal legacy for carbon preservation under redox oscillations remains unclear. The study comprehensively investigated how decadal BC (D-BC) application restrained carbon mineralization of paddy soil via reshaping reactive oxygen species (ROS) dynamics. In situ fluorescence imaging and quantification results showed that D-BC soil inhibited hydroxyl radical (•OH) generation by 22.3% than fresh BC (F-BC) input soil, but elevating hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide (O2•–) accumulation by 36.2% and 25.4% during redox oscillation, respectively. This resulted from its weakened microbial iron reduction and the lower reactivity of Fe(II), which significantly limited Fenton reactions. In contrast, a shift in the microbial community to redox-adapted taxa, lower catalase activity, and enriched dissolved inorganic carbon collectively facilitated the biogenic origin of H2O2 in D-BC soil. Scavenging and correlation analyses revealed that reduced •OH generation led to net suppression in CO2 emission from D-BC soil by >30% via upregulating the enzymatic latch, while enhanced H2O2 accumulation imposed oxidative stress on carbon-degrading microbes. Laboratory verifications confirmed the roles of surface oxidation and persistent free radical attenuation of aged BC in ROS redistribution. The failure of decadal straw (D-Straw) return to reproduce these phenomena suggested that the decadal BC legacy stemmed from a particular redox impact, rather than exogenous carbon input alone. The findings uncovered a new mechanism of BC-induced carbon stability, advancing understanding of the carbon cycle within redox-dynamic zones.

title: Why Can Cross-End Point Transfer Fail in Computational Toxicology? Diagnosing Decision-Structure Incompatibility across 13 End Points under Scaffold-Held-Out Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Cross-end point information sharing may improve toxicity prediction when labeled data are limited, but biologically related end points are not necessarily predictively compatible. We evaluated transfer strategies across 13 toxicity end points using scaffold-disjoint repeated cross-validation with strict leakage control. The benchmark compared data-level pooling with higher-level approaches, including stacking, multitask learning, model-agnostic meta-learning, and frozen-encoder feature augmentation (FEFA). Direct cross-prediction between different end points was generally weak, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.525 across 156 ordered end point pairs, indicating limited standalone portability of end point-specific decision rules. Global data merging reduced macro-average ROC-AUC by 0.0287 relative to end point-specific baselines, whereas several higher-level approaches produced modest gains. The strongest macro-average improvements were observed for stacking (+0.0101 ROC-AUC) and FEFA (+0.0070), although effects varied substantially among end points. Additional decision-structure and representation analyses were consistent with transfer performance being strategy- and target-dependent rather than determined by biological relatedness alone. These findings support leakage-controlled, end point-specific evaluation when using cross-end point learning for chemical toxicity assessment and caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous toxicity data.

title: Feasibility of the frass recirculation method during Hermetia illucens larvae treatment of organic waste streams

Cleaner production of ceramic fracturing proppants from bauxite tailings and oil-based drilling cuttings: process optimization, resource substitution and hazardous-element risk reduction
Preparation of MSCF via MPAM: A thermally stable modified material for the ecological backfilling of mine waste rock
Liquid hydrogen from waste biogas: an integrated process for deep-eutectic-solvent upgrading, steam reforming, and cryogenic liquefaction with energy–exergy–economic optimization
Enhancing the performance and economics of anion exchange membrane electrolysis for renewable hydrogen production
Techno-economic optimization of onboard carbon capture systems under escalating emission penalties using surrogate models
abstract: Onboard carbon capture systems (OCCSs) are emerging as a medium-term response to progressively tightening greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) requirements, motivating assessment of appropriate capacity and operation. This study develops a hierarchical multi-period framework that jointly determines one-time OCCS design and annual operation. Gaussian-process-regression surrogates efficiently replace rate-based process simulations, and the framework is applied to a liquefied-natural-gas-fueled very large crude carrier with a 30 wt% monoethanolamine process. On independent test sets, the surrogates achieved coefficients of determination of at least 0.9992 and mean absolute percentage errors of at most 2.01 %. Without surplus-unit trading, the optimum treats 30.0 % of the highest-load main-engine exhaust and matches capture heat demand primarily to recovered waste heat, reducing life cycle cost by 7.9 % relative to compliance without capture. Tightening the GFI trajectory alone does not necessarily increase capture because capture energy also affects attained GFI. When surplus units are traded, their price determines adoption and scale: installation is economical at 304 USD/ton CO2eq and above but not at 266 USD/ton CO2eq and below, while 342 USD/ton CO2eq drives the designs in all three regulatory scenarios to the maximum available main-engine exhaust flow. At 380 USD/ton CO2eq , gross lifetime capture increases from 199 to 634 kton relative to no trading, but net greenhouse gas avoidance increases only from 147 to 325 kton as parasitic emissions rise. Under the assumed immediate-sale surplus-unit market, the prescribed surplus-unit price and net emissions strongly influence OCCS value alongside the target trajectory.

title: Genetically engineered microorganisms for environmental remediation: An integrated critical review of degradation mechanisms, ecological risks, and regulatory frameworks
Macrophyte-mediated responses of epiphytic biofilms under erythromycin stress in wetland mesocosms
A blockchain and geospatial AI-enabled governance system for illegal gold mining detection and supply chain traceability
The dissent of decarbonization: Sociotechnical controversies in lithium extraction in the Vale do Jequitinhonha, Brazil
abstract: This article describes and analyzes the sociotechnical controversies surrounding lithium exploration in the Vale do Jequitinhonha, Minas Gerais, Brazil, situating them within the context of the global energy transition and the so-called “decarbonization consensus.” The research adopts Actor-Network Theory (ANT) and controversy mapping as a theoretical-methodological approach, making it possible to map the actors, arguments, and disputes that shape the sociotechnical arrangement of lithium mining in the region. The empirical corpus consisted of diverse documents collected through web scraping and monitoring of public debates. The results reveal the conflictual coexistence of antagonistic narratives: on the one hand, lithium as a driver of development, supported by state and corporate discourses that mobilize the idea of overcoming poverty; on the other, mining as a producer of socio-environmental conflicts, denounced by communities, social movements, and researchers. Over time, initial warnings about risks become concrete impacts, broadening the controversy and mobilizing new arenas, such as public hearings, complaints, and legal actions. We conclude that the exploration of minerals demanded by the energy transition, far from being consensual, is traversed by disputes that reveal the production of new sacrifice zones, highlighting the need for more just, participatory, and territorially situated models. By shifting the focus from the “lithium triangle” to the Vale do Jequitinhonha, the article examines a mining frontier that remains little investigated through the lens of controversy mapping.

Towards sustainable aviation: aircraft fuel flow estimation using an improved iTransformer for pollutant emission calculations
abstract: Accurate estimation of aircraft fuel consumption and emissions is essential for sustainable aviation but is constrained by the lack of publicly available fuel flow data and the limited accuracy of existing methods. This study proposes an improved iTransformer-based approach for aircraft fuel flow estimation using ADS-B data. First, key variables influencing fuel flow are identified through Spearman correlation analysis. An LSTM network and a multi-head differential attention mechanism are then incorporated into the iTransformer architecture to improve temporal feature extraction, estimation accuracy, and model generalization. QAR and ADS-B data are preprocessed and analyzed, with the model trained using QAR data and subsequently applied to ADS-B data for fuel flow estimation. The fuel flow estimation yields an average accuracy of 93.7% based on 4,968 flights covering 11 aircraft types. Further estimation of fuel consumption and pollutant emissions was performed on a dataset of 23,756 flights with the same 11 aircraft types, and the overall average accuracy of all estimation results is higher than 90%. The resulting emission estimates are consistent with observed operational characteristics. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to a large-scale dataset of 855,000 flight movements across mainland China in October 2024, enabling nationwide quantification of aviation fuel consumption and emissions. The results demonstrate the robustness and scalability of the proposed approach and highlight its potential to support aviation energy management, emissions monitoring, and sustainable aviation development.

Industrial robotization and provincial green synergy performance in China: Coupling coordination, regional disparities, and dynamic responses
abstract: Rapid industrial automation is becoming an important feature of production systems operating under economic and environmental constraints, while its observed performance implications may emerge with delay and differ across regions. This study examines whether industrial robotization and provincial green synergy performance evolve in tandem, where coordination disparities originate, and how their dynamic relationship unfolds. Using panel data for 30 Chinese provincial-level regions from 2006 to 2023, we employ a shift-share measure of robot installation density and estimate green synergy performance with a super-efficiency slacks-based measure integrating economic output, urban greening, industrial pollution, and carbon emissions. The coupling coordination degree evaluates the alignment of the two systems, the Dagum Gini decomposition identifies the sources of regional disparities, and a panel vector autoregression examines reciprocal temporal predictability and lagged responses. The national coordination degree increased from 0.4810 to 0.7740, while the overall Gini coefficient declined from 0.1685 to 0.1009. Between-region differences remained the largest component of disparity, accounting for 51.14% on average, with the eastern-western gap being the widest. Robotization predicted green synergy performance nationally and in eastern China, with a negative first-lag association followed by a positive second-lag association. By period 10, innovations in robotization accounted for 18.63% of the forecast-error variance in green synergy performance nationally and 34.02% in eastern China. These results reveal a stage-dependent and regionally uneven predictive relationship, although the research design does not identify structural causal effects. The findings highlight the value of coordinating robot deployment with green process redesign, region-specific technical support, and full-cycle performance monitoring.

title: Multi-level governance constraints on the local science–policy–practice interface: Evidence from Ho Chi Minh City flood management
abstract: Stronger collaboration between science, policy and practice is widely acknowledged as essential for addressing escalating climate risks, yet the governance structures shaping such collaboration are often overlooked. This study brings together Multi-level Governance and Science-Policy-Practice Interface (SPPI) scholarship to examine how vertical power relations shape the connection between climate knowledge, policy formulation and practice at the local level, through a case study of Ho Chi Minh City (HCMC)'s urban flood management. Drawing on document analysis, interviews, site visits, and news reports, the findings demonstrate that local flood management efforts are constrained by hierarchical governance procedures. The challenges include: a national preference for conventional approaches that hinders adaptive solutions at the municipal level; top-down planning that creates a mismatch between national objectives and local implementation capacity; and centralised control over budget management, technical standards, and legal reforms, which limits private sector participation and local governments' ability to respond to context-specific challenges. The paper argues that strengthening local government autonomy and enabling more flexible mechanisms for integrating diverse expertise could foster innovation and timely, context-relevant adaptation strategies. Examining the case of HCMC advances understanding of how power relations shape the SPPI and contributes to the growing global literature on the pivotal role of local governments in advancing climate change adaptation and mitigation. It calls for future studies to move beyond a single administrative level to examine how political structure influences the science-policy-practice interface in different social-political contexts.

title: A Land Potential‐Based Framework for Wind Erosion and Sand and Dust Storm Source Mitigation
abstract: ABSTRACT Wind erosion and sand and dust storms are a global challenge. While many management practices to mitigate sources of wind erosion and sand and dust storms have been documented, existing guidance largely emphasizes what practices are available, with limited information on where and under what ecological conditions they should be applied. As a result, mitigation efforts can be ineffective or can exacerbate erosion when implemented without regard to local ecological context. Land potential, or the inherent capacity of land to support vegetation, soil stability, and productivity, provides a basis for aligning mitigation practices with a site's resistance and resilience to erosion. Here, we present a land potential‐based framework to improve the selection, implementation, and evaluation of wind erosion and sand and dust storm source mitigation practices across diverse landscapes. The framework uses land potential assessment with agroecological state concepts to guide decision‐making through the following steps: (1) characterize land potential by soils, topography, and climate to identify resistance and resilience to erosion; (2) identify agroecological states that capture vegetation–soil configurations, thresholds, and feedbacks determining erosion dynamics; (3) identify and monitor wind erosion risk and sand and dust storm source areas; (4) define mitigation targets and benchmarks that guide decision‐making; (5) identify and implement practices to avoid, reduce, reverse, or accept wind erosion; and (6) evaluate mitigation outcomes and adapt management. By linking local‐scale land assessments with mitigation practices, this framework increases the likelihood of successful mitigation and provides scalable decision support for advancing Land Degradation Neutrality and sustainable land management.

title: GAMEMANCIPATION NOW! An intergenerational framework for evaluating games as participatory tools in architecture and urban planning
abstract: Games are increasingly used in architecture and urban planning to support participation, learning, and co-design, yet evaluation remains uneven: studies often report engagement and dialogue while less consistently assessing power relations, agency, and whether game outputs translate into influence in planning and design decisions – especially in intergenerational settings that include children. This paper addresses that gap by proposing the GamEmancipation Framework, a built-environment–specific evaluation tool for analogue and digital participatory games (including geogames) that treats adults and children as co-actors. Grounded in a systematic content analysis of literature spanning participation studies, children’s rights and participation, education, psychology, and planning/game scholarship, the framework operationalises evaluation through four sections: Foundations (structural and methodological conditions), Processes of Participation (phase-by-phase distribution of influence), Outcomes (developmental and transformative capacities, including spatial literacy), and Future & Sustainability (feedback, continuity, and governance coupling). Child-sensitive checkpoints are integrated within the same analytical structure rather than handled as an add-on, and built-environment add-ons foreground spatial relevance and cross-sectoral continuity. We demonstrate application through an illustrative case study of SPECTOR – The Sustainability Inspector, an analogue participatory post-occupancy evaluation game played in three school contexts (the UK, Serbia, and Spain) with 74 children (11–15) and architecture-student facilitators. Using deductive coding of archived interviews, observation accounts, and pupil-produced photographs, we assess the strength and consistency of evidence for each framework category. The application shows strong support for flexible participation, cooperative intergenerational dynamics during play, and spatially grounded evidence-making, while revealing constraints in agenda-setting and weak, context-dependent pathways for feedback, continuity, and institutional uptake. The findings underline that emancipatory trajectories depend not only on in-game participation but also on governance coupling and institutional commitment – an issue that is particularly salient for geogames, where spatial representations can be mistaken for influence without explicit decision pathways. The GamEmancipation Framework provides a transparent, criterion-by-criterion approach for evaluating and comparing participatory games in built-environment contexts, supporting more accountable claims about participation, transformation, and emancipation.

Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
abstract: Abstract Civil wars are a recurring phenomenon undermining development in weak states. Faced with the possibility of costly conflict, why don’t leaders share power? I investigate the role of an unexplored commitment problem, both theoretically and empirically. The model features a leader who can appease challengers by sharing power, but doing so increases their effectiveness at launching a rebellion. I show that commitment worsens as the opposition becomes stronger, and derive testable non-monotonic implications of group strength on power-sharing and conflict. As challengers become stronger, the likelihood of inclusion (positive transfers) increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader prefers to exclude an opposing group and face conflict. I test the model using data on politically relevant ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, their access to executive power, and on armed organizations that claim to represent them. I use within-country variation in population share to proxy for group strength. The empirical findings strongly accord with the predictions of the theory. I then structurally estimate the model parameters and explore policy-relevant counterfactuals, including the effects of democratization, changes in military capacity, financial aid, sanctions, and quotas.

Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

title: Sustainability Reporting on Biodiversity and Ecosystems in the European Forest‐Based Sector: An Institutional Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) emphasises the importance of corporate sustainability reporting on biodiversity and ecosystems, particularly specified in the European Sustainability Reporting Standard E4 (ESRS E4). This study examines how the European forest‐based sector operationalises ESRS E4 through mandatory disclosures and explores the institutional pressures shaping these practices. Using a qualitative content analysis method on 23 sustainability reports, we assess ESRS E4 disclosures and coercive, mimetic and normative pressures. Overall, these pressures manifest in responses ranging from isomorphism and substantive adaptation to tendencies towards means‐ends decoupling related to specific disclosure obligations. The results reveal a contrast between converging transition plans and policies and diverging practices in terms of actions, targets and metrics. Few disclosed financial effects from biodiversity‐related risks were detected. The findings also indicate that effective biodiversity reporting depends not only on regulatory requirements but also on the development of shared reporting and measurement infrastructures.

Contested credibility: Public perceptions of scientists as experts
abstract: Science is widely embraced as an important prerequisite for innovation, and there is widespread support for public investment in science on that basis. However, it remains more contested whether and when science is recognized as a relevant source of expertise in contemporary debates beyond the academic sphere. Drawing on nationally representative survey panels from two European countries (the United Kingdom and Sweden), we investigate whether scientists are perceived as more credible senders of messages regarding societal challenges compared with attribution to other types of expert groups (government, businesspersons, and issue advocates). Evidence from a conjoint analysis paints a rather bleak picture: scientists’ credibility is only superior to that of government officials, but not businesspersons or issue advocates. We furthermore find that scientists are more credible when communicating technological issues than non-technological ones. This pattern can be traced back to three types of perceived sources of distrust (vested interest, partisanship and irrelevance) that are activated more strongly for non-technological issues. The same three sources of distrust also underpin the general credibility disadvantage of scientists as experts. Implications for our understanding of the social contract of science are discussed.

Beyond Equilibrium: Tracing Redox-Driven Pathways That Shape Aqueous and Mineral Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Numerous aqueous and geochemical systems host elements in multiple redox states, with wide ranging implications such as their influence on the formation/dissolution of minerals, water toxicity, and nutrient cycling. To uncover governing mechanisms and complex chemical interactions in geochemical systems, reactive-transport models have increasingly gained importance. However, their predictive capabilities remain limited because existing approaches struggle to accurately account for the full complexities of redox reactions. Here, we develop a reactive-transport framework that leverages recent advances in thermodynamic modeling, speciation chemistry, and redox kinetics. Distinct from traditional models, we uniquely treat redox kinetics along with transport as transient phenomena, decoupled from Gibbs free energy minimization. By ensuring ionic concentrations are governed by nonequilibrium rate laws, this approach allows predicting the tempo-spatial distribution of speciation and precipitation of species across oxidation states. We illustrate the versatility of our framework through two case studies: manganese speciation in natural waters and the fate of dissolved iron in aqueous/porous media. Our framework significantly enhances the modeling of a diverse range of redox-sensitive environments.

title: Condensation Sink Efficiency of Atmospheric Particles Regulated by Their Chemical Compositions and Hygroscopicity
abstract: Abstract Condensation sink (CS) from atmospheric pre-existing particles is a crucial limiting factor for the occurrence of new particle formation (NPF). However, intense NPF events occur frequently in polluted urban areas despite high CS levels. Here, to address this discrepancy, we introduce an efficiency coefficient ε (ε = CSeff/CScal) to quantify the CS efficiency of pre-existing particles toward gaseous H2SO4, where CScal was calculated under the assumption of irreversible uptake. Results demonstrate that ε strongly depends on hygroscopicity and chemical compositions of particles. Under dry conditions, the ε of pure organic particles was less than that of pure inorganic particles, but high humidity increased ε for both. For mixed organic-inorganic particles, the ε was adjusted together by particle chemical compositions and humidity. Exploratory measurements further revealed a decline in CS efficiency for gaseous HIO3. Incorporating ε into field data and models improves cluster survival predictions and sub-3-nm particle formation simulations, potentially explaining the NPF mystery in megacities under high CS and leading to more accurate modeling of NPF impacts.

title: Correction to “A Review: Mechanisms, Processes and Design Principles of Recycling Spent Lithium-Ion Battery and Biomass”
Divergent Catalytic Strategies of Group-6 Propane Monooxygenases in Propane-Stimulated 1,4-Dioxane Biodegradation
abstract: Abstract Group-6 propane monooxygenases (PRMs) catalyze the initial oxidation of 1,4-dioxane (dioxane), a widespread contaminant of emerging concern. Because their expression can be induced by propane, an inexpensive and readily deliverable substrate, PRM-containing microorganisms offer a distinct advantage for propane-based biostimulation strategies targeting dioxane removal. However, functional differences among PRMs from the three major phylogenetic clusters remain poorly understood. Here, three PRMs from Mycobacterium dioxanotrophicus PH-06, Mycobacterium marinum E11, and Mycobacterium sp. ENV421, representing phylogenetic clusters, PRM-I, PRM-II, and PRM-III, respectively, were heterologously expressed in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc2155. ENV421 PRM-III exhibited low substrate affinity but high catalytic capacity toward both dioxane and propane, and moderate resistance to chlorinated solvent inhibition. In contrast, E11 PRM-II displayed high affinity but lower capacity and greater inhibitor sensitivity. PH-06 PRM-I showed comparatively stronger activity toward dioxane than propane relative to the other PRMs. Protein structure analysis suggested that variation in substrate affinity and catalytic turnover is consistent with differences in active-site pocket hydrophobicity, rigidity, and catalytic geometry. Phylogenetic and compositional analyses further suggested horizontal transfer in Clusters I and III. Together, these results highlight substantial functional diversity among group-6 PRMs and offer mechanistic insights for optimizing microbial populations for effective propane-stimulated bioremediation of dioxane.

title: Reducing PFAS Mobility and Plant Uptake in Agricultural Soils via Biochar Amendment
abstract: Abstract Biochar amendment represents a promising in situ strategy for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) mitigation, yet its performance under realistic field conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated PFAS fate in soil–plant–leachate systems under irrigation-water- and biosolids-derived contamination settings. Pinewood biochar (PBC) significantly (P = 0.05) reduced PFAS leaching and plant uptake more so than biosolids-derived biochar (BBC), driven by its higher point of zero charge (PZC), C/H and C/O ratios, and specific surface area, with the strongest mitigation observed for PFHxS and PFOA. Air oxidation and iron oxide modification of PBC further suppressed short-chain PFAS accumulation in plants. Among the tested materials, air-oxidized PBC exhibited the highest mitigation efficiency (ME), reducing leaf bioconcentration factors (BCFs) of PFHxS and PFOA by 1328.5-fold and 285.3-fold, respectively, and suppressing perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) accumulation by 150.8-fold, attributable to enhanced surface area, electrostatic attraction, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) released from biosolids increased the mobility of PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, and PFHxS while reducing the bioavailability and translocation of PFNA and PFOS. Collectively, this work demonstrates that PFAS mitigation by biochar is governed by molecular structures, input pathways, and DOM interactions, providing mechanistic insight for targeted biochar deployment in PFAS-impacted agroecosystems.

Life cycle assessment of North American forest harvesting operations and wood processing for sustainable materials and energy products: A systematic review
abstract: This study provides a systematic review of life cycle assessment for forest harvesting systems in North America, to quantitatively assess the carbon footprint and overall impacts of lumber production and various harvested wood products and their use as biomaterials and bioenergy. The reviewed studies revealed strong regional differentiation in harvesting practices and environmental performance. Mechanized systems in the Southeast US exhibited higher diesel consumption and net carbon removal per hectare due to intensive site preparation and whole-tree harvesting. Pacific Northwest operations relied comparatively more on cable yarding and manual felling on steep terrain, resulting in lower emissions per unit volume. Transportation and residue management were consistently identified as major contributors on a per-unit-volume basis. Processing stages, particularly kiln-drying, were the most energy-intensive processes (5151 MJ/m 3 of lumber in the SE), although more than 70% of energy demand was met using wood-based residues. Sensitivity analysis demonstrated that allocation approach significantly influenced climate impacts. Economic allocation increased the GWP of higher value wood products, whereas mass allocation increased the GWP of low-value byproducts, including dirty chips (251%) or sawdust briquette (2.3-fold), reflecting the lower environmental burden assigned to co-products under economic allocation. Overall, the findings confirm that sustainably managed forest harvesting supply chains function as net carbon sinks while offering significant potential to displace fossil-based energy and materials.
