title: Market and welfare effects of marketing cooperatives in spatial procurement markets
abstract: Abstract Agricultural marketing cooperatives are widely viewed as a mechanism for mitigating oligopsony power in agricultural procurement markets. However, the welfare effects of cooperatives depend on how competing investor‐owned firms respond, and those responses vary with the strategic flexibility available to firms. This paper studies how spatial price discrimination and endogenous location mediate the market and welfare effects of cooperatives in spatial procurement markets. Using a structured counterfactual framework, we compare markets with only investor‐owned firms and mixed markets with both investor‐owned firms and cooperatives across four strategic environments defined by the availability of these strategic margins. We find that strategic flexibility generally attenuates the welfare gains generated by cooperative entry, particularly at low and intermediate transportation costs. This attenuation arises because strategic flexibility increases efficiency in benchmark markets with only investor‐owned firms, leaving less scope for cooperatives to improve market performance. Consequently, strategic flexibility and cooperative ownership emerge as partially substitutable mechanisms for improving procurement‐market performance. Cooperatives therefore deliver their largest welfare gains where competing firms face greater strategic constraints arising from regulation, technology, or physical limitations.

title: Ethnographic Theorizing in Human Resource Management: From Theory‐as‐Design to Theory‐in‐Use
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on human resource management (HRM) has generated influential frameworks for explaining the relationships between HR practices and organizational outcomes. Existing accounts offer less insight into how the frameworks informing those practices acquire meaning, authority, and practical traction in organizational settings. We conceptualize this as a gap between theory‐as‐design and theory‐in‐use and develop ethnographic theorizing as a mode of examining the use‐life of selected design‐oriented HRM frameworks. Our contribution is twofold. First, we specify how sustained immersion, temporal depth, embodied co‐presence, and relational obligation enable researchers to follow frameworks as they are enacted and negotiated. Second, we develop three recursively related analytic moves for theory development— Complement, Complicate, and Reframe —through which ethnographic evidence can elaborate, qualify, or revise existing theoretical accounts. We demonstrate this approach through two ethnographic studies of HR analytics in different organizations. The comparison shows how legitimacy work, identity negotiation, and meaning‐making shaped the enactment of data‐driven HRM in these settings. The paper thus offers a structured approach for studying how established HRM frameworks operate in use and for assessing when situated evidence warrants changes to their constructs, relationships, or boundary conditions. In addition, we discuss implications for HRM theory, research design, and practice.

title: ESG‐linked Executive Compensation and Firm Value: The Mediating Role of Environmental Innovation and Moderating Role of ESG Training
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG)‐linked executive compensation influences firm value and the channels through which its effects emerge. Using panel data of listed firms from STOXX Europe 600 during 2015–2023, the study employs Tobin's Q and price‐to‐book value to assess firm value and robustness, respectively. The empirical analysis uses firm‐ and year‐fixed–effects models complemented by system‐generalized method of moments (GMM) and an event‐study difference‐in‐differences design to address endogeneity. The results show that ESG‐linked compensation is positively associated with environmental innovation. In the baseline fixed‐effects estimates, moving from no ESG‐linked pay to ESG‐linked pay is associated with a 7.6‐point increase in the environmental innovation score, equivalent to approximately 14% of its sample mean, and approximately 5.2% higher firm value. However, the association with firm value is not robust under system‐GMM and event‐study specifications. ESG‐related training conditions the ESG‐linked pay–environmental innovation relation; governance variables do not show consistent moderating effects. The mediation analysis does not support a statistically significant indirect effect. Overall, ESG‐linked pay appears to influence firm behavior more consistently compared with immediate financial outcomes.

title: Lean‐Green Effects and Digital Transformation: Unpacking the Role of Incremental and Radical Green Innovation in Driving Sustainable Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT In the context of an increasingly dynamic industrial landscape, manufacturers are presented with a promising opportunity to enhance their competitive edge while advancing sustainability objectives. This study explores the effects of lean management (LM) and green management (GM) as strategic drivers of sustainable performance (SP), emphasizing the mediating role of incremental (IGI) and radical green innovation (RGI). Grounded in the dynamic capabilities framework, this study examines how LM and GM foster innovation and how digital transformation (DT) moderates these relationships. Using survey data from 310 Portuguese firms and structural equation modeling (SEM), the findings show that both LM and GM significantly contribute to IGI and RGI, which, in turn, enhance economic, environmental, and social sustainability outcomes. DT further strengthens the effects of GM, whereas its interaction with LM enhances the positive effect on IGI but weakens the effect on RGI. The study contributes to innovation and sustainability literature by demonstrating that innovation capabilities are essential conduits through which operational and environmental strategies translate into measurable performance. Practical implications highlight the need for organizations to balance efficiency with strategic innovation and invest in digital tools to scale sustainability efforts.

title: Employing Content Analysis in ESG Research: A Systematic Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT This study systematically reviews the application of content analysis in environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosure research. Although content analysis is widely employed to examine ESG reporting, methodological approaches, disclosure channels and analytical practices remain fragmented, limiting methodological coherence and the cumulative development of knowledge. To synthesise this evolving field, 170 peer‐reviewed articles published in ABS 3, 4 and 4* journals were systematically reviewed following the PRISMA guidelines. Using bibliometric and thematic analyses, the study examines publication trends, methodological developments, disclosure channels and emerging research directions. The findings reveal substantial growth in ESG content analysis research alongside increasing methodological diversification, while also identifying important gaps relating to computational methods, disclosure channels and methodological standardisation. Building on these findings, the study develops an integrative framework grounded in the Ontology–Epistemology–Methodology (OEM) perspective to explain how methodological choices shape the interpretation of ESG disclosures. In addition, a Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM)–based future research agenda comprising eight research propositions is proposed to guide future scholarship. By providing a conceptually integrated synthesis of methodological developments and future research priorities, this review advances understanding of ESG content analysis and offers practical guidance for researchers investigating corporate sustainability communication.

title: Conceptual Change and Sustainable Business Transformation: A Phenomenon‐Driven Review
abstract: ABSTRACT In this article, we ponder profound questions of societal sustainability transitioning through the concept of conceptual change —a category of change that, compared with other scientific domains, has so far received little attention in scholarship of business. We take a phenomenological stance on conceptual change to broach its relevance for the literature on sustainable business transformation. Through a phenomenon‐driven review of when and how such change occurs in for‐profit organizations—which yielded 16 empirical articles—we demonstrate both this relevance and how it is being overlooked to date. Based on the available evidence and following phenomenon‐driven interests for theoretical renewal, we outline a framework and pathways for paying greater attention to intricacies of conceptual change among business organizations as well as its interplay with other dimensions of societal sustainability transitioning.

title: Advancing Sustainable Competitive Advantage through Green Digital Transformation Leadership, Green Technological Innovation and Green Digital Transformation: An Integrated SEM–NCA Approach
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental sustainability has raised global concerns following the increase in carbon emissions due to industrial and commercial activities. As such, this research aims to examine the association between green digital transformation leadership (GDTL) in Malaysian manufacturing companies and sustainable competitive advantage (SCA), with green digital transformation (GDT) and green technology innovation (GTI) playing mediating roles. The strategic importance of leadership in supporting green and digital development efforts is gaining ground, as reflected in Malaysia's ongoing effort to maintain a technological edge while navigating environmental issues. Survey data were gathered from 141 senior management personnel and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA). Based on the elicited outcomes, GDTL significantly increased GDT, GTI and subsequently, SCA. The GDT mediated the GDTL–SCA relationship, denoting the pathways for leadership to promote sustainability. As demonstrated by the NCA outcomes, GDT most significantly influenced SCA. Overall, this study has added depth to the current literature by (1) empirically connecting GDTL with GTI; (2) evidencing the importance of GDT to the achievement of SCA in Malaysia; and (3) providing an integrated framework linking the three components of GDTL, digital transformation, GTI and SCA. The current findings can serve as a guideline for future leaders to navigate digital and green transitions in developing nations.

title: Reductive Incorporation of Technetium-99 in Fe(II)-Doped Layered Double Hydroxide
abstract: Abstract Technetium-99 is a long-lived, high-yield fission product whose solubility is controlled by redox conditions. Here, to explore targeted effluent treatment approaches, pertechnetate (Tc(VII)O4–) reductive retention as Tc(IV) during coprecipitation of Fe(II)-doped Ni–Al–CO3 layered double hydroxide (LDH) was investigated. During LDH formation via base addition to an acidic Ni2+, Al3+, Fe2+, and Tc(VII)O4– bearing solution, there was essentially complete TcO4– removal at low (9.6 Bq/mL) and high (2.9 kBq/mL) concentrations. Characterization of experiments using X-ray diffraction, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) confirmed that, during base titration, a two-stage process occurred, with Al3+ forming amorphous Al (hydr)oxide between pH 4 and 6 in the first stage, followed by hydrolysis of Fe2+/Ni2+ and formation of LDH particles between pH 6 and 9 in stage two. During the first stage, TcO4– was removed from solution, and XAS confirmed it was reduced to Tc(IV) by Fe(II) associated with the amorphous Al (hydr)oxide, forming hydrous Tc(IV)O2-like chains on the Al (hydr)oxide surface. During the second stage, XAS showed that Tc(IV) was incorporated within the newly formed LDH structure. Overall, these data provide novel insights into the application of LDH formation in Tc sequestration and suggest novel effluent treatment pathways to produce an inorganic solid.

Optimal Information and Security Design
abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. Within the class of monotone securities, live-or-die securities are optimal and strictly dominate asset sales. When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal. (JEL D82, D86, G32)

title: Political Voice and (Mortgage) Market Participation: Evidence from the dilution of Voting Rights Act
abstract: Using US Supreme Court’s narrow-decision on Shelby v. Holder as a shock that diluted voting rights of Black Americans in covered counties, we document the relationship between political voice and economic decision-making. We show fewer Black Americans buy homes after their de-facto disenfranchisement, reflected through lower mortgage applications. Among those who apply for mortgages, there is a flight to Black lenders. Leveraging individual-level survey data, we show confidence in government and financial institutions plays a significant role in driving these effects. Our findings demonstrate that the effects of disenfranchisement extend beyond the ballot box to fundamental economic decisions like homeownership.

title: Aggregate fluctuations from firm comovement
PHILLIPS–SOLO ASYMPTOTICS FOR CONTINUOUS-TIME ARMA PROCESSES SAMPLED IN DISCRETE TIME
abstract: Phillips and Solo (1992, Annals of Statistics 20, 971–2001) provided sets of conditions concerning the summability of coefficients and the properties of innovations in discrete-time linear processes such that normalized sums satisfy certain asymptotic properties, such as laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and invariance principles. In this article, we consider ARMA processes in continuous time that are sampled at discrete-time intervals and provide conditions on the continuous-time process such that the results of Phillips and Solo can be utilized for normalized sums of the discrete-time observations. We utilize a state-space representation in the case of stock and flow variables, both of which are a linear combination of the state vector, and derive the relevant asymptotics based on multivariate extensions of the Phillips–Solo results. An illustrative application of the results to unit (zero) root testing is provided.

title: TRUE AND PSEUDO-TRUE PARAMETERS
abstract: Parameter estimates in misspecified models converge to pseudo-true parameter values, which minimize a population objective function. Pseudo-true values often differ from quantities of economic interest, raising questions of how, if at all, they are relevant for decision-making. To study this question, we consider Bayesian decision-makers facing a linear population minimum distance problem. Within a class of priors motivated by the minimum distance objective, we characterize prior sequences under which posteriors concentrate on the pseudo-true value. This convergence is fragile to small changes in priors, implying that pseudo-true values are relevant for decision-making only in special cases. Constructive results are nevertheless possible in this setting, and we derive simple confidence intervals that guarantee correct average coverage for the true parameter under every prior in the class we study, with no bound on the magnitude of misspecification.

title: Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors. Rapid technological progress during catch‐up creates strong demand for reallocating resources from slow to fast adopters, amplifying the consequences of adjustment costs. The amplification fades as technological change gradually slows during convergence to a more advanced and efficient steady state. I evaluate the model using Chinese and German enterprise data and find that differences in development stage account for at least 40% of their labour allocative efficiency gap.

title: Polycrisis and global production networks: a framework for understanding industry dynamics in times of accumulated uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Global production networks (GPNs) are currently impacted by multiple crises. Yet, crises have received little attention in GPN scholarship. This article shows how the entangled drivers of polycrisis affect the economic geographies of suppliers and their integration into GPNs. It develops an analytical framework for exploration of accumulated uncertainties in conjunctural moments of polycrisis. The management of unknown ‘uncertainties’ other than ‘risk’ for lead firms is a key element. Focusing on Bangladesh’s apparel industry, this article explores the industry’s responses and struggles, and provides insights into the wider processes of inclusion and exclusion in the global economy during polycrisis.

title: Time-varying impacts of government spending on CO2 emissions
Selling two units of a customizable good
abstract: A seller can produce two units of a good. Each unit can be customized into one of two versions, and buyers privately learn their valuations for each version. First I consider the case when the second unit costs more to produce than the first. Under certain distributional conditions the search for the optimal mechanism can be restricted to a class where there is no uncertainty about the number of units the buyer will receive, i.e. the buyer chooses whether to get 0, 1, or 2 units. However, there still may be uncertainty over which version the buyer will get. Buyers whose valuation for their favorite version is high, both in absolute terms and relative to the other version, purchase two units of their favorite version with certainty. Buyers with low values are excluded from purchasing. Buyers with values in the intermediate range typically get a lottery over different versions. I compare the fully optimal mechanism with the mechanism that optimally sells each unit separately and show that the solutions coincide when the fully optimal mechanism is deterministic, but they may differ otherwise. In the case when the cost of the second unit is not higher than the cost of the first the optimal mechanism only contains options with 0 and 2 units. The solution in this case can be shown to be isomorphic to a single unit case.

title: From Global Value Chains to Local Jobs: Exploring FDI-induced Job Creation in EU-27
Renewable Natural Resources, Regime Shift and Hysteresis
abstract: Many of the world’s renewable resources are in decline. Optimal harvests with smooth recruitment is well studied but in recent years, ecologists have concluded that tipping points in recruitment are common. Recruitment with a tipping point has low-fecundity below the tipping point and high-fecundity above. When the discounted value of high-fecundity is sufficiently high, there is a high-fecundity steady-state. This steady-state is stable but in some cases, small perturbations may result in large, temporary reductions in recruitment and harvests. Below the tipping point, a low-fecundity steady-state need not exist. When a low-fecundity steady-state does exist, there is an endogenous tipping (Skiba) point: below, harvests converge to the low-fecundity steady-state and above, an austere harvest policy transitions the renewable resource to high-fecundity recruitment. If there is hysteresis in recruitment, the high steady-state may not be stable. Moreover, if the high-/low-fecundity differential is large then following a downward perturbation, fecundity optimally remains low.

abstract: Subscription programs are increasingly central to platform strategy, but their effects on competitors and category demand remain unclear. The authors study restaurant delivery subscriptions using individual-level transaction data on Postmates Unlimited, the first widely available U.S. subscription program in the category, and DoorDash's later DashPass program. Using a matched, staggered difference-in-differences design, they find that signing up for Postmates Unlimited is associated with a 90.4% increase in spending at the focal firm, with no significant average change in competing-firm spending and no offsetting decline in adjacent food categories, consistent with category expansion. Competitive effects depend on customers' prior platform usage. For “singlehomers” (who only used Postmates prior to subscribing), subscribing is associated with increased spending at both the focal firm and competing platforms, even after cancellation. For “multihomers” (who had also previously used competing platforms), the focal-firm effect is larger, and competing-firm spending falls while customers remain subscribed; after cancellation, the focal-firm lift persists, but the decrease in competitor spending does not. DashPass results are broadly similar, but customers with prior Postmates subscription experience show little increase in category spending. Together, these findings suggest subscriptions can both expand markets and capture share, depending on prior platform usage and subscription experience.

title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Funding: The authors received no external funding for this research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03836 .

title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge research support from the Center for Investing at HKUST. Y. Xiong thanks the support by National Natural Science Foundation of China [NSFC 72422007] and the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Project 16501523]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07966 .

title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

title: Perceived Green Innovation Ambidexterity as a Strategic Signal in By‐Product Recycling: Employee Green Behavior, Environmental Consciousness, and Job Satisfaction
abstract: ABSTRACT In by‐product recycling businesses, pursuing green innovation ambidexterity is important, but its benefits depend on how employees enact this strategic orientation. Drawing on signaling theory, we conducted two studies to examine how perceived green innovation ambidexterity is related to employee green behavior and job satisfaction, and investigate the role of individual environmental consciousness in these relationships. For Study 1, we used survey data from 308 by‐product recycling workers in six countries and found that employee green behavior mediated the relationship between perceived green innovation ambidexterity and job satisfaction. Individual environmental consciousness strengthened the effect of perceived green innovation ambidexterity and employee green behavior on job satisfaction. For Study 2, we conducted a scenario‐based experiment with 204 participants, providing supplementary evidence in an experimental setting. Overall, we show how employees interpret green innovation ambidexterity as a strategic signal and translate it into green behavior and job satisfaction, with responses varying according to environmental consciousness.

title: Circular Economy Financial Performance: Sustainability (ESGUI), and Tourism Uncertainty (TUI)
abstract: ABSTRACT Although circular economy investments are seen as an important tool for achieving the SDGs, studies that examine the different sources of uncertainty affecting these investments within a nonlinear framework remain limited. The current literature largely focuses only on traditional uncertainty indices such as EPU, GPR, and pandemic‐related uncertainty. This study fills this gap in literature by including, for the first time in the circular economy literature, two newly developed uncertainty indices, the ESG‐related sustainability uncertainty indices (ESGUI) and the Tourism Uncertainty Index (TUI), alongside traditional uncertainty indicators, and examining their associations with circular economy financial performance. In this study, wavelet power spectrum (WPS), wavelet quantile regression (WQR), wavelet quantile‐on‐quantile regression (WQQR), and Baruník–Křehlík frequency‐domain connectedness (BKFSC) methods were used. The findings show that the relationships between uncertainty and circular economy financial performance differ across investment horizons and market regimes. WQQR results show that the relationships between ESGUI and TUI and circular economy financial performance are nonlinear and vary by market regime. Similarly, the relationships between EPU, GPR, PNDMC, the S&P 500, and circular economy financial performance also differ by market conditions. These findings highlight the importance of considering different sources of uncertainty and general market conditions together when evaluating circular economy financial performance.

title: Biodiversity risk and hotel stock returns: Global evidence from wavelet analysis
abstract: This paper aims to examine the dynamic correlation mechanisms between the S&P Global LargeMidCap Biodiversity Index (GBIO) and share prices of nine major global hotel groups. Based on daily data spanning from June 2019 to July 2025, the research utilises advanced econometric methods including wavelet local multiple correlation, wavelet coherence, wavelet quantile correlation, and rolling window wavelet correlation to reveal that biodiversity risk and hotel industry stock returns exhibit significant non-linear, time-varying, and frequency-dependent characteristics. Empirical results demonstrate that the two maintain a strong and stable positive correlation from a long-term investment perspective (exceeding 64 days), with correlation coefficients generally surpassing 0.8, whilst correlation weakens considerably at short-term scales (2–16 days). Cross-regional comparisons reveal that American hotel groups exhibit the strongest positive correlation with the biodiversity index (averaging 0.56), followed by European enterprises (averaging 0.45), with Asian enterprises showing the weakest correlation (averaging 0.27), reflecting the heterogeneity in ESG factor pricing efficiency across different capital markets. This association strengthened significantly following COVID-19, indicating that biodiversity has become a systematic factor influencing the long-term value of the hotel industry in the post-pandemic era. Portfolio optimization analysis reveals that incorporating GBIO into minimum variance portfolios achieves substantial risk reduction of 44–66% in VaR and hedging effectiveness of 68–89%, with optimal GBIO weights consistently around 0.92 or higher. The study provides crucial empirical evidence for investors' ESG investment decisions and policymakers' biodiversity conservation policy design.

title: A Design Science Approach to Scaling Platform Business Models
abstract: Platform business models are central to the digital economy, yet few achieve sustainable scaling—exponential expansion combined with resource-efficient value creation. Existing research highlights the role of business model design choices and managerial agency in shaping scaling outcomes but offers limited insight into how scalable configurations are generated under uncertainty. We address this question by adopting a design science perspective on platform scaling. A multi-case study of four platforms transitioning from two-sided markets to complex ecosystems reveals how firms generated scaling solutions through blending—the recursive recombination of business model ingredients across industries and geographies. This process was guided by scaling intentions and reinforced through immersion in the digital economy, enabling firms to construct and progressively stabilize novel configurations while shaping ecosystem interdependencies. Over time, recurring patterns in these design practices were codified into simple rules that guided subsequent scaling efforts. These insights contribute to research on platform scaling by shifting attention from identifying effective configurations to explaining how such configurations were generated under uncertainty. They further advance research on heuristics by reconceptualizing simple rules as generative principles that emerge from situated design processes, and extend design science by providing empirical insight into how such processes unfold in established platform firms.

title: Correction: Impatience and entrepreneurship
Body shifted, soul not: migrant identity, social inclusion, and small business success
A reciprocal perspective on internationalization and ESG in EMNEs: The role of digitalization
Resource loss, search distance, and crisis-triggered identity
abstract: We examine why entrepreneurs facing comparable losses during crises search for substitutes at different distances from their incumbent resource pools. We study 27 entrepreneurs who fled Russia following the 2022 war in Ukraine. Building on Conservation of Resources theory, we find that resource-loss severity shaped search distance, but not uniformly: entrepreneurs with modest losses largely substituted within incumbent resource pools. Where severe loss depleted those pools, entrepreneurs drew on what we term crisis-triggered identity (a self-understanding the crisis activated), and their searches diverged, some remaining within familiar domains, others ranging into unfamiliar ones. Entrepreneurs’ losses set how far they must search; who they understand themselves to be sets how far they will.

title: Can linguistic vagueness in annual reports predict supply chain risk?
abstract: Annual reports serve as a critical information channel for corporate stakeholders, especially for supply chain partners. We argue that linguistic vagueness in these reports can function as an early-warning signal for predicting supply chain risk. To test our proposition, we develop a theory-grounded measure of linguistic vagueness by integrating communication vagueness theory with the Word2Vec method. Our analysis of publicly listed companies in China reveals a robust positive association between linguistic vagueness and subsequent supply chain risk. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that this predictive capacity varies under different reputational pressures. Furthermore, by employing interpretable machine learning approaches within an out-of-sample predictive framework, we validate the consistent directional predictive signal via SHAP analysis and solidify the indicator’s predictive robustness. Ultimately, this study establishes linguistic vagueness as an incremental signal that carries significant out-of-sample predictive value for supply chain risk, providing stakeholders with a data-driven approach for proactive risk monitoring.

title: Firm-level effects of AI attention on wages and productivity: A global comparative study
abstract: This paper studies how wages and productivity among publicly listed firms vary with AI attention during a period of uneven AI adoption. AI attention measures the prominence of AI in the country-level information environment. It is distinct from AI adoption. The wage measure captures average staff expenditure on wages and salaries per employee. Using data for 69,783 listed firms in 83 countries over 2004–2023, I measure this attention with Google Trends and combine TWFE, IV–2SLS, and local projections to estimate static and dynamic relationships. Among listed firms in advanced economies (AEs), higher AI attention is associated with lower wages but higher labour productivity and TFP. Listed firms in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) show short-run wage gains and positive productivity responses. These patterns also vary across firms, with wage declines more pronounced among smaller, lower-productivity, and goods-producing listed firms. The sample represents the organised listed corporate sector, which constitutes a particularly selective segment of the firm population in EMDEs; the wider SME, informal, and unlisted sectors remain outside the scope of the analysis. The patterns are consistent with expectations, perceived substitution risk, organisational investment, and workforce composition playing different roles in listed-firm adjustment. • Google Trends measures AI attention for 69,783 listed firms across 83 countries. • Higher AI attention relates to lower wages and higher productivity in AEs. • EMDE listed firms show short-run wage gains and positive productivity responses. • Local projections show persistent and heterogeneous responses to AI attention. • Responses vary by firm size, productivity, sector, and country development level.

title: Alienation and Emotional Labor
Climate Policy Uncertainty and Product Market Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT Using annual data from 276 listed Chinese energy companies from 2009 to 2022, this study investigates the impact of climate policy uncertainty (CPU) on energy companies' product market performance (PMP). The results indicate that CPU significantly enhances enterprise performance in the product market, and subsequent analyses involving variable substitution, tail reduction, and the consideration of potential endogeneity issues confirm the robustness of this conclusion. Additionally, the moderating effects results indicate that among the four types of cross‐border capital flows, cross‐border capital direct investment and cross‐border capital flows from other investments negatively moderate the CPU–PMP relationship, while the overall level of cross‐border capital flows positively moderates the CPU–PMP relationship. Meanwhile, ESG performance and actions with R&D backgrounds positively moderate the CPU–PMP relationship. Moreover, the mediating effect test reveals that CPU influences energy companies' PMP primarily through enhancing technological innovation, alleviating financing constraints, improving the management incentive system, and reducing equity concentration. Lastly, heterogeneity results demonstrate that CPU has a more significant influence on the market performance of non‐SOEs, large‐scale enterprises, profitable companies, non‐transparent companies, enterprises characterized by dispersed equity ownership, and regions with higher stabilization policy efficiency.
journal_name: Journal of International Financial Management & Accounting

title: The effects of aggregate and local extreme weather on financial distress risk: Evidence from China
Blockchain E-invoicing adoption and corporate vertical integration: Evidence from transaction cost theory
Balancing risk communication and accountability concerns in risk management: A study of major public project investments
abstract: Abstract Effective administration of public organizations requires timely responses to emerging risks, yet communicating those risks up the hierarchy can expose operational managers to blame in politicized accountability environments. This study examines how public managers navigated that tension in an analysis of 130 risk reports filed over a seven-year period associated with two major procurement and maintenance projects in the Danish Defence. Using an abductive qualitative approach, we develop a dynamic model of risk management with four phases: (1) risk as an operational concern, (2) turning risk into an organizational problem, (3) assigning blame and accountability, and (4) initiating mitigation and response. We find that risk and accountability communication are interdependent processes rather than independent sequential processes. Operational managers attempt to raise awareness of emerging risks while simultaneously deflecting potential blame and catering to higher-level concerns about public scrutiny. This tension generates pressure to only report when it is absolutely necessary, while higher-level managers often postpone action to avoid political exposure. These practices contribute to delays, projects not meeting specifications, and significant budget overruns. The study advances a dynamic theory of public sector risk management and explains how hierarchical communication practices influence whether, when, and how emerging risks are addressed.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Lack of public service motivation as a value-constraining mechanism in entrepreneurial ecosystems
abstract: This paper examines how public service motivation (PSM) shapes public value creation (PVC) within publicly funded entrepreneurial support organizations (ESOs). As public service ecosystems, ESOs play a pivotal role in entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs), yet how they create public value remains underexplored. While existing research emphasizes PSM at the individual level, less is known about how PSM translates into intentional PVC in boundary-spanning ecosystem contexts. Drawing on an empirical qualitative multi-case study, we show that although ESO staff exhibit a strong commitment to enhancing the public interest, regional-level PVC is constrained by unclear and narrow organizational goals, inconsistent practices, and limited leadership support. Our findings highlight the need for leadership grounded in transformative, supportive, and human-centred practices, as well as leadership collaboration spanning organizational boundaries. This paper clarifies the organizational conditions under which PSM contributes to PVC in hybrid governance settings.

title: Citizens' perceptions of accountability in AI-based public sector decision making
abstract: Research has increasingly focused on identifying and analyzing the key components of accountability in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector. However, much of the existing literature takes a government-centric approach, emphasizing how public organizations implement accountability measures while paying limited attention to citizens' perspectives. This study addresses this gap by empirically examining whom citizens believe should be held accountable and what information about AI-based decisions should be communicated to the public. Using data from a nationally representative sample of U.S. citizens, our analysis reveals several overall trends in public perceptions of accountability for AI-based systems, as well as demographic differences. These findings provide valuable empirical insights to advance research and practice on the use of AI in government.

title: Public Participation as Administrative Practice: Evidence from Federal Entitlement Communities
abstract: Public participation is widely recognized as an important component of democratic governance, yet empirical studies often evaluate participation by the methods employed rather than the institutional structures through which participation is organized within administrative processes. Drawing on an analysis of 289 local jurisdictions receiving federal block grants, this study examines participation as structured administrative practice rather than simply a collection of engagement methods. Using inductive analysis of Consolidated Plans, the study develops a typology of four participation structures: Minimal Compliance, Structured Consultation, Institutionalized Consultation, and Embedded Participation.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: 'We are no longer Allowed to be Human': Officers’ Experiences Policing the Compounding Crises of the COVID-19 Pandemic and Civil Unrest in the United States
abstract: Local police officers are among the most prominent frontline public servants, interacting daily with people, communities, and other agencies and stakeholders. They are, in the most literal sense, street-level bureaucrats. These interactions were greatly tested in the summer of 2020. Police managed – or in some cases refused to manage – enforcement orders for a global pandemic while at the same time policing in the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd. This article explores how officers in three local jurisdictions navigated these dual, compounding crises – which we can certainly expect many more of in the future – and the implications for police interactions, discretion (including de-policing) and job satisfaction. The article concludes with a discussion of how police leaders, local officials and community advocates can better support law enforcement professionals during times of crises.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Does Citizen Political Ideology Shape Bureaucratic Responsiveness? Evidence From an Audit Experiment
abstract: Government workers often take shortcuts when making decisions about delivering public services. When these shortcuts are influenced by stereotypes or bias, citizens may receive unequal treatment. This research examines whether bureaucrats in U.S. housing authorities and parks departments discriminate based on citizen political ideology. Using a pre-registered 2 × 3 email audit experiment ( n = 974), we test whether responsiveness varies when citizens signal conservative views, liberal views, or no political views. The results show that street-level bureaucrats are more likely to respond to citizens signaling conservative views than to citizens with no stated political views. Responsiveness does not differ between citizens signaling liberal views and citizens with no stated political views. However, when a reply is provided, citizens signaling liberal views receive more helpful responses. Interaction models suggest that responsiveness to citizens signaling liberal views differs across public housing authorities and parks departments. These findings suggest that political ideology may shape bureaucratic responsiveness in ways that have implications for fairness in public service delivery.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Health risks of alcohol consumption in Aotearoa New Zealand: modelling to inform low-risk-drinking guidelines
