A broadband and self-driven light sensing optoelectronic device based on a plasmonic MXene-based Ni 2 O 3– X –polymer/TiO 2 heterostructure
abstract: A cost-effective and scalable optoelectronic device based on an MXene-based Ni 2 O 3− X –P1HP (poly(1H-pyrrole))/TiO 2 nanocomposite was fabricated through a facile synthetic strategy involving the incorporation of this composite on additional P1HP seeding layer. The enhanced MXene-based Ni 2 O 3− X –P1HP/TiO 2 /P1HP optoelectronic performance originates from the synergistic integration of multiple semiconductor components with oxygen-deficient Ni 2 O 3− X , whose plasmonic characteristics and defect-rich electronic structure promote efficient light harvesting and charge transport. Under ultraviolet illumination, the fabricated device achieved a maximum responsivity of 2.0 mA W –1 and a specific detectivity of 0.18 × 10 10 Jones. Remarkably, the device maintained substantial photoactivity at lower photon energies (1.6 eV; ∼730 nm), delivering a responsivity of 1.5 mA W –1 and a detectivity of 0.13 × 10 10 Jones, thereby showing efficient operation within the visible–near-infrared spectral region. Morphological investigations revealed the formation of semispherical and rod-like nanostructures with characteristic dimensions of approximately 100 nm. Optical analysis further demonstrated a narrowed band gap of ∼1.48 eV, facilitating enhanced optical absorption across a broad spectral range. In addition, the oxygen-vacancy-rich Ni 2 O 3− X phase introduced localized defect states that promoted hot-carrier generation and suppressed charge recombination. Collectively, these structural and electronic features enable efficient photon harvesting, rapid charge-transfer kinetics, and improved carrier separation, highlighting the potential of this low-cost MXene-based architecture for next-generation optoelectronic sensing applications.

title: Daily Briefing: Tiny doses of LSD seem to boost cognition
Daily briefing: How to rebuild science from ruin
Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.

title: Asymmetric behavioural responses to updating caloric information
abstract: Abstract Calorie labels are widely used as an information disclosure policy, yet their behavioural effects remain debated. Across four studies ( N = 2,067), including one nationally representative online sample of the U.S., we examine how individuals adjust portion-size choices after updating misperceptions about meal calorie content. Using more than 45,000 incentivised calorie estimates and 6,000 food choices, we find that food characteristics, not individual traits, better predict misperceptions, and that larger misestimations are associated with extreme portion choices. Portion-size adjustments after a label reveals the caloric content are substantially smaller than the initial estimation errors. Responses are asymmetric: correcting underestimation is associated with larger reductions in portion size than the increases observed after correcting overestimation. Individuals who estimate calories accurately show little to no adjustment. Increases after correcting overestimation are concentrated among healthier foods and lower-conflict eaters. These results highlight asymmetric behavioural responses to disclosed information and suggest that average calorie changes may obscure important heterogeneity.

title: Voluntary sustainability standards and economic and ecological outcomes: panel evidence from Rwanda’s coffee sector
Is it abundance or scarcity? Reassessing freshwater resources and civil war onset (1960–2023)
The impact of regional growth on internal migration: a district-level analysis for Malawi
Land-based climate policy, land prices, and the green transition trilemma: Evidence from Bolivia
abstract: Land-based climate policies in forest-rich developing economies are often assessed separately, overlooking how land scarcity, land prices, and macroeconomic constraints shape feasibility. This paper examines the macro-financial challenges of sustainable agriculture and forest conservation in Bolivia, where deforestation is high and fiscal and external constraints bind. We develop a dynamic version of the Exposure to Structural Transformation in an Ecologic-Economic Model (D-ESTEEM) to jointly analyse Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) policies for forest conservation and agricultural productivity. The locally calibrated, environmentally extended input-output model combines continuous-time monetary system dynamics, endogenous land prices, and demand-led adjustments in a small open economy. Forest conservation reduces environmental pressures but raises land prices, weakening the competitiveness of land-intensive activities and worsening fiscal and balance-of-payments pressures. Agricultural productivity measures ease land pressures and support output but rely on imported inputs, reinforcing external dependence. Overall, the NDCs improve economic activity and environmental outcomes while worsening fiscal and trade imbalances. Fiscal consolidation and exchange-rate adjustment mitigate some imbalances but entail inflationary pressures or lower output and employment. Environmental gains may therefore come at the cost of macroeconomic fragility. The paper shows how conservation-induced land scarcity and land price dynamics interact with fiscal and balance-of-payments constraints to determine the feasibility of land-based transitions in resource-dependent economies.

title: Disasters bite less deeply, but they do not stop biting: four decades of structural transformation and disaster sensitivity in Vietnam
The Endowment Effect and Seller Behavior: Evidence from the Real Estate Market
abstract: Abstract An endowment effect arises when people demand more to give up a good than they would pay to acquire it. Using a unique dataset that provides complete histories of actual transactions in the real estate market, this study documents a seller‐buyer valuation gap consistent with an endowment effect among real estate owners, regardless of gender or experience. Further comparisons using various homeowners’ purpose and transaction characteristics reveal that whereas homeowners of owner‐occupied properties exhibit a smaller valuation gap, those faced with higher liquidity exhibit a significantly larger valuation gap. These patterns are consistent with endowment‐related behavior, although listing prices may also reflect strategic considerations.

Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.

title: It's in the Small Steps: Navigating Knotted Change‐Stability Tensions in Complex Collaborations
abstract: Abstract Addressing societal challenges requires collaborative arrangements that can adapt to changing environments while maintaining coherence. Existing research highlights collaborative responses to change, yet the processes through which such responses emerge remain poorly understood. Notably, collaborative change involves not only balancing change and stability but also navigating knotted collective‐individual tensions that arise in realigning interests, coordination structures, and operations. To advance understanding of these dynamics, we conduct an in‐depth longitudinal study of collaborative change in a cross‐sector disaster relief partnership. Across successive change stages, we identify stability drivers emerging from collective‐individual tensions that prompted the partners to adopt specific balancing practices. These practices enabled a change process that was incremental and fragile in progression, yet resilient in its cumulative pattern. We develop a process model that explains the dynamics of collaborative change and shows how balancing change and stability enables partners to progressively broaden and occasionally transcend collective‐individual alignment as trust and mutual understanding deepen. This study advances collaboration and paradox theory by exposing balancing practices tailored to collaborative settings that enable adaptation in dynamic environments and by proposing a gradual approach to navigating knotted paradoxes.

title: Everything everywhere all‐at‐once? AI , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

title: Generative AI and the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantages
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantage. We argue that GenAI's impact is conditional on how those opportunities are formed. Discovery opportunities originate from exogenous industry shocks. However, widely available GenAI tools are likely to commoditize opportunity recognition in these settings and thus reduce advantages that might have been generated by exploiting these opportunities. Creation opportunities emerge endogenously, under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, through entrepreneurial action and interaction with the environment. However, GenAI cannot fully resolve the Knightian uncertainty inherent in creation settings, so sustained advantage here depends on whether resources and capabilities developed through creating an opportunity are inimitable. Unawareness opportunities rely on competitive neglect. GenAI may reduce the advantages of firms in these settings when it makes rents legible to potential competitors and when search is directed toward these invisible markets. Managerial Summary Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT and Claude help entrepreneurs spot opportunities, but every competitor can potentially access the same tools. Whether GenAI can create sustained competitive advantages, this paper argues, depends on how an opportunity is formed. When opportunities arise from entrepreneurs noticing an external market shift, GenAI levels the playing field by commoditizing recognition and pushes entrepreneurs to win through execution and hard‐to‐copy complements. When opportunities are created through actions and interactions of entrepreneurs with their environments, GenAI does not fully remove the uncertainty that makes these efforts entrepreneurial but can speed up experimentation. When opportunities emerge from entrepreneurs operating in markets neglected by competitors, GenAI may have a limited effect on advantage unless it makes invisible markets publicly known.

title: Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.

title: Organization and the Signature of Power
abstract: This paper introduces the ‘signature of power’ as a framework to enhance the understanding of politics in organizational studies. We argue for an understanding of contemporary forms of power as a signature that connects and divides two constellations: juridical-political sovereignty (supreme authority) on one side, and economic-managerial government (practical regulation) on the other. These poles have analogies in organizational theory dichotomies like formal versus informal, and institution versus network. The signature of power serves as a heuristic – a discovery mechanism – that enables scholars to navigate and integrate these opposing forces without reducing them to one dominant paradigm. The framework is articulated through four analytical strategies: analytics of government (local, immanent power practices), genealogy of order (historical foundations of governing orders), archaeology of glory (rituals and symbols of supreme authority), and analytics of authority (formal organizational hierarchies and operations). These strategies and their distinct relationships provide a more coherent analytical framework for a multi-paradigm approach to understanding power relations, resistance, and organizational forms. The paper tests this analytic framework through a study of the corporation as a ‘signature of power’ that bridges economic-managerial and juridical-political forms and is shaped by historical shifts and legal innovations. Addressing potential critiques, the paper emphasizes the framework’s adaptability to resistance and its applicability to diverse organizational contexts. This conceptualization encourages intellectual plurality, fostering historically and conceptually informed insight into politics as a set of power-related organizational and institutional practices.

title: Closer to the leader, above the coworkers? How leader gratitude expression shapes employee responses across relational targets
journal_name: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

title: The Hidden Upside of Tech Challenges
abstract: The stresses of technological roadblocks and challenges can result in employee ambivalence and easily lead to disengagement. But tech stress isn’t always bad. New research shows that increasing constructive technology challenges offers employees engaging growth opportunities — if annoying tech hindrances have already been mitigated. The researchers share a three-part approach for creating a stimulating work environment while minimizing tech hurdles and employee ambivalence.

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Mediated Eco‐Design and Environmental Strategy: Human Decision Authority, Sustainability Disclosure, and Lifecycle Accountability
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to generate, simulate, and optimize sustainable product designs. This development creates an environmental strategy problem that existing greenwashing, decoupling, and eco‐innovation theories do not fully explain: an environmentally favorable outcome may be technically real yet difficult for stakeholders to attribute to accountable organizational environmental judgment. This conceptual article develops eco‐algorithmic decoupling as a process attribution gap that may arise, especially for stakeholders who value traceable human environmental judgment, when meaningful human eco‐design decision authority is weak or when disclosures misrepresent the human‐AI division of decision‐making. It distinguishes this process attribution problem from lifecycle incompleteness, a separate accounting problem concerning whether material AI process impacts fall within product claim boundaries and are accounted for or disclosed. The article advances a two‐path credibility model: human decision authority affects perceived moral eco‐integrity and then claim credibility, while lifecycle completeness affects perceived claim completeness and then claim credibility. Disclosure congruence, stakeholder characteristics, and verified environmental performance moderate these paths. The paper contributes to environmental strategy by specifying how AI changes the governance conditions under which eco‐innovation is perceived as credible, accountable, and strategically valuable. It offers propositions, a governance typology, provisional PMEI items, coding rules, and an empirical research agenda for testing AI‐mediated eco‐design credibility.

title: Turning adversity into opportunity: Managerial interventions and employee responses to observed customer mistreatment
abstract: Customer mistreatment is a pervasive challenge in hospitality settings, affecting not only directly targeted employees but also those who witness encounters. Prior research has conceptualized observed customer mistreatment (OCM) through stress and deontic justice lenses, centering on observers’ withdrawal or interpersonal reactions. We shift this perspective by conceptualizing OCM as a service safety incident following which some observers report learning-oriented responses. Study 1 employs the critical incident technique to examine employee and manager accounts and identifies spontaneous observer learning and instances of manager-facilitated reflection. Integrating these findings abductively with cognitive appraisal theory and self-efficacy research, Study 2 tests whether a manager-led post-incident learning/debriefing intervention enhances service self-efficacy, a belief about one’s capability to handle demanding customers, and whether this belief is associated with anticipated responses in a subsequent service encounter. The intervention increased service self-efficacy, which in turn was associated with stronger intended proactive customer service behavior and lower anticipated surface acting. These findings point to the potential value of manager-led post-incident interventions after witnessed mistreatment.

title: Business networks and the persistence of entrepreneurship: evidence from China
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the long run association between business networks and entrepreneurship and regional development in China. We focus on chambers of commerce, bodies which facilitated networking between businesses until private firms were banned by Mao. Our results suggest that the pre-Mao chamber system is associated with long-lasting patterns of business creation and economic output in China, with this influence surviving until the post-1978 return of the market economy. The associations are strongest in the early reform period but weaken over time. We show evidence that historic chambers density is correlated with later social capital, despite major political change.

title: Virtue re-coding: How institutional voids shape ethical practice in international business
abstract: Shared moral vocabularies recur across the Arab world, yet senior executives enact them differently across institutional settings. Drawing on a comparative case study of 45 interviews with Muslim and Christian executives in Lebanon, Iraq, and Egypt, we ask how shared moral resources are re-coded across distinct institutional voids. We develop a mechanism-based account of virtue re-coding: virtue vocabularies such as reputation (sumʿa) and patience (sabr), and morally contested relational practices such as intermediation (wasta), acquire distinct functional meanings through void-specific legitimacy tests. Coordination, security, and procedural voids are associated with three recurring patterns of ethical bricolage, navigational, survivalist, and hierarchical, within which legitimacy calibration modulates enactment through relative legitimacy positioning. Actors also draw the ethics/corruption boundary around wasta differently across voids. The study contributes to IB ethics by explaining how shared virtues become context-specific moral practices, with implications for compliance design and mixed-method extension.

title: Human-robot teams: an Input-Mediator-Output-Input perspective on a new work paradigm

title: Commons governance for international trade: Navigating the efficiency-adaptability paradox in private permissioned blockchain platforms
abstract: Private permissioned blockchain platforms promise to increase the efficiency of international trade networks by offering a hybrid governance arrangement that reduces the transaction and governance costs of international trade administration. However, potential users have declined to join such platforms due to concerns about platforms' commitment to users' interests and platforms' ability to adapt to external shocks and changing business needs. Analyzing the failure of TradeLens, a Maersk/IBM private permissioned blockchain platform, we argue that the very characteristics that increase efficiency also constrain the adaptation of platforms and business models, creating an efficiency-adaptability paradox. To navigate this paradox, we propose a two-layer governance configuration which utilizes private permissioned blockchain to increase transaction efficiency and relational shared governance to guide infrequent, consequential platform adaptation. We then apply principles of commons governance to specify mechanisms for relational shared governance on a global scale. We contribute to theorizing digital platforms the insight that private permissioned blockchain platforms suffer from an efficiency-adaptability paradox and offer a governance configuration for navigating the paradox. We contribute to relational and commons governance theory mechanisms that expand shared governance to a global scale. We connect the governance challenges of private permissioned blockchains to hybrid governance theory by outlining a governance configuration that balances the interests of users and sponsors in voluntary global networks and ecosystems in which market and hierarchy are infeasible. Practically, we describe the governance configuration and mechanisms concretely enough to be implemented by sponsors of global private permissioned blockchain platforms.

title: “Beauty” versus “threat”: how awe influences the desire for luxury goods
Upframing customer vulnerability through a circle of strength
Policy persistence without performance: compensatory legitimacy and the expansion of entrepreneurship education in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: This study examines why entrepreneurship education in Sub-Saharan Africa persists despite limited demonstrable impact. Drawing on institutional and compensatory entrepreneurship theory, we conduct a multi-level abductive study across Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa, and Zambia using 59 interviews with students, faculty, policymakers, and administrators. We show how entrepreneurship education operates as a compensatory legitimacy mechanism linking policy mandates, institutional compliance, and student dissatisfaction. Under conditions of resource constraint and high unemployment, symbolic implementation sustains governmental and university legitimacy despite weak outcomes. We specify the boundary conditions under which entrepreneurship education is likely to function symbolically rather than instrumentally and offer implications for policy design in resource-constrained contexts.

title: Attend But Disengage: How Illusory Superiority Disrupts Sustainable Food Decision‐Making
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing literature often treats the intention–behaviour gap in sustainable food consumption as a single breakdown between intention and action. The present research adopts a process‐oriented perspective, arguing that consumers may disengage at multiple stages when evaluating sustainable food products. Drawing on the Hierarchy of Effects model and the moment‐by‐moment analysis capability of consumer biometric methodologies, we propose that initial attention to sustainability cues is necessary but insufficient to elicit positive emotional responses or support sustainable food purchase decisions. Instead, consumers must become emotionally engaged with the product for sustainability information to progress toward purchase intention. Across four studies, we show that emotional engagement, rather than attention alone, drives purchase intention for sustainable food products. We further demonstrate that illusory superiority bias can reduce emotional engagement because consumers who perceive themselves as more sustainable than others may feel less motivated to engage further with sustainable products. However, when this illusion is corrected, consumers may experience contempt in response to the corrective feedback and in turn, increase emotional engagement with sustainable products as a form of self‐affirmation.

title: Sustainability accounting and reporting: organisational identity construction and enactment in local governments
abstract: Purpose Sustainability accounting and reporting (SAR) has experienced a wide diffusion in the last decades, also in the public sector. It is primarily useful for increasing accountability, transparency and organisational legitimacy. As a consequence, scholars have focused their attention on the external dimensions of SAR and its relationship with organisations' financial performance. This focus has left the internal and managerial dimension of SAR largely underexplored. This article seeks to address this gap by shedding light on the role that SAR can play in the processes of organisational identity construction and enactment. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal case study was conducted to examine the ongoing voluntary adoption of SAR by an Italian pioneer municipality (MoB), and how this practice has contributed to its identity construction and enactment. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and official documents. Findings The research identifies voluntary SAR as both driven by organisational identity and used to construct and enact it in the absence of a public policy. More specifically, SAR contributes to organisational identity construction and enactment by building a collective memory that demonstrates the alignment and consistency between public employees' work and the identity of the organisation to which they belong. Originality/value The research advances the literature on SAR by exploring its contribution to studies on organisational identity. It analyses documents that reflect various phases of organisational processes (planning, accounting and reporting) as organisational practices that contribute to the construction and enactment of organisational identity. The absence of an explicit public policy could be seen as undermining the role of SAR as an accountability tool. Instead, this article shows that voluntary SAR may operate internally as a technology through which organisational identity is articulated, stabilised and enacted over time. This perspective highlights the organisational potential of SAR beyond its external accountability function.

title: Optimal tourism taxation with externalities: A rejoinder on Rosselló-Nadal and Sard (2026)
Quantitative research in tourism: Theoretical and methodological innovations
Adjustment and pivoting in tandem: The evolution of EMNEs in CoPS industries under geopolitical tensions
abstract: The rapid catchup and growing capabilities of emerging-market multinational enterprises (EMNEs) have made them increasingly susceptible to geopolitical tensions, especially in complex product systems (CoPS) industries deeply intertwined with national security and modern industrialization. Through a longitudinal case study of an EMNE in the offshore engineering equipment industry, we develop an integrative framework that illustrates how such firms can navigate the perceived threat of geopolitical tensions while sustaining their global operations, particularly when they have not undergone substantial disruption. We find that, in anticipation of such risks, firms proactively reconfigure their businesses through a dual logic of adjustment (recombining existing elements) and pivoting (integrating novel elements with existing ones) across market, technology, and ecosystem dimensions. Our study extends the strategic choice perspective by framing EMNEs’ evolution as a process in which this dual logic embodies strategic ambidexterity under structural constraints. It further advances the action-based view of dynamic capabilities by specifying how the interplay among multiple strategic dimensions enables sustained firm evolution under the perceived threat of geopolitical tensions.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Negative Marketing Events: The Overlooked Role of Normative Ethics
Differentiation from mentors and the gender productivity gap in research: Evidence from electrical engineering
Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy
abstract: ABSTRACT The field of public administration stands amid genuine crisis. Americans don't trust government or its administrators. Elected officials have attacked the career service as agents of the “deep state” and, though it might be hard to admit, many of public administration's critics have a point. Government's performance too often falls short of what people expect, practitioners too often seem too unresponsive to elected officials, and researchers too often seem to have only fuzzy guidance for practitioners. However, public administration undoubtedly is more important now than ever in translating public goals into effective action, and in bringing to life the democratic aspirations Madison and his colleagues wished for the country at its founding. The field urgently needs new strategies and tactics for solving the new generation of puzzles the country faces. In coming together, practitioners and researchers build on these puzzles to chart an exciting road forward.

title: Impact of Anti‐Money Laundering Enforcement on Suspicious Activity Reporting—Empirical Evidence From Real Estate Agencies in Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the impact of anti‐money laundering (AML) oversight on suspicious activity reports (SARs) filed by real estate agencies in Norway. Using unique data on inspections, sanctions, and confidential SARs, the study estimates the effects of inspections on reporting through a difference‐in‐differences approach. The results show an increase in reporting post‐inspection driven by entities with a low, positive number of prior filings, while report quality remains unchanged. There is no evidence of spillover effects; inspections do not influence the reporting of uninspected entities either geographically close to or affiliated with inspected ones. The findings suggest that AML oversight may create a learning effect for inspected entities but does not lead to sector‐wide improvements beyond local effects. This paper contributes to the modest empirical literature on AML oversight effects and the general literature on regulatory enforcement and provides recommendations for improvements to the AML system.

title: The blurred line between ends and means: how frontline workers factor production attributes into results in performance evaluations
abstract: Results-based performance management assumes that organizational performance can be evaluated by defining and measuring desired results. Yet frontline workers, who translate performance goals into service delivery, may interpret results through their knowledge of how services are produced. We examine whether production attributes enter frontline evaluations of formal results. Drawing on theories of sensemaking and cognitive judgment, we argue that task difficulty and effort provide salient cues through which frontline workers contextualize performance information. We test these expectations using a conjoint survey experiment with 1,371 Danish high school teachers, randomly varying production attributes alongside formal results. Teachers rate schools serving more disadvantaged students more favorably and increase ratings when schools demonstrate greater effort. Both effects exhibit clear dose-response patterns, with effort effects comparable to those of formal results. The findings show that frontline evaluations systematically incorporate production information, revealing how performance management can generate divergent understandings of organizational performance.

title: Assessing performance in collaborative governance networks: testing the Productivity Performance Matrix
