Optimal avoidability in cross-border minimum taxation
abstract: Many tax regimes collect revenue to the extent that other governments do not. This paper develops a theory of how such cross-border minimum taxes should be designed, focusing on choices that affect avoidance of the regime. Making a minimum tax more difficult to avoid retains more firms within the regime but weakens competition among tax havens. Havens then raise their rates toward the minimum, reducing the top-up tax rate on shifted profit. As a result, an avoidable minimum tax can raise more revenue for the governments that impose it than an unavoidable one.

title: Pricing climate risks: Evidence from wildfires and municipal bonds
abstract: How are public finances affected by climate-driven changes in wildfire risk? Using high-resolution meteorological forecasts, land use data, and US municipal bond spreads, we find that municipalities facing greater future wildfire exposure already incur higher borrowing costs: A one standard deviation increase in future wildfire risk is associated with a 7 (8) basis point rise in primary (secondary) market spreads—over 15% of the sample mean. Impacts appear larger in areas with higher minority populations and greater reliance on local revenue. Our study contributes to the broader literature by introducing a new approach to evaluating the capitalization of evolving physical climate risks.

title: The impact of preference programs in public procurement: Evidence from veteran set-asides
Geopoliticizing the Firm: Embraer, Corporate Nationality, and the Geopolitical Constitution of Contracts, Capabilities, and Markets
abstract: Transnational corporations (TNCs) drive fast-changing global economic geographies amid fraught geopolitical relations. However, three influential theoretical accounts of the firm, the nexus of contracts, the resource-based view, and Global Production Networks 2.0, still underspecify how corporate nationality and home–host state geopolitical agendas constitute TNCs’ formation, operations, and strategic management. This omission creates a gap in explaining the connections between geopolitical conditions and TNC operations. This article addresses this gap by geopoliticizing the firm. To this end, it integrates key aspects of the three theoretical accounts into a novel conceptual framework that comprises three analytical mechanisms: geopolitical agenda alignment, territorially defined capability formation, and territorially differentiated product development. Empirically, the article primarily draws on twenty-two interviews with elites across different firms and institutions to examine how Embraer, an aerospace producer, evolved following its establishment in 1969 as an integral part of Brazilian state developmentalism. After privatization in 1994, Embraer simultaneously (dis)engaged with multiple state geopolitical agendas to straddle US–China geopolitical tensions and compete internationally. Such proactive geopolitical (dis)engagement augmented Embraer’s ability to secure contracts, create capabilities, and capture markets across multiple countries. Through this case study, the article demonstrates the importance of conceptualizing the entwinement of TNC activities with both corporate nationality and variegated geopolitical contexts.

title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.

A Century of Stock Market Liquidity and Trading Costs
abstract: ABSTRACT I assemble and examine an annual time series of bid–ask spreads on Dow Jones stocks from 1900 to 2000 and average commission rates for trading NYSE stocks since 1925. Spreads are cyclical, especially during periods of market turmoil. The sum of half‐spreads and one‐way commissions, multiplied by annual turnover, estimates the aggregate cost of trading and drives a wedge between gross and net equity returns. This difference explains only a small part of the observed equity premium, though I show that the gross equity premium is perhaps 1% lower today than it was early in the 1900's. Finally, I find that the transaction cost measures (spreads and turnover), which serve as a proxy for liquidity, predict stock returns 1 year or more ahead and dominate traditional measures such as the dividend yield. The evidence suggests aggregate liquidity is a determinant of expected stock market returns.

title: Selling at the Opening: The “T+1” Rule, Short-term Speculation, and Stock Returns
The Impact of Early Investments in Urban School Systems in the United States
abstract: Cities in the United States dramatically expanded spending on public education after WWI, with the average urban school district increasing per pupil expenditures by over 70 percent by 1924. We provide the first evaluation of these unprecedented investments in public education using a new dataset and plausibly exogenous growth in school spending generated by anti-German sentiment. We find that school resources significantly increased educational attainment and wages later in life, particularly for less advantaged children. Increases in expenditures can explain about 40 percent of the sizable increase in educational attainment of cohorts born between 1895 and 1913. “Every great war in which the United States has played a part has been followed by educational developments of supreme national importance…Although the United States was engaged in the World War less than two years, the effects upon education resulting from this brief period of warfare will perhaps prove to be as far-reaching and as important as those growing out of any previous war…Undoubtedly the World War was the most important factor in awakening the American public to the inadequacy of its educational provisions and in arousing the States to vigorous efforts to improve educational conditions.” —Fletcher Harper Swift, Biennial Survey of Education 1920–1922, Volume 1, (1924, pp. 1–2).

title: School timing, sleep, and adolescent behavior: Evidence from lottery-assigned start times
Revisiting the price elasticity of charitable giving: Meta-analysis of tax incentives and matching donations
abstract: This paper presents the first quantitative meta-analysis of the price elasticity of charitable giving under both rebate and matching schemes. We compile 137 elasticity estimates from 26 experimental papers and synthesize them using random-effects and multilevel models. Charitable giving is highly price-responsive: the pooled meta-analytic mean elasticity of total donations is −1.75, indicating that lowering the effective price of giving substantially increases charitable revenue. Although we observe considerable between-study heterogeneity and some evidence of publication bias, bias-adjusted estimates remain negative. Furthermore, elasticity is substantially more negative under matching (−2.44) than under rebate (−0.73), contradicting the theoretical prediction of equivalence but aligning with the original experimental findings in this literature. The rebate-matching difference is attenuated when moving from laboratory to field settings, although it persists.

title: Estimation of Agent-Based Models using the Wasserstein Distance
Human rights economics
abstract: This article proposes a theoretical framework that systematically integrates human rights and economic analysis, addressing gaps in previous attempts linking theory and policy. Rather than developing a new theoretical approach, we work within a standard social planner setting in which a social welfare function embeds both fiscal constraints and rights-based valuations, ensuring Pareto-efficient outcomes while guaranteeing minimum rights. Conceptually, we link principles, policy instruments, and outcomes, highlighting shared structures across disciplines and enabling policy design that balances efficiency, equity, and transparency. Empirically, a case study of universal social protection strategies in South Africa illustrates how economic, human rights, and integrated approaches produce different priorities: targeted basic income maximizes fiscal efficiency, the universal transfer maximizes equality and rights, and the integrated perspective favors the expansion of the existing system as the second-most rights-consistent and most cost efficient option. This fully integrated framework demonstrates that human rights economics is not a slogan, nor merely the economics of human rights or rights within economics, but a true integration of both—practically applicable, context-sensitive, and offering a pathway to fiscally sustainable, socially inclusive, and administratively feasible policies.

title: Economic impacts of pasture degradation at the municipal level: Evidence from Minas Gerais, Brazil
Government positions and climate change: paradigmatic conflict versus consensus in environmental performance
abstract: Historically, environmental policy was framed as a fundamental trade-off between economic growth and ecological preservation. Since the mid-1980s, however, this dichotomy has been largely replaced by the paradigm of ecological modernization, expressed in concepts like “green growth” and “sustainable development,” which hold that economic growth and environmental protection are mutually reinforcing. This shift was accompanied by the assumption that a broad political consensus on reconciling economic growth and environmental protection would lead to superior environmental outcomes. Yet, the persistent gap between climate targets and actual emission trends necessitates a critical re-evaluation of this “consensus” approach and of whether the original antagonism between environmental protection and economic growth has genuinely been overcome. To assess this claim, this study tests six distinct conceptualizations of government ideology and policy focus, analyzing government positions across 35 advanced democracies from 1990 to 2021. The findings show that neither the focus on technocratic environmental issues, nor the classic left-right divide, nor the newer, more encompassing green-alternative versus traditional-authoritarian dimension predicts emissions performance. Instead, emissions decline where governments adopt growth-critical positions and even more where environmental ideology contrasts growth-oriented productionism with growth-critical environmental protection. This suggests that the depoliticization of climate policy may be part of the problem: ideological contestation over growth itself, not environmental consensus, emerges as the more effective driver of decarbonization.

title: A beta-binomial algorithm for forecasting the price of crude oil
The effects of R&D tax credit and market competition policies on firms’ zero-leverage behaviour
abstract: Abstract Motivated by the characteristics of R&D and its co-movement with the rising prevalence of zero-leverage firms over the past four decades, we investigate the effects of US R&D tax incentive and import tariff policies on zero-leverage behaviour. We find that the number of R&D-intensive firms has increased since the introduction of the R&D tax credit in 1981, and that zero-leverage firms are disproportionately concentrated among R&D firms. Both the increase in R&D investment and the rising sensitivity of leverage decisions to R&D contribute to this pattern. In addition, intensified market competition driven by tariff reductions significantly increases the likelihood of zero leverage among R&D firms, but not among non-R&D firms. Overall, our findings suggest that R&D tax incentives and trade liberalisation policies have played important roles in shaping the long-term trend of zero-leverage behaviour in the United States.
journal_name: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting

title: The profitability of bank capital and household debt
abstract: This paper examines the conditions under which the profitability of banking capital can exceed that of industrial capital. In a benchmark scenario where banks extend credit only to industrial firms, the industrial sector dominates in terms of return on equity unless two conditions are jointly satisfied: financial intermediation costs must be sufficiently low, and the industrial sector’s leverage must be sufficiently high. The analysis is then extended to a more realistic environment in which banks also lend to households, who finance large expenditures—such as housing, vehicles, and education—through bank credit. In this setting, the return on bank equity can exceed that of industrial capital whenever the flow of household interest payments is sufficiently large, even if bank funding costs remain high or industrial leverage is modest. Thus, household debt service can constitute an additional and potentially important source of bank profitability relative to the industrial sector. Using U.S. quarterly data for 1984–2020, an ARDL bounds test provides empirical support for cointegration between the bank–industry profitability differential and aggregate household debt-service payments.

title: Functional Upgrading in Global Value Chains
Emerging Research Frontiers in Business Cycle Synchronization: A Review of Measurement, Evolution, and Driving Forces
abstract: ABSTRACT Offering new evidence on business cycle synchronization (BCS) has received special attention in recent decades owing to the structural shifts witnessed in the world economy. Hence, this study provides a survey of the literature on business cycle synchronization. The study aims to understand: (a) the definition, (b) measurement, (c) evolution, (d) determinants/driving forces, and (e) propose future research directions. This study highlights that correlation, dynamic correlation, the concordance index, the absolute growth differential, the decoupling index, and the network approach are the key measures of synchronization. While trade integration, financial integration, specialization, and policy similarity have emerged as key drivers, other factors, such as the global financial cycle, geographical proximity, and political factors, also drive synchronization. To track the evolution, this study delves into historical evidence, conventional wisdom, the world business cycle, sectoral and regional business cycles, the financial crisis perspective, the euro area, and the decoupling hypothesis. Finally, this study reveals that although economies are broadly synchronized during a specific period, they exhibit distinct synchronization patterns across different economies and groups at various time periods. Given the long‐standing and unsettled literature, these findings are highly relevant for policymakers, and the suggested research directions open avenues for future research.

title: Review of Literature on Corporate Cash Holdings and Future Research Agenda in an ESG Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT This study synthesizes the literature on corporate cash holdings under an ESG framework and develops a theoretically grounded future research agenda. Based on a systematic review of 116 studies screened from Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection, the literature is categorized into five streams: impacts of aggregate ESG, environmental, social, and governance factors on cash holdings, and reverse effects of cash holdings/financial slack on ESG‐related outcomes. ESG reshapes three established cash‐holding motives: the insurance value of liquidity, the financing wedge between internal and external funds, and agency costs of retained cash. The E, S, and G pillars present distinct mechanisms tied to environmental commitments, stakeholder/labor claims, and liquidity governance. Stronger ESG can reduce cash by lowering risk, financing frictions, or agency costs, while strategic liquidity needs, stakeholder commitments, and adverse ESG shocks may increase cash demand. Reverse evidence shows accumulated liquidity funds ESG investment and supports employment resilience, forming a dynamic bidirectional ESG‐cash relationship. Methodologically, OLS and fixed‐effects regressions dominate the literature, while quasi‐experimental, structural, and machine‐learning approaches remain rare. Future research could explore nonlinear, co‐determined ESG‐cash dynamics via E‐DSGE modeling, real‐options analysis, AI‐enabled liquidity management, and ESG contagion in strategic alliances.

title: Mitigating time-varying buyer power through farmer commodity storage
abstract: Abstract Buyer market power is a significant concern in many agricultural product procurement markets. Research almost exclusively treats such buyer power as a static element of agricultural market structure, despite evidence that buyer power varies across the marketing season for many commodities and locations. We study buyer power as a time-varying phenomenon and analyze the role of commodity storage in mitigating such power and increasing farmer incomes. Data-driven simulations show that strategic storage can generate significant farm income gains and risk reduction. Key factors determining welfare impacts are magnitudes and expected changes in buyer power and farmers’ storage efficiency and risk preferences.

title: Corridors in Shallow Lakes: The Case of Intermediate Pollution
abstract: Abstract We study optimal management of the standard shallow lake model with special attention to the damage caused by the accumulated phosphorus in the water of the lake. The occurrence of a tipping point leads to a stronger increase in the damage after moving from the low-damage to the high-damage regime, because of the loss of ecosystem services. We modify the standard quadratic damage function by introducing a jump in marginal damage when moving from the low-damage to the high-damage regime. Connecting the lower and the higher marginal damage functions yields a continuous piecewise linear marginal damage function with a strong increase around the jump. In addition to the well-known oligotrophic and eutrophic steady states, we find that a third steady state can occur, separated by two Skiba points. This implies that a corridor or a basin of attraction arises between these two Skiba points where optimal management of the lake stabilizes the amount of phosphorus somewhere in the middle instead of either moving to the low-damage or to the high-damage regime, as is the result in the standard knife-edge case with one Skiba point.

title: A Cross‐Country Study of Carbon Risk and Financial Constraints: The Role of Carbon Disclosure Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether firm‐level carbon risk affects financial constraints and whether the quality of carbon disclosure moderates this relationship. Using 16,274 firm‐year observations from 50 countries from 2007 to 2023, we find that higher carbon risk is associated with greater financial constraints. The result is robust to entropy balancing, Heckman correction, instrumental variables and a quasi‐natural experiment based on the 2013 UK carbon disclosure regulation. High‐quality disclosure weakens this association, suggesting that transparency reduces financing frictions by lowering information asymmetry. Additional analyses show that governance, monitoring and institutional context shape the financing consequences of carbon risk.

title: The Effect of a Miscarriage Compared to a Completed Pregnancy on Mental Health Care Use, Labour Market and Family Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT Miscarriages occur in about 15% of recognised pregnancies and often cause grief and stress. We investigate the effect of a miscarriage on mental health care use, labour market and family outcomes of women and their partners using an event study framework applied to Dutch linked administrative data. After a miscarriage, women's use of mental health care temporarily increase compared to before the miscarriage, while their partner's use is unaffected. Furthermore, miscarriages affect labour market trajectories and reduce the probability of living together. Results are similar when comparing the effects of a miscarriage with the effects of having a child using a matched sample of women with a completed pregnancy.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Do Tax Incentives Enhance Entrepreneurship? Evidence from Value‐Added Tax Reform in China
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the causal effect of tax incentives on entrepreneurship. Using a staggered Value‐Added Tax (VAT) reform in China as an exogenous shock to conduct difference‐in‐differences estimation, we find that tax cuts have a considerable positive effect on local entrepreneurship. A plausible mechanism driving our findings is the ease of financial constraints. Our results are robust to a battery of endogeneity and robustness tests. We find that regions with high levels of institutional quality, trust, or a commercial culture undergo greater entrepreneurship after the VAT reform. Overall, this study provides a timely policy evaluation of the importance of tax incentives in promoting entrepreneurship in a typical emerging market.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: The Tipping Point: Interest Rates and Financial Stability
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of interest rates on bank stability in a standard bank‐run model. Banks invest in long‐term assets, whose value decreases with interest rates, and set deposit rates to optimally insure depositors' liquidity risk. Liquidity‐risk insurance implies banks earn interest margins, which increase with interest rates. Hence, interest rates have two countervailing effects: they reduce the value of banks' long‐term assets while widening their margins. First, the paper characterizes the parametric condition under which an effect dominates. The condition implies interest‐rate risk is captured by banks' maturity mismatch adjusted for deposits' effective duration. Second, the paper solves for the interest‐rate level that tips banks into instability. Quantification points to the possibility of a negative effective maturity mismatch, making the tipping point a lower bound on interest rates.

title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.

title: EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

title: Unpacking the micro–macro transmission mechanism: how home-country culture selectively shapes cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial internationalization
abstract: Abstract International business accounts treat national culture as a country-level antecedent that shifts average export propensity uniformly, leaving the individual-level mechanisms producing within-country heterogeneity in internationalization intensity unspecified. We address this micro–macro transmission gap using social cognitive theory, examining how individualism versus collectivism and risk avoidance versus tolerance selectively recalibrate three cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial export decisions: perceived self-efficacy, perceived opportunity availability, and fear of failure. Our multilevel analysis of 40,529 observations across 41 countries spanning 2010–2019 reveals divergent rather than uniform moderation: individualism amplifies self-efficacy and opportunity availability beliefs through the social validation pathway, while risk avoidance constrains opportunity availability beliefs and fear of failure through the anticipatory self-regulation and outcome expectancy pathways. Fear of failure’s directional relationship with internationalization is contingent on the expectations of failure costs that the home-country cultural environment establishes through the outcome expectancy pathway, rather than being uniformly inhibitory as prior frameworks assume. These findings advance international business microfoundations theory by specifying the observable transmission pathways through which national cultural dimensions produce heterogeneous export intensity outcomes within the same national context. For policymakers, the findings imply that interventions to strengthen self-efficacy or opportunity awareness work best when calibrated to a country’s cultural profile.

title: Correction: National identity rhetoric under bilateral geopolitical tensions: evidence from Taiwanese MNEs
Generative AI use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

title: The Signaling Role of Seemingly Myopic Investment Behavior
Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Pension Research Council of Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, as well as the Retirement and Savings Institute at HEC Montréal, for generous research funding. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08268 .

title: The Efficiency Trap of Agentic AI in Human Resource Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Agentic AI transforms HRM from data‐driven support to autonomous execution. Organizations deploy these recursive workflows to eliminate human implementation variance, yet we challenge the assumption that such alignment remains optimal. Drawing on Weick's theory of loose coupling, we argue that delegating HR execution to agentic AI creates algorithmic tight coupling. While this generates immediate hyper‐fit, the removal of strategic slack leads to structural calcification, compromising organizational resilience during polycrises. Human line managers provide a critical buffer, enabling the sensemaking necessary to absorb systemic shocks. In contrast, agentic AI workflows governed by instrumental rationality lack the value rationality required for complex organizing. We propose a governance framework to reconcile machine‐driven consistency with the human stewardship required to preserve long‐term organizational adaptability.

title: Machine Learning Instrument Variables for Causal Inference
abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

title: Diversification versus Consumption Motives for Early Exercise of Employee Stock Options
Do Audit Committee Characteristics Influence Climate‐Related Disclosure? Evidence From Italian Listed Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Research concerning the determinants of corporate climate disclosure has primarily focused on the board of directors, whereas evidence regarding the audit committee (AC), whose oversight directly influences the reporting process, remains limited and inconclusive. Drawing on agency and stakeholder theories, this study examines whether AC characteristics explain the extent of climate‐related disclosure. We hand‐code a 13‐item Climate Disclosure Index aligned with the Task Force on Climate‐related Financial Disclosures from the 2024 non‐financial reports of 211 Italian‐listed firms and estimate hierarchical regressions. AC gender diversity and meeting frequency are positively and significantly associated with disclosure extent, whereas AC size and independence are not; firms in environmentally sensitive industries (ESI) exhibit a greater disclosure extent than non‐ESI firms. Results hold across several robustness tests, including Tobit regression, regional controls, and entropy balancing. These findings provide implications for managers and policymakers, highlighting the need to promote AC activism and gender diversity as essential internal mechanisms to enhance corporate accountability in response to the climate crisis.

title: Boards of Directors and Voluntary Carbon Disclosure: Evidence From Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether Italy's concentrated ownership environment alters the effectiveness of board‐level governance mechanisms as drivers of voluntary carbon disclosure quality, in line with the institutional theory, challenging the assumptions of standard agency and stakeholder theories. Using a sample of 60 Italian listed non‐financial companies over 2015–2023, we employ the Carbon Disclosure Project scores as a measure of disclosure quality. The presence of a corporate social responsibility committee is the only governance mechanism consistently associated with the disclosure quality across all specifications. Board independence exhibits a significant negative effect, consistent with the symbolic compliance hypothesis, according to which independent directors in blockholder‐dominated firms may function as compliance figures rather than effective monitors. Board size, gender diversity, and CEO duality are not significantly associated with disclosure quality. Further analysis shows that the CSR committee effect is stronger in carbon‐intensive industries and weaker in family‐controlled firms. Family ownership also attenuates the negative effect of board independence, suggesting that concentrated ownership selectively conditions, rather than uniformly suppresses, governance effectiveness. Results are robust to alternative estimators, lag structures, and endogeneity tests. Overall, the findings provide novel evidence that governance–disclosure relationships documented in dispersed ownership settings do not readily extend to blockholder‐dominated environments, with important implications for governance reforms in similar institutional contexts.

title: Decoupling Sustainability Reporting and Social Media Communication After a Sustainability Scandal: Strategic Silence, Selective Disclosure and Legitimacy Stabilisation
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how corporate sustainability disclosure evolves across a legitimacy‐threatening event by analysing the interaction between formal sustainability reporting and social media communication. Using a qualitative, longitudinal, event‐centred single‐case design, the study investigates a major Italian organic meat producer over the 2021–2024 period through formal sustainability reporting, Facebook content and stakeholder interactions, regulatory and contextual documents and selected economic indicators. Findings reveal a marked divergence across corporate‐controlled disclosure channels. Formal sustainability reporting remained active and progressively expanded, whereas sustainability‐related Facebook communication sharply contracted after the scandal despite continued overall platform activity. Stakeholder interactions shifted from predominantly routine and positive before the scandal to markedly critical during it, before progressively normalising in 2024. The study contributes to the literature by conceptualising strategic silence as topic‐specific avoidance within active communication, identifying multi‐channel communication fragmentation and showing how post‐scandal dynamics may involve delayed and selective acknowledgement alongside legitimacy stabilisation without comprehensive legitimacy repair.

title: Capability Configurations Linking Circular Economy Practices to Sustainable Supply Chain Performance: A Theory‐Building Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Circular economy ( CE ) practices do not automatically result in sustainable supply chain performance (SSCP), indicating the need for a conceptual explanation of how capabilities support the translation of CE practices into SSCP. This study employed a Scopus‐based theory‐building systematic literature review followed by cross‐study conceptual synthesis. The synthesis identified three complementary capability configurations with different yet interrelated functions: Information‐Digital‐Adaptive and Relational‐Integration primarily serve enabling roles by supporting information processing, analytics, visibility, collaboration, and coordination, whereas Operational‐Adaptive serves a transmitting role by translating enabling resources and CE requirements into coordinated and adaptive supply chain responses. The effectiveness of these configurations is context‐dependent and may vary with industry dynamism, supply chain integration, technological readiness, institutional and stakeholder pressures, and firm and resource characteristics. The proposed framework extends Dynamic Capability Theory by shifting attention from individual capabilities toward capability complementarity, differentiated functional roles, and contextual cross‐capability mechanisms.

title: The Rise of Carbon Finance: A Bibliometric Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Carbon finance has emerged as a critical mechanism for mobilizing capital toward climate change mitigation and supporting the transition to low‐carbon economies. However, its intellectual development remains fragmented across environmental economics, financial economics, sustainability, and climate policy. This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric assessment of carbon finance research, examining its growth trajectory, intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, thematic evolution, and emerging research frontiers. Using 1610 Scopus‐indexed publications from 1993 to 2026, the study integrates performance analysis, citation impact, science mapping, network analysis, thematic visualization, Bradford's law, Lotka's law, journal quality indicators, and life cycle analysis. The findings reveal substantial growth, particularly following the Paris Agreement, alongside a concentrated intellectual structure in which China leads publication productivity, whereas the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan demonstrate strong citation influence. Collaboration networks indicate increasing internationalization, although research remains concentrated among a limited number of authors and institutions. Thematic evolution demonstrates a shift from carbon markets, emissions trading, and environmental regulation toward green finance, sustainable investment, climate‐related financial risk, renewable‐energy financing, ESG integration, and digital finance. The study contributes by extending the temporal coverage of previous bibliometric reviews, integrating multiple analytical approaches, and explicitly tracing the progressive financialization of carbon finance. It reconciles divergent patterns in productivity, citation influence, collaboration, and development across countries and disciplines. By identifying structural patterns, emerging themes, and underexplored research frontiers, the study provides an evidence‐based agenda for future research and informs policymakers, standard‐setters, investors, and practitioners seeking to advance sustainable financial systems and climate transition strategies.

title: Correction to “Strategic integration of environmental sustainability in inland logistics: A multi‐criteria decision‐making approach”
abstract: An error occurred in the calculations when applying Formula 2, where a negative sign ('-') was inadvertently used in the numerator instead of the positive sign ('+') specified in the formula.Formula 2 as presented in the article is correct and the revised results are reflected in the updated Tables 4, 5, 6 and Figure 1.

title: Bio In, Garbage Out? A Review of Paradoxes and Trade‐Offs in the Circular Bioeconomy
abstract: ABSTRACT The circular bioeconomy (CBE) is increasingly presented as a promising way to advance corporate environmental sustainability by combining the use of renewable, bio‐based resources with circular economy principles of resource efficiency and lifecycle management. However, despite growing interest in the CBE, limited attention has been paid to the tensions that emerge in its implementation across the value cycle. This gap matters, as the transition to the CBE requires substantial technological, organizational, regulatory, and market changes that create competing yet interdependent demands for firms and other stakeholders. Drawing on paradox theory as a detective theoretical lens, this study systematically reviews 58 articles to identify and map the tensions characterizing the CBE. In doing so, we distinguish between trade‐offs and paradoxes, examine where these tensions are located, and assess how they concentrate across the CBE value cycle. Our findings indicate that tensions arise unevenly—with the highest concentration occurring during the procurement and processing of raw materials—and that issues related to resource availability, technological development, supply chain adaptation, and regulatory uncertainty are particularly significant. By providing a systemic account of tensions within the CBE, this study extends research on sustainability transitions and offers a foundation for understanding the contradictory demands that firms must navigate as they pursue circular bio‐based strategies.

title: Smart Industry and Ecological Sustainability: Industry 4.0 Technologies, Renewables, and the US Production Ecological Footprint
abstract: ABSTRACT The United States ranks 5th globally in terms of the per capita ecological footprint (ECF) and 2nd in terms of the total ECF and is responsible for intensive energy consumption, resource exploitation, and carbon‐intensive industrial production. However, achieving sustainable industrial development requires understanding which ecological modernization pathways are associated with reducing environmental pressures in the long run. Our study evaluates the long‐term associations of AI and eco‐innovation, supply chain efficiency, industrial renewable energy consumption, GDP growth, and foreign direct investment with the ECF in the United States. In terms of methodology, the study employs autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) using US data from 1990 to 2023. The long‐run ARDL estimation suggests that AI and eco‐innovation, supply chain efficiency, and industrial renewable energy consumption are statistically significant and negatively associated with the ECF in the country over the long run. In contrast, GDP growth and foreign direct investment are significant positive ECF drivers within long‐run dynamics. However, supply chain efficiency shows the largest estimated negative long‐term association with ECF among the modernization pathways examined. Nevertheless, this result is model‐specific evidence rather than proof of universal superiority in comparison with other modernization pathways. Alternative long‐run estimators provide additional support for the baseline associations, although the alternative‐indicator specifications reveal sensitivity to variable measurement. In addition, the Toda–Yamamoto Granger causality results suggest that FDI follows unidirectional predictive precedence toward ECF. Overall, the findings suggest that ecological modernization in the United States operates through innovation capability, operational efficiency, and energy transition, each of which is associated with ECF through a different mechanism. Federal policymakers may consider prioritizing these ecological modernizers as long‐term complementary pathways and set combined policy actions to reduce ECF in the country.

title: Sustainable Dreams, Overlooked Realities: Closing the Design–Outcome Gap in Sustainable Business Models
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable business models (SBMs) are enablers of the circular economy ( CE ) and sustainability. However, its adoption does not always improve environmental performance. This study investigates the conditions under which SBM design does (or does not) produce the expected environmental benefits. We conducted a secondary cross‐case analysis of three use‐oriented product–service–system (PSS) business model (BM) implemented by three distinct Swedish companies that previously had been assessed using business model life cycle assessment (BM‐LCA). Across the cases, environmental performance outcomes were not primarily determined by BM main property (i.e., reuse, sharing, or rental) as such, but by a set of conditions (e.g., product return rates, enabling infrastructure, location, and consumer behavior). Overall, the results show that sustainability benefits are not inherent to SBM archetypes. A key learning is that the singular design focus, institutional pressure to “show” sustainability, and lack of quantitative assessment contribute to the poor environmental performance of the SBM in the studied cases. We also show that the absence of empirical validation can foster a wishful thinking that well‐intentioned environmental efforts are enough. The study contributes by specifying conditions that shape SBM's environmental performance, clarifying when and why environmental performance outcomes of SBMs can diverge from their design expectations. We further show how BM‐LCA can be integrated into SBM analysis to operationalize and test the sustainability assumptions embedded in BM design. This positions BM‐level, life cycle–based assessment as a structured decision‐support and learning tool for assessing and refining SBMs.

title: Regulatory Governance and Sustainable Logistics Performance in India: The Conditional Role of Operational Capabilities
abstract: ABSTRACT Logistics performance is critical to economic competitiveness and resilient supply networks, particularly in emerging economies facing technological, infrastructural, workforce, environmental, and institutional constraints. However, limited attention has been given to how regulatory governance conditions the effects of these operational factors on logistics performance. This study examines the determinants of sustainable logistics performance in India's transportation sector, focusing on the moderating role of government policies and regulatory compliance. Drawing on Institutional Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Innovation Diffusion Theory, an integrated framework links transportation infrastructure, technology adoption and automation, system integration, supply chain (SC) coordination, environmental factors, and driver shortage and turnover to logistics performance. The proposed relationships are examined using partial least squares structural equation modeling with moderation analysis. The findings indicate that transportation infrastructure, technology adoption and automation, system integration, SC coordination, and environmental factors are positively associated with logistics performance, whereas driver shortage and turnover are negatively associated. Government policies and regulatory compliance moderates two relationships: They mitigate the negative association between driver shortage and logistics performance but attenuate the positive association between SC coordination and performance. The findings highlight the need for regulatory frameworks that address workforce constraints without limiting coordination and operational flexibility. The study contributes to sustainable logistics research by demonstrating that regulatory governance can condition, rather than uniformly determine, the performance effects of operational capabilities.

title: Antecedents, Mediators, Moderators and Outcomes of Circular Business Models: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Circular business models (CBMs) have gained increasing scholarly attention as organisations seek to transition toward more sustainable and regenerative economic systems. Despite this growing body of research, the literature remains fragmented across disciplines and lacks an integrated understanding of the drivers, mechanisms, contextual conditions and outcomes associated with CBM implementation. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic literature review of 477 peer‐reviewed articles published between 2017 and 2024 spanning business, management, environmental science and sustainability disciplines. Through an inductive synthesis of recurring patterns, four higher‐order dimensions were identified: antecedents, mediators, moderators and outcomes. These dimensions form the basis of the AMMO framework, a causal model that links organisational and ecosystem‐level drivers to sustainability outcomes through mediating mechanisms and moderating contextual conditions. By consolidating dispersed insights into a coherent explanatory model, this study advances CBM theorising, outlines a structured research agenda for future research and provides practical guidance for managers and policymakers seeking to identify key drivers, mechanisms and boundary conditions for circular transitions.

title: Emotional labor in the age of service robots: Comparing hospitality and other service sectors through service robot support, ego depletion, and service performance
How value representation formats influence project cognition and project portfolio decisions
Interpretable machine learning for customer satisfaction optimization
abstract: Purpose Understanding how dining experiences are transformed into customer satisfaction judgments is central to hospitality competitiveness. Using high-dimensional user-generated content on tourism dining experiences, this study aims to examine whether shared three-factor classifications coexist with segment-specific differences in satisfaction relationships. Design/methodology/approach The authors analyze 82,105 Yelp restaurant reviews from nine market segments based on price level, cuisine type and restaurant category. Bidirectional encoder representations from transformers-based aspect mining and clustering extract attribute–sentiment pairs. Ensemble models estimate nonlinear predictive relationships, and SHAP decomposes their predictions to support attribute classification, segment-specific satisfaction functions and diagnostic prioritization. Findings Empirical results reveal a basic-dominant pattern together with segment-level variation in estimated penalty–reward magnitudes, satisfaction-function shapes and diagnostic priorities. This pattern remains largely stable under alternative impact asymmetry thresholds and the procedure based on penalty-reward contrast analysis. Categorical stability can therefore coexist with segment-contingent differences in evaluative weight and relationship form. Practical implications Theoretically, the findings highlight the value of extending attribute classification with segment-specific satisfaction-function analysis, because segment heterogeneity is expressed within, and not only between, three-factor categories. Practically, managers can use the framework to diagnose service attributes with higher marginal predictive utility and develop more targeted, segment-specific improvement priorities. Originality/value This study refines the categorical interpretation of three-factor theory by showing that a shared attribute classification does not imply an invariant satisfaction relationship. Segment heterogeneity can occur within a shared category through differences in penalty–reward magnitude and satisfaction-function shape, not only through category shifts.

title: Political risk insurance in the digital age: How CPA moderates negative investor reactions following head of government attacks on social media
The role of leadership on employee mental ill‐health through workplace disruption: A systematic review and meta‐analysis of longitudinal research
abstract: Abstract As socio‐global events more frequently disrupt workplaces, understanding leadership's dynamic and context‐sensitive role in shaping employee wellbeing during periods of uncertainty has become increasingly important. Drawing on the Conservation of Resources Theory, this study synthesized current longitudinal evidence on the association between leadership and mental ill‐health (i.e. stress, burnout, psychological distress). We systematically reviewed 106 longitudinal studies, and meta‐analysed 191 time‐lagged effect sizes, to compare direct leadership associations and the moderating role of workplace disruption. Twenty‐four studies reported a disruptive workplace context, identified by the novelty, criticality or discontinuity of the event. Meta‐analytic results revealed that leadership styles differed in the magnitude of their peak observed association with employee mental ill‐health outcomes. Servant Leadership showed the strongest negative association with burnout across all leadership styles, although evidence was mixed across other outcomes. Destructive/Abusive Leadership styles had consistently strong effects across all mental ill‐health outcomes. Workplace disruption weakened the negative association of Supportive Leadership and stress, but further amplified the positive association between Autocratic Leadership and psychological distress. Statistical analyses and narrative commentary identified key opportunities to improve future longitudinal leadership research. Organizations can leverage these findings to promote sustainable leadership behaviours that enhance mental health generally and through adversity.

title: Different strokes for different folks: how firms’ language complexity influences Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) rating divergence?
The evolving role of organisational foresight: Implications for the food service industry
abstract: This article examines the evolving role of organisational foresight (OF), by integrating economics of innovation and managerial economics perspectives. The analysis investigates the interplay between foresight practices, coordination of routines and innovation, and how OF can be adopted to address mounting environmental and social challenges in the underexplored context of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) of the food service industry (FSI). Hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling on data collected from 204 managers of Brazilian FSI firms via an online questionnaire, complemented by a subsequent qualitative investigation. The results reveal that OF positively affects coordination of routines and innovation of firms. Innovation also positively affects green corporate social responsibility (GCSR) and sustainable performance (SP) of firms. Coordination of routines plays a mediating role that strengthens the association between OF and innovation. Furthermore, innovation mediates the relationship between OF and GCSR, as well as between OF and SP. In the context of FSI SMEs, foresight appears as a more informal, experiential sense-making capability. Although OF is a systematic process of thinking strategically about the future, OF per se is not enough. Firms should integrate a selection of dynamic capabilities into OF to strengthen their innovation, GCSR, and sustainable performance. The formalisation of additional management capabilities related to the coordination of routines, can make this process more effective. OF can shift from a theoretical exercise towards more socially- and environmentally-oriented actions which should be embedded into the culture of FSI firms.

title: Beyond a Name: The CAPE Framework for Names, Nicknames, and (Nick)Naming in Marketing
More to gain, less to lose? Chinese firms’ US patenting strategies amidst decoupling
abstract: US-China geopolitical tensions have produced decoupling policies that restrict Chinese firms’ access to most assets within strategic industries in the US. Yet Chinese firms in strategic industries can still legally obtain patents in the US, though doing so poses political risks and even this access may be restricted in the future. How do Chinese firms seek assets abroad in this new geopolitical environment? Drawing on the Attention-Based View, we argue that decoupling redirects attention of managers at Chinese firms in strategic industries to significantly increase US patenting because restrictions on alternative assets heighten patents’ relative value, reduce the perceived costs of exploiting them aggressively, and create urgency to secure them before access is potentially restricted. In contrast, managers with lived experience in the US or politically similar markets are theorized to perceive greater political risks of this strategy, leading their firms to increase patenting less. Using a difference-in-differences approach analyzing USPTO patent filings by publicly-listed Chinese firms from 2013–2023, we find support for our hypotheses. Robustness checks, including tests showing no comparable increase in patenting by the Chinese firms in other major foreign markets, corroborate these results. Further, supplementary analysis indicates that the increase in patenting is associated with fewer claims per patent — a pattern consistent with the strategic use of patents, potentially as weapons and transactable assets, rather than proportionally greater inventiveness. Our findings highlight how geopolitical decoupling intensifies firms’ pursuit of still-accessible assets in host markets, tempered by managers’ attention to political risks.

title: Media Framing, Solidarity, and Tourism in Wartime
abstract: This study examines how the framing of newspaper articles shapes place solidarity and associated tourism implications during the Russia-Ukraine war, and how these framing effects vary according to national values of the countries in which the articles were published. Drawing on framing theory, Hofstede’s national values, and the place solidarity concept, we analyze 379 newspaper articles from 46 countries using quantitative content analysis and categorical principal component analysis. Justice- and threat-focused frames in newspapers are associated with place solidarity, which is linked to media-represented tourism implications such as willingness to visit Ukraine, hospitality toward Ukrainians, and perceived tourism spillovers. Several national values moderate these relationships, indicating contingent framing effects. The study advances understanding of how media narratives construct solidarity during crises and how cultural contexts influence tourism outcomes.

title: How the European Union Fell Out of Love With Open‐Source Software
abstract: ABSTRACT This article explains why the European Commission diluted the 2004 European Interoperability Framework's provisions favoring open‐source software and open standards when it revised the framework in 2010. Using an extended Multiple Streams Framework with a technology stream, the study shows how pro‐openness policy entrepreneurs secured the 2004 provisions and why incumbent advocacy became more effective during revision. Drawing on annotated drafts and expert interviews, the study traces actors' lobbying strategies across the problem, politics, and policy streams and examines how technology‐stream developments altered the feasibility and political salience of competing solutions. The analysis shows how changing standards and licensing dynamics, incumbent advocacy, and declining political support for the earlier pro‐openness package enabled a new coupling around business‐model neutrality and licensing flexibility, diluting the 2004 provisions. Beyond the European case, the study informs debates on open‐source artificial intelligence and advances theory on institutional dynamics in regulatory governance.
