Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
abstract: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment. (JEL G1, G2)

title: Input sourcing, trade liberalization, and diversifying mergers

Real Activity and Uncertainty Shocks: The Long and the Short of It
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a nonrecursive VAR identification strategy that separately identifies short‐term and long‐term uncertainty shocks by exploiting sign restrictions implied by a stylized framework and a DSGE model featuring both types of shocks. We find that long‐term uncertainty shocks exert strong and persistent effects on real activity, whereas short‐term shocks have limited real effects. We use the DSGE model to study their differential propagation and show that time‐to‐build is an important ingredient allowing the model to account for the stark empirical asymmetry in investment and, in turn, output—both contract sharply after long‐term shocks but only modestly after short‐term shocks.

title: “Demographic Change and Migration: Facts, Models and Policy Implications” – An Introduction to the Special Issue
abstract: Demographic change, driven by lower fertility rates and declining mortality, is a central long-run phenomenon impacting all major economies around the world.The papers in this special issue study the interactions between demographic change, internal and external migration, technological progress, and economic development, with a particular focus on Asian economies.Scientific collaboration represents one form of cross-border interaction through which knowledge and human capital contribute to economic development.When the international migration of researchers is subject to frictions, international cooperation in the production of scientific output becomes crucial.In Scientific Isolation?The Consequences of Trump's China Initiative on Chinese Research , by Philippe

title: Asset Market Participation, Redistribution, and Asset Pricing
abstract: ABSTRACT We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons. We interpret these patterns using a production‐based asset‐pricing model with limited participation and external habits. Aggregate (relative) consumption captures variation in the price (quantity) of risk. Technology shocks drive macroeconomic fluctuations, whereas redistributive shocks generate large short‐run movements in inequality and are the main source of priced risk. This points to a macro‐finance disconnect between the drivers of business cycles and those governing risk premia.

title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

title: The Perils of Overreaction
abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

title: A Better Cycle-Breaker for Direct Democracy?
External reference pricing versus price controls under endogenous product quality
abstract: Motivated by the high prices of branded/patented pharmaceuticals in many parts of the world, this paper analyzes price regulations in a two-country (home and foreign) model where a single home firm serves both markets and its R&D investment determines product quality. We study two types of price regulations: direct price controls (PCs) and external reference pricing (ERP) under which the price that the firm is permitted to charge locally depends upon its price abroad. We show that although ERP undermines R&D incentives, its implementation can raise home welfare. However, home’s optimal ERP policy is too restrictive from a joint welfare perspective. Furthermore, if the foreign market is subject to a PC, home prefers ERP to a PC due to strategic considerations that come into play due to the international price linkage created by ERP.

title: Leveraging surplus electricity: Profitability of Bitcoin mining as a national strategy in South Korea

Robust portfolio choice under a continuum of downside risk preferences

Personality, longevity insurance, and the timing of Social Security claiming
abstract: Abstract Delaying a Social Security claim buys a larger inflation‐indexed annuity, a form of longevity insurance. Because claiming‐age adjustments are uniform within birth cohorts, delay is worth more to those likely to live longer, so traits that predict longer lives should predict later claiming. In the Health and Retirement Study, we relate Big Five traits measured before receipt to the age at first reported Social Security income of any type between 62 and 70. Converting each trait's mortality difference into the claiming age maximizing expected present value gives a benchmark for observed timing. Timing moves toward the benchmark for traits predicting shorter lives, by less than mortality implies, with openness the exception. Conscientiousness, the strongest longevity predictor, implies about 6 months of later claiming per standard deviation, yet we detect no later receipt. Personality makes observable a mortality difference that claiming models treat as latent.

title: Ecological macroeconomics models? Caveat emptor
abstract: Ecological Macroeconomic Integrated Assessment Models (EM-IAMs) have emerged as tools for exploring post-growth narratives and challenging the dominant discourse of continuous economic growth. Their use may be strategically advantageous: by employing modelling approaches that are epistemically legitimate within economics, EM-IAMs can contest the growth paradigm with their own tools. Yet, the framing of socio-ecological processes in EM-IAMs, through quantification and evaluative logics, risks interfering with the other goal of EM-IAMs; to address social inequality and injustices. As such, EM-IAMs risk operating as what ecologist Langdon Winner coined as ‘conceptual Trojan horse’. We question whether EM-IAMs may truly provide “robust modelling tools to explore alternative future scenarios, enabling the ex-ante evaluation of direct and indirect effects of policies on well-being, employment, and the ecosystem” (Ecological Economics, 2025). Our doubts rest upon complexity that does not reduce uncertainty, the politics of model simplification, the limitations of EM-IAM models for aspects that resist quantification, the reinforcement of historical power imbalances, and, ultimately, the performative effects of models themselves. We suggest that, rather than extending EM-IAMs to incorporate well-being analysis, we should adopt a different approach to modelling, learning from ecological values; appreciating diversity, variability in space and time, self-regulation, and entanglements.

title: China’s institution-building amidst (dynamic) network effects: how will the relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions evolve?
abstract: How will the regime complex of balance-of-payments lending evolve amidst ongoing global power shifts? In this paper, we challenge the hitherto static outlook on the viability of external institutional change within the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) institutional environment. Dominant views in International Political Economy suggest that the IMF’s current focality will persist as China’s reformist approach to balance-of-payments lending and strong network effects favoring the IMF induce (inter-)institutional inertia. In contrast, we argue that the interests of challenger states – particularly China – and their exposure to network effects are dynamic. Depending on challengers’ evolving reformist or revisionist interests and their dynamic exposure to network effects, we derive pathways for external institutional change toward multiple inter-institutional relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions. Based on theoretical extrapolation and empirical trends, we claim that institutional hedging is a probable pathway for China’s institution-building efforts in the near future. For the more distant future, we introduce complementary layering and conflictual counter-institutionalization as highly contingent possibilities and discuss how the (inter-)actions of challengers and defenders during the hedging phase may shape their (non-)materialization. We thereby offer a methodologically innovative and policy-relevant outlook on future institutional change in international finance.

title: The Association Between Physician Organizational Form and Opioid Prescribing
abstract: In theory, there are several reasons why physician organizational form might affect the price, quantity, and quality of physician services. In this paper, we examine the association between three aspects of physician organizational form and opioid prescribing: solo versus group practice; integration with a hospital versus independent practice; and the average age of the other physicians in the physician's group. We present three key findings. First, physicians who switch from solo to group practice, particularly large-group practice, significantly reduce their prescribing relative to those who stay in solo practice. Conversely, physicians who switch from group to solo practice significantly increase their prescribing by approximately the same amount. Second, physicians who switch from independent to hospital-integrated practice (and those who switch from integrated to independent practice) generally do not significantly change their prescribing. Third, among group-practice physicians, there are significant differences in prescribing by the average of age of physicians in the group, holding constant the physician's own age and other characteristics of the group, the physician, and the physician's patients. Physicians in groups with a higher average age (excluding the index physician) prescribe more intensively and are more likely to write inappropriate opioid prescriptions than physicians in younger groups-holding other factors constant.

title: How Has the Health of the United States Population Changed? Evidence From Biomarkers
abstract: Population health is a central input into social welfare, but health itself is complex and multidimensional. Mapping multiple dimensions of health into a single population health index may require strong assumptions about how to aggregate and weight across dimensions. This study adopts a novel nonparametric approach to rank individual health as a function of seven biomarkers associated with major domains of physiological health: body mass index (BMI), glycohemoglobin (HbA1c), total cholesterol, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and white blood cell (WBC). This approach avoids arbitrary weighting while requiring only monotonicity and quasi-concavity. Using NHANES data from 1988 to 2018, we document a significant deterioration in the U.S. health distribution, with declines concentrated in the lower tail. Counterfactual decompositions show that one-third of the negative shift can be attributed to an aging, more racially and ethnically diverse population, leaving a remaining portion unexplained by observed factors. The findings highlight the value of distribution-sensitive multidimensional health measures for monitoring health inequality and targeting preventive care.

title: Europe Adrift
abstract: Europe is adrift in the face of great turmoil and transformation. The liberal international order that emerged after the Cold War has disintegrated and the EU lacks a coherent strategic vision for responding to, let alone shaping, the emergent world order. There has been a shift away from market liberalism and toward state interventionism in pursuit of strategic autonomy. While the EU seeks to be more assertive internationally, its efforts are haunted by legacies from the neoliberal era that continue to limit its capacity for effective action. Herein lies the challenge. Europe struggles to overcome internal difficulties while simultaneously facing a security threat from Russia, erratic neo-mercantilism from the US, a competitiveness challenge from China, and declining goodwill in the Global South, all in the context of rapid environmental change. This special issue takes the dynamics of intensifying global inter-state competition as an entry point to survey the erosion of European security, growth and normative power. A Europe Adrift speaks to how the foundations of this erosion were laid on the basis of EU regulatory statehood, the contradictions revealed in the EU’s evolving governance architecture and how European power and prosperity are being reshaped in unexpected ways.

title: Marx and Engels on the Lumpenproletariat and the Poor Laws
abstract: What if the English Poor Laws helped reproduce the social conditions Marx and Engels associated with the lumpenproletariat? This paper argues that their critique of the Poor Laws and their concept of the lumpenproletariat form part of a common analysis of capitalist accumulation and the production of relative surplus population. Marx and Engels understood poor relief as a mechanism embedded in capitalist reproduction, stabilising dependency, exerting downward pressure on wages, and fragmenting the working class. The lumpenproletariat, situated at the lowest strata of pauperism, serves as a conceptual bridge between surplus population and the institutional regulation of poverty. By clarifying this connection, the article repositions Marx and Engels within nineteenth-century debates on poverty and highlights their divergence from classical political economy, particularly regarding the structural limits of reform within capitalism.

Winning at Defense by Playing Offense: Discrediting by Target Firms in Activist Hedge Fund Campaigns
abstract: Prior research highlights the far-reaching strategic and governance consequences for firms targeted in activist hedge fund (AHF) campaigns. Yet, how target firm executives and directors can effectively defend against these campaigns remains underexplored. Drawing on impression management (IM) theory, we reason that executives and directors use discrediting in their public rebuttal letters to negatively influence shareholders’ evaluations of AHFs’ reputation. To nuance this prediction, we develop a taxonomy distinguishing between source-focused discrediting, which directly attacks AHFs’ reputation, and message-focused discrediting, which challenges the validity of AHFs’ claims to indirectly tarnish their reputation. We theorize that both discrediting subtypes enhance target firms’ defense success, particularly when deployed in combination. Adopting a temporal perspective on IM theory, we further argue that the effectiveness of discrediting diminishes as more time elapses between an AHF’s public attack and executives and directors’ rebuttal. A manual content analysis of 841 rebuttal letters issued during U.S. AHF campaigns (2000–2023) provides robust support for these predictions. Beyond contributing to shareholder activism research by offering new insights into the determinants of campaign outcomes, our study advances IM theory by conceptualizing discrediting as a multidimensional influence tactic and exploring its effectiveness and temporal dynamics in adversarial contexts.

Robust Auction Design with Support Information
abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00714 .

title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72671091, 72371079, and 72501192, and Key Program 72432005] and the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangdong Province [Grant 2023B1515020045]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03608 .

title: Consumer scheduling of experiential activities in shopping centers
Challenge for some, hindrance for others? How stress appraisals shape employee performance of essential and nonessential work during crises
abstract: Anecdotes during crises frequently highlight essential employees who maintain critical services and perform effectively under adversity. This raises a central question: which types of work are more (vs less) likely to be performed effectively during crises, and why? Drawing on the Transactional Theory of Stress, we propose that performing essential (vs nonessential) work during crises facilitates challenge appraisals and reduces hindrance appraisals of the work performed, which in turn enhances in-role performance and taking charge behaviors. We further propose that organizational adaptive capacity functions as a contextual resource that strengthens these beneficial appraisals. We test our framework in a two-wave multisource survey conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic and two preregistered experiments simulating organizational crises. Results provide broad support for our theorizing. At both occupational and task levels, higher levels of challenge (Studies 1 and 2) and lower levels of hindrance appraisals (Studies 1, 2, and 3) mediate the relationship between essential (vs nonessential) work and performance. The moderating role of organizational adaptive capacity was only supported in our field study. This research advances our understanding of how the socially constructed labels of “essential” versus “nonessential” work shape employee appraisals and performance during crises.

title: From control to co‐construction in identity regulation: A systematic review and an agenda for future research
abstract: Abstract This systematic review synthesises findings from 112 peer‐reviewed articles (1995–2026) to provide a comprehensive and timely understanding of identity regulation, diverse navigation strategies, and multifaceted outcomes. It reveals identity regulation as a multi‐level phenomenon extending to organisations, managers, and teams as distinct targets of regulation beyond the traditional employee focus. It maps the multi‐level mechanisms through which identity is shaped and the diverse strategies individuals (employees and managers) employ to navigate these pressures—from conformity, (dis)‐identification, sensemaking, and balancing to resistance and proactive identity work. The review reveals multifaceted and often paradoxical outcomes affecting individuals physically, emotionally, socially, and ethically, as well as influencing team and organisational dynamics. Notably, findings strongly suggest that a co‐constructive regulatory approach fostering agency yields significantly more positive consequences than a traditional control‐centric approach. This review highlights a conceptual shift from a control‐centric approach towards a co‐constructive approach, proposing a detailed research agenda to significantly advance the field in this dynamic direction.

title: Signaling Climate Transition Capacity: How Environmental Expenditures Attenuate the Carbon Risk Premium
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the pricing of carbon risk among publicly listed firms in Asia. We first develop a theoretical model of the carbon risk premium grounded in information asymmetry, which posits that a firm's environmental expenditures serve as a credible signal of its climate transition capacity. We then test these predictions using a novel panel dataset of 144 green bond issuers from 2005 to 2023. Our empirical analysis confirms the existence of a statistically significant, positive carbon risk premium in the region. Crucially, and consistent with our theoretical framework, we find that this premium is attenuated for firms with higher environmental expenditures. We further uncover that the modest scale of this premium is driven by investor heterogeneity: Long‐term institutional investors penalize high‐emitting firms but reward those with significant environmental spending, while short‐term strategic entities exhibit opposing behavior. Based on these findings, policymakers can mobilize corporate resources to address the carbon risk premium through three complementary levers: implementing stringent climate policy, enhancing climate finance taxonomies, and mandating standardized transition risk disclosure.

title: CEO Tenure and Sustainable Growth: Non‐Linear Effects and Strategic Trade‐Offs Between Sustainability Dimensions
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how CEO tenure influences firm sustainable growth across economic and social dimensions and whether it is associated with sustainability trade‐offs. Prior research has largely focused on short‐term performance measures and linear CEO tenure effects, providing limited evidence on sustainable growth and potential trade‐offs across sustainability dimensions. Using panel data from 272 publicly listed Vietnamese firms from 2011 to 2022, we employ fixed‐effects models, system GMM, and seemingly unrelated regression. The results show that CEO tenure has non‐linear effects on sustainable growth: a U‐shaped relationship with economic sustainability and an inverted U‐shaped relationship with social sustainability. Evidence of a negative residual correlation between the two dimensions suggests the possibility of sustainability trade‐offs among these two aspects. Furthermore, the relationship between CEO tenure and sustainability trade‐offs is evident only among firms with positive economic sustainability. This study contributes to the CEO tenure and sustainability literature by demonstrating that CEO tenure affects sustainable growth differently across economic and social dimensions and by identifying the non‐linear nature of these relationships. It also extends the sustainability trade‐off literature by showing that CEO tenure is associated with sustainability trade‐offs under specific performance conditions, offering important implications for board succession planning, executive monitoring, and the pursuit of balanced long‐term sustainable growth. These findings highlight the multidimensional and dynamic nature of CEO tenure effects on sustainable growth.

title: The Cost of Being Green: Sustainability‐Linked Eco‐Friction, Trade‐Off Tolerance, and Tourist Satisfaction in Island Reviews
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainability is often assumed to enhance tourism value, yet tourists do not always evaluate green practices positively in lived service encounters. This study examines sustainability‐linked evaluation in island and coastal tourism by distinguishing eco‐delight from eco‐friction, defined as environmentally anchored inconvenience rather than generic dissatisfaction. Using 138,683 Google Maps and TripAdvisor reviews from 10 destinations in Southeast and East Asia, we apply bilingual dictionary‐based text analysis and review‐level econometric modeling. Separate bilingual dictionaries, environmental anchoring rules, manual validation, and broad‐versus‐strict sensitivity analyses are used to reduce construct overlap and make classification uncertainty explicit. In the broad sample, eco‐delight is positively associated with review rating, whereas eco‐friction is negatively associated with it. The negative association of eco‐friction is stronger than the positive association of eco‐delight, indicating sustainability‐specific asymmetric negativity rather than only generic negativity bias. Positive trade‐off tolerance weakens this penalty in the broad specification, but the interaction does not replicate in the much smaller strict eco‐core sample. Accordingly, the text‐derived variables are interpreted as imperfect indicators of sustainability‐linked discourse rather than as latent psychological measures. The study reframes sustainable tourism experience as a trade‐off structure rather than a uniformly positive green premium.

title: Green Innovation Through Artificial Intelligence: Sectoral and Regional Perspectives of China
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed manufacturing and promotes firms' green innovation. Concurrently, the significance of green innovation plays an important role in supporting firms' environmental transformation. Against this backdrop, the present study investigates the dynamic relationship between AI and firms' green innovation (FGI), with a specific focus on Chinese manufacturing firms. The results show that manufacturing companies with extensive AI adoption demonstrate heightened levels of green innovation. Furthermore, the study explores the heterogeneous impact of AI on FGI across different types of firms and regions. Notably, AI has a stronger effect on FGI within the eastern region and significantly drives green innovation in non‐SOE, high‐tech, and non‐labor‐intensive firms compared to their counterparts in SOE, labor‐intensive, and non‐tech industries. Additionally, AI contributes to the enhancement of FGI by stimulating investments in green research and development (R&D), reducing operational costs, and facilitating digital transformation initiatives. The study also illuminates the influence of environmental regulations in amplifying AI's promotion of FGI in manufacturing firms. Finally, based on the pragmatic assessments, valuable policy implications are discussed.

title: Linking managerial coaching to engagement in the service-profit chain: Evidence in a quick-service restaurant context
Agentic AI Personalization in Advertising: Realizing the True Potential of N = 1
abstract: With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), we have come closer than ever to achieving the holy grail of personalizing advertisements to individual consumers, i.e., the ideal of N = 1. AI-driven ad serving platforms act with unprecedented agency, dynamically creating highly tailored appeals and experiences. Such “agentic AI personalization” has both positive and negative consequences. This article traces the evolution from analog personalization to agentic personalization. It then explicates the latter concept in terms of breadth, depth, and length of personalized messaging. It overviews the processes underlying agentic AI personalization and describes the dualities inherent in both its foundation and operation. Finally, it offers a theoretical framework for studying the effects of agentic AI personalization on consumer responses to advertisements, followed by an illustrative set of propositions for empirical testing.

title: The 8th Industrial Marketing Management Summit: relationships, regulation, and reconfiguration in B2B markets
The future workplace: developing the human-machine symbioscape
abstract: Purpose This paper develops the concept of the human-machine symbioscape to explain how work environments shape collaboration between humans and AI-enabled machines. Extending servicescape thinking from customer-employee encounters to hybrid human-machine work systems, the paper positions environmental design as a core antecedent of human–machine adaptive collaboration, with particular relevance for service and frontline settings where visibility, coordination, and role clarity are critical. Design/methodology/approach The paper is conceptual and theory building in nature. It synthesises insights from biological symbiosis, servicescape research, sociotechnical and sociomaterial theory, organisational sensemaking and team adaptation research to develop a deductive typology of the human-machine symbioscape as a three-tiered environmental construct, its cue categories, and its design-critical properties. The framework is further illustrated through a structured coding of relevant human-machine collaboration studies. Findings The paper conceptualises the symbioscape as a three-tier environmental architecture comprising physical–digital, socio-relational, and institutional–ecosystem conditions. Across these tiers, six cue categories shape what human and AI-enabled actors can notice, how they coordinate work, and how collaborative routines are reinforced over time. Drawing on Weick's sensemaking theory, the framework links these tiers to enactment, selection, and retention processes, and explains how they influence adaptation speed, adaptation effectiveness, and adaptation persistence in human–AI collaboration. Research limitations/implications The paper is purely conceptual and does not empirically test the proposed relationships. Its evidence base is limited to published studies and illustrative coding, with a strong emphasis on service and frontline contexts. It identifies an agenda for future research around operationalising symbioscape constructs, testing the proposed relationships empirically, and examining how individual tiers and cross-tier configurations jointly affect human–machine work. Practical implications The symbioscape framework provides managers with a structured lens for designing AI-enabled workplaces. It highlights how deliberate choices in physical–digital visibility and interface design, socio-relational workflow sequencing and interaction load, and institutional governance, training, and role architecture can improve the speed, quality and durability of human–machine adaptation. The framework can be used to diagnose service work environments, where frontline employees must coordinate with intelligent systems under conditions of customer presence, temporal pressure, and operational variability. Originality/value The paper introduces the symbioscape as a novel, three-tier environmental construct for human–machine collaboration, extending the servicescape from customer–employee encounters to hybrid human–AI work systems. It adds a missing environmental layer to human-machine collaboration research by systematically integrating dispersed insights on context into a coherent framework that links environmental cue structures to sensemaking and adaptation outcomes. For scholars, it offers an integrative conceptual architecture; for practitioners, it provides a foundation for designing and structuring future workplaces that foster adaptive human–machine collaboration.

title: Halting Biodiversity Loss Requires a Different Kind of Management Research
abstract: The first business and biodiversity assessment by the Intergovernmental Science‑Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services concludes that voluntary corporate action cannot halt biodiversity loss without broader shifts in the policy, economic, financial, social, and knowledge systems that shape business behavior and environmental outcomes. Yet management research on biodiversity remains largely firm-centric, attending to what individual firms measure, disclose, and do, while often overlooking these wider systems. We propose four interrelated research priorities to reorient the field: the political economy of inaction, the limits of organizational capability, the viability of organizing beyond growth, and reconceptualizing the firm–nature relationship. Pursuing them requires research that is interdisciplinary—drawing on insights beyond management—and transdisciplinary, co‑producing decision‑relevant knowledge with the actors who shape and experience biodiversity outcomes.

title: The critical foundations of truly sustainable environmental auditing
abstract: This essay addresses the urgent need for transformative action in environmental governance and examines how environmental auditing can support diagnostic and transformative agency within social-ecological systems. This requires a radical conceptual reconfiguration of environmental audit. To this end, the essay advances five conceptual foundations for a more impactful and sustainable approach. These include: an overarching commitment to Earth system stability; transcending an organization-centric paradigm; repositioning environmental auditing as a first-order function that drives, rather than follows, accounting; leveraging diverse forms of accounts to generate diagnostic insights into what truly matters within social-ecological systems; and actively coordinating accountability processes. Collectively, these foundations reposition environmental audit as a dynamic practice for nurturing meaningful change in social-ecological systems.

Shared Policy Commitments in the Buyer Ego‐Network and Buyer Financial Performance: A Multiplex Network Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Public commitments to sustainability policies have become common practice among buyer and supplier companies facing growing sustainability imperatives. Firms often pursue these commitments to address societal expectations and comply with institutional norms rather than to achieve efficiency, frequently endorsing them without a comprehensive assessment of their performance implications. Within the supply chain, when multiple firms commit to similar policies, alignment emerges across network members through shared policy commitments. Such shared commitments differ from traditional buyer–supplier coordinated alignment by introducing an additional layer of complexity beyond contractual dynamics, with potential performance consequences. Adopting an embeddedness perspective, the authors analyze 240 multiplex ego networks that capture both shared policy commitments and structural ties. Results show that shared policy commitments within a buyer ego‐network, between a buyer and its direct suppliers or among those suppliers, are positively associated with the focal buyer's financial performance, with each direction's association conditional on the level of the other. However, the findings also reveal a curvilinear relationship: buyer performance declines as network members' commitments become increasingly centered on the same policies. Network interconnectedness through contractual ties serves as a moderator, unlocking additional benefits of shared commitments. This study provides theoretical and practical insights for managing shared commitments in the buyer ego‐network while avoiding over‐embeddedness.

title: From Experience to Memory: Emotional Pathways in Skip-Gen Travel
abstract: Skip-gen travel, in which grandparents travel with grandchildren without parents, has received increasing attention, yet how such experiences are emotionally interpreted and remembered in later life remains underexplored. This study examines relationships among experiential characteristics, emotions, memory, and post-travel outcomes, drawing on memorable tourism experience research and psychological perspectives on emotion and memory. Using survey data from 790 Chinese grandparents and follow-up interviews with 57 participants, the findings show that rewarding experiential characteristics are associated with positive emotions, whereas stress and fatigue are associated with negative emotions. Positive emotions are positively associated with memory, while negative emotions show a negative association. Memory is associated with well-being, emotional closeness, and behavioral intentions. These relationships are stronger among non-co-residing grandparents, with qualitative findings highlighting variation in relational context within both groups. The findings suggest designing meaningful intergenerational activities, reducing strain for older travelers, and considering family context in skip-gen travel offerings.

title: Archetypal Digital Nomads’ Typology and Implications for Tourism Destinations
abstract: Digital nomadism, characterized by the integration of work and travel, is reshaping how mobile visitors engage with tourism destinations, services, and infrastructure. Drawing on 25 empirically derived work-leisure boundary management practices identified from 224 digital diaries and 32 praxiographic interviews, this study applies archetypal analysis to develop a typology of six digital nomad archetypes. The findings reveal that different configurations of temporal, spatial, material, social, and psycho-emotional practices produce distinct patterns of destination and service engagement. The study advances tourism theory by explaining heterogeneity within digital nomad lifestyle mobility through a practice-based perspective, showing how tourism resources acquire different functions according to work-leisure boundary configurations. The resulting typology explains variations in the use of accommodation, coworking spaces, digital infrastructure, and local services, providing actionable insights for destination planning, hospitality service design, infrastructure development, and tourism policy.

title: Trust or Scrutiny? The Technology Readiness Paradox in Travel Planning With Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now drafts travel itineraries that travelers cannot easily verify. Integrating privacy calculus theory with a dual-pathway trust model, this study examines how system attributes shape tourist trust and continued usage, and how technology readiness conditions those links. A two-wave panel (433 Chinese and European travelers), a validation wave (372), and 42 interviews were analyzed using structural equation modeling, importance–performance map analysis, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and thematic analysis. Data transparency and content authenticity raised both cognitive and affective trust, and affective trust sustained continued usage most strongly. Technology readiness reversed the expected pattern: readier travelers scrutinized fluent output rather than relying on it, weakening the behavioral effect of trust. Providers should replace generic privacy notices with in-context, verifiable data-use disclosures and checkable citations, and segment interfaces so that ready travelers receive verification tools and less-ready travelers receive reassurance. Regulators can make verifiability, not fluency, the disclosure standard.

title: Sick of change? Sickness absence following ownership conversions in Norwegian kindergartens
abstract: Abstract The expansion of mixed-provider welfare systems has intensified debates about the consequences of public, nonprofit, and for-profit provision. Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. We depart from research suggesting that ownership conversions can disrupt employee-organization value congruence as well as change the incentive structures. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Norwegian childcare services (2015-2019), we examine whether ownership conversions are associated with changes in employee sickness absence. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that sickness absence increases following nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions. At the same time, public-to-for-profit transitions show little consistent relationship with sickness absence. These findings suggest that employee responses to ownership change are shaped less by the public-private divide than by differences in organizational missions and values. More broadly, the study highlights organizational value congruence as a potential mechanism linking ownership arrangements to employee well-being, and suggests that the nonprofit-for-profit boundary may be more consequential for employees than the conventional public-private divide.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Synthetic humanitarianism and algorithmic witnessing: generative AI and the politics of humanitarian representation
abstract: Humanitarian organisations have begun deploying generative AI imagery in their campaigns, a practice this article terms synthetic humanitarianism. The article asks what conceptual framework is required to analyse the ethical and communicative implications of this practice. Drawing on witnessing theory, decolonial critiques of humanitarian visibility, and technocolonialism, I argue that synthetic humanitarianism intensifies extractive and colonial logics that have structured humanitarian communication since its institutional emergence. I develop the concept of algorithmic witnessing to name the communicative condition in which generative AI systems produce the relations of testimony and moral address without any act of witnessing having taken place and, in the typical case, without the participation of those represented. The framework specifies four dimensions, testimonial fabrication, epistemic extraction, delanguaging, and stereoscopic automation, and I apply it to thirteen documented cases of generative AI image use in humanitarian communications between 2022 and 2025. The analysis demonstrates that these dimensions form a mutually reinforcing system in which the elimination of situated meaning-making enables fabricated testimony and the computational encoding of colonial visual archives produces automated stereotype. I argue that the most significant consequence of synthetic humanitarianism is political rather than epistemological. The displacement of situated meaning-making by algorithmic production tends to eliminate the last structural point at which affected communities could intervene in their own representation.

title: From Gender Antagonism to Inclusive Solidarity? Trade Union Membership and Attitudes Toward Women's Employment
abstract: ABSTRACT Why and to what extent do union members differ from non‐members in attitudes toward women's employment? This study argues that a masculinized conception of work has historically underpinned gender antagonism in trade unionism, and that the rise of right‐wing populism may have hindered recent progress toward gender equality among union members. Analyzing the European Values Study data, I find that union members hold more egalitarian attitudes toward women's employment than non‐members on average. This relationship further varies across individual and institutional characteristics. After the financial crisis, however, the positive association has weakened particularly in countries where right‐wing populism is influential.
