title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

title: Untangling time and prematurity in brain development
abstract: Cerebellar developmental differences between preterm- and term-born children persist into early childhood

title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

title: Caught by chirality
abstract: Altermagnets are identified by the handedness of their collective magnetic excitations

title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF 2
abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.

title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error
abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.

title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.

title: Whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate, Danionella cerebrum
abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.

title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.

title: Spawning Season: An Experiment in Queer Parenthood Spawning Season: An Experiment in Queer Parenthood Joseph Osmundson Bloomsbury, 2026, 208 pp.
Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs
abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.

title: It’s not perfect—but it’s me
Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.

title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis
abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium–derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.

title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice
abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.

title: A Martian meteorite that formed ≳4.1 billion years ago samples Mars’ early crust and mantle
abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18 O, before ejection into space by an impact.

Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
abstract: Abstract Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

title: Political Parties as Drivers of US Polarization: 1927–2018
Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights
State capacity and wildfire mitigation: Evidence from state-led forest conservation in China
Offshoring and voting patterns in the US
Strategic Ignorance and Information Design
People, places, and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
abstract: Abstract In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues—the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density—are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

title: Impacts of Corporate Tax Cuts on Firms and Workers: Evidence from Small Businesses
abstract: This paper assesses the effects of corporate tax cuts on small firms and their workers. Following a reform in Quebec, Canada, firms receiving tax cuts expand and their workers’ earnings increase compared to workers and firms without tax cuts. We estimate that overall workers bear 35 percent of the tax burden, with larger incidence falling on those with ownership in the companies they work at, through increased profits. Additionally, workers across each tercile of the within-firm earnings distribution benefit from tax cuts, possibly because fair-wage concerns matter when after-tax profits rise due to close interactions among workers in small corporate environments. (JEL D22, H22, H25, J31, L25)

title: The Pass-Through of Retail Crime
abstract: This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers. (JEL D22, H22, H76, K42, L81)

title: On-Demand Assistance: Experimental Evidence from Indonesia
abstract: Given labor informality in developing countries, addressing employment shocks is challenging. We study Indonesia’s new approach for on-demand online applications for temporary cash assistance and online job training. Through 20 lotteries over two years, 11 million beneficiaries were selected. In nationwide representative surveys matched with administrative data, most beneficiaries report not receiving the assistance, with no detectable impact on employment or consumption. In contrast, survey data from applicants with working phones reveal high reported take-up and higher incomes. The results suggest that, while flexible, on-demand assistance has potential, design features that allow for flexibility could hinder receipt and, thus, impact. (JEL E21, E24, I38, J24, J46, O15)

title: Trade Protection along Supply Chains
abstract: We study the effects of trade protection along supply chains. We focus on temporary trade barriers against China, which has been the main target of US trade protection during the last decades. To deal with endogeneity concerns, we use an instrumental variable strategy, exploiting changes in the identity of swing states across presidential terms and heterogeneous exposure to these political shocks across industries. We find that politically motivated trade protection generates winners and losers: It fosters employment growth in protected industries but hampers employment growth in downstream industries. Our estimates imply a negative overall impact on US jobs. (JEL D72, F13, F14, L14, O19, P33)

title: Childhood Health Shocks and the Intergenerational Transmission of Inequality
abstract: This paper documents a socioeconomic gradient in adult labor market penalties stemming from a single chronic and treatable childhood health shock in a country with universal access to health care. Using childhood onset type 1 diabetes, Danish administrative registry data, and causal forests, we estimate substantial variation in the employment and earnings penalties at age 30. These penalties vary systematically with parental income and maternal educational attainment. Our findings help explain the income-health gradient and have important implications for policy discussions related to the design of health care systems. (JEL H51, I12, I13, I18, J16, J23, J31)

title: Polluted IPOs
abstract: Chinese companies must undergo a review by a regulator-appointed committee before proceeding with initial public offerings (IPOs). We find that firms—particularly, politically unconnected ones—are more likely to pass this review on polluted days (i.e., with a high level of PM2.5). The effect appears driven by reduced cognitive capacity among reviewers, reflected in fewer and simpler questions raised during review sessions. Notably, firms approved on polluted days show no significant performance difference from other firms within three years after the IPO. The findings suggest that pollution-induced cognitive fatigue may paradoxically reduce distortions in a politically influenced approval process. (JEL D22, G24, G32, K22, P28, P31, Q52)

title: The Role of Race in the Legal Representation of Low-Income Defendants
abstract: Little is known about the role of race in the defense of low-income defendants by court-appointed attorneys. Exploiting the quasirandom assignment of court-appointed attorneys to cases, we test whether attorneys secure better deals for same-race defendants. Results indicate that while Black and White attorneys are similarly effective at representing White defendants, Black defendants who are represented by White rather than Black attorneys are 14–16 percent more likely to have their charges dismissed and 15–26 percent less likely to be incarcerated. Moreover, we find no evidence that having a different-race attorney increases the likelihood of reoffending in the future. (JEL H76, J15, K14, K42)

title: How Effective Are R&D Tax Incentives? Reconciling the Micro and Macro Evidence
abstract: Recent firm-level studies find R&D tax incentives to be much more effective at stimulating firms’ R&D investment than aggregate analyses suggest. Based on a distributed analysis of official R&D survey and administrative tax relief microdata for 19 OECD countries, we show that two factors can reconcile these contrasting results. First, the limited uptake of R&D tax incentives in most countries makes aggregate studies underestimate the effectiveness of R&D tax incentives. Secondly, R&D tax incentives are (much) less effective for large and R&D-intensive firms, which account for a small share of R&D-performing firms but most aggregate R&D tax relief. (JEL D22, H25, H32, L25, O31)

title: Can You Erase the Mark of a Criminal Record? Labor Market Impacts of Criminal Record Remediation
abstract: We investigate whether removing a previously obtained criminal record improves employment outcomes. We estimate the causal impact of criminal record remediation laws that have been widely enacted with the goal of improving employment opportunities for millions of individuals with records. We find consistent evidence that removing an existing record does not improve labor market outcomes, on average. A notable exception is participation in gig work through online platforms, which often screen workers based on their records but not their employment histories. The evidence is consistent with records initially scarring labor market trajectories in a way that is difficult to undo later. (JEL H76, J22, J23, K14, K42, M51)

title: The Unintended Consequences of Academic Leniency
Prioritizing Benefit? How Low-Income Patients Respond to Prescription Cost Sharing
abstract: This paper measures how cost sharing impacts older low-income patients, exploiting a discontinuity in eligibility for a prescription drug subsidy for those who lose access to the Medicaid-linked program. Higher drug prices resulting from subsidy loss lead to a 40 percent reduction in prescription expenditures, driven by a 16 percent quantity reduction of prescriptions filled. Patients economize on purchases of higher-priced drugs, irrespective of their health benefits. For example, patients reduce insulin purchases by 35 percent. There is no evidence that cost sharing prompts switching from branded drugs to generics. This behavior suggests that cost sharing reduces prescription accessibility without enhancing cost-effectiveness. (JEL D24, I11, I18, I32, I38, L65)

title: Inclusive Teaching: Spotting Social Isolation in the Classroom
abstract: We evaluate an intervention aimed at addressing social isolation in classrooms. The treatment provides teachers with their students’ social networks and information on developmental risks associated with social exclusion. Using friendship data and incentive-compatible measures, we find that the intervention reduces social isolation and antisocial behavior but does not increase prosocial behavior. Lower antisocial behavior enhances economic efficiency, reflected in higher average student payoffs and reduced inequality. Our findings highlight the personal and communal benefits of addressing social exclusion and antisocial peer dynamics in schools. (JEL D91, I21, I24, I28, J13, Z13)

title: A Matter of Time? Measuring Effects of Public Schooling Expansions on Families
abstract: We leverage pronounced changes in the availability of public schooling for young children—through duration expansions to the kindergarten day—to better understand how an implicit childcare subsidy affects mothers and families. Exploiting full-day kindergarten variation across place and time from 1992 through 2022 and novel data on state-level policy changes, combined with a comparison of children of typical kindergarten-age to older children, we measure effects on parental labor supply and family childcare expenses. Full-day kindergarten expansions were responsible for as much as 24 percent of the growth in employment of mothers with kindergarten-age children in this time frame. (JEL H75, I21, J12, J13, J16, J22)

title: China’s Nationwide CO 2 Emissions Trading System: A General Equilibrium Assessment
abstract: China’s CO 2 emissions trading system, the world’s largest, aims to significantly reduce CO 2 emissions. The system is a tradable performance standard (TPS), differing from cap and trade (C&T). We provide a dynamic general equilibrium assessment that uniquely considers institutional and fiscal features of China that affect policy costs and distributional impacts. Key findings: The TPS’s environmental benefits exceed its costs by a factor of five or more. Interactions with the fiscal system reduce or eliminate the TPS’s cost disadvantage relative to C&T. Introducing auctioning as a complementary source of allowance supply can reduce costs by 30 percent. (JEL D58, O13, P28, Q54, Q58)

title: The Effect of Deactivating Facebook and Instagram on Users’ Emotional State
abstract: We estimate the effect of social media deactivation on users’ emotional state in two large randomized experiments before the 2020 US election. People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety, relative to controls who deactivated for just the first of those six weeks. People who deactivated Instagram for those six weeks reported a 0.041 standard deviation improvement relative to controls. Exploratory analysis suggests that the Facebook effect is driven by people over 35, while the Instagram effect is driven by women under 25. (JEL D12, D91, I31, J16, L82)

title: Identifying Tax Compliance from Variation in Tax Policy: Theory and Empirics
abstract: Governments increasingly use changes in tax rules to combat evasion. We develop a general approach to point-identify tax compliance along with supply and demand elasticities. Identification requires data on prices and quantities, variation in tax policy, and a demand or supply shifter. We illustrate our approach using data on Airbnb collection agreements, where taxes are enforced by shifting the statutory burden away from hosts and onto renters via the platform. We find that taxes are paid on roughly 0 to 1.6 percent of Airbnb transactions prior to enforcement. (JEL H25, H26, H71, K34, L83)

title: When should firms promote consumer learning? An experimental study
Age Discrimination in the Labour Market, Depression and Coping Strategies

title: Host-country media discourse and China’s economic presence in Africa
abstract: China’s economic engagement in Africa takes place in changing host-country discourse environments, yet the consequences of adverse media reporting for China’s overseas presence remain unclear. We argue that worsening media tone can signal rising operating risk and may therefore trigger adjustment across different margins of presence. Using an annual panel of 54 African countries for 2010–2023, we construct lagged media-tone shocks from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone and estimate their dynamic association with Chinese project personnel and FDI stocks. We combine Double Machine Learning with two-way fixed effects, conventional fixed-effects benchmarks, balanced-sample checks and an Afrobarometer exercise. The evidence is consistent with a selective-adjustment pattern. Negative media-tone shocks are associated with a delayed reduction in Chinese project personnel, with effects that emerge at the three- and four-year horizons. Positive shocks show no comparable expansion effect. Chinese overseas presence adjusts primarily to negative shifts in discourse through the more flexible personnel margin, while FDI stocks respond slowly and less consistently. The host country’s institutional context also influences the staffing response. The findings suggest that hostile discourse becomes especially materially consequential when it is likely to translate into operating risk.

title: Environmental Policy and Automation
When immigrants meet exporters: A reassessment of the migrant-native wage gap
China’s fiscal stimulus, global financial intermediaries, and international spillovers
Medicated Optimism
abstract: Do people experiencing depression form accurate expectations about losing their jobs? Linking Estonian panel survey data to administrative employment, diagnosis, and prescription records, I track within-person changes in expected job loss and subsequent realized job loss as individuals move into and out of depression and depression medication. Using individual fixed effects and controls for depression severity and physical health, I find that as the same worker enters the medicated depression state from no depression, expected job loss falls by 3.6 percentage points while realized job loss rises by 5.1 percentage points. The resulting 8.7 percentage-point fall in the forecast error is split almost evenly between less over-prediction among workers who keep their jobs and more under-prediction among workers who lose them. This shift toward optimism is larger for medication classes more closely linked to reward-related pathways and is absent when prescribed medication is not purchased. The welfare implications are two-sided: more optimistic beliefs may reduce worry about job loss, but workers who understate rising risk may prepare less for a separation.

title: Passive market impact: a point process approach
Intra-Horizon Risk Measures and Continuation Liquidity Requirements in Commodity Futures Markets
abstract: Traditional Value at Risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES) measures that are based on terminal loss may underestimate the risk induced by interim price movements. In this article, we evaluate the intra-horizon risk measures MaxVaR and MaxES as measures of the continuation liquidity buffer required to sustain futures positions. We propose models with asymmetric jumps and/or seasonal volatility and generate out-of-sample MaxVaR and MaxES forecasts over 10-, 22-, and 66-day horizons. Using data for heating oil, natural gas, corn, and soybeans from 2000 to 2021, we find that considering both asymmetric jumps and seasonal volatility generates the most accurate MaxVaR and MaxES forecasts. Liquidity buffers that are based on these measures also exhibit substantial seasonal variation and significant asymmetry between long and short positions. Furthermore, comparisons with initial margins indicate that continuation liquidity buffers represent a substantial component of the total liquidity capacity required to initiate and maintain futures positions.

title: Pursuing fiscal credibility, performing fiscal discipline: epistemic politics and status seeking in Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession
abstract: There is a prolific literature on the politics of austerity, highlighting how its confidence effects arise from fiscal retrenchment embodying and signalling a credible commitment to markets’ interests. However, I argue that this implicitly performative account of fiscal credibility is too functionalist, underplaying how states continually negotiate it with different audiences. To overcome these issues, this article develops an alternative theorisation of (fiscal) credibility as a perlocutionary performative, meaning it is dependent on felicitous conditions to be brought about. Channelling a ‘practice-based constructivist’ framework through an ‘epistemic politics’ and ‘status seeking’ lens, I use archival and biographical research to study Italy and Spain’s Eurozone accession during the 1990s. My argument is that the success of their austerity programmes, and therefore of their accession strategies, depended on a series of cognitive and strategic dynamics beyond fiscal retrenchment – mainly, based on the epistemic politics of multilateral surveillance, national status claims to fiscal credibility, and the social construction of ‘credibility’ under a broad set of fiscal and non-fiscal parameters. As such, this article contributes to recent constructivist research on the practical life of ideas and on epistemic politics, showing the dynamics of construction, performance, and contestation surrounding austerity and fiscal credibility.

title: The semi-periphery's ‘defence dividend’: redistribution of labour in Europe's defence industry
abstract: The ramp up of European defence industrial production raises a critical question for the future shape and competitiveness of the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB): will it continue to be dominated and limited by core European Union (EU) producers or is there an ongoing redistribution of defence production? We argue a significant redistribution is underway, although not caused by recent geopolitical shocks, but by the long-term agency of the semi-periphery itself. Our analysis identifies a distinct long-term pathway of defence-industrial upgrading in Eastern and Central Europe (ECE), which unfolds within the broader context of Dependent Market Economies (DMEs) and which we term the Militarised DME (M-DME). The EU’s recent geoeconomic turn did not create this trajectory but validated and accelerated it. Using time-series cluster analysis of EU arms export data, we identify a sustained rise in high-value-added (HVA) exports associated primarily with indigenously controlled actors. Ultimately, our findings point to a contested re-division of labour that predates the current security crisis and has important implications for European strategic autonomy, industrial integration, and the future shape of the EDTIB.
